\chapter{Mathematical Foundations of Natural Language
Processing}\label{mathematical-foundations-of-natural-language-processing}

From Tokens and Probability to Transformers, Retrieval, and Responsible
AI

\hfill\break

Natural language processing is the study of how language can be
represented, modeled, learned, retrieved, generated, and evaluated by
computational systems. This book develops NLP from a mathematical point
of view, with enough Python computation to make the ideas concrete and
testable.

This book is designed for students in applied mathematics, statistics,
data science, computer science, and related quantitative programs who
want to understand modern NLP beyond package usage. The central theme is
that language data can be studied through familiar mathematical
structures: finite sets, vectors, matrices, probability distributions,
optimization problems, graphs, geometry, and topology.

\section{What makes this book
mathematical?}\label{what-makes-this-book-mathematical}

Rather than beginning with software libraries, the book begins with
objects and operations.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
NLP idea
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mathematical viewpoint
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Computational object
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Tokens & Elements of a finite alphabet & strings, integer ids \\
Documents & Empirical measures or vectors & token lists, count
vectors \\
Vocabulary & Finite set with indexing & dictionaries, arrays \\
Language model & Conditional probability distribution & tables or neural
networks \\
Embedding & Map into a vector space & dense matrix rows \\
Similarity & Inner product, norm, or metric & cosine score, distance
matrix \\
Attention & Similarity-weighted averaging operator & query-key-value
matrices \\
Transformer & Nonlinear operator on sequences & stacked attention and
feedforward blocks \\
Retrieval & Nearest-neighbor search in representation space & ranked
document lists \\
Evaluation & Statistical estimation under uncertainty & metrics,
confidence intervals \\
Responsible NLP & Error analysis across populations and contexts &
audits, calibration, bias diagnostics \\
\end{longtable}
}

The goal is not only to run an NLP model. The goal is to understand what
the model is doing, what assumptions it makes, when it works, and how to
diagnose its failures.

\section{Intended audience}\label{intended-audience}

The book assumes basic familiarity with:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  linear algebra: vectors, matrices, inner products, projections,
  eigenvalues, and singular value decomposition;
\item
  probability: conditional probability, likelihood, entropy,
  expectation, and random variables;
\item
  statistics: classification, estimation, empirical risk, validation,
  and uncertainty;
\item
  Python: NumPy, pandas, matplotlib, and basic machine learning
  workflows.
\end{itemize}

No prior NLP background is required. The computer labs are written for
independent study and include the necessary background before
programming begins.

\section{How to use this book}\label{how-to-use-this-book}

Each chapter is organized around four layers.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Conceptual layer:} What is the NLP problem and why does it
  matter?
\item
  \textbf{Mathematical layer:} What objects, maps, distributions, or
  optimization problems define the method?
\item
  \textbf{Computational layer:} How can the idea be implemented in
  Python on a small transparent example?
\item
  \textbf{Critical layer:} What can go wrong, and how should we evaluate
  or audit the method?
\end{enumerate}

A recommended weekly workflow is:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  read the chapter overview and mathematical explanation;
\item
  work through the examples by hand for a small toy corpus;
\item
  open the corresponding lab in Google Colab;
\item
  complete the guided exercises;
\item
  write a short reflection on what the model assumes and where it may
  fail.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{Shaded}

\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} probability distributions}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} sparse and dense vector spaces}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} neural sequence maps}

The same mathematical ideas appear repeatedly:

\begin{itemize}

  \textbf{Linearity:} document-term matrices, embeddings, projections,
  attention scores, and low-rank adaptation.
\item
  \textbf{Probability:} likelihood, language modeling, entropy,

\item
  \textbf{Optimization:} cross-entropy minimization, stochastic
  gradients, AdamW, clipping, and regularization.
\item
  \textbf{Geometry:} similarity, clustering, anisotropy, hubness,
  positional encoding, and representation diagnostics.
\item
  \textbf{Graphs:} co-occurrence networks, dependency structures,
  knowledge graphs, message passing, and retrieval links.
\item
  \textbf{Evaluation:} metrics, uncertainty, subgroup analysis,
  factuality, robustness, and responsible deployment.
\end{itemize}

\chapter{Introduction}\label{introduction}

Why Natural Language Processing Is a Mathematical Subject

\hfill\break

Natural language processing is often introduced through applications:
search engines, translation systems, chatbots, summarizers, speech
interfaces, and large language models. This book takes a different but
complementary route. It asks: \textbf{what mathematical objects are
being manipulated when a machine processes language?}

The answer is richer than a single method or model. Language can be
represented as strings, finite sets, sequences, sparse vectors,
probability distributions, matrices, graphs, geometric point clouds, and
learned nonlinear maps. Modern NLP is powerful because these
representations can be connected: tokens become vectors, vectors become
probability models, probability models become neural networks, neural
networks become attention-based sequence operators, and these operators
become components of retrieval and generation systems.

This book develops NLP through that mathematical chain.

\section{Goals of the book}\label{goals-of-the-book}

The main goal is to help students understand NLP as a mathematical
discipline, not only as a collection of software tools. By the end of
the book, students should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  represent text using tokens, vocabularies, vectors, matrices, and
  probability distributions;
\item
  derive and implement basic probabilistic language models;
\item
  understand text classification through Bayes rules, likelihoods, and
  decision boundaries;
\item
  explain document-term matrices, TF-IDF, cosine similarity, SVD, and
  embedding geometry;
\item
  implement the core computations behind attention and transformer
  blocks;
\item
  interpret autoregressive language modeling through conditional
  probability and cross-entropy;
\item
  build small retrieval and retrieval-augmented generation systems;
\item
  evaluate NLP systems using metrics, uncertainty, calibration, and
  subgroup analysis;
\item
  connect NLP to information theory, optimization, graphs, geometry,
  topology, and ethics.
\end{enumerate}

The book is intentionally mathematical, but it is also computational.
Each major idea is paired with a transparent Python implementation,
usually on a small corpus that students can inspect directly.

\section{Why a mathematical
approach?}\label{why-a-mathematical-approach}

Many NLP systems are large, but their core ideas can be studied on small
examples. A sentence such as

\begin{quote}
language models learn patterns from text
\end{quote}

can already illustrate much of the mathematical structure of NLP.

It can be treated as:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Viewpoint
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mathematical object
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example question
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
string processing & sequence of characters & How should text be
normalized? \\
tokenization & finite sequence from a vocabulary & What counts as a word
or subword? \\
vectorization & vector in \(\mathbb R^d\) & Which coordinates represent
the document? \\
probability & empirical or learned distribution & How surprising is the
next token? \\
geometry & point in a metric or inner product space & Which texts are
similar? \\
neural modeling & parameterized nonlinear map & How are features learned
from data? \\
attention & weighted averaging operator & Which tokens should influence
each other? \\
evaluation & statistical estimator & How reliable is the measured
performance? \\
responsibility & decision under social constraints & Who is harmed by
errors or bias? \\
\end{longtable}
}

A mathematical perspective helps students see common structure across
many models. For example, cosine similarity in TF-IDF retrieval,
nearest-neighbor search in embedding space, attention scores in
transformers, and reranking in retrieval-augmented generation all
involve comparing representations. Cross-entropy appears in language
modeling, classification, calibration, and preference learning. Matrix
factorization appears in latent semantic analysis, embedding learning,
low-rank adaptation, and representation diagnostics.

\section{The central pipeline}\label{the-central-pipeline}

A simplified NLP pipeline is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{raw text}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} tokens}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} vocabulary indices}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} vectors or embeddings}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} model scores}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} probability distributions}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} predictions, retrieved documents, or generated text}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} evaluation and auditing}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Each arrow hides mathematical choices. Tokenization determines the
sample space. Vectorization determines what information is preserved.
The model class determines which dependencies can be learned. The loss
function determines what the system is optimized to do. The evaluation
protocol determines what failures are visible.

One guiding theme of the book is therefore:

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Note}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Every NLP system is a sequence of mathematical modeling decisions. Good
NLP requires understanding those decisions, not merely running the final
model.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Prerequisites}\label{prerequisites}

The book is written for advanced undergraduate students, master's
students, or beginning PhD students in applied mathematics, statistics,
data science, computer science, computational linguistics, or related
fields.

Useful background includes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{linear algebra:} vectors, matrices, inner products, norms,
  projections, eigenvalues, and singular value decomposition;
\item
  \textbf{probability:} conditional probability, likelihood,
  expectation, entropy, Bayes rule, and random variables;
\item
  \textbf{statistics and machine learning:} classification, validation,
  loss functions, empirical risk, and basic evaluation metrics;
\item
  \textbf{calculus and optimization:} gradients, gradient descent,
  stochastic gradients, and regularization;
\item
  \textbf{Python:} basic programming with lists, dictionaries, NumPy
  arrays, pandas data frames, and matplotlib plots.
\end{itemize}

Students do not need prior NLP experience. The computer labs are
designed for independent study and introduce the needed background
before programming begins.

\section{Notation}\label{notation}

The following notation is used throughout the book.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(V\) & vocabulary set \\
\(|V|\) & vocabulary size \\
\(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T\) & token sequence of length \(T\) \\
\(d\) & embedding dimension or feature dimension \\
\(X \in \mathbb R^{n \times d}\) & data matrix with \(n\) examples and
\(d\) features \\
\(p(x)\) & probability of token, document, or event \(x\) \\
\(p(x_t \mid x_{<t})\) & autoregressive next-token probability \\
\(\theta\) & model parameters \\
\(\ell(\theta)\) & loss function or objective \\
\(q, k, v\) & query, key, and value vectors in attention \\
\(Q, K, V\) & query, key, and value matrices \\
\(A\) & attention weight matrix or adjacency matrix, depending on
context \\
\end{longtable}
}

For a probability distribution \(p\) over a finite set \(V\), entropy is
written as

\[
H(p) = -\sum_{x \in V} p(x) \log p(x).
\]

For two distributions \(p\) and \(q\), cross-entropy is

\[
H(p,q) = -\sum_{x \in V} p(x) \log q(x),
\]

and KL divergence is

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p \Vert q) = \sum_{x \in V} p(x) \log \frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\]

For vectors \(u,v \in \mathbb R^d\), cosine similarity is

\[
\operatorname{cos}(u,v) = \frac{u \cdot v}{\|u\|\,\|v\|}.
\]

The attention operation is usually written as

\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.
\]

These formulas will appear repeatedly in different contexts.

\section{Computational philosophy}\label{computational-philosophy}

The labs avoid treating NLP models as black boxes. Instead, students are
asked to build small versions of the main algorithms. The goal is not to
compete with industrial-scale models. The goal is to understand the
computations well enough to inspect, modify, and evaluate them.

For example, students will implement:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  tokenization and vocabulary construction;
\item
  document-term matrices and TF-IDF;
\item
  n-gram language models and smoothing;
\item
  Naive Bayes classification;
\item
  cosine retrieval and SVD-based latent spaces;
\item
  word embeddings from co-occurrence statistics;
\item
  attention and self-attention from matrix operations;
\item
  transformer-style blocks;
\item
  autoregressive decoding methods;
\item
  retrieval metrics and transparent RAG pipelines;
\item
  fairness, calibration, and bias diagnostics.
\end{itemize}

Whenever possible, the book uses small datasets created inside the
notebook. This makes the mathematical structure visible. Students can
print the vocabulary, inspect the matrix entries, compute probabilities
by hand, and compare manual calculations with Python output.

\section{How to use the computer
labs}\label{how-to-use-the-computer-labs}

The labs are located in the \texttt{labs/} folder and are designed to
open directly in Google Colab. Each lab follows the same
independent-study structure:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Background before programming.} The lab explains the core
  mathematical idea before code appears.
\item
  \textbf{Small transparent data.} Students work with short corpora or
  toy examples before moving to larger settings.
\item
  \textbf{Guided implementation.} Important formulas are translated into
  Python step by step.
\item
  \textbf{Diagnostics.} Students inspect intermediate objects such as
  vocabularies, matrices, probabilities, hidden states, attention
  weights, or retrieval rankings.
\item
  \textbf{Exercises.} Each lab contains tasks that require modification,
  experimentation, and interpretation.
\item
  \textbf{Mini-project.} Each lab ends with an open-ended extension
  suitable for independent study.
\item
  \textbf{AI-assisted reflection.} Students are encouraged to use AI
  tools to explain, critique, and test their reasoning, but not to
  replace their own mathematical work.
\end{enumerate}

A productive workflow is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{read the chapter}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} open the corresponding Colab lab}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} run every cell}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} change the toy data}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} answer the exercises}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} write a short reflection}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} connect the result back to the formulas}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Responsible use of AI tools}\label{responsible-use-of-ai-tools}

Because NLP is closely connected to modern generative AI, this book
treats AI tools as objects of study and as possible learning assistants.
Students may use AI systems to ask for explanations, generate test
examples, or compare interpretations. However, they should verify all
claims through computation, derivation, or source checking.

A useful rule is:

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Important}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Use AI to ask better questions, not to avoid mathematical reasoning.

\end{tcolorbox}

For each AI-assisted prompt in the labs, students should record:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the question they asked;
\item
  the answer they received;
\item
  what they verified independently;
\item
  what was unclear, incomplete, or incorrect;
\item
  how the result connects to the mathematical model.
\end{itemize}

This habit is especially important in later chapters on evaluation,
retrieval-augmented generation, fairness, and responsibility.

\section{Chapter roadmap}\label{chapter-roadmap}

The book has seven parts.

\subsection{Part I. Language as Data}\label{part-i.-language-as-data-1}

Chapters 1--3 introduce text as data. Students learn what NLP studies,
how text becomes tokens and vocabularies, and how documents become
vectors. These chapters establish the finite-set and vector-space
foundations of the book.

\subsection{Part II. Probability Models for
Language}\label{part-ii.-probability-models-for-language-1}

Chapters 4--6 develop probability models. Students study empirical
distributions, likelihood, entropy, n-gram language models, smoothing,
and Naive Bayes classification. These chapters show how language
modeling begins with conditional probability.

\subsection{Part III. Linear Algebra of
Language}\label{part-iii.-linear-algebra-of-language-1}

Chapters 7--9 develop vector space methods, embeddings, and geometry.
Students study document-term matrices, TF-IDF, SVD, word embeddings,
cosine similarity, anisotropy, hubness, clustering, and semantic
directions.

\subsection{Part IV. Neural Networks for
Sequences}\label{part-iv.-neural-networks-for-sequences-1}

Chapters 10--12 introduce neural networks for text. Students study
embedding lookup, pooling, recurrent neural networks, backpropagation
through time, LSTM cells, GRU cells, and gated memory.

\subsection{Part V. Attention and
Transformers}\label{part-v.-attention-and-transformers-1}

Chapters 13--16 develop attention, self-attention, transformer blocks,
and positional encoding. These chapters form the mathematical core of
modern NLP architectures.

\subsection{Part VI. Large Language Models and
Retrieval}\label{part-vi.-large-language-models-and-retrieval-1}

Chapters 17--20 study autoregressive language models, training
objectives, retrieval, RAG, and evaluation. Students learn how
next-token prediction, decoding, fine-tuning, retrieval, calibration,
and uncertainty interact in modern systems.

\subsection{Part VII. Advanced Mathematical
Perspectives}\label{part-vii.-advanced-mathematical-perspectives-1}

Chapters 21--25 connect NLP to information theory, optimization, graphs,
topology, geometry, ethics, bias, and responsibility. These chapters
invite students to view NLP as part of a larger mathematical and social
ecosystem.

\section{Suggested study questions}\label{suggested-study-questions}

Students should return to these questions throughout the course:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the sample space?
\item
  What information is preserved by the representation?
\item
  What information is lost?
\item
  What probability distribution is being estimated or optimized?
\item
  What geometry does the representation create?
\item
  What loss function defines success during training?
\item
  What metric defines success during evaluation?
\item
  What kinds of examples are likely to fail?
\item
  Who is affected by the errors?
\item
  What evidence supports the final conclusion?
\end{enumerate}

These questions help connect early chapters on tokens and vectors with
later chapters on transformers, retrieval, and responsible AI.

\section{A first example: language as counting and
prediction}\label{a-first-example-language-as-counting-and-prediction}

Consider a tiny corpus:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models learn from text}
\NormalTok{language models predict text}
\NormalTok{retrieval systems use text}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

From this corpus, we can construct a vocabulary

\[
V = \{\text{from}, \text{language}, \text{learn}, \text{models}, \text{predict}, \text{retrieval}, \text{systems}, \text{text}, \text{use}\}.
\]

Each document can be represented as a vector in \(\mathbb R^{|V|}\). A
language model can estimate probabilities such as

\[
p(\text{text} \mid \text{predict}).
\]

A retrieval system can compare a query vector with document vectors. A
neural model can learn dense embeddings for the same tokens. An
attention model can compute which earlier words influence a later
prediction.

Thus a simple corpus already contains the central mathematical objects
of the book: sets, vectors, matrices, probabilities, optimization
problems, and evaluation criteria.

\section{What this book is not}\label{what-this-book-is-not}

This book is not a catalog of every NLP library or a survey of every
current model. Modern NLP changes quickly, and software APIs change even
faster. Instead, this book focuses on durable mathematical principles.
Students who understand these principles will be better prepared to
learn new architectures, evaluate new systems, and use future tools
responsibly.

\section{Final perspective}\label{final-perspective}

Natural language is human, contextual, and social. Mathematical models
of language are useful because they simplify language into structures
that can be computed with. But every simplification has consequences. A
responsible mathematical approach therefore asks both technical and
critical questions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the model?
\item
  What does the model optimize?
\item
  What does the model ignore?
\item
  How do we know whether it works?
\item
  What happens when it fails?
\end{itemize}

The purpose of this book is to give students the mathematical and
computational tools to answer these questions carefully.

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Learning Roadmap}\label{learning-roadmap}

A Guided Path Through Mathematical Natural Language Processing

\hfill\break

This roadmap explains how to move through \emph{Mathematical Foundations
of Natural Language Processing}. It connects the 25 chapters, 25 Google
Colab labs, mathematical prerequisites, learning milestones, and
possible project directions.

Natural language processing can look like a collection of separate
tools: tokenizers, classifiers, embeddings, transformers, retrieval
systems, and evaluation metrics. The purpose of this book is to show
that these tools are connected by a small number of mathematical ideas.

The main journey is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{raw text}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} tokens and vocabularies}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} vectors and matrices}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} probability models}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} embeddings and geometry}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} neural sequence maps}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} attention and transformers}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} language models and retrieval}
\NormalTok{  {-}\textgreater{} evaluation, auditing, and responsible use}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Students should not try to memorize every method. Instead, they should
ask the same questions in every chapter:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the mathematical object?
\item
  What map or probability distribution is being learned?
\item
  What loss function or evaluation criterion is used?
\item
  What assumptions are made?
\item
  What can fail, and how can we diagnose it?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Part I. Language as Data}\label{part-i.-language-as-data-2}

\textbf{Goal:} Convert raw text into mathematical objects.

In this part, students learn that NLP begins with representation. A
sentence is not directly a vector or probability distribution. It must
first be segmented, normalized, indexed, and counted.

similarity, and explain why preprocessing choices affect downstream
models.

\section{Part II. Probability Models for
Language}\label{part-ii.-probability-models-for-language-2}

\textbf{Goal:} Model language using finite probability distributions.

This part introduces the probabilistic view of NLP. A language model
assigns probabilities to tokens or token sequences. A classifier assigns
probabilities or scores to labels. Smoothing, likelihood, and entropy
become central tools.

\section{Part III. Linear Algebra of
Language}\label{part-iii.-linear-algebra-of-language-2}

\textbf{Goal:} Understand language as geometry in high-dimensional
vector spaces.

This part moves from sparse document vectors to dense word embeddings.
Students learn that similarity, projection, low-rank approximation, and
clustering are not merely computational tricks; they are geometric
operations.

\section{Part IV. Neural Networks for
Sequences}\label{part-iv.-neural-networks-for-sequences-2}

sequence maps.

This part introduces neural networks for text. Students first study
embedding lookup and pooling, then learn why order-sensitive models such
as RNNs and gated RNNs were historically important.

\section{Part V. Attention and
Transformers}\label{part-v.-attention-and-transformers-2}

\textbf{Goal:} Build the mathematical core of modern transformer models.

This part studies attention as a matrix operator. Students learn how
queries, keys, values, masks, positional encodings, residual
connections, and normalization combine into a transformer block.

\section{Part VI. Large Language Models and

training, retrieval, and evaluation.

Students study autoregressive factorization, training objectives,
supervised fine-tuning, preference learning, retrieval-augmented
generation, and model evaluation.

\section{Part VII. Advanced Mathematical
Perspectives}\label{part-vii.-advanced-mathematical-perspectives-2}

\textbf{Goal:} Use deeper mathematical viewpoints to understand and
audit NLP systems.

The final part returns to the mathematical foundations and uses them as
diagnostic tools. Information theory measures uncertainty and
divergence. Optimization explains training dynamics. Graphs model
relations. Topology studies shape. Ethics and responsibility ask whether
models should be trusted in context.

\section{Three possible learning
pathways}\label{three-possible-learning-pathways}

Different students may use the book in different ways.

\subsection{Pathway A. Mathematical foundations
first}\label{pathway-a.-mathematical-foundations-first}

This pathway is best for students who want a rigorous conceptual
foundation before studying large models.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Chapters 1{-}{-}9}
\NormalTok{then 21{-}{-}22}
\NormalTok{then 10{-}{-}20}
\NormalTok{then 23{-}{-}25}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This path emphasizes tokens, vectors, probability, geometry, information
theory, and optimization before modern architectures.

\subsection{Pathway B. Modern NLP systems
first}\label{pathway-b.-modern-nlp-systems-first}

This pathway is best for students who want to reach transformers, LLMs,
and RAG quickly.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Chapters 1{-}{-}3}
\NormalTok{then 10}
\NormalTok{then 13{-}{-}20}
\NormalTok{then 4{-}{-}9 and 21{-}{-}25 as deeper foundations}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This path introduces the main system components early, then returns to
the mathematical foundations in more depth.

\subsection{Pathway C. Full semester
course}\label{pathway-c.-full-semester-course}

This pathway is best for a 14-week graduate course.

3 & 5--6 & 5--6 & \(n\)-gram models, Naive Bayes \\
4 & 7--8 & 7--8 & vector space retrieval, embeddings \\
5 & 9--10 & 9--10 & embedding geometry, neural text models \\
6 & 11--12 & 11--12 & RNNs, LSTMs, GRUs \\
7 & 13--14 & 13--14 & attention and self-attention \\
8 & 15--16 & 15--16 & transformers and positional encoding \\
9 & 17--18 & 17--18 & autoregressive LMs and training objectives \\
10 & 19--20 & 19--20 & retrieval, RAG, evaluation \\
11 & 21--22 & 21--22 & information theory and optimization \\
12 & 23--24 & 23--24 & graphs, topology, geometry \\
13 & 25 & 25 & ethics, bias, responsibility \\
14 & project presentations & project notebooks & synthesis and
communication \\
\end{longtable}
}

\section{Independent-study workflow}\label{independent-study-workflow}

For each chapter, students should complete the following cycle.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Read the chapter.} Focus on definitions, equations, and
  examples.
\item
  \textbf{Reproduce one calculation by hand.} For example, compute a
  cosine similarity, one row of attention, or one Naive Bayes log-score.
\item
  \textbf{Open the Colab lab.} Run all cells once before changing
  anything.
\item
  \textbf{Modify one variable.} Change a smoothing parameter, embedding
  dimension, threshold, temperature, or graph radius.
\item
  \textbf{Explain the effect.} Write two or three sentences connecting
  the result to the mathematics.
\item
  \textbf{Complete the exercises.} Use the hints only after attempting
  the problem.
\item
  \textbf{Complete the mini-project.} Extend the lab to a new toy
  dataset or new diagnostic question.
\item
  \textbf{Write a reflection.} State one assumption, one limitation, and
  one possible improvement.
\end{enumerate}

The following milestones can be used for self-assessment or course
grading.

Neural modeling & Explain embeddings, softmax, cross-entropy, gradients,

\section{Suggested final project
directions}\label{suggested-final-project-directions}

A good final project should combine mathematics, computation, and
critical evaluation. Possible directions include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Transparent retrieval system:} compare TF-IDF, dense toy
  embeddings, hybrid retrieval, and reranking on a course-document
  corpus.
\item
  \textbf{Small language model study:} train and evaluate an \(n\)-gram
  or small neural next-token model with different smoothing or decoding
  choices.
\item
  \textbf{Embedding geometry audit:} compare nearest neighbors, PCA
  plots, anisotropy, hubness, and semantic directions across corpora.
\item
  \textbf{RAG reliability audit:} build a small RAG system and evaluate
  retrieval quality, citation support, and answer faithfulness.
\item
  \textbf{Fairness and calibration study:} evaluate a text classifier
  across subgroups and study threshold, calibration, and uncertainty
  tradeoffs.
\item
  \textbf{Graph representation project:} build a co-occurrence,
  dependency, or knowledge graph and analyze PageRank, communities, or
  message passing.
\item
  \textbf{Topology of embeddings:} build neighborhood graphs or
  Vietoris--Rips summaries for embeddings and compare geometric shape
  across labels or domains.
\end{enumerate}

A strong project report should include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a clear research question;
\item
  the mathematical representation used;
\item
  the dataset and preprocessing choices;
\item
  the model or algorithm;
\item
  quantitative results;
\item
  visualizations or diagnostic tables;
\item
  limitations and responsible-use discussion.
\end{itemize}

\section{Closing perspective}\label{closing-perspective}

The central message of the book is that modern NLP is not magic. It is a
layered mathematical system. Text is discretized into tokens. Tokens
become vectors. Vectors define probabilities, similarities, graphs, and
neural maps. Models are trained by optimization and judged by
statistical evidence. Responsible use requires understanding not only
how a model works, but also where it fails.

Students who complete this roadmap should be able to read modern NLP
papers and systems with a clearer question in mind:

\begin{quote}
What are the objects, maps, probabilities, losses, and assumptions
behind this language system?
\end{quote}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Notation and Core Notions}\label{notation-and-core-notions}

A compact reference for mathematical NLP

\hfill\break

This page collects the main notation, conventions, and core notions used
throughout the book. It is designed as a quick reference for students
moving between chapters, computer labs, and projects.

Natural language processing combines discrete objects, continuous
representations, probability models, optimization algorithms, and
evaluation protocols. The same symbol may appear in several contexts, so
this page explains the standard meaning used in this book and notes when
a symbol has context-dependent interpretations.

\section{1. General conventions}\label{general-conventions}

Unless otherwise stated:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  vectors are column vectors;
\item
  matrices are written with capital letters;
\item
  finite sets are written with capital letters such as \(V\), \(D\), and
  \(C\);
\item
  random variables are written with capital letters such as \(X\) and
  \(Y\);
\item
  observed values are written with lowercase letters such as \(x\) and
  \(y\);
\item
  logarithms are natural logarithms unless base \(2\) is explicitly
  stated;
\item
  probabilities are defined over finite sets in most chapters;
\item
  all examples use small corpora so that the mathematical structure is
  visible.
\end{itemize}

A recurring theme is that an NLP pipeline is a composition of maps:

\[
\text{text} \longrightarrow \text{tokens} \longrightarrow \text{indices} \longrightarrow \text{vectors} \longrightarrow \text{scores} \longrightarrow \text{probabilities} \longrightarrow \text{decisions}.
\]

Each arrow represents a modeling choice.

\section{2. Text, tokens, and
vocabularies}\label{text-tokens-and-vocabularies}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Typical chapter use
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(s\) & raw text string & preprocessing and tokenization \\
\(x_t\) & token at position \(t\) & sequences and language models \\
\(x_{1:T}\) & token sequence \(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T\) & sequence
modeling \\
\(T\) & sequence length & RNNs, attention, transformers \\
\(V\) & vocabulary set & tokenization and vectorization \\
\(|V|\) & vocabulary size & language models and embeddings \\
\(w\) & a word, subword, or token type & vocabulary-level quantities \\
\(\iota\) & indexing map from tokens to integers & token ids \\
\(\langle\mathrm{unk}\rangle\) & unknown token & out-of-vocabulary
handling \\
\(\langle\mathrm{bos}\rangle\) & beginning-of-sequence token & language
modeling \\
\(\langle\mathrm{eos}\rangle\) & end-of-sequence token & language
modeling \\
\(\langle\mathrm{pad}\rangle\) & padding token & batching
variable-length sequences \\
\end{longtable}
}

A tokenizer maps a string to a finite sequence:

\[
\tau(s) = (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T), \qquad x_t \in V.
\]

The vocabulary is not just a list of words. It determines the sample
space for probability models and the coordinate system for count
vectors.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Note}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Changing the tokenizer changes the mathematical problem. A word
tokenizer, character tokenizer, and subword tokenizer produce different
vocabularies, different sequence lengths, and different probability
distributions.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{3. Documents and corpora}\label{documents-and-corpora}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(d_i\) & document \(i\) \\
\(D\) & document collection or corpus \\
\(n\) & number of documents or examples \\
\(m\) & vocabulary size, often \(m=|V|\) \\
\(c(w,d)\) & count of token \(w\) in document \(d\) \\
\(\mathrm{tf}(w,d)\) & term frequency of token \(w\) in document
\(d\) \\
\(\mathrm{df}(w)\) & document frequency of token \(w\) \\
\(\mathrm{idf}(w)\) & inverse document frequency of token \(w\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

A corpus can be represented as a list of token sequences:

\[
D = \{x^{(1)}_{1:T_1}, x^{(2)}_{1:T_2}, \ldots, x^{(n)}_{1:T_n}\}.
\]

A document-term matrix is usually written as

\[
X \in \mathbb R^{n \times m},
\]

where row \(i\) represents document \(d_i\) and column \(j\) represents
token \(w_j\).

\section{4. Vectors, matrices, and
geometry}\label{vectors-matrices-and-geometry}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(x \in \mathbb R^d\) & feature vector or embedding \\
\(d\) & feature dimension or embedding dimension \\
\(X \in \mathbb R^{n \times d}\) & data matrix with \(n\) examples and
\(d\) features \\
\(E \in \mathbb R^{|V| \times d}\) & embedding matrix \\
\(e_w\) & embedding vector for token \(w\) \\
\(\lVert x \rVert\) & Euclidean norm of \(x\) \\
\(x^\top y\) & inner product of vectors \(x\) and \(y\) \\
\(\cos(x,y)\) & cosine similarity \\
\(G = XX^\top\) & Gram matrix of pairwise inner products \\
\end{longtable}
}

The cosine similarity between two nonzero vectors is

\[
\cos(x,y) = \frac{x^\top y}{\lVert x \rVert\lVert y \rVert}.
\]

This score appears in TF-IDF retrieval, embedding search, clustering,
nearest neighbors, and some attention interpretations.

\subsection{Matrix factorization}\label{matrix-factorization}

For a matrix \(X \in \mathbb R^{n \times d}\), the singular value
decomposition is

\[
X = U\Sigma V^\top.
\]

In NLP, low-rank approximations are used to reveal latent structure:

\[
X_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^\top.
\]

The same idea appears in latent semantic analysis, embedding geometry,
representation diagnostics, and low-rank adaptation.

\section{5. Probability and language
models}\label{probability-and-language-models}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(p(x)\) & probability of event or token \(x\) \\
\(p(x,y)\) & joint probability \\
\(p(y \mid x)\) & conditional probability \\
\(\hat p\) & empirical distribution estimated from data \\
\(\theta\) & model parameters \\
\(p_\theta\) & probability distribution defined by parameters
\(\theta\) \\
\(\ell(\theta)\) & loss or negative log-likelihood \\
\(L(\theta)\) & objective function \\
\end{longtable}
}

A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences. The
autoregressive factorization is

\[
p_\theta(x_{1:T}) = \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}),
\]

where \(x_{<t} = x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}\).

The negative log-likelihood for one sequence is

\[
-\log p_\theta(x_{1:T}) = -\sum_{t=1}^T \log p_\theta(x_t \mid x_{<t}).
\]

Per-token average negative log-likelihood is cross-entropy when the data
distribution is fixed.

\section{6. Information theory}\label{information-theory}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(H(p)\) & entropy of distribution \(p\) \\
\(H(p,q)\) & cross-entropy between true distribution \(p\) and model
\(q\) \\
\(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q)\) & Kullback--Leibler divergence from \(p\)
to \(q\) \\
\(I(X;Y)\) & mutual information between \(X\) and \(Y\) \\
\(\mathrm{PMI}(x,y)\) & pointwise mutual information \\
\(\mathrm{PPL}\) & perplexity \\
\end{longtable}
}

Entropy measures average uncertainty:

\[
H(p) = -\sum_{x \in V} p(x)\log p(x).
\]

Cross-entropy measures average code length when data come from \(p\) but
are coded using \(q\):

\[
H(p,q) = -\sum_{x \in V} p(x)\log q(x).
\]

KL divergence is the excess cross-entropy:

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\Vert q) = \sum_{x \in V} p(x)\log\frac{p(x)}{q(x)}.
\]

Perplexity is often used to report language-model quality:

\[
\mathrm{PPL} = \exp\{H\}.
\]

Lower perplexity usually means the model assigns higher probability to
the observed tokens, but it does not automatically imply better
factuality, usefulness, fairness, or safety.

\section{7. Classification notation}\label{classification-notation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(y\) & class label \\
\(C\) & set of classes \\
\(K\) & number of classes \\
\(p(y \mid x)\) & posterior class probability \\
\(\hat y\) & predicted class \\
\(W\) & classifier weight matrix \\
\(b\) & bias vector \\
\(z\) & logits or unnormalized scores \\
\end{longtable}
}

A common linear classifier computes logits

\[
z = Wx + b,
\]

then converts logits to probabilities using softmax:

\[
\mathrm{softmax}(z)_j = \frac{\exp(z_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(z_k)}.
\]

The cross-entropy loss for a true class \(y\) is

\[
\ell(z,y) = -\log \mathrm{softmax}(z)_y.
\]

\section{8. Neural network notation}\label{neural-network-notation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(h_t\) & hidden state at position \(t\) \\
\(c_t\) & LSTM cell state at position \(t\) \\
\(\sigma\) & sigmoid function \\
\(\tanh\) & hyperbolic tangent nonlinearity \\
\(\phi\) & generic nonlinear activation \\
\(W\), \(U\), \(b\) & neural-network parameters \\
\(\nabla_\theta L\) & gradient of objective with respect to
parameters \\
\(\eta\) & learning rate \\
\end{longtable}
}

A simple recurrent neural network has the form

\[
h_t = \phi(W_x x_t + W_h h_{t-1} + b).
\]

A feedforward layer has the form

\[
h = \phi(Wx+b).
\]

Training usually means solving an empirical risk minimization problem:

\[
\min_\theta \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f_\theta(x_i),y_i).
\]

\section{9. Attention and
transformers}\label{attention-and-transformers}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(q\) & query vector \\
\(k\) & key vector \\
\(v\) & value vector \\
\(Q\) & query matrix \\
\(K\) & key matrix \\
\(V\) & value matrix \\
\(A\) & attention weight matrix \\
\(d_k\) & key/query dimension \\
\(M\) & attention mask \\
\(P\) & positional encoding matrix \\
\end{longtable}
}

Scaled dot-product attention is

\[
\mathrm{Attention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)V.
\]

The matrix

\[
A = \mathrm{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} + M\right)
\]

contains attention weights. Each row is usually a probability
distribution over source positions.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Warning}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Attention weights are useful diagnostics, but they are not automatically
faithful explanations of model behavior. They show one internal
weighting pattern, not the full causal reason for a prediction.

\end{tcolorbox}

A transformer block combines attention, residual connections,
normalization, and feedforward layers. A simplified encoder block is

\[
Z_1 = \mathrm{LayerNorm}(X + \mathrm{SelfAttention}(X)),
\]

\[
Z_2 = \mathrm{LayerNorm}(Z_1 + \mathrm{FFN}(Z_1)).
\]

\section{10. Retrieval and RAG
notation}\label{retrieval-and-rag-notation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(q\) & user query, or query vector depending on context \\
\(d_i\) & document or chunk \(i\) \\
\(r(q,d_i)\) & retrieval score for query \(q\) and document \(d_i\) \\
\(\mathrm{top}_k(q)\) & top \(k\) retrieved documents for query \(q\) \\
\(\mathrm{rel}(q,d)\) & relevance label \\
\(\mathrm{Recall@}k\) & fraction of relevant items retrieved in top
\(k\) \\
\(\mathrm{Precision@}k\) & fraction of top \(k\) results that are
relevant \\
\(\mathrm{MRR}\) & mean reciprocal rank \\
\(\mathrm{nDCG}\) & normalized discounted cumulative gain \\
\end{longtable}
}

A retrieval system ranks documents by a score:

\[
r(q,d_i) = \mathrm{sim}(\psi(q),\psi(d_i)),
\]

where \(\psi\) is a representation map and \(\mathrm{sim}\) is a
similarity function.

A retrieval-augmented generation system can be summarized as

\[
\text{query} \longrightarrow \text{retrieve context} \longrightarrow \text{generate answer conditioned on context}.
\]

When evaluating RAG, separate the retrieval problem from the generation
problem. A wrong answer may be caused by poor retrieval, poor context
use, hallucination, or ambiguity in the question.

\section{11. Graph notation}\label{graph-notation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(G=(N,E)\) & graph with node set \(N\) and edge set \(E\) \\
\(A\) & adjacency matrix \\
\(D\) & degree matrix, or corpus depending on context \\
\(L=D-A\) & graph Laplacian \\
\(\tilde A\) & normalized or self-loop augmented adjacency matrix \\
\(N(i)\) & neighborhood of node \(i\) \\
\(h_i\) & node representation \\
\end{longtable}
}

A graph convolution layer often has the form

\[
H' = \phi(\tilde AHW),
\]

where \(H\) is a matrix of node features, \(W\) is a learnable weight
matrix, and \(\tilde A\) controls message passing.

Graph views of language include dependency graphs, word co-occurrence
graphs, document-term bipartite graphs, citation graphs, and knowledge
graphs.

\section{12. Topology and geometry
notation}\label{topology-and-geometry-notation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Symbol
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(X\) & finite point cloud or data matrix \\
\(d(x,y)\) & distance between points \(x\) and \(y\) \\
\(\epsilon\) & scale parameter \\
\(G_\epsilon\) & neighborhood graph at scale \(\epsilon\) \\
\(\beta_0\) & number of connected components \\
\(\beta_1\) & number of one-dimensional loops \\
\(\mathrm{VR}_\epsilon(X)\) & Vietoris--Rips complex at scale
\(\epsilon\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

A Vietoris--Rips complex at scale \(\epsilon\) contains a simplex
whenever all its vertices are pairwise within distance \(\epsilon\).

For NLP, topology is used as a diagnostic lens: it can help compare
embedding spaces, detect clustering, study loops or branches in
representation trajectories, and summarize how local neighborhoods
change with scale.

\section{13. Evaluation and responsibility
notation}\label{evaluation-and-responsibility-notation}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(\mathrm{TP}\) & true positives \\
\(\mathrm{FP}\) & false positives \\
\(\mathrm{TN}\) & true negatives \\
\(\mathrm{FN}\) & false negatives \\
\(\mathrm{Acc}\) & accuracy \\
\(\mathrm{Prec}\) & precision \\
\(\mathrm{Rec}\) & recall \\
\(F_1\) & harmonic mean of precision and recall \\
\(\mathrm{ECE}\) & expected calibration error \\
\(g\) & group or subgroup variable \\
\(\Delta_g\) & performance gap across groups \\
\end{longtable}
}

Precision and recall are

\[
\mathrm{Precision} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FP}},
\]

\[
\mathrm{Recall} = \frac{\mathrm{TP}}{\mathrm{TP}+\mathrm{FN}}.
\]

The \(F_1\) score is

\[
F_1 = \frac{2\cdot \mathrm{Precision}\cdot \mathrm{Recall}}{\mathrm{Precision}+\mathrm{Recall}}.
\]

Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities match empirical
frequencies. Fairness and responsibility require checking not only
global averages but also subgroup errors, uncertainty, data provenance,
privacy, and possible misuse.

Some symbols are used differently in different contexts. The local
meaning should be clear from the chapter.

\section{16. Reading formulas in this
book}\label{reading-formulas-in-this-book}

Many formulas should be read both algebraically and computationally. For
example,

\[
z = Wx+b
\]

means all of the following at once:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  algebraically, a linear map followed by a translation;
\item
  geometrically, a projection onto score directions;
\item
  statistically, a model for class logits;
\item
  computationally, a matrix multiplication plus broadcasting;
\item
  pedagogically, a place where dimensions must match.
\end{enumerate}

When studying a new formula, ask:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  What are the dimensions of all objects?
\item
  Which quantities are fixed data and which are parameters?
\item
  Which operation creates the output?
\item
  What loss or metric will evaluate the output?
\item
  What failure modes are hidden by the notation?
\end{itemize}

\section{17. Python naming conventions used in
labs}\label{python-naming-conventions-used-in-labs}

The labs use Python variable names that mirror the mathematical
notation.

In code, \texttt{V} can conflict with the value matrix in attention. For
this reason, labs often use \texttt{vocab} for the vocabulary and
\texttt{V\_values} for the value matrix.

\section{18. Minimal checklist for
students}\label{minimal-checklist-for-students}

Before starting a chapter or lab, check that you can identify:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  the input object;
\item
  the output object;
\item
  the representation space;
\item
  the probability distribution or scoring function;
\item
  the loss, metric, or diagnostic;
\item
  the assumptions made by the representation;
\item
  one possible failure mode.
\end{enumerate}

This checklist turns notation into understanding. The goal is not to
memorize symbols, but to recognize the mathematical structure behind NLP
systems.

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Mathematical Background}\label{mathematical-background}

Core tools for studying natural language processing

\hfill\break

Natural language processing uses many kinds of mathematics at once. A
tokenizer creates finite sets. A document becomes a vector. A language
model becomes a conditional probability distribution. A transformer
becomes a composition of matrix maps, nonlinearities, normalizations,
and optimization steps. This page collects the main background ideas
used throughout the book.

This background chapter is not meant to replace a full course in linear
algebra, probability, statistics, optimization, graph theory, or
topology. Instead, it gives a compact map of the mathematical objects
that appear repeatedly in NLP. Students can read this page before
starting the book, and then return to the relevant sections while
working through the chapters and labs.

\section{How to use this page}\label{how-to-use-this-page}

Use this page as a reference while reading the book.

and SVD \\

graphs \\

A useful study habit is to ask four questions whenever a new NLP method
appears.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the input set?
\item
  What mathematical representation is assigned to each input?
\item
  What function, probability distribution, or optimization problem is
  being used?
\item
  What metric or loss tells us whether the method worked?
\end{enumerate}

\section{1. Finite sets, maps, and
indexing}\label{finite-sets-maps-and-indexing}

Most NLP systems begin by converting text into discrete symbols.

A \textbf{vocabulary} is a finite set

\[
V = \{w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_m\}.
\]

An \textbf{indexing map} assigns each token to an integer:

\[
\iota: V \to \{0,1,\ldots,m-1\}.
\]

After indexing, a sentence such as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models learn patterns}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

may become a sequence of token ids such as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{[12, 7, 35, 19]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This is mathematically important because neural networks do not operate
directly on English words. They operate on arrays of numbers.

\subsection{Key ideas}\label{key-ideas}

map & tokenizer, embedding lookup, classifier \\

token \\

}

}

\section{2. Vectors and matrices}\label{vectors-and-matrices}

Once words and documents are indexed, they are commonly represented as
vectors.

A vector in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) is an ordered list of real numbers:

\[
\mathbf{x} = (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_d).
\]

A document-term vector might record how often each word appears in a
document. If the vocabulary is

\[
V=\{\text{data},\text{language},\text{model},\text{probability}\},
\]

then the document

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language model language}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

has count vector

\[
\mathbf{x}=(0,2,1,0).
\]

A collection of \(n\) documents can be represented by a document-term
matrix

\[
X \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times m},
\]

where row \(i\) represents document \(i\) and column \(j\) represents
token \(w_j\).

\subsection{Inner products and norms}\label{inner-products-and-norms}

The dot product of two vectors is

\[
\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{y}=\sum_{j=1}^d x_jy_j.
\]

The Euclidean norm is

\[
\|\mathbf{x}\|_2=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^d x_j^2}.
\]

The cosine similarity is

\[
\cos(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y})=
\frac{\mathbf{x}\cdot \mathbf{y}}{\|\mathbf{x}\|_2\|\mathbf{y}\|_2}.
\]

Cosine similarity is widely used in NLP retrieval because it compares
vector direction rather than raw magnitude. This is useful when two
documents have similar topic proportions but different lengths.

\subsection{Important matrix
operations}\label{important-matrix-operations}

\end{longtable}
}

\section{3. Linear transformations and
embeddings}\label{linear-transformations-and-embeddings}

An \textbf{embedding} maps a discrete object into a vector space. For
example, a word embedding is a function

\[
e: V \to \mathbb{R}^d.
\]

If the vocabulary has \(m\) words, an embedding table is a matrix

\[
E \in \mathbb{R}^{m\times d}.
\]

The row \(E_{j,:}\) is the vector representation of token \(w_j\).

The embedding lookup for token id \(j\) can be written as

\[
\mathbf{e}_j = E_{j,:}.
\]

Equivalently, if \(\mathbf{u}_j\) is the one-hot vector for token \(j\),
then

\[
\mathbf{e}_j = \mathbf{u}_j^T E.
\]

This identity explains why embedding lookup is a computationally
efficient version of multiplying by a large matrix.

\subsection{What embeddings try to
preserve}\label{what-embeddings-try-to-preserve}

Embeddings are useful when geometric relationships encode linguistic
relationships.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Geometric relation & Linguistic interpretation \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
small distance & similar meaning or usage \\
large dot product & high compatibility or relevance \\
common direction & shared semantic or syntactic change \\
cluster & group of related words or documents \\
subspace & latent topic, style, or feature \\
\end{longtable}
}

Embeddings are not perfect. They may encode frequency artifacts, social
bias, domain shift, and spurious correlations. This is why the book
repeatedly connects representation learning with diagnostics and
evaluation.

\section{4. Projection, orthogonality, and least
squares}\label{projection-orthogonality-and-least-squares}

A projection finds the closest point in a subspace. If \(U\) is a
subspace of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), the projection of \(\mathbf{x}\) onto
\(U\) is the vector \(\mathbf{p}\in U\) that minimizes

\[
\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{p}\|_2.
\]

Projection appears in NLP when we reduce dimension, remove a direction
from embeddings, or fit linear models.

If \(A\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times d}\) and \(\mathbf{b}\in \mathbb{R}^n\),
the least-squares problem is

\[
\min_{\mathbf{w}\in \mathbb{R}^d}\|A\mathbf{w}-\mathbf{b}\|_2^2.
\]

The normal equation is

\[
A^TA\mathbf{w}=A^T\mathbf{b}.
\]

In modern machine learning, we usually solve such problems with
numerical optimization rather than explicitly forming the inverse.

\section{5. Singular value
decomposition}\label{singular-value-decomposition}

The singular value decomposition, or SVD, is one of the most important
matrix tools in this book. For a matrix \(X\in \mathbb{R}^{n\times m}\),
the SVD has the form

\[
X = U\Sigma V^T.
\]

Here:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  columns of \(U\) describe directions among documents;
\item
  columns of \(V\) describe directions among terms or features;
\item
  diagonal entries of \(\Sigma\) are singular values, ordered from
  largest to smallest.
\end{itemize}

A rank-\(k\) approximation is

\[
X_k = U_k\Sigma_k V_k^T.
\]

This is the best rank-\(k\) approximation to \(X\) in Frobenius norm:

\[
X_k = \arg\min_{\operatorname{rank}(Y)\leq k}\|X-Y\|_F.
\]

In NLP, SVD appears in latent semantic analysis, dimensionality
reduction, visualization, denoising, and embedding diagnostics.

\section{6. Probability distributions}\label{probability-distributions}

A probability distribution on a finite set \(V\) assigns a number
\(p(w)\) to each \(w\in V\) such that

\[
p(w)\geq 0,\qquad \sum_{w\in V}p(w)=1.
\]

In NLP, finite distributions appear everywhere:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  token frequency distributions;
\item
  next-token distributions;
\item
  class posterior probabilities;
\item
  attention weights;
\item
  retrieval scores after normalization.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Conditional probability}\label{conditional-probability}

The conditional probability of \(y\) given \(x\) is

\[
P(y\mid x)=\frac{P(x,y)}{P(x)}.
\]

A classifier estimates \(P(y\mid x)\). A language model estimates

\[
P(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}).
\]

The chain rule gives

\[
P(x_1,\ldots,x_T)=\prod_{t=1}^T P(x_t\mid x_1,
\ldots,x_{t-1}).
\]

This identity is the mathematical basis of autoregressive language
modeling.

\section{7. Likelihood, log-likelihood, and maximum
likelihood}\label{likelihood-log-likelihood-and-maximum-likelihood}

Suppose a model with parameter \(\theta\) assigns probability
\(p_\theta(x_i)\) to each training example \(x_i\). The likelihood is

\[
L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(x_i).
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i).
\]

Maximum likelihood estimation chooses

\[
\hat\theta=\arg\max_\theta \ell(\theta).
\]

Equivalently, many machine learning algorithms minimize the negative
log-likelihood:

\[
\hat\theta=\arg\min_\theta -\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(x_i).
\]

In language modeling, this becomes the token-level cross-entropy loss.

\section{8. Entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, and
perplexity}\label{entropy-cross-entropy-kl-divergence-and-perplexity}

Information theory provides the language for uncertainty and prediction
quality.

The entropy of a distribution \(p\) on \(V\) is

\[
H(p)=-\sum_{w\in V}p(w)\log p(w).
\]

Entropy measures uncertainty. A concentrated distribution has low
entropy. A nearly uniform distribution has high entropy.

The cross-entropy from \(p\) to \(q\) is

\[
H(p,q)=-\sum_{w\in V}p(w)\log q(w).
\]

The KL divergence from \(p\) to \(q\) is

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{w\in V}p(w)\log\frac{p(w)}{q(w)}.
\]

The identity

\[
H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
\]

shows that cross-entropy is minimized when \(q=p\).

If average token cross-entropy is measured using natural logarithms,
perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{PPL}=\exp(H).
\]

Perplexity can be interpreted as an effective number of choices per
token.

\section{9. Bayes rule and
classification}\label{bayes-rule-and-classification}

Bayes rule states

\[
P(y\mid x)=\frac{P(x\mid y)P(y)}{P(x)}.
\]

For classification, the denominator \(P(x)\) is the same for all
classes, so the Bayes decision rule is

\[
\hat y = \arg\max_y P(x\mid y)P(y).
\]

Naive Bayes assumes that features are conditionally independent given
the class. For a count vector

\[
\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_m),
\]

the multinomial Naive Bayes score has the form

\[
\log P(y)+\sum_{j=1}^m x_j\log P(w_j\mid y).
\]

This formula is simple, interpretable, and surprisingly strong for many
text classification problems.

\section{10. Softmax and attention
weights}\label{softmax-and-attention-weights}

The softmax function converts real-valued scores into probabilities.
Given scores

\[
\mathbf{z}=(z_1,\ldots,z_m),
\]

the softmax distribution is

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_j=
\frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum_{k=1}^m e^{z_k}}.
\]

For numerical stability, compute softmax as

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(\mathbf{z})_j=
\frac{e^{z_j-c}}{\sum_{k=1}^m e^{z_k-c}},
\qquad c=\max_k z_k.
\]

In attention, the score between query \(\mathbf{q}\) and key
\(\mathbf{k}\) is often

\[
\frac{\mathbf{q}\cdot \mathbf{k}}{\sqrt{d}}.
\]

The attention output is a weighted average of value vectors:

\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d}}\right)V.
\]

This formula is one of the central mathematical expressions in modern
NLP.

\section{11. Differentiation, gradients, and
backpropagation}\label{differentiation-gradients-and-backpropagation}

Training a neural model means minimizing a loss function. If

\[
L(\theta)
\]

is a loss depending on parameters \(\theta\), the gradient

\[
\nabla_\theta L
\]

points in the direction of steepest increase. Gradient descent updates
parameters by

\[
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\nabla_\theta L(\theta_t),
\]

where \(\eta>0\) is the learning rate.

Backpropagation is repeated use of the chain rule. If

\[
z=f(y),\qquad y=g(x),
\]

then

\[
\frac{dz}{dx}=\frac{dz}{dy}\frac{dy}{dx}.
\]

In a neural network, every layer contributes one part of this chain.

\subsection{Common losses}\label{common-losses}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Task
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
binary classification & logistic loss & \(-y\log p-(1-y)\log(1-p)\) \\

\(-\sum_t \log p(x_t\mid x_{<t})\) \\

\(-\log\sigma(s^+-s^-)\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\section{12. Optimization algorithms}\label{optimization-algorithms}

Full-batch gradient descent uses all training data for each update.
Stochastic gradient descent uses small random batches. For mini-batch
\(B_t\), the update is

\[
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta\frac{1}{|B_t|}\sum_{i\in B_t}\nabla_\theta L_i(\theta_t).
\]

Momentum smooths updates:

\[
v_{t+1}=\beta v_t + \nabla L(\theta_t),
\]

\[
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta v_{t+1}.
\]

Adam and AdamW adapt learning rates using running estimates of first and
second moments of gradients. These methods are standard in training
transformer models.

\subsection{Practical optimization
issues}\label{practical-optimization-issues}

\section{13. Sequences and recurrence}\label{sequences-and-recurrence}

A text is not only a bag of words. It is an ordered sequence

\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T.
\]

A recurrent neural network updates a hidden state by

\[
\mathbf{h}_t=\phi(W_x\mathbf{x}_t+W_h\mathbf{h}_{t-1}+\mathbf{b}),
\]

where \(\phi\) is a nonlinear activation function.

The hidden state is a summary of previous tokens. The challenge is that
long chains of matrix multiplications can produce vanishing or exploding
gradients. LSTMs and GRUs address this issue with gates that control
memory flow.

\section{14. Transformers and residual
computation}\label{transformers-and-residual-computation}

A transformer block combines several operations:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  self-attention;
\item
  residual connection;
\item
  layer normalization;
\item
  feedforward network;
\item
  another residual connection;
\item
  another layer normalization.
\end{enumerate}

A simplified encoder block can be written as

\[
Y = \operatorname{LayerNorm}(X + \operatorname{SelfAttention}(X)),
\]

\[
Z = \operatorname{LayerNorm}(Y + \operatorname{FFN}(Y)).
\]

The residual terms help preserve information and improve gradient flow.
Layer normalization stabilizes the scale of activations.

\section{15. Positional encoding}\label{positional-encoding}

Self-attention alone is permutation equivariant: if token order is
permuted, outputs are permuted in the same way. To model word order,
transformers add position information.

A token representation often has the form

\[
\mathbf{z}_t = \mathbf{e}_{x_t}+\mathbf{p}_t,
\]

where \(\mathbf{e}_{x_t}\) is the token embedding and \(\mathbf{p}_t\)
is a position vector.

Sinusoidal positional encodings use functions such as

\[
\sin\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2j/d}}\right),
\qquad
\cos\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2j/d}}\right).
\]

Relative position methods modify attention scores according to token
distance. Rotary positional embedding, or RoPE, rotates query and key
vectors by position-dependent angles.

\section{16. Graphs and language}\label{graphs-and-language}

A graph consists of vertices and edges:

\[
G=(V,E).
\]

Graphs appear in NLP in many ways:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  dependency parse graphs;
\item
  word co-occurrence graphs;
\item
  document similarity graphs;
\item
  knowledge graphs;
\item
  retrieval citation graphs;
\item
  conversation graphs.
\end{itemize}

The adjacency matrix \(A\) is defined by

\[
A_{ij}=1
\]

if there is an edge from node \(i\) to node \(j\), and \(0\) otherwise.
Weighted graphs allow nonnegative edge weights.

The degree matrix \(D\) has diagonal entries

\[
D_{ii}=\sum_j A_{ij}.
\]

The graph Laplacian is

\[
L=D-A.
\]

Graph neural networks update node features by mixing information from
neighbors. A simple graph convolution has the form

\[
H^{(\ell+1)}=\sigma(\widetilde A H^{(\ell)}W^{(\ell)}),
\]

where \(\widetilde A\) is a normalized adjacency matrix.

\section{17. Metrics, ranking, and retrieval
evaluation}\label{metrics-ranking-and-retrieval-evaluation}

Retrieval systems rank documents according to a score. If \(q\) is a
query and \(d\) is a document, a retrieval score might be

\[
s(q,d)=\cos(\mathbf{q},\mathbf{d}).
\]

The output is an ordered list of documents. Evaluation must respect
ranking.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Metric
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
What it measures
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
precision@k & fraction of top-\(k\) documents that are relevant \\
recall@k & fraction of all relevant documents found in top \(k\) \\
MRR & reciprocal rank of the first relevant document \\
MAP & average precision across relevant documents \\
nDCG & relevance-weighted ranking quality with discount for lower
ranks \\
\end{longtable}
}

For retrieval-augmented generation, evaluation must check both retrieval
and generation. A good answer may fail because the retriever missed the
right evidence, or because the generator ignored the evidence.

\section{18. Statistics and
uncertainty}\label{statistics-and-uncertainty}

Evaluation metrics are estimates computed on finite datasets. They have
uncertainty.

If a model has accuracy \(\hat p\) on \(n\) independent examples, an
approximate standard error is

\[
\sqrt{\frac{\hat p(1-\hat p)}{n}}.
\]

For complex metrics, bootstrap resampling is often more useful. A
bootstrap procedure repeatedly samples the evaluation set with
replacement, recomputes the metric, and uses the resulting empirical
distribution to estimate uncertainty.

\subsection{Confusion matrix}\label{confusion-matrix}

For binary classification, the confusion matrix records:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& predicted positive & predicted negative \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
actual positive & TP & FN \\
actual negative & FP & TN \\
\end{longtable}
}

The most common metrics are

\[
\operatorname{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},
\]

\[
\operatorname{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},
\]

\[
F_1=\frac{2\cdot \operatorname{precision}\cdot \operatorname{recall}}
{\operatorname{precision}+\operatorname{recall}}.
\]

\section{19. Geometry and topology of
representations}\label{geometry-and-topology-of-representations}

A set of embeddings can be treated as a finite metric space. Given
points

\[
\mathbf{x}_1,\ldots,\mathbf{x}_n\in \mathbb{R}^d,
\]

we can compute pairwise distances

\[
d_{ij}=\|\mathbf{x}_i-\mathbf{x}_j\|_2.
\]

A neighborhood graph connects points whose distance is below a scale
\(\epsilon\). As \(\epsilon\) changes, the graph may gain or lose
connected components.

Topology studies properties such as connected components and loops.
Persistent homology studies how such properties change across scale.

In NLP, these ideas can help diagnose representation spaces. For
example:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Are embeddings organized into clusters?
\item
  Are there hubs that appear near too many points?
\item
  Does the representation collapse into a narrow cone?
\item
  Are trajectories through generated text smooth or unstable?
\item
  Do different groups or domains occupy different regions?
\end{itemize}

\section{20. Responsible mathematical
modeling}\label{responsible-mathematical-modeling}

Responsible NLP is not separate from mathematics. It uses mathematical
tools to ask whether systems behave reliably and fairly.

Examples include:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Concern
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mathematical diagnostic

\bottomrule\noalign{}

unequal error rates & subgroup precision, recall, false positive rate \\

distribution shift & train-test divergence, importance weighting \\

}

A model is not responsible simply because it has high average accuracy.
The errors must be understood by context, subgroup, uncertainty, and
consequences.
