\section{Key takeaways}\label{key-takeaways}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Text must be converted into finite mathematical objects before
  modeling.
\item
  A tokenizer is a map \(\tau:A^*\to V^*\).
\item
  A vocabulary determines the dimension of one-hot vectors and count
  vectors.
\item
  Count vectors and document-term matrices are the first bridge from NLP
  to linear algebra.
\item
  Word tokenization is interpretable but has serious unknown-word
  problems.
\item
  Subword tokenization balances vocabulary size, sequence length, and
  coverage.
\item
  Tokenization changes the probability space of language modeling.
\item
  In AI systems, tokenization affects context length, retrieval,
  prompting, and computational cost.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-1}

Classical treatments of text representations, tokenization, and
document-term matrices appear in information retrieval and statistical
NLP sources such as Manning et al. (2008), Manning and Schuetze (1999),
and Jurafsky and Martin (2024). Subword tokenization and byte-pair
encoding connect classical compression ideas with modern neural language
modeling.

\chapter{Documents as Vectors}\label{documents-as-vectors}

Term-document matrices, TF-IDF, and cosine geometry

\hfill\break

After text has been tokenized, the next classical step in NLP is to
represent each document by a vector. This chapter develops document
vectors from a mathematical point of view. We build count vectors,
term-document matrices, normalized frequency vectors, TF-IDF vectors,
and cosine similarity. The goal is not only to compute these objects,
but to understand what assumptions they encode and why they still matter
in modern AI systems such as search engines and retrieval-augmented
generation.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-2}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  define a document-vector representation as a map from token sequences
  to \(R^d\);
\item
  construct count vectors and document-term matrices from a corpus;
\item
  distinguish counts, binary indicators, relative frequencies, and
  normalized vectors;
\item
  explain TF-IDF as a mathematical weighting scheme for term
  specificity;
\item
  compute cosine similarity and interpret it geometrically;
\item
  rank documents in response to a query using sparse vector operations;
\item
  describe the statistical assumptions behind bag-of-words models;
\item
  implement document-vector methods in Python without relying on
  black-box NLP libraries;
\item
  use interactive visualizations to study how TF-IDF and normalization
  change retrieval;
\item
  use AI tools critically to test, explain, and improve vector-space
  representations.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Why documents become
vectors}\label{why-documents-become-vectors}

A document is naturally a sequence of tokens. If the vocabulary is

\[
V = \{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_d\},
\]

then a tokenized document has the form

\[
x=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_m), \qquad t_k \in V.
\]

Many mathematical and statistical methods, however, operate on vectors
and matrices. The basic idea of this chapter is to replace a token
sequence by a vector

\[
\phi(x) \in R^d,
\]

where the \(j\)th coordinate measures how strongly token \(v_j\) appears
in the document.

\textbf{Central idea.} A document-vector model is a representation map

\[
\phi:V^* \to R^d.
\]

Different choices of \(\phi\) produce different mathematical models.
Count vectors, TF-IDF vectors, binary vectors, probability vectors, and
neural embeddings are all representation maps.

The simplest representation ignores word order and records only token
counts. Although this loses information, it produces a useful
finite-dimensional object. In classical NLP and information retrieval,
this is called the \textbf{vector space model}.

\section{Corpus, vocabulary, and
notation}\label{corpus-vocabulary-and-notation}

Let

\[
D = (x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_n)
\]

be a corpus of \(n\) tokenized documents. Each document \(x_i\) is a
finite sequence over the vocabulary \(V\).

We use the following notation throughout the chapter:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Symbol & Meaning \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(n\) & number of documents \\
\(d\) & vocabulary size \\
\(x_i\) & document \(i\) \\
\(v_j\) & vocabulary token \(j\) \\
\(c_{ij}\) & count of token \(v_j\) in document \(x_i\) \\
\(X\) & document-term matrix \\
\(q\) & query vector \\
\(s_i\) & similarity score between document \(i\) and query \\
\end{longtable}
}

The central matrix is

\[
X = (c_{ij}) \in R^{n \times d},
\]

where

\[
c_{ij}=\#\{k : t_{ik}=v_j\}.
\]

Here \(t_{ik}\) is the \(k\)th token in document \(x_i\).

\subsection{Row convention}\label{row-convention}

In this book we usually use the row convention:

\[
X_{i\cdot} = \text{vector representation of document } x_i.
\]

Thus each row is a document and each column is a term. Some books use
the transpose convention, where columns are documents. Both are valid,
but dimensions must be tracked carefully.

\textbf{Dimension check.} If \(X \in R^{n \times d}\) and a query vector
is \(q \in R^d\), then raw document-query scores have the form

\[
Xq \in R^n.
\]

The output contains one score for each document.

\section{Count vectors}\label{count-vectors}

The count vector of a document \(x\) is

\[
c(x)=(c_1(x),c_2(x),\ldots,c_d(x)) \in N^d,
\]

where

\[
c_j(x)=\#\{k:t_k=v_j\}.
\]

For example, suppose

\[
V=\{\text{data},\text{language},\text{learning},\text{models},\text{token}\}.
\]

If

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{data data learning models}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is the document, then

\[
c(x)=(2,0,1,1,0).
\]

The count vector answers the question: \textbf{How many times does each
vocabulary term appear?}

\subsection{What counts preserve and
lose}\label{what-counts-preserve-and-lose}

The count vector preserves token frequency but discards order. For
example, the two documents

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{models predict language}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language predict models}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

have the same count vector. Therefore, the count-vector map is not
injective.

\textbf{Bag-of-words assumption.} A count vector treats a document as a
multiset of tokens rather than as an ordered sequence. Mathematically,
this means the representation is invariant under permutations of the
token positions.

If \(\pi\) is a permutation of \(\{1,2,\ldots,m\}\) and

\[
x=(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_m),
\]

then the permuted document

\[
\pi x=(t_{\pi(1)},t_{\pi(2)},\ldots,t_{\pi(m)})
\]

satisfies

\[
c(\pi x)=c(x).
\]

This invariance is both a strength and a weakness. It makes the model
simple and robust, but it cannot distinguish syntax, negation, or word
order.

\section{Binary vectors}\label{binary-vectors}

Sometimes we care only whether a token appears, not how often. The
binary representation is

\[
b_j(x)=
\begin{cases}
1, & c_j(x)>0,\\
0, & c_j(x)=0.
\end{cases}
\]

Thus

\[
b(x) \in \{0,1\}^d.
\]

Binary vectors are useful when repeated occurrences should not dominate.
For example, if one document repeats the word ``model'' many times, a
raw count vector may make it appear overly similar to any query
containing ``model.'' Binary vectors reduce this effect.

\section{Relative-frequency vectors}\label{relative-frequency-vectors}

Raw counts depend strongly on document length. If one document is twice
as long as another, its count vector may have a larger norm simply
because it contains more words. A simple correction is to divide by the
document length.

Let

\[
|x| = \sum_{j=1}^d c_j(x)
\]

be the total number of vocabulary tokens in document \(x\). The
relative-frequency vector is

\[
p_j(x)=\frac{c_j(x)}{|x|}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,d.
\]

Then

\[
p(x) \in R^d, \qquad p_j(x)\ge 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^d p_j(x)=1.
\]

Thus \(p(x)\) is an empirical probability distribution over the
vocabulary.

\textbf{Statistical viewpoint.} If a document is modeled as a sample
from a multinomial distribution over \(V\), then the relative-frequency
vector is the maximum likelihood estimate of the token probability
vector for that document.

This interpretation connects document vectors to statistics. A document
is not merely a string; it can be viewed as data generated by an unknown
distribution on words.

\section{The document-term matrix}\label{the-document-term-matrix}

Given \(n\) documents and \(d\) vocabulary terms, the count vectors form
a matrix

\[
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
--- & c(x_1)^T & ---\\
--- & c(x_2)^T & ---\\
& \vdots & \\
--- & c(x_n)^T & ---
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{n\times d}.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
X_{ij}=c_j(x_i).
\]

This matrix is usually sparse because most documents contain only a
small fraction of all vocabulary terms.

\subsection{Example}\label{example}

Consider the corpus

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{machine\ learning\ models\ learn\ from\ data}
\item
  \texttt{language\ models\ predict\ the\ next\ token}
\item
  \texttt{statistics\ studies\ data\ uncertainty\ and\ models}
\end{enumerate}

Using the vocabulary

\[
V=\{\text{data},\text{language},\text{learning},\text{models},\text{predict},\text{statistics},\text{token}\},
\]

the document-term matrix is

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&0&1&1&0&0&0\\
0&1&0&1&1&0&1\\
1&0&0&1&0&1&0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The first row says that the first document contains \texttt{data},
\texttt{learning}, and \texttt{models} once each.

\section{Python example: building a document-term
matrix}\label{python-example-building-a-document-term-matrix}

The following code builds a vocabulary and document-term matrix from
scratch. This is useful because it exposes the mathematical object
directly.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch03-document-term-matrix}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ re}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\NormalTok{corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"machine learning models learn from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language models predict the next token"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"statistics studies data uncertainty and models"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"learning from data helps statistical models"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
\NormalTok{    text }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ text.lower()}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ re.findall(}\VerbatimStringTok{r"}\PreprocessorTok{[a{-}z]}\OperatorTok{+}\VerbatimStringTok{"}\NormalTok{, text)}

\NormalTok{tokenized }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [tokenize(doc) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ corpus]}

\CommentTok{\# Build vocabulary in alphabetical order for reproducibility.}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(token }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc))}
\NormalTok{token\_to\_id }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{token: j }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, token }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(corpus), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)), dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, doc }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(tokenized):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc:}
\NormalTok{        X[i, token\_to\_id[token]] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{X\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(X, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\SpecialStringTok{f"doc\_}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{i}\OperatorTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"} \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(corpus))])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(X\_df)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The output matrix is the basic object used by many classical NLP
algorithms. Notice that the matrix construction requires only
tokenization, a vocabulary map, and counting.

\section{Linear algebra viewpoint}\label{linear-algebra-viewpoint}

Once documents are represented as vectors, we can use linear algebra.

Let

\[
x,y \in R^d
\]

be two document vectors. We may compute:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  their dot product \(x^Ty\);
\item
  their norms \(\|x\|_1\), \(\|x\|_2\), or \(\|x\|_\infty\);
\item
  their angle through cosine similarity;
\item
  their distance, such as \(\|x-y\|_2\);
\item
  their projection onto a low-dimensional subspace.
\end{itemize}

The dot product is

\[
x^Ty=\sum_{j=1}^d x_jy_j.
\]

For count vectors, this quantity is large when the two documents share
many terms with high counts.

However, dot products are sensitive to length. A longer document tends
to have a larger norm and may receive a large dot product even when it
is not especially similar in content.

\section{Cosine similarity}\label{cosine-similarity}

Cosine similarity normalizes by vector length:

\[
\operatorname{cos}(x,y)=\frac{x^Ty}{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2},
\]

provided \(x\ne 0\) and \(y\ne 0\).

Geometrically, this is the cosine of the angle between \(x\) and \(y\).
It measures direction rather than magnitude. If \(x\) and \(y\) point in
the same direction, then their cosine similarity is \(1\). If they are
orthogonal, the similarity is \(0\).

For nonnegative document vectors, cosine similarity lies between \(0\)
and \(1\).

\textbf{Scale invariance.} For any \(a>0\) and \(b>0\),

\[
\operatorname{cos}(ax,by)=\operatorname{cos}(x,y).
\]

Therefore, cosine similarity ignores positive rescaling of documents.
This is useful when document lengths differ.

\subsection{Matrix form of cosine
retrieval}\label{matrix-form-of-cosine-retrieval}

Suppose \(X\in R^{n\times d}\) contains document vectors and
\(q\in R^d\) is a query vector. The raw dot-product scores are

\[
r=Xq \in R^n.
\]

The cosine scores are

\[
s_i=\frac{X_{i\cdot}q}{\|X_{i\cdot}\|_2\|q\|_2}, \qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]

If we define the row-normalized matrix

\[
\widetilde X_{i\cdot}=\frac{X_{i\cdot}}{\|X_{i\cdot}\|_2}
\]

and the normalized query

\[
\widetilde q=\frac{q}{\|q\|_2},
\]

then

\[
s=\widetilde X\widetilde q.
\]

Thus retrieval by cosine similarity is matrix-vector multiplication
after normalization.

\section{Python example: cosine
search}\label{python-example-cosine-search}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch03-cosine-search}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ re}

\NormalTok{corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"machine learning models learn from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language models predict the next token"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"statistics studies data uncertainty and models"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"learning from data helps statistical models"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ re.findall(}\VerbatimStringTok{r"}\PreprocessorTok{[a{-}z]}\OperatorTok{+}\VerbatimStringTok{"}\NormalTok{, text.lower())}

\NormalTok{tokenized }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [tokenize(doc) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ corpus]}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(token }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc))}
\NormalTok{token\_to\_id }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{token: j }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, token }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ vectorize(tokens):}
\NormalTok{    vec }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokens:}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ token\_to\_id:}
\NormalTok{            vec[token\_to\_id[token]] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ vec}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.vstack([vectorize(doc) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized])}

\NormalTok{query }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"data learning models"}
\NormalTok{q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ vectorize(tokenize(query))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cosine\_similarity\_matrix(X, q):}
\NormalTok{    q\_norm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(q)}
\NormalTok{    X\_norms }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scores }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (X\_norms }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ q\_norm)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ scores}

\NormalTok{scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ cosine\_similarity\_matrix(X, q)}
\NormalTok{ranking }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{scores)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ rank, i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(ranking, start}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{rank}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{. score=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{scores[i]}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{corpus[i]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This code shows that document retrieval can be written as a small linear
algebra problem.

\section{Term frequency}\label{term-frequency}

Raw counts can be transformed before similarity is computed. The first
transformation is \textbf{term frequency}.

A simple term frequency is

\[
\operatorname{tf}_{ij}=c_{ij}.
\]

A length-normalized term frequency is

\[
\operatorname{tf}_{ij}=\frac{c_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^d c_{ik}}.
\]

A log-scaled term frequency is

\[
\operatorname{tf}_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
1+\log(c_{ij}), & c_{ij}>0,\\
0, & c_{ij}=0.
\end{cases}
\]

The log transform reduces the effect of repeated occurrences. For
example, a term appearing ten times should not always be ten times as
important as a term appearing once.

\section{Document frequency and inverse document
frequency}\label{document-frequency-and-inverse-document-frequency}

Some words appear in many documents. These common terms often have low
discriminative value. For example, words such as \texttt{the},
\texttt{and}, \texttt{model}, or \texttt{data} may appear frequently in
a technical corpus.

The document frequency of token \(v_j\) is

\[
\operatorname{df}_j=\#\{i:c_{ij}>0\}.
\]

It counts how many documents contain the term at least once.

The inverse document frequency is commonly defined as

\[
\operatorname{idf}_j=\log\left(\frac{n+1}{\operatorname{df}_j+1}\right)+1.
\]

The added \(1\) in numerator and denominator is smoothing. It avoids
division by zero and keeps the weight finite. Other conventions are also
used.

\textbf{Interpretation.} If \(\operatorname{df}_j/n\) is the empirical
probability that a random document contains token \(v_j\), then

\[
\log\left(\frac{n}{\operatorname{df}_j}\right)
\]

is the negative logarithm of this empirical probability. Rare terms
receive larger weights because they are more informative for
distinguishing documents.

\section{TF-IDF vectors}\label{tf-idf-vectors}

The TF-IDF weight of term \(v_j\) in document \(x_i\) is

\[
w_{ij}=\operatorname{tf}_{ij}\operatorname{idf}_j.
\]

In matrix form, if \(T=(\operatorname{tf}_{ij})\) and

\[
D_{\operatorname{idf}}=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{idf}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{idf}_d),
\]

then the TF-IDF matrix is

\[
W=TD_{\operatorname{idf}}.
\]

This is a column weighting of the term-frequency matrix. Terms that
appear in many documents get smaller weights. Terms that appear in fewer
documents get larger weights.

\subsection{Why TF-IDF is useful}\label{why-tf-idf-is-useful}

TF-IDF balances two effects:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Within-document importance.} A term is important if it appears
  often in a particular document.
\item
  \textbf{Across-document specificity.} A term is more informative if it
  does not appear in almost every document.
\end{enumerate}

Thus TF-IDF is a simple way to say:

\begin{quote}
A good keyword should be frequent in this document but not too frequent
across the whole corpus.
\end{quote}

\section{Python example: TF-IDF from
scratch}\label{python-example-tf-idf-from-scratch}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch03-tfidf-from-scratch}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\CommentTok{\# X is the document{-}term count matrix from the previous example.}
\NormalTok{n, d }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape}

\CommentTok{\# Term frequency: length{-}normalized counts.}
\NormalTok{doc\_lengths }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{TF }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ doc\_lengths}

\CommentTok{\# Document frequency.}
\NormalTok{df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Smoothed inverse document frequency.}
\NormalTok{idf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log((n }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (df }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}

\CommentTok{\# TF{-}IDF matrix.}
\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ TF }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ idf}

\NormalTok{W\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(W, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\SpecialStringTok{f"doc\_}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{i}\OperatorTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"} \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n)])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(W\_df.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The resulting matrix has the same shape as the count matrix, but its
entries have changed. Common tokens receive smaller column weights,
while more specific tokens receive larger column weights.

\section{Comparing count vectors and TF-IDF
vectors}\label{comparing-count-vectors-and-tf-idf-vectors}

Count vectors often reward documents that share common terms with the
query. TF-IDF vectors reward documents that share more specific terms.

Suppose the query is

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language token prediction}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A count-vector search might rank a document highly because it contains
\texttt{language} and \texttt{token}. TF-IDF may increase the importance
of \texttt{token} if it appears in only a few documents.

This distinction matters in academic settings. For example, in a corpus
of course descriptions, words such as \texttt{course},
\texttt{students}, and \texttt{methods} may appear everywhere. Words
such as \texttt{Bayesian}, \texttt{topology}, or \texttt{transformer}
may be more specific.

The following interactive component lets you adjust the IDF strength and

The HTML version of this chapter contains an interactive Plotly.js

\section{The geometry of sparse document
vectors}\label{the-geometry-of-sparse-document-vectors}

Document vectors often live in very high dimensions. A vocabulary may
contain thousands or millions of tokens, while a single document uses
only a small subset. Therefore, most entries of a document vector are
zero.

This creates a sparse geometry:

\[
\#\{j:x_j\ne 0\} \ll d.
\]

Sparse vectors are computationally useful because we do not need to
store or multiply by all zero entries. They are also geometrically
interesting. Two randomly chosen short documents may have no terms in
common, which makes their dot product zero.

\subsection{Orthogonality in sparse
spaces}\label{orthogonality-in-sparse-spaces}

If two count vectors have disjoint supports, then

\[
x^Ty=0.
\]

For nonnegative vectors, this means their cosine similarity is zero. In
a large vocabulary, many pairs of documents may be nearly orthogonal
even if they are topically related but use different words.

For example, the documents

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{neural network training}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{deep learning optimization}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

are semantically related, but a simple bag-of-words model may give low
similarity if the exact words do not overlap. This limitation motivates
later chapters on latent semantic analysis, word embeddings, and
transformer representations.

\section{Stop words and projection}\label{stop-words-and-projection}

A common preprocessing step removes very frequent words such as
\texttt{the}, \texttt{and}, \texttt{of}, and \texttt{to}.
Mathematically, stop-word removal is a coordinate projection.

Let \(S\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots,d\}\) be the set of coordinates
corresponding to terms we keep. The projection map is

\[
P_S:R^d\to R^{|S|},
\]

where

\[
P_S(x)=(x_j)_{j\in S}.
\]

This map discards coordinates. It can improve retrieval by removing
noise, but it can also remove meaningful words in some contexts. For
example, \texttt{not} is often a stop word in generic lists, but it is
crucial for sentiment analysis.

\textbf{Modeling warning.} Stop-word removal is not universally safe. It
is a projection that may remove coordinates relevant to the task.

\section{Statistical model behind
bag-of-words}\label{statistical-model-behind-bag-of-words}

The bag-of-words representation can be derived from a multinomial model.

Suppose document \(x_i\) has length \(m_i\) and is generated by
independent draws from a categorical distribution

\[
\theta_i=(\theta_{i1},\ldots,\theta_{id}),
\]

where

\[
\theta_{ij}\ge 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^d \theta_{ij}=1.
\]

The probability of observing counts

\[
c_i=(c_{i1},\ldots,c_{id})
\]

is

\[
P(c_i\mid \theta_i)=\frac{m_i!}{c_{i1}!c_{i2}!\cdots c_{id}!}\prod_{j=1}^d \theta_{ij}^{c_{ij}}.
\]

The log-likelihood, ignoring the multinomial coefficient, is

\[
\ell(\theta_i)=\sum_{j=1}^d c_{ij}\log \theta_{ij}.
\]

Maximizing this subject to \(\sum_j \theta_{ij}=1\) gives

\[
\widehat\theta_{ij}=\frac{c_{ij}}{m_i}.
\]

Thus the relative-frequency vector is the maximum likelihood estimate of
the document's token distribution under this simplified model.

\subsection{What the model assumes}\label{what-the-model-assumes}

The multinomial bag-of-words model assumes:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  token order is irrelevant;
\item
  tokens are conditionally independent given \(\theta_i\);
\item
  each document has its own word distribution;
\item
  dependence between neighboring words is ignored.
\end{enumerate}

These assumptions are false for real language, but they give a
mathematically transparent baseline.

\section{Connection to
classification}\label{connection-to-classification}

Document vectors are not only used for retrieval. They can also be used
for classification.

Suppose each document has a label

\[
y_i\in \{1,2,\ldots,K\}.
\]

A linear classifier has the form

\[
f(x_i)=\arg\max_{k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}} \left(w_k^T\phi(x_i)+b_k\right).
\]

Here \(\phi(x_i)\) may be a count vector, TF-IDF vector, or another
document representation. The same vectorization step supports logistic
regression, support vector machines, naive Bayes, and neural networks.

For binary classification, a common model is

\[
P(y_i=1\mid x_i)=\sigma(w^T\phi(x_i)+b),
\]

where

\[
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.
\]

This shows how vector-space NLP connects directly to statistics and
machine learning.

\section{Low-dimensional visualization by
SVD}\label{low-dimensional-visualization-by-svd}

Because document vectors are high-dimensional, we often visualize them
by projecting to two dimensions. A simple method is singular value
decomposition.

Let \(W\in R^{n\times d}\) be a centered or weighted document-term
matrix. Its singular value decomposition is

\[
W=U\Sigma V^T.
\]

The best rank-\(k\) approximation in Frobenius norm is

\[
W_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^T.
\]

For visualization, we often use the rows of

\[
U_2\Sigma_2\in R^{n\times 2}
\]

as two-dimensional document coordinates.

\textbf{Preview.} This idea leads to latent semantic analysis, which
studies low-rank structure in document-term matrices. Chapter 7 returns
to this topic in detail.

\section{Python example: two-dimensional document
map}\label{python-example-two-dimensional-document-map}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch03-svd-visualization}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}

\CommentTok{\# Use the TF{-}IDF matrix W from the earlier example.}
\CommentTok{\# Center columns so the SVD highlights differences among documents.}
\NormalTok{W\_centered }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ W.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{U, S, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(W\_centered, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{coords }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U[:, :}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ S[:}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{plt.figure(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{plt.scatter(coords[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], coords[:, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, text }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(corpus):}
\NormalTok{    plt.annotate(}\SpecialStringTok{f"doc\_}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{i}\OperatorTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{, (coords[i, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], coords[i, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]))}
\NormalTok{plt.axhline(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, linewidth}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.axvline(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, linewidth}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"first SVD coordinate"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"second SVD coordinate"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.title(}\StringTok{"Documents projected to two dimensions"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This visualization is not a replacement for the full high-dimensional
representation. It is a diagnostic tool that helps us inspect whether
documents cluster by topic or vocabulary.

\section{Evaluation of retrieval}\label{evaluation-of-retrieval}

A document-vector method is often used for retrieval: given a query,
return a ranked list of documents. To evaluate retrieval, we need
relevance judgments.

For a query \(q\), let

\[
R(q)\subseteq \{1,2,\ldots,n\}
\]

be the set of relevant documents. If a system returns the top \(k\)
documents

\[
A_k(q),
\]

then precision at \(k\) is

\[
\operatorname{Precision@}k=\frac{|A_k(q)\cap R(q)|}{k}.
\]

Recall at \(k\) is

\[
\operatorname{Recall@}k=\frac{|A_k(q)\cap R(q)|}{|R(q)|}.
\]

Precision measures how many retrieved documents are relevant. Recall
measures how many relevant documents were retrieved.

For course search, advising chatbots, and RAG systems, retrieval
evaluation is essential. A language model can only answer from useful
evidence if the retrieval step finds useful evidence.

\section{AI component: document vectors in RAG
systems}\label{ai-component-document-vectors-in-rag-systems}

Modern retrieval-augmented generation systems often use neural
embeddings rather than TF-IDF. However, the mathematical pipeline is
similar:

\[
\text{document} \xrightarrow{\phi} R^p,
\qquad
\text{query} \xrightarrow{\phi} R^p,
\qquad
\text{rank by similarity}.
\]

In classical vector search, \(\phi\) may be TF-IDF. In neural vector
search, \(\phi\) may be a transformer embedding model. The retrieval
step still depends on geometry: dot products, cosine similarity, nearest
neighbors, and ranking.

\textbf{AI-assisted learning activity.} Ask an AI system:

\begin{quote}
Give three short documents for which TF-IDF search succeeds and three
short documents for which TF-IDF search fails. For each failure, explain
the mathematical reason in terms of vocabulary overlap, synonymy,
negation, or word order.
\end{quote}

Then verify the examples by computing count vectors and cosine
similarities yourself.

\section{AI component: auditing a
representation}\label{ai-component-auditing-a-representation}

When using AI tools to help build NLP systems, ask the tool to make the
representation assumptions explicit. A useful prompt is:

\begin{quote}
I am representing documents using TF-IDF vectors. List the mathematical
assumptions of this representation. Which assumptions are problematic
for sentiment analysis, course advising, and mathematical text search?
\end{quote}

A good answer should mention at least:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  loss of word order;
\item
  dependence on exact vocabulary overlap;
\item
  sensitivity to tokenization;
\item
  inability to understand synonyms unless they share terms;
\item
  possible removal of important stop words;
\item
  limited handling of negation;
\item
  dependence on the corpus used to compute IDF.
\end{itemize}

Use AI tools as mathematical critics, not as replacements for
mathematical verification.

\section{Worked example: hand
calculation}\label{worked-example-hand-calculation}

Consider three documents with vocabulary

\[
V=\{a,b,c,d\}.
\]

Suppose the count matrix is

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&1&0&0\\
1&0&2&0\\
0&1&0&3
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Let the query be

\[
q=(1,1,0,0)^T.
\]

The raw dot-product scores are

\[
Xq=
\begin{bmatrix}
3\\
1\\
1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The Euclidean norms are

\[
\|q\|_2=\sqrt{2},
\]

\[
\|X_{1\cdot}\|_2=\sqrt{5}, \qquad
\|X_{2\cdot}\|_2=\sqrt{5}, \qquad
\|X_{3\cdot}\|_2=\sqrt{10}.
\]

Thus the cosine scores are

\[
s_1=\frac{3}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{2}}=\frac{3}{\sqrt{10}},
\]

\[
s_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}},
\]

and

\[
s_3=\frac{1}{\sqrt{10}\sqrt{2}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{20}}.
\]

Therefore, document 1 is most similar to the query.

This small example illustrates the full retrieval calculation:
vectorize, multiply, normalize, rank.

\section{Common pitfalls}\label{common-pitfalls}

\subsection{Pitfall 1: confusing rows and
columns}\label{pitfall-1-confusing-rows-and-columns}

Always state whether documents are rows or columns. In this book,
documents are rows.

\subsection{Pitfall 2: forgetting zero
vectors}\label{pitfall-2-forgetting-zero-vectors}

Cosine similarity is undefined when one vector has zero norm. This can
happen if a query contains no vocabulary terms.

\subsection{Pitfall 3: assuming TF-IDF understands
meaning}\label{pitfall-3-assuming-tf-idf-understands-meaning}

TF-IDF is a lexical method. It does not know that \texttt{doctor} and
\texttt{physician} are related unless the corpus and vocabulary create
indirect associations.

\subsection{Pitfall 4: ignoring corpus
dependence}\label{pitfall-4-ignoring-corpus-dependence}

IDF weights depend on the corpus. If the corpus changes, the IDF weights
change.

\subsection{Pitfall 5: treating preprocessing as
neutral}\label{pitfall-5-treating-preprocessing-as-neutral}

Lowercasing, punctuation removal, stop-word removal, and stemming all
change the mathematical representation.

\section{Chapter summary}\label{chapter-summary-1}

The main construction in this chapter is the document-vector map

\[
\phi:V^*\to R^d.
\]

The simplest choice is the count vector. From count vectors we build the
document-term matrix

\[
X\in R^{n\times d}.
\]

We then transform this matrix using normalization and TF-IDF weighting.
Similarity between documents or between a query and documents is often
measured by cosine similarity:

\[
\operatorname{cos}(x,y)=\frac{x^Ty}{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2}.
\]

These ideas form the classical foundation of search and retrieval. They
also prepare us for modern NLP, where documents and queries are
represented by learned dense vectors instead of sparse TF-IDF vectors.
