\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-2}

The vector space model and TF-IDF are classical foundations of
information retrieval. For more detail, see Manning et al. (2008) and
Manning and Schuetze (1999). Modern NLP still uses the same underlying
linear algebra ideas, even when the representation map is learned by a
neural network rather than manually constructed. Later chapters connect
these ideas to latent semantic analysis, word embeddings, and
transformer-based retrieval.

\part{Part II. Probability Models for Language}

\chapter{Probability and Language}\label{probability-and-language}

Random tokens, conditional distributions, likelihood, entropy, and
perplexity

\hfill\break

Natural language has uncertainty. A sentence may continue in many
possible ways, a word may have several meanings, and the same document
may be assigned different labels depending on context. This chapter
develops the probabilistic viewpoint needed for modern NLP. We treat
tokens, sentences, labels, and model outputs as random objects. The goal
is to understand language modeling as conditional probability estimation
and supervised NLP as learning probability distributions from data.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-3}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  describe a token sequence as a realization of random variables over a
  finite vocabulary;
\item
  distinguish empirical token frequencies, population probabilities, and
  model probabilities;
\item
  use the chain rule of probability to factor the probability of a
  sentence;
\item
  explain why language modeling is conditional distribution estimation;
\item
  derive maximum likelihood estimation for a unigram model;
\item
  compute negative log-likelihood, cross-entropy, entropy, KL
  divergence, and perplexity;
\item
  explain the difference between generative and discriminative NLP
  models;
\item
  implement simple probability models for text using Python;
\item
  use an interactive Plotly.js visualization to explore entropy,
  temperature, and next-token probabilities;
\item
  use AI tools to critique probabilistic assumptions without treating
  the AI response as a proof.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Why probability enters NLP}\label{why-probability-enters-nlp}

In the previous chapters, we treated text as data: strings, token
sequences, count vectors, and document-term matrices. These
representations are useful, but they do not yet answer questions such
as:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  How likely is a sentence?
\item
  Which word is most likely to come next?
\item
  How uncertain is a model's prediction?
\item
  How should a classifier combine evidence from many words?
\item
  How should we compare two language models statistically?
\end{itemize}

Probability provides the mathematical language for these questions.

Suppose the vocabulary is

\[
V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_d\}.
\]

A single token can be modeled as a random variable

\[
W:\Omega \to V,
\]

where \(\Omega\) is an underlying sample space. For a sentence or
document of length \(T\), we use a sequence of random variables

\[
W_1,W_2,\ldots,W_T,
\]

with each \(W_t\) taking values in \(V\). A particular observed sentence
is a realization

\[
w_{1:T}=(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T).
\]

\textbf{Central idea.} A probabilistic language model assigns
probabilities to token sequences:

\[
p(w_{1:T})=P(W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_T=w_T).
\]

Modern large language models usually estimate conditional probabilities
of the form

\[
p(w_t \mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}).
\]

A probability model does not claim that language is random in a
philosophical sense. Rather, it gives a mathematical way to represent
uncertainty from the viewpoint of an observer who has partial
information.

\section{Probability distributions on a finite
vocabulary}\label{probability-distributions-on-a-finite-vocabulary}

For a fixed vocabulary \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\), a probability
distribution over tokens is a vector

\[
p=(p_1,p_2,\ldots,p_d) \in R^d
\]

such that

\[
p_j \geq 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^d p_j = 1.
\]

The set of all such vectors is the probability simplex

\[
\Delta^{d-1}
=\left\{p\in R^d: p_j\geq 0,\ \sum_{j=1}^d p_j=1\right\}.
\]

If \(p_j=P(W=v_j)\), then \(p\) is the distribution of the random token
\(W\).

\subsection{Example}\label{example-1}

Let

\[
V=\{\text{data},\text{language},\text{model},\text{learns}\}.
\]

One possible token distribution is

\[
p=(0.35,0.25,0.30,0.10).
\]

This means

\[
P(W=\text{data})=0.35, \qquad P(W=\text{learns})=0.10.
\]

A model's prediction at a particular position in a sentence is also a
probability vector in a simplex. If a neural language model reads the
context

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

then it may output a conditional distribution

\[
p_\theta(\cdot \mid \text{language models}) \in \Delta^{d-1}.
\]

The subscript \(\theta\) denotes trainable model parameters.

\section{Empirical distributions}\label{empirical-distributions}

In practice we do not know the true population distribution of language.
We observe a corpus and estimate probabilities from counts.

Let \(c_j\) be the number of times token \(v_j\) appears in a corpus and
let

\[
N=\sum_{j=1}^d c_j
\]

be the total number of vocabulary tokens. The empirical token
distribution is

\[
\widehat p_j=\frac{c_j}{N}, \qquad j=1,\ldots,d.
\]

This is a probability vector because \(\widehat p_j\geq 0\) and

\[
\sum_{j=1}^d \widehat p_j
=
\sum_{j=1}^d \frac{c_j}{N}
=
\frac{1}{N}\sum_{j=1}^d c_j
=1.
\]

\textbf{Empirical distribution.} A corpus turns counts into
probabilities by normalization:

\[
\widehat p_j=\frac{\text{count of }v_j}{\text{total token count}}.
\]

This is the simplest statistical estimator in language modeling.

\subsection{Python example: empirical token
probabilities}\label{python-example-empirical-token-probabilities}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ math}

\NormalTok{corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"language models learn from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"data models predict tokens"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language data has structure"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"models learn probability"}
\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ text.lower().split()}

\NormalTok{tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ corpus:}
\NormalTok{    tokens.extend(tokenize(doc))}

\NormalTok{counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(tokens)}
\NormalTok{N }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(counts.values())}
\NormalTok{empirical\_p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{token: count }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ N }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ counts.items()\}}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Token counts:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(counts)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Empirical probabilities:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(empirical\_p.items()):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{token}\SpecialCharTok{:12s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Token counts:
Counter({'models': 3, 'data': 3, 'language': 2, 'learn': 2, 'from': 1, 'predict': 1, 'tokens': 1, 'has': 1, 'structure': 1, 'probability': 1})

Empirical probabilities:
data         0.188
from         0.062
has          0.062
language     0.125
learn        0.125
models       0.188
predict      0.062
probability  0.062
structure    0.062
tokens       0.062
\end{verbatim}

The output is an empirical distribution on the vocabulary built from the
corpus. This distribution is not a deep model, but it is the
mathematical beginning of language modeling.

\section{Population distribution, data distribution, and model
distribution}\label{population-distribution-data-distribution-and-model-distribution}

It is useful to distinguish three distributions.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Distribution
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Meaning
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Usually known?
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\(p^*\) & true data-generating distribution of language in the target
domain & no \\
\(\widehat p\) & empirical distribution from the observed corpus &
yes \\
\(p_\theta\) & model distribution with parameters \(\theta\) & yes after
training \\
\end{longtable}
}

The true distribution \(p^*\) is an idealized object. It represents the
probability law of text in the population or domain we care about. We
never observe \(p^*\) directly. Instead, we observe samples and build an
empirical approximation \(\widehat p\). Training tries to choose
parameters \(\theta\) so that \(p_\theta\) is close to \(p^*\), using
the corpus as evidence.

A clean statistical formulation is:

\[
\text{Choose }\theta\text{ so that }p_\theta\text{ assigns high probability to observed text.}
\]

This principle leads to maximum likelihood estimation.

\section{Maximum likelihood for a unigram
model}\label{maximum-likelihood-for-a-unigram-model}

The simplest language model assumes that tokens are independent and
identically distributed from a vocabulary distribution \(p\).

Let the corpus tokens be

\[
w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_N.
\]

The unigram model says

\[
P(W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_N=w_N)
=
\prod_{i=1}^N p(w_i).
\]

If token \(v_j\) appears \(c_j\) times, the likelihood is

\[
L(p)
=
\prod_{j=1}^d p_j^{c_j}.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(p)
=
\log L(p)
=
\sum_{j=1}^d c_j\log p_j.
\]

We maximize \(\ell(p)\) subject to

\[
p_j\geq 0,\qquad \sum_{j=1}^d p_j=1.
\]

Ignoring zero-count boundary details, use a Lagrange multiplier:

\[
\mathcal L(p,\lambda)
=
\sum_{j=1}^d c_j\log p_j
+
\lambda\left(1-\sum_{j=1}^d p_j\right).
\]

For \(c_j>0\),

\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal L}{\partial p_j}
=
\frac{c_j}{p_j}-\lambda=0.
\]

Therefore

\[
p_j=\frac{c_j}{\lambda}.
\]

Using \(\sum_j p_j=1\) gives

\[
1=\sum_{j=1}^d \frac{c_j}{\lambda}
=\frac{N}{\lambda},
\]

so \(\lambda=N\). Hence the maximum likelihood estimator is

\[
\widehat p_j=\frac{c_j}{N}.
\]

\textbf{MLE for the unigram model.} Under the independent-token model,
the maximum likelihood estimate of the token probability is the
empirical frequency:

\[
\widehat p_j=\frac{c_j}{N}.
\]

This derivation is important because it shows how a simple counting rule
is actually a likelihood-based statistical estimator.

\section{Sentences and the chain
rule}\label{sentences-and-the-chain-rule}

A sentence is not just a bag of independent tokens. Word order and
context matter. The full probability of a sequence is

\[
P(W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_T=w_T).
\]

The chain rule of probability gives the exact factorization

\[
P(w_1,\ldots,w_T)
=
P(w_1)P(w_2\mid w_1)P(w_3\mid w_1,w_2)\cdots P(w_T\mid w_1,
\ldots,w_{T-1}).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
P(w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^T P(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1}),
\]

where \(w_{1:t-1}=(w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1})\).

\textbf{Language modeling problem.} Estimate the conditional
distribution

\[
P(W_t=\cdot \mid W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_{t-1}=w_{t-1}).
\]

A language model is a machine for producing this distribution.

This formula is exact. The difficulty is statistical and computational:
there are many possible histories \(w_{1:t-1}\). N-gram models solve
this by truncating the history. Transformers solve it by learning a
flexible representation of the history through attention.

\section{Conditional probability and
prediction}\label{conditional-probability-and-prediction}

The basic object in next-token prediction is a conditional probability.
Given a context \(C\), a language model outputs

\[
p_\theta(v_j\mid C),\qquad j=1,\ldots,d.
\]

This is a probability vector satisfying

\[
p_\theta(v_j\mid C)\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^d p_\theta(v_j\mid C)=1.
\]

The most likely next token is

\[
\widehat w
=
\arg\max_{v_j\in V} p_\theta(v_j\mid C).
\]

But the full probability vector is more informative than only the
maximum. It tells us how uncertain the model is. For example, after the
context

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{machine learning models can}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

the model may assign high probability to several plausible next tokens
such as ``predict,'' ``learn,'' ``classify,'' or ``generate.'' A
deterministic answer hides that uncertainty.

\section{Negative log-likelihood}\label{negative-log-likelihood}

Suppose a model assigns probability \(p_\theta(w_i)\) to each observed
token \(w_i\). The likelihood of the observed corpus is

\[
L(\theta)=\prod_{i=1}^N p_\theta(w_i).
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta)=\sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(w_i).
\]

Instead of maximizing log-likelihood, machine learning usually minimizes
negative log-likelihood:

\[
\operatorname{NLL}(\theta)
=
-\sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(w_i).
\]

For a sequence model, this becomes

\[
\operatorname{NLL}(\theta)
=
-\sum_{t=1}^T \log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1}).
\]

The negative sign appears because optimization algorithms are often
written as minimization algorithms. Minimizing negative log-likelihood
is equivalent to maximizing likelihood.

\subsection{Python example: negative
log-likelihood}\label{python-example-negative-log-likelihood}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{observed\_tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{model\_p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.40}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.15}
\NormalTok{\}}

\NormalTok{nll }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(math.log(model\_p[token]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ observed\_tokens)}
\NormalTok{avg\_nll }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ nll }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(observed\_tokens)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Negative log{-}likelihood:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(nll, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Average negative log{-}likelihood:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(avg\_nll, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Perplexity:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(math.exp(avg\_nll), }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Negative log-likelihood: 4.8283
Average negative log-likelihood: 1.2071
Perplexity: 3.3437
\end{verbatim}

The average negative log-likelihood is also the empirical cross-entropy
of the observed data relative to the model.

\section{Entropy}\label{entropy}

Entropy measures uncertainty in a probability distribution. For a
distribution \(p\) on \(V\), the entropy is

\[
H(p)=-\sum_{j=1}^d p_j\log p_j.
\]

We use the convention \(0\log 0=0\), interpreted as a limit.

If \(p\) is concentrated on one token, entropy is small. If \(p\) is
spread evenly across many tokens, entropy is large.

\subsection{Example}\label{example-2}

For a four-token vocabulary, compare

\[
p=(1,0,0,0)
\]

and

\[
q=\left(\frac14,\frac14,\frac14,\frac14\right).
\]

Then

\[
H(p)=0,
\]

while

\[
H(q)=-4\left(\frac14\log\frac14\right)=\log 4.
\]

The uniform distribution has the largest entropy among distributions on
four outcomes.

\subsection{Python example: entropy of token
distributions}\label{python-example-entropy-of-token-distributions}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ entropy(probs):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \OperatorTok{{-}}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(p }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ math.log(p) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ p }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ probs }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ p }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sharp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.03}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{spread }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{]}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Entropy of sharp distribution:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(entropy(sharp), }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Entropy of spread distribution:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(entropy(spread), }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Entropy of sharp distribution: 0.428
Entropy of spread distribution: 1.3863
\end{verbatim}

In NLP, entropy helps quantify uncertainty in token prediction. A model
with high next-token entropy is unsure among many possible
continuations. A model with low next-token entropy strongly prefers a
small number of continuations.

\section{Cross-entropy}\label{cross-entropy}

Suppose \(p\) is the true distribution and \(q\) is a model
distribution. The cross-entropy from \(p\) to \(q\) is

\[
H(p,q)=-\sum_{j=1}^d p_j\log q_j.
\]

This measures the expected negative log-probability assigned by model
\(q\) when the data are drawn from \(p\).

If \(p\) is replaced by an empirical distribution \(\widehat p\), then

\[
H(\widehat p,q)
=
-\sum_{j=1}^d \widehat p_j\log q_j.
\]

Using \(\widehat p_j=c_j/N\), we get

\[
H(\widehat p,q)
=
-\sum_{j=1}^d \frac{c_j}{N}\log q_j
=
-\frac1N \sum_{j=1}^d c_j\log q_j.
\]

This is average negative log-likelihood.

\textbf{Cross-entropy and training.} When we train a language model with
next-token prediction, the usual loss is empirical cross-entropy:

\[
-\frac1N \sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(w_i\mid \text{context}_i).
\]

Thus cross-entropy is not just an evaluation metric. It is the main
training objective for many language models.

\section{KL divergence}\label{kl-divergence}

The Kullback-Leibler divergence from \(p\) to \(q\) is

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)
=
\sum_{j=1}^d p_j\log\frac{p_j}{q_j}.
\]

It satisfies

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\geq 0,
\]

with equality if \(p=q\) on the support of \(p\).

The relationship between entropy, cross-entropy, and KL divergence is

\[
H(p,q)=H(p)+D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q).
\]

Since \(H(p)\) does not depend on the model \(q\), minimizing
cross-entropy is equivalent to minimizing KL divergence from the data
distribution to the model distribution.

This identity gives a clean mathematical interpretation of
language-model training:

\[
\text{training reduces the discrepancy between the data distribution and the model distribution.}
\]

\section{Perplexity}\label{perplexity}

Perplexity is a common metric for language models. If the average
negative log-likelihood per token is

\[
\overline L
=
-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(w_i\mid \text{context}_i),
\]

then perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{PPL}=\exp(\overline L).
\]

If logarithms base \(2\) are used, then

\[
\operatorname{PPL}=2^{\overline L_2}.
\]

Perplexity can be interpreted as an effective number of equally likely
choices. For example, a perplexity of \(10\) roughly means the model is
as uncertain as if it were choosing among \(10\) equally likely tokens
at each step.

\textbf{Important caution.} Lower perplexity usually means better
next-token prediction on similar data, but it does not automatically
mean better reasoning, truthfulness, robustness, or usefulness.

\section{Interactive HTML: temperature, entropy, and next-token
uncertainty}\label{interactive-html-temperature-entropy-and-next-token-uncertainty}

The softmax function converts scores, or logits, into probabilities.
Given logits \(z_1,\ldots,z_d\) and temperature \(T>0\), define

\[
p_j(T)=\frac{\exp(z_j/T)}{\sum_{k=1}^d \exp(z_k/T)}.
\]

Small temperature makes the distribution sharper. Large temperature
makes it flatter. This affects entropy and perplexity.

The HTML version of this chapter contains an interactive Plotly.js
visualization. It lets the reader change the softmax temperature \(T\)
and observe how the next-token distribution, entropy, and effective
perplexity change.

\subsection{Mathematical lesson from the
interactive}\label{mathematical-lesson-from-the-interactive}

The temperature transformation

\[
p_j(T)=\frac{\exp(z_j/T)}{\sum_{k=1}^d \exp(z_k/T)}
\]

is not a new training procedure. It is a transformation of the output
distribution. When \(T<1\), the largest logits become more dominant.
When \(T>1\), the probabilities become more balanced. Thus temperature
controls randomness in generation by changing the entropy of the
next-token distribution.

\section{Conditional language models as statistical
estimators}\label{conditional-language-models-as-statistical-estimators}

Let \(C_t=(W_1,\ldots,W_{t-1})\) denote the context before position
\(t\). A conditional language model estimates

\[
p^*(w_t\mid C_t).
\]

The model is a parameterized function

\[
f_\theta:C_t \mapsto p_\theta(\cdot\mid C_t)\in \Delta^{d-1}.
\]

Training data consist of context-target pairs

\[
(C_i,y_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,N,
\]

where \(y_i\) is the observed next token. The empirical cross-entropy
loss is

\[
\widehat R(\theta)
=
-\frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(y_i\mid C_i).
\]

This is the same mathematical structure whether \(f_\theta\) is an
n-gram table, a recurrent neural network, or a transformer.

\textbf{Unified view.} Classical and neural language models differ in
how they represent the context \(C\) and parameterize
\(p_\theta(\cdot\mid C)\), but they share the same probabilistic target:
estimate a conditional distribution over the next token.

\section{From counts to conditional
probabilities}\label{from-counts-to-conditional-probabilities}

A simple conditional model estimates probabilities from co-occurrence
counts. Let \(a\) be a previous token and \(b\) be a next token. Define

\[
c(a,b)=\#\{t: w_{t-1}=a,\ w_t=b\}
\]

and

\[
c(a)=\sum_{b\in V} c(a,b).
\]

The empirical conditional probability is

\[
\widehat P(W_t=b\mid W_{t-1}=a)
=
\frac{c(a,b)}{c(a)}.
\]

This is the bigram maximum likelihood estimator. Chapter 5 develops this
idea systematically.

\subsection{Python example: conditional next-token
probabilities}\label{python-example-conditional-next-token-probabilities}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ defaultdict, Counter}

\NormalTok{sentences }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"language models learn from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language models predict tokens"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"models learn probability from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"data models learn patterns"}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{bigram\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ defaultdict(Counter)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ sentence }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ sentences:}
\NormalTok{    toks }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tokenize(sentence)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ a, b }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(toks[:}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], toks[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:]):}
\NormalTok{        bigram\_counts[a][b] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{previous\_token }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"models"}
\NormalTok{total\_after\_previous }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(bigram\_counts[previous\_token].values())}
\NormalTok{conditional\_probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
\NormalTok{    token: count }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ total\_after\_previous}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ bigram\_counts[previous\_token].items()}
\NormalTok{\}}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Next{-}token distribution after \textquotesingle{}}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{previous\_token}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{\textquotesingle{}:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(conditional\_probs.items()):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"P(}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{token}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{previous\_token}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{) = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Next-token distribution after 'models':
P(learn | models) = 0.750
P(predict | models) = 0.250
\end{verbatim}

This model uses only the previous token as context. It is simple enough
to inspect by hand, but it already illustrates the central
conditional-probability structure of language modeling.

\section{Zero probabilities and
smoothing}\label{zero-probabilities-and-smoothing}

A serious problem occurs when a token sequence has not appeared in the
training corpus. If \(c(a,b)=0\), then the maximum likelihood bigram
estimate gives

\[
\widehat P(b\mid a)=0.
\]

This means the model says the event is impossible. But in language,
unseen does not mean impossible. A small training corpus cannot contain
every valid phrase.

A common remedy is smoothing. For example, add-alpha smoothing estimates

\[
\widehat P_\alpha(b\mid a)
=
\frac{c(a,b)+\alpha}{c(a)+\alpha d},
\]

where \(\alpha>0\) and \(d=|V|\).

When \(\alpha=1\), this is called add-one smoothing or Laplace
smoothing.

\textbf{Smoothing principle.} Smoothing moves probability mass away from
observed events and assigns some mass to unseen events. It is a
statistical correction for finite data.

Chapter 5 studies smoothing in more detail for n-gram language models.

\section{Generative and discriminative probabilistic
models}\label{generative-and-discriminative-probabilistic-models}

Many NLP tasks involve a label \(Y\) and an input text \(X\). For
example:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(X\) is a movie review and \(Y\) is its sentiment label;
\item
  \(X\) is an email and \(Y\) indicates spam or not spam;
\item
  \(X\) is a student question and \(Y\) is the correct resource
  category.
\end{itemize}

There are two common probabilistic viewpoints.

\subsection{Generative modeling}\label{generative-modeling}

A generative model describes the joint distribution

\[
P(X,Y).
\]

Using the product rule,

\[
P(X,Y)=P(Y)P(X\mid Y).
\]

For classification, Bayes' rule gives

\[
P(Y\mid X)=\frac{P(X\mid Y)P(Y)}{P(X)}.
\]

Naive Bayes, developed in Chapter 6, is a generative text classifier. It
models how each class generates words.

\subsection{Discriminative modeling}\label{discriminative-modeling}

A discriminative model directly estimates

\[
P(Y\mid X).
\]

Logistic regression, neural classifiers, and transformer classifiers are
usually discriminative models. They do not need to model the probability
of the text itself; they only model the label distribution given the
text.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Type
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Models
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Main object
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Generative & Naive Bayes, language models & \(P(X,Y)\) or \(P(X)\) \\
Discriminative & Logistic regression, neural classifiers &
\(P(Y\mid X)\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

Both viewpoints are useful. Generative models are often interpretable
and useful with limited data. Discriminative models are often more
accurate when sufficient labeled data are available.

\section{Bayesian updating for text
classification}\label{bayesian-updating-for-text-classification}

Bayes' rule is central to probabilistic NLP classification. Suppose
\(Y\in\{0,1\}\) is a class label and \(X\) is a text. Then

\[
P(Y=1\mid X)
=
\frac{P(X\mid Y=1)P(Y=1)}{P(X)}.
\]

Since

\[
P(X)=P(X\mid Y=0)P(Y=0)+P(X\mid Y=1)P(Y=1),
\]

we can compute the posterior probability of the class once we have class
priors and class-conditional text probabilities.

This equation is the mathematical foundation of Naive Bayes classifiers.
Its practical success depends on how we model \(P(X\mid Y)\).

\section{Worked example: a tiny probabilistic
classifier}\label{worked-example-a-tiny-probabilistic-classifier}

Suppose we classify short texts into two labels:

\[
Y\in\{\text{positive},\text{negative}\}.
\]

Assume equal class priors:

\[
P(Y=\text{positive})=P(Y=\text{negative})=\frac12.
\]

Let the text be represented by tokens. A simple generative model
estimates class-conditional token probabilities. Suppose

\[
P(\text{good}\mid \text{positive})=0.30,
\qquad
P(\text{good}\mid \text{negative})=0.05,
\]

and

\[
P(\text{clear}\mid \text{positive})=0.20,
\qquad
P(\text{clear}\mid \text{negative})=0.10.
\]

For the two-token document

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{good clear}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and under the naive conditional independence approximation,

\[
P(X\mid Y=\text{positive})
=0.30\cdot 0.20=0.060,
\]

while

\[
P(X\mid Y=\text{negative})
=0.05\cdot 0.10=0.005.
\]

Multiplying by equal priors gives scores

\[
0.5\cdot 0.060=0.030,
\qquad
0.5\cdot 0.005=0.0025.
\]

The posterior probability of the positive class is

\[
\frac{0.030}{0.030+0.0025}\approx 0.923.
\]

Therefore the model predicts positive sentiment.

\subsection{Python example: tiny Bayesian
classifier}\label{python-example-tiny-bayesian-classifier}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{priors }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"positive"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"negative"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{class\_token\_probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"positive"}\NormalTok{: \{}\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"clear"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{\},}
    \StringTok{"negative"}\NormalTok{: \{}\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"clear"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{\}}

\NormalTok{document }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"clear"}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{unnormalized }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{\}}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ label }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ priors:}
\NormalTok{    score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ priors[label]}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ document:}
\NormalTok{        score }\OperatorTok{*=}\NormalTok{ class\_token\_probs[label][token]}
\NormalTok{    unnormalized[label] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ score}

\NormalTok{normalizing\_constant }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(unnormalized.values())}
\NormalTok{posterior }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
\NormalTok{    label: score }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ normalizing\_constant}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ label, score }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ unnormalized.items()}
\NormalTok{\}}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Unnormalized scores:"}\NormalTok{, unnormalized)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Posterior probabilities:"}\NormalTok{, posterior)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Prediction:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(posterior, key}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{posterior.get))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Unnormalized scores: {'positive': 0.03, 'negative': 0.0025000000000000005}
Posterior probabilities: {'positive': 0.923076923076923, 'negative': 0.07692307692307694}
Prediction: positive
\end{verbatim}

This small calculation previews Chapter 6. The important point here is
not the particular classifier, but the probabilistic structure: prior,
likelihood, posterior, and normalization.

\section{Log probabilities and numerical
stability}\label{log-probabilities-and-numerical-stability}

Products of many probabilities become extremely small. For a sentence of
length \(T\), the probability

\[
\prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1})
\]

may underflow on a computer. Therefore NLP systems usually work with log
probabilities:

\[
\log \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1})
=
\sum_{t=1}^T \log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1}).
\]

Log probabilities turn products into sums, making computation more
stable and easier to optimize.

\subsection{Python example: product versus log
probability}\label{python-example-product-versus-log-probability}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{100}

\NormalTok{product\_prob }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1.0}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ p }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ probs:}
\NormalTok{    product\_prob }\OperatorTok{*=}\NormalTok{ p}

\NormalTok{log\_prob }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(math.log(p) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ p }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ probs)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Product probability:"}\NormalTok{, product\_prob)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Log probability:"}\NormalTok{, log\_prob)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Product probability: 1.2676506002282316e-170
Log probability: -391.20230054281404
\end{verbatim}

For long sequences, the raw probability may be too small to interpret
directly. The log probability remains manageable.

\section{Statistical assumptions in probabilistic
NLP}\label{statistical-assumptions-in-probabilistic-nlp}

A mathematical NLP model is built from assumptions. Some assumptions are
explicit; others are hidden in the architecture or training data.

Important assumptions include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Sampling assumption.} The training corpus is representative of
  the target distribution.
\item
  \textbf{Tokenization assumption.} The chosen tokens preserve the
  relevant information.
\item
  \textbf{Context assumption.} The model uses enough context to predict
  the target.
\item
  \textbf{Stationarity assumption.} The relationship between context and
  token does not change too much between training and deployment.
\item
  \textbf{Loss assumption.} Cross-entropy is an appropriate objective
  for the downstream goal.
\item
  \textbf{Evaluation assumption.} Test data represent the kinds of
  examples where the model will be used.
\end{enumerate}

These assumptions are not merely philosophical. When they fail, a model
may have low training loss but poor real-world behavior.

\section{AI component: using AI to audit probabilistic
assumptions}\label{ai-component-using-ai-to-audit-probabilistic-assumptions}

AI tools can help test understanding, generate examples, and critique
assumptions. However, AI explanations should be checked mathematically.

\subsection{Prompt 1: Explain the model
object}\label{prompt-1-explain-the-model-object}

Ask an AI assistant:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{In mathematical terms, explain why a next{-}token language model estimates a conditional probability distribution. Use the notation p\_theta(w\_t | w\_1, ..., w\_\{t{-}1\}). Then give one example where the model may be uncertain.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Check the answer for the following:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Does it distinguish probability distribution from a single prediction?
\item
  Does it correctly state that probabilities over the vocabulary sum to
  one?
\item
  Does it confuse the model distribution with the true data
  distribution?
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Prompt 2: Derive the unigram
MLE}\label{prompt-2-derive-the-unigram-mle}

Ask:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Derive the maximum likelihood estimator for a unigram language model over a finite vocabulary. Use a Lagrange multiplier and show why the answer is c\_j / N.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Then verify each step:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Is the likelihood written as \(\prod_j p_j^{c_j}\)?
\item
  Is the constraint \(\sum_j p_j=1\) included?
\item
  Is the solution normalized correctly?
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Prompt 3: Critique
perplexity}\label{prompt-3-critique-perplexity}

Ask:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Give three reasons why a lower perplexity language model may not always be better for a real NLP application.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A good answer should mention domain shift, factuality, alignment with
task goals, robustness, or evaluation mismatch.

\textbf{AI study rule.} Use AI to generate explanations and
counterexamples, but always reduce probabilistic claims to definitions:
sample space, random variables, distributions, conditioning, likelihood,
and loss.

\section{Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes}

\subsection{Mistake 1: Treating the most likely token as the whole
model}\label{mistake-1-treating-the-most-likely-token-as-the-whole-model}

A language model returns a full probability distribution. The argmax
token is only one summary of that distribution.

\subsection{Mistake 2: Confusing frequency with
probability}\label{mistake-2-confusing-frequency-with-probability}

Empirical frequency estimates probability from data, but it is not the
same as the unknown population probability.

\subsection{Mistake 3: Ignoring the role of the
context}\label{mistake-3-ignoring-the-role-of-the-context}

The probability of a token depends on context. For example,
\(P(\text{bank})\) and \(P(\text{bank}\mid \text{river})\) represent
different quantities.

\subsection{Mistake 4: Comparing raw likelihoods across corpora of
different
lengths}\label{mistake-4-comparing-raw-likelihoods-across-corpora-of-different-lengths}

Longer corpora usually have smaller raw likelihoods. Use average
log-likelihood, cross-entropy, or perplexity to compare across datasets.

\subsection{Mistake 5: Assuming low perplexity implies high-quality
generation}\label{mistake-5-assuming-low-perplexity-implies-high-quality-generation}

Perplexity measures next-token prediction on a distribution. It does not
directly measure truthfulness, reasoning, safety, or usefulness.

\section{Chapter summary}\label{chapter-summary-2}

This chapter introduced the probabilistic foundation of NLP.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A token is modeled as a random variable taking values in a finite
  vocabulary.
\item
  A sentence is a sequence of random variables.
\item
  A language model assigns probabilities to token sequences or
  conditional probabilities to next tokens.
\item
  Empirical frequencies estimate probability distributions from corpora.
\item
  The unigram maximum likelihood estimator is the empirical token
  distribution.
\item
  The chain rule factors a sentence probability into conditional
  next-token probabilities.
\item
  Cross-entropy and negative log-likelihood are the central training
  losses for language models.
\item
  Entropy measures uncertainty; perplexity exponentiates average
  negative log-likelihood.
\item
  Generative models estimate \(P(X,Y)\) or \(P(X)\); discriminative
  models estimate \(P(Y\mid X)\).
\item
  Probabilistic models are useful only when their assumptions match the
  intended data and task.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Exercises}\label{exercises-3}

\subsection{Conceptual exercises}\label{conceptual-exercises-2}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Let \(V=\{a,b,c\}\) and \(p=(0.2,0.5,0.3)\). Verify that
  \(p\in \Delta^2\) and compute \(H(p)\).
\item
  Explain the difference between \(p^*\), \(\widehat p\), and
  \(p_\theta\) in your own words.
\item
  Give an example of a context \(C\) where the next-token distribution
  should have high entropy. Give another where it should have low
  entropy.
\item
  Why is the chain rule factorization of \(P(w_{1:T})\) exact, while an
  n-gram approximation is not exact?
\item
  Explain why raw likelihood is difficult to compare across test sets of
  different lengths.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Mathematical exercises}\label{mathematical-exercises-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item
  Let a corpus over \(V=\{v_1,v_2,v_3\}\) have counts \((10,5,5)\).
  Compute the unigram MLE.
\item
  For the distribution \(p=(1/2,1/4,1/4)\), compute entropy using
  natural logarithms.
\item
  Let \(p=(0.5,0.5)\) and \(q=(0.9,0.1)\). Compute \(H(p,q)\) and
  \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\).
\item
  Suppose a model assigns probabilities \(0.5\), \(0.25\), and \(0.1\)
  to three observed next tokens. Compute the total negative
  log-likelihood, average negative log-likelihood, and perplexity.
\item
  Derive the MLE for a Bernoulli token model with vocabulary
  \(V=\{0,1\}\) and show that it equals the sample proportion.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Python exercises}\label{python-exercises}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\item
  Write a Python function that takes a list of tokens and returns the
  empirical probability distribution.
\item
  Write a Python function that computes entropy for any probability
  vector.
\item
  Write a Python function that computes cross-entropy between an
  empirical distribution and a model distribution.
\item
  Build a bigram count table from a small corpus and compute
  \(\widehat P(b\mid a)\) for several choices of \(a\).
\item
  Modify the bigram probability code to use add-alpha smoothing. Compare
  \(\alpha=0\), \(\alpha=0.1\), and \(\alpha=1\).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Mini-project: probabilistic language
audit}\label{mini-project-probabilistic-language-audit}

Choose a small corpus of 20 to 50 short documents, such as course
descriptions, news headlines, or abstract titles. Build a probability
audit with the following parts:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  tokenize the corpus and construct the vocabulary;
\item
  compute empirical unigram probabilities;
\item
  compute entropy of the unigram distribution;
\item
  build a bigram table and inspect next-token distributions after five
  selected tokens;
\item
  compute smoothed and unsmoothed probabilities for unseen bigrams;
\item
  write a short interpretation of what the probability model captures
  and what it misses.
\end{enumerate}

The final report should include at least one table of probabilities, one
plot, and one paragraph explaining the assumptions behind the model.
