\chapter{N-Gram Language Models}\label{n-gram-language-models}

Markov assumptions, conditional probability tables, smoothing,
generation, and perplexity

\hfill\break

An \(n\)-gram language model is one of the simplest mathematical models
of language. It predicts the next token using only the previous \(n-1\)
tokens. Although modern transformer language models are much more
powerful, \(n\)-gram models remain an essential starting point because
their assumptions, estimators, failures, and evaluation metrics can be
written down exactly. In this chapter we study \(n\)-gram models as
finite-state conditional probability models estimated from counts.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-4}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  define unigrams, bigrams, trigrams, and general \(n\)-grams;
\item
  explain the Markov approximation behind an \(n\)-gram language model;
\item
  estimate \(n\)-gram probabilities by maximum likelihood from corpus
  counts;
\item
  represent an \(n\)-gram model as a conditional probability table over
  contexts;
\item
  explain why zero counts create zero probabilities for unseen
  sentences;
\item
  derive and implement add-\(\alpha\) smoothing;
\item
  compute sentence log-probability, average negative log-likelihood,
  cross-entropy, and perplexity;
\item
  sample text from a fitted \(n\)-gram model;
\item
  compare unigram, bigram, and trigram models mathematically and
  computationally;
\item
  use AI tools to critique a language model's assumptions without
  outsourcing the reasoning.
\end{enumerate}

\section{\texorpdfstring{Why study \(n\)-gram
models?}{Why study n-gram models?}}\label{why-study-n-gram-models}

An \(n\)-gram model is not a modern state-of-the-art NLP model. However,
it is mathematically transparent. Nearly every important idea in
language modeling appears in a simple form:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  language as a probability distribution on token sequences;
\item
  conditioning on previous context;
\item
  maximum likelihood estimation;
\item
  sparse data and overfitting;
\item
  smoothing and regularization;
\item
  evaluation by cross-entropy and perplexity;
\item
  generation by sequential sampling.
\end{itemize}

Modern neural language models replace explicit count tables with
high-dimensional nonlinear functions, but they still model conditional
probabilities of the form

\[
p_\theta(w_t \mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}).
\]

The \(n\)-gram model is the finite-table version of the same idea.

\textbf{Central idea.} An \(n\)-gram model approximates

\[
P(W_t=w_t \mid W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_{t-1}=w_{t-1})
\]

by conditioning only on the most recent \(n-1\) tokens:

\[
P(W_t=w_t \mid W_{t-n+1}=w_{t-n+1},\ldots,W_{t-1}=w_{t-1}).
\]

This is a mathematical simplification: the entire past is compressed
into a short context.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Tokens, contexts, and
\(n\)-grams}{Tokens, contexts, and n-grams}}\label{tokens-contexts-and-n-grams}

Let

\[
V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_d\}
\]

be a finite vocabulary. A token sequence is

\[
w_{1:T}=(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T), \qquad w_t\in V.
\]

An \(n\)-gram is a consecutive block of \(n\) tokens:

\[
(w_t,w_{t+1},\ldots,w_{t+n-1}).
\]

Common cases are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Model
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Unit
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Example from \texttt{language\ models\ learn\ probability}
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
unigram & one token & \texttt{language}, \texttt{models},
\texttt{learn}, \texttt{probability} \\
bigram & two tokens & \texttt{language\ models}, \texttt{models\ learn},
\texttt{learn\ probability} \\
trigram & three tokens & \texttt{language\ models\ learn},
\texttt{models\ learn\ probability} \\
\end{longtable}
}

For prediction, it is useful to split an \(n\)-gram into a context and a
next token. For an \(n\)-gram model, the context length is \(n-1\):

\[
h_t=(w_{t-n+1},\ldots,w_{t-1}), \qquad \text{next token } w_t.
\]

The model estimates

\[
p(w_t\mid h_t).
\]

For a bigram model, the context is one token. For a trigram model, the
context is two tokens.

\section{The chain rule and the Markov
approximation}\label{the-chain-rule-and-the-markov-approximation}

From Chapter 4, the chain rule gives the exact factorization

\[
P(W_{1:T}=w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(W_t=w_t\mid W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_{t-1}=w_{t-1}).
\]

This formula is exact but not directly useful for estimation when \(T\)
is large. The number of possible histories grows explosively. The
\(n\)-gram approximation assumes that the conditional distribution
depends only on the most recent \(n-1\) tokens:

\[
P(W_t=w_t\mid W_1=w_1,\ldots,W_{t-1}=w_{t-1})
\approx
P(W_t=w_t\mid W_{t-n+1}=w_{t-n+1},\ldots,W_{t-1}=w_{t-1}).
\]

Therefore,

\[
P(w_{1:T})
\approx
\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(w_t\mid w_{t-n+1:t-1}).
\]

Here \(w_{a:b}\) denotes the subsequence \((w_a,w_{a+1},\ldots,w_b)\).

\textbf{Markov viewpoint.} A bigram model is a first-order Markov chain
on the vocabulary:

\[
P(W_t=w_t\mid W_1,\ldots,W_{t-1})
\approx
P(W_t=w_t\mid W_{t-1}).
\]

A trigram model is a second-order Markov model because it conditions on
the previous two tokens.

This does not mean language truly has such short memory. It means we
choose a tractable approximation.

\section{Boundary tokens}\label{boundary-tokens}

A practical language model needs to represent the beginning and end of a
sentence. We usually add special tokens such as

\[
\langle s\rangle, \qquad \langle/ s\rangle.
\]

For a bigram model, the sentence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models learn}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is transformed into

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\textless{}s\textgreater{} language models learn \textless{}/s\textgreater{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and contributes the bigrams

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(\textless{}s\textgreater{}, language), (language, models), (models, learn), (learn, \textless{}/s\textgreater{})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

For a trigram model, we often add two start tokens:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\textless{}s\textgreater{} \textless{}s\textgreater{} language models learn \textless{}/s\textgreater{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

so that the first real word can be predicted from a two-token context.

Mathematically, boundary tokens allow every position to have a context
of the required length.

\section{Maximum likelihood estimation for
bigrams}\label{maximum-likelihood-estimation-for-bigrams}

Let \(C(u,v)\) denote the number of times token \(u\) is followed by
token \(v\) in the training corpus. Let

\[
C(u)=\sum_{v\in V} C(u,v)
\]

be the number of times \(u\) appears as a context token. The maximum
likelihood estimator for a bigram model is

\[
\widehat p(v\mid u)=\frac{C(u,v)}{C(u)}.
\]

This is simply a row-normalized count table.

\subsection{Derivation}\label{derivation}

For a fixed context \(u\), suppose we observe counts

\[
C(u,v_1),C(u,v_2),\ldots,C(u,v_d).
\]

We want to estimate a conditional probability vector

\[
p(\cdot\mid u)=(p(v_1\mid u),\ldots,p(v_d\mid u))\in \Delta^{d-1}.
\]

The conditional likelihood for this row is

\[
L_u(p)=\prod_{j=1}^{d} p(v_j\mid u)^{C(u,v_j)}.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_u(p)=\sum_{j=1}^{d} C(u,v_j)\log p(v_j\mid u).
\]

We maximize \(\ell_u(p)\) subject to

\[
\sum_{j=1}^{d}p(v_j\mid u)=1.
\]

Using a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\),

\[
\mathcal{L}(p,\lambda)
=
\sum_{j=1}^{d}C(u,v_j)\log p(v_j\mid u)
+
\lambda\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d}p(v_j\mid u)-1\right).
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(p(v_j\mid u)\) gives

\[
\frac{C(u,v_j)}{p(v_j\mid u)}+\lambda=0.
\]

Thus

\[
p(v_j\mid u)=-\frac{C(u,v_j)}{\lambda}.
\]

Summing over \(j\) and using the constraint gives

\[
1=\sum_{j=1}^{d}p(v_j\mid u)
=-\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{j=1}^{d}C(u,v_j)
=-\frac{C(u)}{\lambda}.
\]

So \(\lambda=-C(u)\) and therefore

\[
\widehat p(v_j\mid u)=\frac{C(u,v_j)}{C(u)}.
\]

This derivation is important because it shows that the count ratio is
not merely intuitive. It is the maximum likelihood estimate under a
multinomial model.

\section{\texorpdfstring{General \(n\)-gram maximum likelihood
estimator}{General n-gram maximum likelihood estimator}}\label{general-n-gram-maximum-likelihood-estimator}

Let \(h\) be a context of length \(n-1\). For example, in a trigram
model,

\[
h=(u_1,u_2).
\]

Let \(C(h,v)\) be the number of times context \(h\) is followed by token
\(v\), and let

\[
C(h)=\sum_{v\in V}C(h,v).
\]

The maximum likelihood estimator is

\[
\widehat p(v\mid h)=\frac{C(h,v)}{C(h)}.
\]

The same Lagrange multiplier argument applies independently to each
context row.

\textbf{Conditional probability table.} An \(n\)-gram model is a
collection of probability vectors

\[
\{p(\cdot\mid h): h\in V^{n-1}\}.
\]

Each row belongs to the probability simplex \(\Delta^{d-1}\).

For bigrams, this table is a \(d\times d\) matrix. For trigrams, it is a
\(d^2\times d\) table. For general \(n\), the number of possible
contexts is \(d^{n-1}\), which grows quickly.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Python example: building an \(n\)-gram model
from
scratch}{Python example: building an n-gram model from scratch}}\label{python-example-building-an-n-gram-model-from-scratch}

The following code builds an \(n\)-gram count model, estimates
probabilities, and displays the next-token distribution for a chosen
context.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter, defaultdict}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ math}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ random}

\NormalTok{corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"language models learn from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language models predict tokens"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"statistical models learn probability"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"neural models learn representations"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"data science uses probability models"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"models predict language tokens"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(sentence):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ sentence.lower().split()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ add\_boundaries(tokens, n):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"\textless{}s\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (n }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ tokens }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"\textless{}/s\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ fit\_ngram(corpus, n}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    context\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter()}
\NormalTok{    next\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ defaultdict(Counter)}
\NormalTok{    vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{([}\StringTok{"\textless{}s\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"\textless{}/s\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{])}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ sentence }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ corpus:}
\NormalTok{        tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ add\_boundaries(tokenize(sentence), n)}
\NormalTok{        vocab.update(tokens)}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tokens)):}
\NormalTok{            context }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{tuple}\NormalTok{(tokens[i }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ n }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:i])}
\NormalTok{            word }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tokens[i]}
\NormalTok{            context\_counts[context] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{            next\_counts[context][word] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{    vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts}

\NormalTok{vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ fit\_ngram(corpus, n}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{context }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{,)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Vocabulary:"}\NormalTok{, vocab)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Context count:"}\NormalTok{, context\_counts[context])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Next{-}token counts after \textquotesingle{}models\textquotesingle{}:"}\NormalTok{, next\_counts[context])}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{MLE next{-}token probabilities:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ next\_counts[context].most\_common():}
\NormalTok{    prob }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ count }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ context\_counts[context]}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"P(}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{word}\SpecialCharTok{:16s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | models) = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Vocabulary: ['</s>', '<s>', 'data', 'from', 'language', 'learn', 'models', 'neural', 'predict', 'probability', 'representations', 'science', 'statistical', 'tokens', 'uses']
Context count: 6
Next-token counts after 'models': Counter({'learn': 3, 'predict': 2, '</s>': 1})

MLE next-token probabilities:
P(learn            | models) = 0.500
P(predict          | models) = 0.333
P(</s>             | models) = 0.167
\end{verbatim}

The model has learned, from this tiny corpus, which words tend to follow
\texttt{models}.

\section{The zero-probability
problem}\label{the-zero-probability-problem}

Maximum likelihood \(n\)-gram models assign probability zero to any
next-token event not observed in the training corpus:

\[
C(h,v)=0
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\widehat p(v\mid h)=0.
\]

This is a serious issue. If a single bigram in a test sentence has
probability zero, then the entire sentence probability becomes zero:

\[
\prod_{t=1}^{T}\widehat p(w_t\mid h_t)=0.
\]

The log-probability becomes undefined because \(\log 0=-\infty\).

\subsection{Example}\label{example-3}

Suppose the training corpus contains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models learn}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

but never contains

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models explain}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A bigram model may estimate

\[
\widehat p(\text{explain}\mid \text{models})=0,
\]

even though the phrase is perfectly reasonable. The zero probability
reflects limited data, not linguistic impossibility.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Add-\(\alpha\)
smoothing}{Add-\textbackslash alpha smoothing}}\label{add-alpha-smoothing}

A simple solution is add-\(\alpha\) smoothing. For \(\alpha>0\), define

\[
\widehat p_\alpha(v\mid h)
=
\frac{C(h,v)+\alpha}{C(h)+\alpha |V|}.
\]

The numerator adds \(\alpha\) pseudo-counts to every possible next
token. The denominator adds the total pseudo-count mass \(\alpha |V|\).

When \(\alpha=1\), this is called add-one or Laplace smoothing. Smaller
values such as \(\alpha=0.1\) often behave better in language modeling
because the vocabulary may be large.

\textbf{Smoothing as regularization.} Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing moves
each empirical row toward the uniform distribution:

\[
\widehat p_\alpha(\cdot\mid h)
=
\frac{C(h)}{C(h)+\alpha |V|}\widehat p_{\text{MLE}}(\cdot\mid h)
+
\frac{\alpha |V|}{C(h)+\alpha |V|}\,u,
\]

where \(u(v)=1/|V|\).

This formula shows that smoothing is a convex combination of the
empirical MLE distribution and the uniform distribution.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Python example: add-\(\alpha\)
probabilities}{Python example: add-\textbackslash alpha probabilities}}\label{python-example-add-alpha-probabilities}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ next\_token\_distribution(context, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{    total }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ context\_counts[context]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ \{}
\NormalTok{        word: (next\_counts[context][word] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (total }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d)}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ vocab}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ word }\OperatorTok{!=} \StringTok{"\textless{}s\textgreater{}"}
\NormalTok{    \}}

\NormalTok{context }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{,)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ alpha }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\SpecialStringTok{alpha = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{alpha}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{==} \FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{:}
        \CommentTok{\# MLE: show only observed words to avoid many zeros}
\NormalTok{        dist }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
\NormalTok{            word: next\_counts[context][word] }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ context\_counts[context]}
            \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ vocab}
            \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ context\_counts[context] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \KeywordTok{and}\NormalTok{ next\_counts[context][word] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}
\NormalTok{        \}}
    \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        dist }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ next\_token\_distribution(context, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(dist.items(), key}\OperatorTok{=}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])[:}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{]:}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"P(}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{word}\SpecialCharTok{:16s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | models) = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}

alpha = 0.0
P(learn            | models) = 0.500
P(predict          | models) = 0.333
P(</s>             | models) = 0.167

alpha = 0.1
P(learn            | models) = 0.413
P(predict          | models) = 0.280
P(</s>             | models) = 0.147
P(data             | models) = 0.013
P(from             | models) = 0.013
P(language         | models) = 0.013
P(models           | models) = 0.013
P(neural           | models) = 0.013

alpha = 1.0
P(learn            | models) = 0.190
P(predict          | models) = 0.143
P(</s>             | models) = 0.095
P(data             | models) = 0.048
P(from             | models) = 0.048
P(language         | models) = 0.048
P(models           | models) = 0.048
P(neural           | models) = 0.048
\end{verbatim}

As \(\alpha\) increases, probability mass spreads more evenly across the
vocabulary.

\section{Sentence probability and
log-probability}\label{sentence-probability-and-log-probability}

Let \(w_{1:T}\) be a sentence after adding boundary tokens. Under an
\(n\)-gram model,

\[
p(w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=n}^{T}p(w_t\mid w_{t-n+1:t-1}).
\]

In computation, we usually work with log-probabilities:

\[
\log p(w_{1:T})
=
\sum_{t=n}^{T}\log p(w_t\mid w_{t-n+1:t-1}).
\]

This is numerically more stable because products of many small
probabilities can underflow to zero.

\subsection{Python example: sentence
log-probability}\label{python-example-sentence-log-probability}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sentence\_logprob(sentence, n, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ add\_boundaries(tokenize(sentence), n)}
\NormalTok{    d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{    logp }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{    details }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tokens)):}
\NormalTok{        context }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{tuple}\NormalTok{(tokens[i }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ n }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:i])}
\NormalTok{        word }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tokens[i]}
\NormalTok{        count\_context }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ context\_counts[context]}
\NormalTok{        count\_pair }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ next\_counts[context][word]}
\NormalTok{        prob }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (count\_pair }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (count\_context }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d)}
\NormalTok{        logp }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ math.log(prob)}
\NormalTok{        details.append((context, word, prob))}

    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ logp, details}

\NormalTok{sentence }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"language models learn probability"}
\NormalTok{logp, details }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sentence\_logprob(sentence, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Sentence:"}\NormalTok{, sentence)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Log{-}probability:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(logp, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Probability:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(math.exp(logp), }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Factors:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ context, word, prob }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ details:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"P(}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{word}\SpecialCharTok{:16s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{context}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{) = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Sentence: language models learn probability
Log-probability: -8.2631
Probability: 0.00025785

Factors:
P(language         | ('<s>',)) = 0.1852
P(models           | ('language',)) = 0.2381
P(learn            | ('models',)) = 0.2593
P(probability      | ('learn',)) = 0.1429
P(</s>             | ('probability',)) = 0.1579
\end{verbatim}

The sentence probability is a product of local next-token probabilities.

\section{Cross-entropy and
perplexity}\label{cross-entropy-and-perplexity}

Let a test corpus contain \(N\) predicted tokens. Suppose the model
assigns probability \(p_i\) to the correct token at position \(i\). The
average negative log-likelihood is

\[
\operatorname{NLL}_{\text{avg}}
=
-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_i.
\]

When natural logarithms are used, this quantity is measured in nats per
token. The perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{Perplexity}
=
\exp\left(\operatorname{NLL}_{\text{avg}}\right).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\operatorname{Perplexity}
=
\left(\prod_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{p_i}\right)^{1/N}.
\]

So perplexity is the geometric mean of the inverse probabilities
assigned to the correct next tokens.

\textbf{Interpretation.} Lower perplexity is better. A perplexity of
\(10\) roughly means that, on average, the model is as uncertain as
choosing uniformly among \(10\) plausible next tokens.

This interpretation is approximate, but it is useful for intuition.

\subsection{Python example: evaluating
perplexity}\label{python-example-evaluating-perplexity}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ evaluate\_perplexity(test\_corpus, n, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    total\_logp }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{    total\_tokens }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ sentence }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ test\_corpus:}
\NormalTok{        tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ add\_boundaries(tokenize(sentence), n)}
\NormalTok{        d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tokens)):}
\NormalTok{            context }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{tuple}\NormalTok{(tokens[i }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ n }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:i])}
\NormalTok{            word }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tokens[i]}
\NormalTok{            prob }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (next\_counts[context][word] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (context\_counts[context] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d)}
\NormalTok{            total\_logp }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ math.log(prob)}
\NormalTok{            total\_tokens }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{    avg\_nll }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{total\_logp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ total\_tokens}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ math.exp(avg\_nll), avg\_nll}

\NormalTok{test\_corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"language models predict probability"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"neural models learn language"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ alpha }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    ppl, avg\_nll }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ evaluate\_perplexity(test\_corpus, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"alpha=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{alpha}\SpecialCharTok{:3.1f\}}\SpecialStringTok{  avg NLL=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{avg\_nll}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{  perplexity=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{ppl}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
alpha=0.1  avg NLL=1.926  perplexity=6.861
alpha=0.5  avg NLL=2.097  perplexity=8.141
alpha=1.0  avg NLL=2.253  perplexity=9.513
\end{verbatim}

Perplexity depends on the test set, the vocabulary, the tokenization
scheme, the order \(n\), and the smoothing method. Comparing
perplexities is meaningful only when these conditions are comparable.

\section{Interactive HTML: smoothing and next-token
uncertainty}\label{interactive-html-smoothing-and-next-token-uncertainty}

The interactive below uses a small bigram corpus. Move the smoothing
slider to see how add-\(\alpha\) smoothing changes the conditional
distribution after the context word \texttt{models}. The bar chart shows
the next-token probabilities. The table also reports the entropy of the
distribution.

The key mathematical pattern is shrinkage. When \(\alpha\) is small, the
distribution is close to the empirical count distribution. When
\(\alpha\) is large, the distribution moves toward uniform.

\section{\texorpdfstring{Sampling text from an \(n\)-gram
model}{Sampling text from an n-gram model}}\label{sampling-text-from-an-n-gram-model}

A fitted \(n\)-gram model is generative. Starting with boundary tokens,
repeatedly sample the next token from

\[
p(\cdot\mid h_t).
\]

Then update the context and continue until the end token appears.

\subsection{Python example: bigram
generation}\label{python-example-bigram-generation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sample\_next(distribution):}
\NormalTok{    words }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(distribution.keys())}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(distribution.values())}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ random.choices(words, weights}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{probs, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ generate\_ngram(n, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, max\_steps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{, seed}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    random.seed(seed)}
\NormalTok{    context }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{tuple}\NormalTok{([}\StringTok{"\textless{}s\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (n }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    generated }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(max\_steps):}
\NormalTok{        dist }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ next\_token\_distribution(context, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{alpha)}
\NormalTok{        word }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sample\_next(dist)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ word }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"\textless{}/s\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{break}
\NormalTok{        generated.append(word)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ n }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            context }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{tuple}\NormalTok{((}\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(context) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ [word])[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{(n }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):])}

    \ControlFlowTok{return} \StringTok{" "}\NormalTok{.join(generated)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ seed }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(generate\_ngram(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, vocab, context\_counts, next\_counts, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, seed}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{seed))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
statistical representations language models learn neural science models learn probability tokens language models predict representations data tokens uses science uses
data science uses learn probability models predict tokens
tokens tokens
language neural models predict representations
language from language language data learn tokens representations representations
\end{verbatim}

The generated text may be grammatical in small fragments, but it often
lacks long-range coherence. This is a mathematical consequence of the
short-context assumption.

\section{Comparing unigram, bigram, and trigram
models}\label{comparing-unigram-bigram-and-trigram-models}

A unigram model assumes tokens are independent:

\[
p(w_{1:T})\approx \prod_{t=1}^{T}p(w_t).
\]

A bigram model keeps one previous token:

\[
p(w_{1:T})\approx \prod_{t=1}^{T}p(w_t\mid w_{t-1}).
\]

A trigram model keeps two previous tokens:

\[
p(w_{1:T})\approx \prod_{t=1}^{T}p(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1}).
\]

As \(n\) increases, the model can represent richer local structure. But
the number of possible contexts grows as

\[
|V|^{n-1}.
\]

This creates a bias-variance tradeoff.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Model & Context length & Strength & Weakness \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
unigram & 0 & stable estimates & ignores order \\
bigram & 1 & captures local transitions & limited memory \\
trigram & 2 & captures short phrases & sparse counts \\
larger \(n\) & \(n-1\) & more context & severe sparsity \\
\end{longtable}
}

\textbf{Bias-variance viewpoint.} Small \(n\) gives high bias because
the model is too simple. Large \(n\) can give high variance because many
contexts have few or no observations. Smoothing partially controls
variance but cannot fully solve the curse of dimensionality.

\section{Backoff and interpolation}\label{backoff-and-interpolation}

Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing is simple but not always strong enough. Two
common ideas are backoff and interpolation.

\subsection{Backoff}\label{backoff}

If a trigram context is rare or unseen, use a lower-order model:

\[
p(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1})
\quad \longrightarrow \quad
p(w_t\mid w_{t-1})
\quad \longrightarrow \quad
p(w_t).
\]

The model backs off from specific context to more general context.

\subsection{Interpolation}\label{interpolation}

Interpolation combines several orders:

\[
p(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1})
=
\lambda_3 p_3(w_t\mid w_{t-2},w_{t-1})
+
\lambda_2 p_2(w_t\mid w_{t-1})
+
\lambda_1 p_1(w_t),
\]

where

\[
\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\geq 0,
\qquad
\lambda_1+\lambda_2+\lambda_3=1.
\]

This is a convex combination of probability distributions. It is
mathematically similar to ensemble methods and shrinkage estimators.

\section{Matrix viewpoint for bigram
models}\label{matrix-viewpoint-for-bigram-models}

For a vocabulary of size \(d\), a bigram model can be represented by a
transition matrix

\[
P\in R^{d\times d},
\]

where

\[
P_{ij}=P(W_t=v_j\mid W_{t-1}=v_i).
\]

Each row is a probability vector:

\[
P_{ij}\geq 0,
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^{d}P_{ij}=1.
\]

Thus \(P\) is a row-stochastic matrix. A distribution \(\pi_t\) over the
current token evolves by

\[
\pi_{t+1}=\pi_t P.
\]

This connects bigram language modeling to finite Markov chains.

\subsection{Python example: transition
matrix}\label{python-example-transition-matrix}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Build a smoothed bigram transition matrix over the full vocabulary.}
\CommentTok{\# Using the full vocabulary makes each row a probability vector.}
\NormalTok{selected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ vocab}
\NormalTok{index }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{word: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, word }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(selected)\}}
\NormalTok{alpha }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.2}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ u }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ selected:}
\NormalTok{    row }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{    context }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (u,)}
\NormalTok{    denom }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ context\_counts[context] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(selected)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ v }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ selected:}
\NormalTok{        row.append((next\_counts[context][v] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ denom)}
\NormalTok{    P.append(row)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Rows approximately sum to 1:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, row }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(selected, P))[:}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{]:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{word}\SpecialCharTok{:12s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ row sum = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(row)}\SpecialCharTok{:.6f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Transition probability P(models {-}\textgreater{} learn):"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(P[index[}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{]][index[}\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{]])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Rows approximately sum to 1:
</s>         row sum = 1.000000
<s>          row sum = 1.000000
data         row sum = 1.000000
from         row sum = 1.000000
language     row sum = 1.000000
learn        row sum = 1.000000
models       row sum = 1.000000
neural       row sum = 1.000000

Transition probability P(models -> learn):
0.35555555555555557
\end{verbatim}

The transition matrix view is useful because it exposes the connection
between NLP and stochastic processes.

\section{Worked hand calculation}\label{worked-hand-calculation}

Consider the corpus consisting of two sentences:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\textless{}s\textgreater{} a b \textless{}/s\textgreater{}}
\NormalTok{\textless{}s\textgreater{} a c \textless{}/s\textgreater{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The bigram counts after context \texttt{a} are

\[
C(a,b)=1,
\qquad
C(a,c)=1,
\qquad
C(a)=2.
\]

With no smoothing,

\[
\widehat p(b\mid a)=\frac{1}{2},
\qquad
\widehat p(c\mid a)=\frac{1}{2}.
\]

If the vocabulary is

\[
V=\{a,b,c,d,\langle/ s\rangle\},
\]

then \(|V|=5\). With add-\(\alpha\) smoothing and \(\alpha=1\),

\[
\widehat p_1(b\mid a)=\frac{1+1}{2+5}=\frac{2}{7},
\]

\[
\widehat p_1(c\mid a)=\frac{2}{7},
\]

and the unseen word \(d\) receives

\[
\widehat p_1(d\mid a)=\frac{0+1}{2+5}=\frac{1}{7}.
\]

This example shows both the benefit and cost of smoothing: unseen events
get nonzero probability, but observed events lose some probability mass.

\section{AI-assisted learning
component}\label{ai-assisted-learning-component-1}

AI systems can be helpful for studying \(n\)-gram models, but they
should be used as mathematical assistants rather than answer engines.

\subsection{Prompt 1: audit an
assumption}\label{prompt-1-audit-an-assumption}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I am studying n{-}gram language models. Explain the Markov assumption in a bigram model. Give one example where it works reasonably well and one example where it fails because of long{-}range dependence. Do not use code.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

After reading the response, check whether the explanation distinguishes
clearly between an exact identity and an approximation.

\subsection{Prompt 2: verify a
derivation}\label{prompt-2-verify-a-derivation}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Derive the maximum likelihood estimator for P(v | h) in an n{-}gram model using a Lagrange multiplier. Use counts C(h,v). Then explain why the estimator is undefined when C(h)=0.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

You should verify that the final answer is

\[
\widehat p(v\mid h)=\frac{C(h,v)}{C(h)}.
\]

\subsection{Prompt 3: critique
smoothing}\label{prompt-3-critique-smoothing}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{In an n{-}gram model, add{-}alpha smoothing gives P\_alpha(v | h) = (C(h,v)+alpha)/(C(h)+alpha |V|). Explain this formula as shrinkage toward the uniform distribution. What problem does it solve, and what new problem can it introduce?}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A strong answer should mention zero probabilities, probability mass
redistribution, and the fact that large vocabularies can make add-one
smoothing too strong.

\subsection{Prompt 4: connect to modern language
models}\label{prompt-4-connect-to-modern-language-models}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Compare an n{-}gram language model and a transformer language model from a mathematical point of view. Focus on how each estimates P(w\_t | context), how the context is represented, and why transformers can use longer{-}range dependencies.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This helps students see why Chapter 5 belongs in a modern NLP book
rather than only in a historical survey.

\section{Mathematical summary}\label{mathematical-summary-1}

The main formulas of this chapter are:

\[
P(w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T}P(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1})
\]

for the exact chain rule,

\[
P(w_t\mid w_{1:t-1})
\approx
P(w_t\mid w_{t-n+1:t-1})
\]

for the \(n\)-gram Markov approximation,

\[
\widehat p(v\mid h)=\frac{C(h,v)}{C(h)}
\]

for maximum likelihood estimation,

\[
\widehat p_\alpha(v\mid h)=\frac{C(h,v)+\alpha}{C(h)+\alpha |V|}
\]

for add-\(\alpha\) smoothing, and

\[
\operatorname{Perplexity}
=
\exp\left(-\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\log p_i\right)
\]

for evaluation.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain in your own words why the exact chain rule is not enough to
  build a practical language model.
\item
  What is the difference between a bigram model and a trigram model?
\item
  Why does increasing \(n\) reduce bias but increase variance?
\item
  Why can an unseen bigram force an entire sentence to have probability
  zero?
\item
  Explain add-\(\alpha\) smoothing as a convex combination of the
  empirical distribution and the uniform distribution.
\item
  Why is perplexity related to average uncertainty?
\item
  Give an example of a sentence where a bigram model misses important
  long-range information.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}

  MLE probabilities.

\item
  For the same counts, compute add-\(0.5\) smoothed probabilities.

\item

\section{Mini-project: small-domain language
model}\label{mini-project-small-domain-language-model}

Choose a small text domain, such as course descriptions, research
abstracts, textbook section titles, or advising questions. Build
unigram, bigram, and trigram models.

Your report should include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  the tokenization rule;
\item
  the vocabulary size;
\item
  the number of observed contexts for each model order;
\item
  several next-token predictions for selected contexts;
\item
  generated text samples;
\item
  perplexity on a held-out set;
\item
  a discussion of where the Markov assumption succeeds and fails.
\end{enumerate}

For a mathematically stronger project, include the transition matrix for
the bigram model and analyze row entropies.

\section{Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-2}

The corresponding computer lab should guide students through:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  building \(n\)-gram counts from scratch;
\item
  deriving and implementing MLE probabilities;
\item
  implementing add-\(\alpha\) smoothing;
\item
  computing sentence log-probability and perplexity;
\item
  generating text by sequential sampling;
\item
  visualizing smoothing effects with Plotly;
\item
  comparing unigram, bigram, and trigram models.
\end{itemize}

This lab is an important bridge between probability theory and modern
neural language modeling. The next chapters will use the same
probabilistic ideas in text classification and representation learning.

\chapter{Naive Bayes and Text
Classification}\label{naive-bayes-and-text-classification}

Bayes decision rules, multinomial likelihoods, smoothing, and linear
log-odds

\hfill\break

Text classification is the supervised learning problem of assigning a
label to a document. A document may be an email, review, abstract, news
article, student question, or clinical note. In this chapter we develop
one of the most important classical models for this task: \textbf{Naive
Bayes}. The model is simple, fast, interpretable, and mathematically
transparent. Its main lesson is that a probabilistic model for documents
can lead to a linear decision rule in word-count features.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-5}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  formulate text classification as a statistical decision problem;
\item
  derive the Bayes classifier under zero-one loss;
\item
  define the multinomial Naive Bayes model for count vectors;
\item
  estimate class priors and class-conditional token probabilities from
  data;
\item
  explain the conditional independence assumption and why it is called
  ``naive'';
\item
  derive the log-score form \[
  s_c(x)=\log \widehat \pi_c+\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\log \widehat \theta_{cj};
  \]
\item
  show that Naive Bayes is a linear classifier in count-vector space;
\item
  implement Naive Bayes from scratch in Python;
\item
  use add-\(\alpha\) smoothing to avoid zero probabilities;
\item
  evaluate a text classifier with confusion matrices, precision, recall,
  and \(F_1\) score;
\item
  use AI tools to critique assumptions, detect data leakage, and explain
  classifier behavior.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Why Naive Bayes matters}\label{why-naive-bayes-matters}

Naive Bayes is not a modern large language model. However, it remains a
useful mathematical baseline for NLP because it makes the modeling
assumptions explicit.

The model answers a clean question:

\begin{quote}
If documents in class \(c\) generate tokens according to a
class-specific probability distribution, which class most likely
generated a new document?
\end{quote}

This question leads naturally to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Bayes' theorem;
\item
  maximum likelihood estimation;
\item
  multinomial distributions;
\item
  Dirichlet/additive smoothing;
\item
  log-likelihood ratios;
\item
  linear decision boundaries;
\item
  interpretable feature weights.
\end{itemize}

Modern neural classifiers often achieve higher accuracy, but Naive Bayes
gives a clear first model against which more complicated systems should
be compared.

\textbf{Central idea.} A count vector
\(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\in \mathbb{N}^d\) records how often each vocabulary
token appears in a document. Multinomial Naive Bayes estimates

\[
P(Y=c\mid X=x)
\]

by combining a class prior \(P(Y=c)\) with a class-conditional token
model \(P(X=x\mid Y=c)\).

\section{Text classification as a supervised learning
problem}\label{text-classification-as-a-supervised-learning-problem}

Let

\[
\mathcal{Y}=\{1,2,\ldots,K\}
\]

be a finite label set. Examples include:

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Task
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Input
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Label set
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
sentiment analysis & movie review &
\(\{\text{negative},\text{positive}\}\) \\
spam detection & email & \(\{\text{ham},\text{spam}\}\) \\
topic classification & news article &
\(\{\text{sports},\text{business},\text{science},\ldots\}\) \\
intent classification & student question &
\(\{\text{transfer credit},\text{course registration},\text{visa},\ldots\}\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

A training dataset is

\[
D_n=\{(d_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n,
\]

where \(d_i\) is a document and \(y_i\in \mathcal{Y}\) is its label.
After choosing a representation map

\[
\phi: \text{documents}\longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d,
\]

we obtain feature vectors

\[
x_i=\phi(d_i)\in \mathbb{R}^d.
\]

For Naive Bayes, the most common representation is a count vector:

\[
x_i=(x_{i1},x_{i2},\ldots,x_{id})\in \mathbb{N}^d,
\]

where \(x_{ij}\) is the number of times vocabulary token \(v_j\) appears
in document \(d_i\).

The goal is to learn a classifier

\[
f:\mathbb{N}^d\longrightarrow \mathcal{Y}.
\]

\section{The Bayes classifier}\label{the-bayes-classifier}

Assume \((X,Y)\) is a random pair with \(X\in \mathbb{N}^d\) and
\(Y\in \mathcal{Y}\). Under zero-one loss,

\[
L(\widehat y,y)=
\begin{cases}
0, & \widehat y=y,\\
1, & \widehat y\neq y,
\end{cases}
\]

the best possible prediction rule, if the true distribution were known,
is the \textbf{Bayes classifier}:

\[
f^*(x)=\arg\max_{c\in \mathcal{Y}} P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]

This rule chooses the class with the largest posterior probability.

By Bayes' theorem,

\[
P(Y=c\mid X=x)
=
\frac{P(X=x\mid Y=c)P(Y=c)}{P(X=x)}.
\]

For classification, the denominator \(P(X=x)\) does not depend on \(c\).
Therefore,

\[
f^*(x)=\arg\max_{c\in \mathcal{Y}} P(X=x\mid Y=c)P(Y=c).
\]

This is the maximum a posteriori, or MAP, decision rule.

\textbf{Bayes decision rule.} To classify \(x\), compare the posterior
scores

\[
P(X=x\mid Y=c)P(Y=c), \qquad c=1,\ldots,K.
\]

Naive Bayes becomes a usable classifier after we specify and estimate
the class-conditional distribution \(P(X=x\mid Y=c)\).

\section{The multinomial event model}\label{the-multinomial-event-model}

Let

\[
V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_d\}
\]

be the vocabulary. In the multinomial Naive Bayes model, each class
\(c\) has a token probability vector

\[
\theta_c=(\theta_{c1},\theta_{c2},\ldots,\theta_{cd})\in \Delta^{d-1},
\]

where

\[
\theta_{cj}\ge 0, \qquad \sum_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}=1.
\]

The interpretation is:

\[
\theta_{cj}=P(\text{a randomly drawn token is }v_j\mid Y=c).
\]

Now suppose a document has length

\[
m=\sum_{j=1}^d x_j.
\]

The multinomial model assumes that, conditional on the class, the
document's tokens are generated by repeated draws from \(\theta_c\). The
probability of observing the count vector \(x\) is

\[
P(X=x\mid Y=c)
=
\frac{m!}{x_1!x_2!\cdots x_d!}
\prod_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}^{x_j}.
\]

The multinomial coefficient counts how many token sequences have the
same count vector.

For classification, if the document \(x\) is fixed, the coefficient

\[
\frac{m!}{x_1!x_2!\cdots x_d!}
\]

does not depend on the class \(c\). Therefore the MAP classifier can
ignore it:

\[
\widehat y
=
\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}
\pi_c\prod_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}^{x_j},
\]

where \(\pi_c=P(Y=c)\) is the class prior.

\section{The conditional independence
assumption}\label{the-conditional-independence-assumption}

The word ``naive'' refers to the conditional independence assumption. In
sequence form, if a document has tokens

\[
w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_m,
\]

the model assumes

\[
P(w_1,\ldots,w_m\mid Y=c)
\approx
\prod_{t=1}^m P(w_t\mid Y=c).
\]

That is, after conditioning on the class label, the tokens are treated
as independent draws from a class-specific distribution.

This is a strong assumption. Natural language has grammar, word order,
collocations, phrases, and long-range dependence. For example, in real
text,

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{not good}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

is not the same as the two independent words \texttt{not} and
\texttt{good}. Yet Naive Bayes often works surprisingly well for topic
and sentiment tasks because the presence of highly class-indicative
words can dominate the classification score.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Note}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The Naive Bayes assumption is usually false as a generative model of
language. The important question is not whether the model is literally
true, but whether the resulting decision rule is useful and
interpretable for a particular task.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Estimating the parameters}\label{estimating-the-parameters}

Suppose we have training examples

\[
(x_i,y_i),\qquad i=1,\ldots,n.
\]

\subsection{Class priors}\label{class-priors}

The maximum likelihood estimate of the class prior is

\[
\widehat \pi_c
=
\frac{n_c}{n},
\]

where

\[
n_c=\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf{1}\{y_i=c\}
\]

is the number of training documents in class \(c\).

\subsection{Token probabilities}\label{token-probabilities}

Let

\[
N_{cj}=\sum_{i:y_i=c} x_{ij}
\]

be the total number of times token \(v_j\) appears in documents with
label \(c\). Let

\[
N_c=\sum_{j=1}^d N_{cj}
\]

be the total number of tokens in class \(c\). The maximum likelihood
estimate is

\[
\widehat \theta_{cj}
=
\frac{N_{cj}}{N_c}.
\]

\subsection{Derivation by constrained
optimization}\label{derivation-by-constrained-optimization}

For a fixed class \(c\), the likelihood for \(\theta_c\) is proportional
to

\[
L_c(\theta_c)
=
\prod_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}^{N_{cj}}.
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell_c(\theta_c)
=
\sum_{j=1}^d N_{cj}\log \theta_{cj},
\]

subject to

\[
\sum_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}=1.
\]

Using a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\), define

\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta_c,\lambda)
=
\sum_{j=1}^d N_{cj}\log \theta_{cj}
+\lambda\left(1-\sum_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}\right).
\]

The stationarity condition gives

\[
\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}}{\partial \theta_{cj}}
=
\frac{N_{cj}}{\theta_{cj}}-\lambda=0.
\]

Hence

\[
\theta_{cj}=\frac{N_{cj}}{\lambda}.
\]

Summing over \(j\) gives

\[
1=\sum_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}=\frac{1}{\lambda}\sum_{j=1}^d N_{cj}=\frac{N_c}{\lambda},
\]

so \(\lambda=N_c\). Therefore

\[
\widehat \theta_{cj}=\frac{N_{cj}}{N_c}.
\]

\section{\texorpdfstring{Zero probabilities and add-\(\alpha\)
smoothing}{Zero probabilities and add-\textbackslash alpha smoothing}}\label{zero-probabilities-and-add-alpha-smoothing}

The maximum likelihood estimator assigns probability zero to any token
that never appears in class \(c\):

\[
N_{cj}=0 \quad \Longrightarrow \quad \widehat \theta_{cj}=0.
\]

This creates a serious problem. If a test document contains even one
such token, then

\[
\prod_{j=1}^d \widehat \theta_{cj}^{x_j}=0
\]

for that class. The model may rule out a class entirely because of one
unseen word.

To avoid this, we use add-\(\alpha\) smoothing:

\[
\widehat \theta_{cj}^{(\alpha)}
=
\frac{N_{cj}+\alpha}{N_c+\alpha d},
\qquad \alpha>0.
\]

Common choices include \(\alpha=1\) for Laplace smoothing and smaller
values such as \(\alpha=0.1\) or \(\alpha=0.01\) for less aggressive
smoothing.

\subsection{Bayesian interpretation}\label{bayesian-interpretation}

Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing can be interpreted through a symmetric
Dirichlet prior on each class token vector:

\[
\theta_c\sim \operatorname{Dirichlet}(\alpha,\ldots,\alpha).
\]

The smoothed estimate

\[
\frac{N_{cj}+\alpha}{N_c+\alpha d}
\]

is the posterior predictive probability of the next token being \(v_j\)
after observing the class-specific token counts.

\textbf{Smoothing as regularization.} Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing shrinks
the estimated token distribution away from the boundary of the simplex.
No token receives probability zero, so every class remains possible for
every document.

\section{Log-scores and numerical
stability}\label{log-scores-and-numerical-stability}

The product

\[
\pi_c\prod_{j=1}^d \theta_{cj}^{x_j}
\]

can be extremely small. In computation, multiplying many small
probabilities may underflow to zero. Taking logarithms avoids this
problem and converts products into sums:

\[
s_c(x)
=
\log \pi_c+
\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\log \theta_{cj}.
\]

The classifier is

\[
\widehat y
=
\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{Y}} s_c(x).
\]

Because the logarithm is increasing, maximizing the log-score is
equivalent to maximizing the original posterior numerator.

\section{Naive Bayes as a linear
classifier}\label{naive-bayes-as-a-linear-classifier}

The score for class \(c\) can be written as

\[
s_c(x)=b_c+w_c^\top x,
\]

where

\[
b_c=\log \pi_c,
\qquad
w_c=(\log \theta_{c1},\ldots,\log \theta_{cd})^\top.
\]

Thus multinomial Naive Bayes is a linear classifier in count-vector
space.

For binary classification with classes \(1\) and \(0\), compare
log-scores:

\[
s_1(x)-s_0(x)
=
\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}
+
\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\log\frac{\theta_{1j}}{\theta_{0j}}.
\]

The decision rule is

\[
\widehat y=1
\quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad
\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}
+
\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\log\frac{\theta_{1j}}{\theta_{0j}}>0.
\]

The decision boundary is the hyperplane

\[
\log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}
+
\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\log\frac{\theta_{1j}}{\theta_{0j}}=0.
\]

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Tip}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The weights

\[
\log\frac{\theta_{1j}}{\theta_{0j}}
\]

are interpretable. A large positive value means token \(v_j\) strongly
favors class \(1\) over class \(0\). A large negative value means the
token strongly favors class \(0\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{Relation to logistic
regression}\label{relation-to-logistic-regression}

Both Naive Bayes and logistic regression can produce linear decision
boundaries, but they estimate different objects.

Naive Bayes is a \textbf{generative} model. It estimates

\[
P(Y=c),
\qquad
P(X=x\mid Y=c),
\]

and then uses Bayes' theorem to obtain a classifier.

Logistic regression is a \textbf{discriminative} model. It estimates the
conditional probability directly:

\[
P(Y=c\mid X=x).
\]

For binary classification, logistic regression models

\[
P(Y=1\mid X=x)
=
\sigma(\beta_0+\beta^\top x),
\]

where

\[
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.
\]

Naive Bayes may work well with small data because it imposes strong
probabilistic structure. Logistic regression may work better with enough
labeled data because it directly optimizes conditional prediction.

\section{Bernoulli Naive Bayes}\label{bernoulli-naive-bayes}

The multinomial model uses token counts. Another common model uses
binary features:

\[
z_j=\mathbf{1}\{\text{token }v_j\text{ appears in the document}\}.
\]

For each class \(c\), Bernoulli Naive Bayes estimates

\[
\rho_{cj}=P(Z_j=1\mid Y=c).
\]

The class-conditional probability is

\[
P(Z=z\mid Y=c)
=
\prod_{j=1}^d \rho_{cj}^{z_j}(1-\rho_{cj})^{1-z_j}.
\]

The log-score becomes

\[
s_c(z)
=
\log \pi_c+
\sum_{j=1}^d
\left[z_j\log \rho_{cj}+(1-z_j)\log(1-\rho_{cj})\right].
\]

Bernoulli Naive Bayes models word presence or absence; multinomial Naive
Bayes models word counts. For longer documents, multinomial Naive Bayes
is often more natural. For short texts, binary presence features can be
useful.

\section{Worked example by hand}\label{worked-example-by-hand}

Suppose the vocabulary is

\[
V=\{\texttt{win},\texttt{meeting},\texttt{free}\}.
\]

There are two classes:

\[
\mathcal{Y}=\{\text{spam},\text{ham}\}.
\]

Assume the estimated parameters are:

\[
\widehat \pi_{\text{spam}}=0.4,
\qquad
\widehat \pi_{\text{ham}}=0.6,
\]

and

  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3636}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3636}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
token

Consider the document

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{free win free}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Its count vector is

\[
x=(1,0,2).
\]

The spam log-score is

\[
\log(0.4)+1\log(0.50)+0\log(0.05)+2\log(0.45).
\]

The ham log-score is

\[
\log(0.6)+1\log(0.05)+0\log(0.70)+2\log(0.25).
\]

Since \texttt{win} and \texttt{free} are much more likely under the spam
token distribution, the spam score will be larger.

\section{Python example: training from
scratch}\label{python-example-training-from-scratch}

The following code implements multinomial Naive Bayes without using a
machine learning library. The point is to see the mathematical
quantities directly.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ re}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter, defaultdict}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\NormalTok{train\_docs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"free money win now"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"spam"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"win a free prize"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"spam"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"cheap offer free entry"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"spam"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"meeting schedule for project"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ham"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"project meeting tomorrow"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ham"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"please review the project schedule"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ham"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{test\_docs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"free project prize"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"meeting tomorrow schedule"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"win free offer"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"please review money"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ re.findall(}\VerbatimStringTok{r"}\PreprocessorTok{[a{-}z]}\OperatorTok{+}\VerbatimStringTok{"}\NormalTok{, text.lower())}

\CommentTok{\# Build vocabulary from training documents.}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(\{tok }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc, label }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ train\_docs }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenize(doc)\})}
\NormalTok{token\_to\_index }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{tok: j }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, tok }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}
\NormalTok{classes }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(\{label }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_, label }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ train\_docs\})}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Vocabulary:"}\NormalTok{, vocab)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Classes:"}\NormalTok{, classes)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Vocabulary: ['a', 'cheap', 'entry', 'for', 'free', 'meeting', 'money', 'now', 'offer', 'please', 'prize', 'project', 'review', 'schedule', 'the', 'tomorrow', 'win']
Classes: ['ham', 'spam']
\end{verbatim}

Now estimate the class priors and class-conditional token distributions.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{alpha }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1.0}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(classes)}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}

\NormalTok{class\_doc\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(label }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_, label }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ train\_docs)}
\NormalTok{class\_token\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{c: np.zeros(d, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes\}}
\NormalTok{class\_total\_tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{c: }\FloatTok{0.0} \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes\}}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc, label }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ train\_docs:}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenize(doc):}
\NormalTok{        j }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ token\_to\_index[tok]}
\NormalTok{        class\_token\_counts[label][j] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{        class\_total\_tokens[label] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{priors }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{c: class\_doc\_counts[c] }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(train\_docs) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes\}}
\NormalTok{theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{\}}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes:}
\NormalTok{    theta[c] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (class\_token\_counts[c] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (class\_total\_tokens[c] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d)}

\NormalTok{prior\_table }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"class"}\NormalTok{: classes, }\StringTok{"prior"}\NormalTok{: [priors[c] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes]\})}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(prior\_table)}

\NormalTok{theta\_table }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(theta, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(theta\_table.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

            ham   spam

meeting   0.103  0.034

please    0.069  0.034

\end{verbatim}

Define prediction using log-scores.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ vectorize(doc):}
\NormalTok{    x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(d, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenize(doc):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ token\_to\_index:}
\NormalTok{            x[token\_to\_index[tok]] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ x}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ log\_scores(doc):}
\NormalTok{    x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ vectorize(doc)}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{\}}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes:}
\NormalTok{        scores[c] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log(priors[c]) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(x }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.log(theta[c]))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ scores}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ predict(doc):}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ log\_scores(doc)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(scores, key}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{scores.get), scores}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ test\_docs:}
\NormalTok{    pred, scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ predict(doc)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"Document: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{doc}\SpecialCharTok{!r\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Prediction:"}\NormalTok{, pred)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Scores:"}\NormalTok{, \{c: }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(scores[c], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes\})}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Document: 'free project prize'
Prediction: spam
Scores: {'ham': -9.409, 'spam': -8.716}

Document: 'meeting tomorrow schedule'
Prediction: ham
Scores: {'ham': -7.905, 'spam': -10.795}

Document: 'win free offer'
Prediction: spam
Scores: {'ham': -10.795, 'spam': -7.617}

Document: 'please review money'
Prediction: ham
Scores: {'ham': -9.409, 'spam': -10.102}
\end{verbatim}

\section{Python example: interpretable log-odds
weights}\label{python-example-interpretable-log-odds-weights}

For binary classification, the log-odds weight for token \(v_j\) is

\[
\log\frac{\widehat\theta_{\text{spam},j}}{\widehat\theta_{\text{ham},j}}.
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{positive\_class }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"spam"}
\NormalTok{negative\_class }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"ham"}

\NormalTok{log\_odds }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log(theta[positive\_class] }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ theta[negative\_class])}
\NormalTok{weights }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"token"}\NormalTok{: vocab,}
    \StringTok{"log\_odds\_spam\_vs\_ham"}\NormalTok{: log\_odds}
\NormalTok{\}).sort\_values(}\StringTok{"log\_odds\_spam\_vs\_ham"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(weights.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
       token  log_odds_spam_vs_ham
4       free                 1.386
16       win                 1.099
6      money                 0.693
10     prize                 0.693
1      cheap                 0.693
7        now                 0.693
0          a                 0.693
2      entry                 0.693
8      offer                 0.693
3        for                -0.693
9     please                -0.693
12    review                -0.693
14       the                -0.693
15  tomorrow                -0.693
5    meeting                -1.099
13  schedule                -1.099
11   project                -1.386
\end{verbatim}

Tokens with positive log-odds push the classifier toward \texttt{spam}.
Tokens with negative log-odds push it toward \texttt{ham}.

\section{Python example: accuracy and confusion
matrix}\label{python-example-accuracy-and-confusion-matrix}

Here is a tiny evaluation example. In a real project, train and test
sets should be separated carefully.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{labeled\_test }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"free project prize"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"spam"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"meeting tomorrow schedule"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ham"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"win free offer"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"spam"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"please review money"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"ham"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{confusion }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{classes, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{classes)}
\NormalTok{correct }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc, true\_label }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ labeled\_test:}
\NormalTok{    pred\_label, \_ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ predict(doc)}
\NormalTok{    confusion.loc[true\_label, pred\_label] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{    correct }\OperatorTok{+=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(pred\_label }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ true\_label)}

\NormalTok{accuracy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ correct }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(labeled\_test)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Accuracy:"}\NormalTok{, accuracy)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(confusion)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Accuracy: 1.0
      ham  spam
ham     2     0
spam    0     2
\end{verbatim}

For binary classification with positive class \texttt{spam}, define:

\[
\text{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},
\qquad
\text{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN},
\]

and

\[
F_1=\frac{2\cdot \text{precision}\cdot \text{recall}}{\text{precision}+\text{recall}}.
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{pos }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"spam"}
\NormalTok{neg }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"ham"}
\NormalTok{TP }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ confusion.loc[pos, pos]}
\NormalTok{FP }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ confusion.loc[neg, pos]}
\NormalTok{FN }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ confusion.loc[pos, neg]}

\NormalTok{precision }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ TP }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (TP }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ FP) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ TP }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ FP }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{recall }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ TP }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (TP }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ FN) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ TP }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ FN }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{f1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ precision }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ recall }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (precision }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ recall) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ precision }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ recall }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(\{}
    \StringTok{"precision"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(precision), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
    \StringTok{"recall"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(recall), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
    \StringTok{"f1"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(f1), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
{'precision': 1.0, 'recall': 1.0, 'f1': 1.0}
\end{verbatim}

\section{Interactive HTML: smoothing and
log-odds}\label{interactive-html-smoothing-and-log-odds}

The next interactive component shows how add-\(\alpha\) smoothing
changes token probabilities and log-odds weights. The example uses two
classes and four tokens. Move the smoothing slider and token-count
sliders to see how the decision score changes.

The HTML version of this chapter contains an interactive Plotly.js
component for exploring how add-\(\alpha\) smoothing changes Naive Bayes
log-odds weights and predictions. In PDF output, the same ideas can be
studied by running the Python code examples above.

\section{Statistical interpretation of
smoothing}\label{statistical-interpretation-of-smoothing}

Smoothing changes a classifier in two ways.

First, it prevents impossible events. Every token receives positive
probability in every class:

\[
\widehat \theta_{cj}^{(\alpha)}>0.
\]

Second, it reduces the magnitude of extreme log-odds weights. If a token
appears many times in one class and zero times in another, the
unsmoothed log-ratio would be infinite. Smoothing makes the ratio
finite:

\[
\log\frac{N_{1j}+\alpha}{N_{0j}+\alpha}
+
\log\frac{N_0+\alpha d}{N_1+\alpha d}.
\]

Thus smoothing acts like a regularizer on the classifier's feature
weights.

\section{Model assumptions and failure
modes}\label{model-assumptions-and-failure-modes}

Naive Bayes works best when class-indicative tokens are strong and word
order is not essential. It can fail when meaning depends on syntax,
negation, or context.

\subsection{Failure mode 1: negation}\label{failure-mode-1-negation}

The phrases

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{good}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

and

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{not good}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

have different meanings. A unigram Naive Bayes model may treat
\texttt{good} as positive even when preceded by \texttt{not}.

Possible remedy: add bigram features such as \texttt{not\_good}.

\subsection{Failure mode 2: repeated correlated
words}\label{failure-mode-2-repeated-correlated-words}

Because Naive Bayes multiplies token probabilities, repeated correlated
words may make the model overconfident. The model behaves as though each
occurrence contributes independent evidence.

Possible remedy: use binary features, stronger smoothing, feature
selection, or a discriminative model.

\subsection{Failure mode 3: dataset
leakage}\label{failure-mode-3-dataset-leakage}

If the training data contains label artifacts, the classifier may learn
shortcuts. For example, if all spam examples contain a footer phrase not
present at deployment time, the model may appear accurate in validation
but fail in practice.

Possible remedy: inspect feature weights and validate on realistic
held-out data.

\section{AI-assisted learning
component}\label{ai-assisted-learning-component-2}

Use AI tools as a mathematical tutor and model auditor, not as a
replacement for your own derivations.

\subsection{Prompt 1: explain the
assumption}\label{prompt-1-explain-the-assumption}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\NormalTok{Explain the conditional independence assumption using probability notation.}
\NormalTok{Then give two examples where this assumption is false in natural language.}

\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

After receiving an answer, check whether it correctly distinguishes

\[
P(w_1,\ldots,w_m\mid Y=c)
\]

from

\]

\section{A complete mathematical
summary}\label{a-complete-mathematical-summary}

The multinomial Naive Bayes pipeline can be summarized as follows.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Choose a vocabulary
\end{enumerate}

\[
V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{1}
\tightlist
\item
  Represent each document as a count vector
\end{enumerate}

\[
x\in \mathbb{N}^d.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{2}
\tightlist
\item
  Estimate class priors
\end{enumerate}

\[
\widehat \pi_c=\frac{n_c}{n}.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  Estimate smoothed token probabilities
\end{enumerate}

\[
\widehat \theta_{cj}
=
\frac{N_{cj}+\alpha}{N_c+\alpha d}.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{4}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute class log-scores
\end{enumerate}

\[
s_c(x)=\log \widehat \pi_c+
\sum_{j=1}^d x_j\log \widehat \theta_{cj}.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\tightlist
\item
  Predict
\end{enumerate}

\[
\widehat y=\arg\max_{c\in\mathcal{Y}}s_c(x).
\]

The classifier is probabilistic in origin but linear in its final
scoring form.

\section{Exercises}\label{exercises-5}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Bayes rule.} Starting from Bayes' theorem, derive the MAP
  classification rule \[
  \widehat y=\arg\max_c P(X=x\mid Y=c)P(Y=c).
  \]
\item
  \textbf{Multinomial likelihood.} Let \(x\in\mathbb{N}^d\) with
  \(m=\sum_j x_j\). Write the multinomial probability \(P(X=x\mid Y=c)\)
  and identify which factor can be ignored for classification.
\item
  \textbf{MLE derivation.} Use Lagrange multipliers to derive \[
  \widehat \theta_{cj}=\frac{N_{cj}}{N_c}.
  \]
\item
  \textbf{Smoothing.} Suppose \(d=1000\), \(N_c=5000\), \(N_{cj}=0\),
  and \(\alpha=1\). Compute the smoothed probability of token \(v_j\) in
  class \(c\).
\item
  \textbf{Log-odds.} In a binary classifier, show that the Naive Bayes
  decision boundary is a hyperplane in \(\mathbb{R}^d\).
\item
  \textbf{Interpretability.} Suppose a token has log-odds weight \(3.2\)
  for spam versus ham. Interpret this value as a ratio of
  class-conditional token probabilities.
\item
  \textbf{Bernoulli versus multinomial.} Give an example of a task where
  binary word-presence features may be better than count features.
\item
  \textbf{Negation.} Construct a small example showing why unigram Naive
  Bayes can mishandle negation.
\item
  \textbf{Implementation.} Modify the Python code above so that unknown
  test tokens are mapped to a special
  \texttt{\textless{}unk\textgreater{}} token.
\item
  \textbf{AI critique.} Ask an AI tool to explain Naive Bayes. Then
  identify one place where the answer is incomplete, imprecise, or
  missing a mathematical assumption.
\end{enumerate}
