\section{What to remember}\label{what-to-remember}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Naive Bayes is a generative classifier: it models \(P(Y)\) and
  \(P(X\mid Y)\).
\item
  The multinomial model treats a document as a bag of token counts.
\item
  The conditional independence assumption is mathematically convenient
  but linguistically false.
\item
  Add-\(\alpha\) smoothing prevents zero probabilities and regularizes
  log-odds weights.
\item
  The MAP rule becomes a linear classifier in count-vector space.
\item
  The feature weights are interpretable through log-ratios of
  class-conditional token probabilities.
\item
  Naive Bayes is a useful baseline before using larger neural NLP
  models.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-3}

Naive Bayes is a classical method in statistical NLP and information
retrieval. For broader context, see Manning and Schuetze (1999), Manning
et al. (2008), and Jurafsky and Martin (2024). The relationship between
generative and discriminative classifiers is also connected to standard
material in statistical learning theory.

\part{Part III. Linear Algebra of Language}

\chapter{Vector Space Models}\label{vector-space-models}

Document-term matrices, cosine retrieval, SVD, and latent semantic
structure

\hfill\break

In the previous chapters, documents were represented by count vectors,
TF-IDF vectors, and probabilistic models. In this chapter we study these
representations from a systematic linear-algebraic point of view. A
corpus becomes a matrix, documents become rows, vocabulary terms become
columns, similarity becomes an inner product, and latent semantic
structure is extracted by projection onto low-dimensional subspaces.

The central mathematical tool is the singular value decomposition. It
turns a large sparse document-term matrix into a sequence of best
low-rank approximations. This gives the classical method known as
\textbf{latent semantic analysis} and also prepares us for modern
embedding models.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-6}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  represent a corpus as a document-term matrix \(X\in R^{n\times d}\);
\item
  interpret rows, columns, row space, column space, rank, and Gram
  matrices in NLP terms;
\item
  compute document similarity using inner products and cosine
  similarity;
\item
  express retrieval scores in matrix form;
\item
  explain why normalization changes the geometry of document comparison;
\item
  state the singular value decomposition and connect it to eigenvalue
  problems;
\item
  use the Eckart--Young--Mirsky theorem to justify low-rank
  approximation;
\item
  construct latent semantic analysis from a truncated SVD;
\item
  compare raw vector-space retrieval with low-rank latent retrieval;
\item
  implement the main ideas in Python using NumPy;
\item
  use Plotly.js to visualize latent document geometry;
\item
  use AI tools to critique representation choices, identify hidden
  assumptions, and explain model behavior.
\end{enumerate}

Throughout this chapter, \(R\) denotes the real numbers. In code we use
ordinary NumPy arrays, but the mathematical object is a matrix
representation of a finite corpus.

\section{The main object: a document-term
matrix}\label{the-main-object-a-document-term-matrix}

Let

\[
D=\{d_1,d_2,\ldots,d_n\}
\]

be a corpus of \(n\) documents, and let

\[
V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_d\}
\]

be a fixed vocabulary of \(d\) tokens. A vector-space model chooses a
representation map

\[
\phi:D\longrightarrow R^d.
\]

The \(i\)th document is represented by

\[
x_i=\phi(d_i)=(x_{i1},x_{i2},\ldots,x_{id})\in R^d.
\]

The full corpus is represented by the matrix

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
--- & x_1^T & ---\\
--- & x_2^T & ---\\
& \vdots & \\
--- & x_n^T & ---
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{n\times d}.
\]

The entry \(X_{ij}\) is the weight of term \(v_j\) in document \(d_i\).
Depending on the representation, \(X_{ij}\) may be a count, a binary
indicator, a relative frequency, or a TF-IDF weight.

\textbf{Document-term matrix.} A corpus is converted into a matrix

\[
X\in R^{n\times d},
\]

where rows index documents and columns index vocabulary terms. Most
classical NLP methods can be described as operations on this matrix.

This viewpoint is powerful because it reduces many NLP operations to
familiar linear algebra:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}ll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
NLP operation & Linear algebra operation \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
represent a document & choose a row vector \(x_i\in R^d\) \\
compare two documents & compute \(x_i^T x_j\) or cosine similarity \\
compare all documents & compute the Gram matrix \(XX^T\) \\
compare all terms & compute the Gram matrix \(X^TX\) \\
remove unimportant dimensions & project onto a subspace \\
find latent topics & compute a low-rank approximation \\
search with a query & compute matrix-vector scores \(Xq\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

\section{Rows, columns, and geometry}\label{rows-columns-and-geometry}

The row vector \(x_i\in R^d\) describes document \(d_i\) as a point in
vocabulary space. The \(j\)th column

\[
X_{:j}=\begin{bmatrix}X_{1j}\\X_{2j}\\\vdots\\X_{nj}\end{bmatrix}\in R^n
\]

describes how term \(v_j\) is distributed across documents.

These two perspectives are dual:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  rows describe \textbf{documents by terms};
\item
  columns describe \textbf{terms by documents}.
\end{itemize}

The document Gram matrix is

\[
G_D=XX^T\in R^{n\times n},
\]

with entries

\[
(G_D)_{ij}=x_i^Tx_j.
\]

The term Gram matrix is

\[
G_T=X^TX\in R^{d\times d},
\]

with entries

\[
(G_T)_{jk}=X_{:j}^T X_{:k}.
\]

Thus \(G_D\) measures document-document similarity, while \(G_T\)
measures term-term co-occurrence similarity.

\textbf{Two Gram matrices.}

\[
XX^T \quad \text{compares documents},
\]

while

\[
X^TX \quad \text{compares terms}.
\]

The singular value decomposition links these two matrices through the
same singular values.

\section{Inner product retrieval}\label{inner-product-retrieval}

Suppose a query is represented by a vector

\[
q\in R^d.
\]

A simple retrieval score for document \(d_i\) is

\[
s_i=x_i^Tq.
\]

For the whole corpus, the score vector is

\[
s=Xq\in R^n.
\]

Documents with larger scores are considered more relevant. This is the
foundation of classical vector-space search.

The inner product has a clear meaning for nonnegative text vectors:

\[
x_i^Tq=\sum_{j=1}^d x_{ij}q_j.
\]

Only terms that appear in both the document and the query contribute
positively. Large weights produce larger scores.

However, raw inner products favor long documents because long documents
tend to have larger norms. To reduce this length bias, we often use
cosine similarity.

\section{Cosine similarity and normalized
geometry}\label{cosine-similarity-and-normalized-geometry}

For nonzero vectors \(x,y\in R^d\), the cosine similarity is

\[
\operatorname{cos}(x,y)=\frac{x^Ty}{\lVert x\rVert_2\lVert y\rVert_2}.
\]

This is the inner product after projecting both vectors to the unit
sphere:

\[
\widehat x=\frac{x}{\lVert x\rVert_2},
\qquad
\widehat y=\frac{y}{\lVert y\rVert_2}.
\]

Then

\[
\operatorname{cos}(x,y)=\widehat x^T\widehat y.
\]

Cosine similarity compares direction rather than magnitude. In document
analysis, direction often represents relative term usage, while
magnitude is partly influenced by document length.

If \(\widetilde X\) is the row-normalized document matrix, then all
pairwise cosine similarities are contained in

\[
C=\widetilde X\widetilde X^T.
\]

Similarly, query scores are

\[
s=\widetilde X\widehat q.
\]

\textbf{Normalization changes the model.} Raw inner products ask: ``How
much weighted vocabulary overlap is there?'' Cosine similarity asks:
``How similar are the directions of the two term-weight vectors?'' These
are different statistical assumptions about what should count as
similarity.

\section{Python example: building a document-term
matrix}\label{python-example-building-a-document-term-matrix-1}

The following example uses a small corpus. The goal is not to build a
production search engine, but to expose every mathematical step.

\section{Python example: cosine search from
scratch}\label{python-example-cosine-search-from-scratch}

Now we represent a query and rank the documents by cosine similarity.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ vectorize\_query(query, vocab\_index):}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab\_index), dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenize(query):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ vocab\_index:}
\NormalTok{            q[vocab\_index[token]] }\OperatorTok{+=} \FloatTok{1.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ q}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ row\_normalize(A, eps}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    norms }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(A, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(norms, eps)}

\NormalTok{query }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"matrix decomposition for latent semantic search"}
\NormalTok{q\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ vectorize\_query(query, token\_to\_col)}

\NormalTok{Xn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_normalize(X\_counts)}
\NormalTok{qn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ q\_counts }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(q\_counts), }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{cos\_scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Xn }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ qn}

\NormalTok{ranking }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{cos\_scores)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ rank, i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(ranking, start}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{rank}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{. score=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{cos\_scores[i]}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | label=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{labels[i]}\SpecialCharTok{:15s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{corpus[i]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The formula used here is exactly

\[
s=\widetilde X\widehat q.
\]

This is a complete vector-space retrieval system in a few lines of
NumPy.

\section{Term weighting as diagonal
scaling}\label{term-weighting-as-diagonal-scaling}

Raw count matrices are often not the best representation. Common words
may dominate similarity. TF-IDF corrects this by increasing the weight
of terms that are frequent in a document but rare across the corpus.

Let

\[
\operatorname{tf}_{ij}=X_{ij}
\]

or a transformed frequency such as \(\log(1+X_{ij})\). The document
frequency of term \(j\) is

\[
\operatorname{df}_j=\#\{i:X_{ij}>0\}.
\]

A smoothed inverse document frequency is

\[
\operatorname{idf}_j=\log\left(\frac{1+n}{1+\operatorname{df}_j}\right)+1.
\]

Then

\[
X^{\operatorname{tfidf}}_{ij}=\operatorname{tf}_{ij}\operatorname{idf}_j.
\]

In matrix form, this is column scaling:

\[
X^{\operatorname{tfidf}}=XW,
\]

where

\[
W=\operatorname{diag}(\operatorname{idf}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{idf}_d).
\]

Thus TF-IDF is not just a heuristic. It is a diagonal linear
transformation of the feature space.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tfidf\_transform(X):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(X }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    idf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log((}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ n) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ df)) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ idf, idf}

\NormalTok{X\_tfidf, idf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tfidf\_transform(X\_counts)}

\NormalTok{idf\_table }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"term"}\NormalTok{: vocab, }\StringTok{"idf"}\NormalTok{: idf\}).sort\_values(}\StringTok{"idf"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{idf\_table.head(}\DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The only change is the geometry of the feature space. The similarity

\section{Rank and latent structure}\label{rank-and-latent-structure}

The rank of \(X\) is

\[
\operatorname{rank}(X)=\dim(\operatorname{Row}(X))=\dim(\operatorname{Col}(X)).
\]

In NLP, a high-dimensional vocabulary space often contains redundancy:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  different words may carry related meanings;
\item
  topics create correlations among terms;
\item
  document collections often lie near lower-dimensional structures;
\item
  noise and rare words inflate the apparent dimension.
\end{itemize}

A low-rank approximation tries to replace \(X\) by a simpler matrix

\[
X_k\in R^{n\times d},
\qquad
\operatorname{rank}(X_k)\le k,
\]

where \(k\ll \min(n,d)\).

The goal is to keep the most important geometric structure while
discarding high-dimensional noise.

\section{Singular value
decomposition}\label{singular-value-decomposition-1}

Every matrix \(X\in R^{n\times d}\) has a singular value decomposition

\[
X=U\Sigma V^T,
\]

where:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(U\in R^{n\times r}\) has orthonormal columns;
\item
  \(V\in R^{d\times r}\) has orthonormal columns;
\item
  \(\Sigma=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r)\);
\item
  \(r=\operatorname{rank}(X)\);
\item
  \(\sigma_1\ge \sigma_2\ge \cdots\ge \sigma_r>0\).
\end{itemize}

The columns of \(U\) are left singular vectors. The columns of \(V\) are
right singular vectors. The singular values measure how much variation
lies in each singular direction.

The SVD diagonalizes the two Gram matrices:

\[
XX^T=U\Sigma^2U^T,
\]

and

\[
X^TX=V\Sigma^2V^T.
\]

Thus left singular vectors describe principal directions among
documents, while right singular vectors describe principal directions
among terms.

\section{Best low-rank approximation}\label{best-low-rank-approximation}

For \(k<r\), define

\[
U_k=[u_1,\ldots,u_k],
\qquad
V_k=[v_1,\ldots,v_k],
\qquad
\Sigma_k=\operatorname{diag}(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_k).
\]

The rank-\(k\) truncated SVD approximation is

\[
X_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^T.
\]

The Eckart--Young--Mirsky theorem says that \(X_k\) is the best
rank-\(k\) approximation to \(X\) in Frobenius norm:

\[
X_k=\arg\min_{\operatorname{rank}(A)\le k}\lVert X-A\rVert_F.
\]

Moreover,

\[
\lVert X-X_k\rVert_F^2=\sum_{j=k+1}^r \sigma_j^2.
\]

This theorem is the mathematical foundation of latent semantic analysis.

\textbf{SVD interpretation for NLP.} The truncated SVD replaces sparse
surface-level term matching by a lower-dimensional coordinate system.
Documents that do not share many exact words may become close if they
have similar coordinates in the latent space.

\section{Latent semantic analysis}\label{latent-semantic-analysis}

Latent semantic analysis, or LSA, applies truncated SVD to a
term-weighted document matrix such as \(X^{\operatorname{tfidf}}\).

Let

\[
X\approx X_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^T.
\]

The row vector

\[
z_i=(U_k\Sigma_k)_{i:}\in R^k
\]

is a \(k\)-dimensional latent representation of document \(d_i\). The
row vector

\[
t_j=(V_k\Sigma_k)_{j:}\in R^k
\]

may be interpreted as a latent representation of term \(v_j\).

A query vector \(q\in R^d\) can be projected into the same latent
coordinate system by

\[
z_q=q^TV_k\in R^k.
\]

Then retrieval can be performed by comparing \(z_q\) with the document
coordinates \(z_i\).

There are several conventions for scaling latent coordinates. The
important point is that documents and queries are compared after
projection onto the subspace spanned by the top right singular vectors.

\section{Python example: SVD and low-rank
coordinates}\label{python-example-svd-and-low-rank-coordinates}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\NormalTok{U, singular\_values, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(X, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sv\_table }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"component"}\NormalTok{: np.arange(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(singular\_values) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{),}

\NormalTok{\})}

\begin{Shaded}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ truncated\_svd\_coordinates(X, k):}

\section{Reconstruction error}\label{reconstruction-error}

A rank-\(k\) approximation is useful only if it captures enough
structure. The following code computes reconstruction error for each
possible \(k\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ svd\_reconstruction(X, k):}
\NormalTok{    U, s, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(X, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ (U[:, :k] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ s[:k]) }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Vt[:k, :]}

\NormalTok{rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ k }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(X.shape) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    Xk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ svd\_reconstruction(X, k)}
\NormalTok{    error }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Xk, }\BuiltInTok{ord}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"fro"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    relative\_error }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ error }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X, }\BuiltInTok{ord}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"fro"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    rows.append((k, error, relative\_error))}

\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(rows, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\StringTok{"k"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"frobenius\_error"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"relative\_error"}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Interactive HTML: latent semantic
projection}\label{interactive-html-latent-semantic-projection}

The interactive below uses a small fixed document-term matrix. Move the
slider to choose the rank \(k\) used by a precomputed low-rank
representation. The plot shows how documents move as the latent
dimension changes. The displayed quantity is the cumulative
singular-value energy

\[
\frac{\sum_{j=1}^k\sigma_j^2}{\sum_{j=1}^r\sigma_j^2}.
\]

This example is intentionally small. In real corpora, the visual
separation of topics may be much more subtle, and the first two
dimensions may not capture everything important.

\section{Low-rank retrieval}\label{low-rank-retrieval}

In raw vector-space retrieval, the query score is computed in the
original vocabulary space:

\[
s=Xq.
\]

In LSA retrieval, we first project the query into the latent
right-singular-vector space:

\[
z_q=q^TV_k.
\]

The document coordinates are

\[
Z=XV_k=U_k\Sigma_k.
\]

Then the latent retrieval score is

\[
s_i=z_i^Tz_q.
\]

In matrix form,

\[
s=Zz_q^T.
\]

If cosine similarity is desired, normalize the latent document
coordinates and the latent query coordinate before scoring.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ lsa\_search(X, q, k):}
\NormalTok{    U, s, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(X, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    Vk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Vt[:k, :].T}
\NormalTok{    Z\_docs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Vk}
\NormalTok{    z\_query }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Vk}
\NormalTok{    Zn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_normalize(Z\_docs)}
\NormalTok{    zqn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ z\_query }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(z\_query), }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Zn }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ zqn}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ k }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ lsa\_search(X\_tfidf, q\_tfidf, k}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{k)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\SpecialStringTok{Rank k=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{k}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ rank, i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{scores), start}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
        \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{rank}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{. score=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{scores[i]}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ | }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{corpus[i]}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Low-rank retrieval may retrieve documents that do not share many exact
query words but lie in a related latent direction. This is the main
advantage of LSA over purely surface-level matching.

\section{How LSA handles synonymy and
polysemy}\label{how-lsa-handles-synonymy-and-polysemy}

Two common language difficulties are \textbf{synonymy} and
\textbf{polysemy}.

Synonymy means that different words have related meanings. For example,
``car'' and ``automobile'' may not match exactly in a count-vector
model. If they occur in similar document contexts, a low-rank model may
place them near each other.

Polysemy means that one word has multiple meanings. For example,
``bank'' may refer to a financial institution or a river bank. A simple
vector-space model assigns one column to the token ``bank,'' so it
cannot fully separate meanings. LSA may partially separate contexts
through document-level directions, but it still lacks the contextual
flexibility of modern neural embeddings.

\textbf{What LSA can and cannot do.} LSA can discover linear correlation
structure in a corpus. It cannot truly understand syntax, word order, or
context-dependent meaning. Its strength is low-rank linear geometry; its
limitation is that language is not purely linear bag-of-words geometry.

\section{Centering, scaling, and preprocessing as linear
transformations}\label{centering-scaling-and-preprocessing-as-linear-transformations}

Many preprocessing steps can be described as transformations of \(X\).

\subsection{Row normalization}\label{row-normalization}

Row normalization replaces each document vector by

\[
\widehat x_i=\frac{x_i}{\lVert x_i\rVert_2}.
\]

This maps documents to the unit sphere in \(R^d\).

\subsection{Column scaling}\label{column-scaling}

TF-IDF is column scaling:

\[
X\mapsto XW.
\]

This changes the metric by giving different importance to different
vocabulary dimensions.

\subsection{Stop-word removal}\label{stop-word-removal}

Removing a set of stop-word columns is projection onto a coordinate
subspace. If \(S\) is the set of retained columns, then

\[
X\mapsto XP_S,
\]

where \(P_S\) selects the retained vocabulary coordinates.

\subsection{Centering}\label{centering}

Centering subtracts the column mean:

\[
X_c=X-\mathbf{1}\mu^T,
\]

where

\[
\mu=\frac{1}{n}X^T\mathbf{1}.
\]

Centering is standard in PCA, but it must be used carefully in sparse
nonnegative text matrices because it destroys sparsity and creates
negative entries.

\section{PCA and LSA: same theorem, different data
convention}\label{pca-and-lsa-same-theorem-different-data-convention}

PCA is usually applied to centered data. LSA is usually applied to
uncentered TF-IDF data. Both use the SVD.

For centered data \(X_c\), PCA finds directions maximizing variance:

\[
v_1=\arg\max_{\lVert v\rVert=1}\lVert X_cv\rVert_2^2.
\]

The solution is the top right singular vector of \(X_c\).

LSA instead applies SVD to a sparse term-weight matrix, often without
centering:

\[
X^{\operatorname{tfidf}}=U\Sigma V^T.
\]

The purpose is not variance analysis in the classical statistical sense,
but low-rank semantic approximation for retrieval and representation.

\section{A statistical
interpretation}\label{a-statistical-interpretation}

A document-term matrix can be viewed as data sampled from an underlying
distribution. Suppose each document is generated from a mixture of
latent topics. Then terms that often occur together across documents
produce correlated columns in \(X\).

A low-rank model assumes that much of this correlation can be explained
by a small number of latent factors. Informally,

\[
X\approx AB^T,
\]

where

\[
A\in R^{n\times k}
\]

contains document factors and

\[
B\in R^{d\times k}
\]

contains term factors.

The SVD gives the best unconstrained linear factorization under squared
error. Later models, such as nonnegative matrix factorization and topic
models, impose additional constraints or probabilistic assumptions.

\section{Worked hand calculation}\label{worked-hand-calculation-1}

Consider three documents and four terms:

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1&0&0\\
1&0&1&0\\
0&0&1&1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The document Gram matrix is

\[
XX^T=
\begin{bmatrix}
2&1&0\\
1&2&1\\
0&1&2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Thus documents 1 and 2 overlap in one term, documents 2 and 3 overlap in
one term, and documents 1 and 3 do not overlap. The cosine similarity
matrix is obtained by dividing each row and column by document norms.
Since every row has norm \(\sqrt{2}\),

\[
C=\frac{1}{2}XX^T
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1&1/2&0\\
1/2&1&1/2\\
0&1/2&1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

This example shows why vector-space models can be understood entirely
through matrix products.

\section{AI-assisted learning
activities}\label{ai-assisted-learning-activities}

AI tools can help students learn vector-space models, but they should be
used as mathematical assistants rather than answer machines.

\subsection{Activity 1: representation
audit}\label{activity-1-representation-audit}

Give an AI tool the following prompt:

\begin{quote}
I represented documents using TF-IDF vectors and cosine similarity. List
the mathematical assumptions behind this representation. Which
assumptions might fail for short student advising questions?
\end{quote}

Then revise the output by checking whether it mentions:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  bag-of-words independence from word order;
\item
  sparse high-dimensional geometry;
\item
  length normalization;
\item
  rare-term upweighting;
\item
  vocabulary mismatch;
\item
  synonymy and polysemy.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Activity 2: explain the SVD in NLP
terms}\label{activity-2-explain-the-svd-in-nlp-terms}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Explain \(X\approx U_k\Sigma_kV_k^T\) to a student who knows linear
algebra but not NLP. Interpret \(U_k\), \(\Sigma_k\), and \(V_k\) for a
document-term matrix.
\end{quote}

Then identify whether the explanation correctly distinguishes document
coordinates from term directions.

\subsection{Activity 3: adversarial query
design}\label{activity-3-adversarial-query-design}

Create two queries:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  one that should work well with TF-IDF cosine search;
\item
  one that should fail because it uses synonyms not present in the
  corpus.
\end{enumerate}

Ask an AI tool to predict which query will fail and why. Then test the
prediction using Python.

\section{Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing documents and terms.} If \(X\in R^{n\times d}\),
  rows are documents and columns are terms. Some books use the transpose
  convention, so always check the orientation.
\item
  \textbf{Using raw inner products without thinking about length.} Long
  documents can dominate raw scores.
\item
  \textbf{Calling SVD topics probabilities.} SVD factors are real-valued
  and may be negative. They are not probability distributions.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming low-rank always improves retrieval.} Low-rank
  projection can remove noise, but it can also remove important rare
  information.
\item
  \textbf{Overinterpreting two-dimensional plots.} A 2D map may be
  useful for visualization but may not preserve all relevant distances.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Exercises}\label{exercises-6}

\subsection{Conceptual exercises}\label{conceptual-exercises-4}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(X\in R^{n\times d}\) be a document-term matrix. Explain the NLP
  meaning of \(XX^T\) and \(X^TX\).
\item
  Why does cosine similarity reduce document-length bias compared with a
  raw inner product?
\item
  Explain TF-IDF as a diagonal column-scaling operation.
\item
  What does it mean for a corpus matrix to be approximately low rank?
\item
  Why can LSA retrieve related documents that do not share exact query
  words?
\item
  Give one limitation of LSA caused by the bag-of-words assumption.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Mathematical exercises}\label{mathematical-exercises-3}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Prove that cosine similarity is the inner product of normalized
  vectors.
\item
  Let \(X=U\Sigma V^T\). Show that \(XX^T=U\Sigma^2U^T\) and
  \(X^TX=V\Sigma^2V^T\).
\item
  For the matrix \[
  X=
  \begin{bmatrix}
  1&1&0\\
  1&0&1\\
  0&1&1
  \end{bmatrix},
  \] compute \(XX^T\) and the cosine similarity matrix.
\item
  Suppose \(X_k=U_k\Sigma_kV_k^T\). Show that \(X_kV_k=U_k\Sigma_k\).
\item
  Let \(q\in R^d\) be a query vector. Derive the latent query coordinate
  \(z_q=q^TV_k\) and the latent score \(s_i=z_i^Tz_q\).
\item
  If \(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_r\) are the singular values of \(X\),
  compute the fraction of Frobenius energy captured by the first \(k\)
  components.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Computational exercises}\label{computational-exercises-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Add three new documents to the corpus and recompute the TF-IDF matrix.
\item
  Compare search rankings using counts, TF-IDF, and LSA with \(k=2\).
\item
  Plot the singular values of the document-term matrix.
\item
  Remove common words such as ``models'' and ``language'' and observe
  how the retrieval rankings change.
\item
  Replace cosine similarity with Euclidean distance after row
  normalization. What changes?
\item
  Try \(k=1,2,3,4\) for LSA retrieval. Which value gives the most
  sensible ranking for the sample query?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Mini-project: a small mathematical search
engine}\label{mini-project-a-small-mathematical-search-engine-1}

Build a small search engine for a focused corpus, such as course
descriptions, research abstracts, advising FAQs, or textbook chapter
summaries.

Your report should include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  the tokenization rule;
\item
  the vocabulary size;
\item
  the definition of the document-term matrix;
\item
  the weighting scheme;
\item
  the similarity measure;
\item
  a comparison between TF-IDF search and LSA search;
\item
  at least one failure case;
\item
  a mathematical explanation of the failure case.
\end{enumerate}

A strong project should include both formulas and code. The goal is not
only to produce rankings, but to explain the geometry behind the
rankings.

\section{Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-3}

The corresponding Python lab should guide students through:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  constructing document-term matrices from scratch;
\item
  implementing cosine similarity;
\item
  building a TF-IDF search engine;
\item
  computing the SVD of a weighted corpus matrix;
\item
  visualizing document embeddings in two dimensions;
\item
  comparing raw and low-rank retrieval;
\item
  writing a short mathematical interpretation of the results.
\end{itemize}

This chapter is the bridge from count-based NLP to embedding-based NLP.
In the next chapter, we move from document vectors to word embeddings,
where the goal is to learn dense vector representations of individual
tokens from co-occurrence structure.

\chapter{Word Embeddings}\label{word-embeddings}

Distributional semantics, matrix factorization, skip-gram models, and
geometry of meaning

\hfill\break

In Chapter 7, a document was represented as a vector in vocabulary
space. The coordinates of that vector were counts, TF-IDF weights, or
low-rank latent coordinates derived from a document-term matrix. In this
chapter we reverse the viewpoint: instead of representing documents by
words, we represent \textbf{words themselves} as vectors.

A word embedding is a map from a discrete vocabulary into a continuous
vector space. This is one of the central mathematical ideas in modern
NLP. It converts symbolic data into geometric data: words have lengths,
angles, neighborhoods, projections, and directions. Once words become
vectors, we can use linear algebra, probability, optimization, and
geometry to study meaning.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-7}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  define a word embedding as a function \(e:V\to R^m\);
\item
  explain how one-hot vectors differ from dense embeddings;
\item
  construct co-occurrence matrices from a corpus;
\item
  interpret the distributional hypothesis mathematically;
\item
  compute empirical probabilities for word-context pairs;
\item
  define pointwise mutual information and positive PMI;
\item
  connect matrix factorization to word embeddings;
\item
  derive the skip-gram softmax objective;
\item
  explain negative sampling as a computational approximation;
\item
  state the GloVe weighted least-squares objective;
\item
  analyze embedding geometry using norms, cosine similarity, and
  analogies;
\item
  implement toy embeddings from scratch in Python;
\item
  visualize embedding spaces with Plotly and Plotly.js;
\item
  use AI tools to critique embedding assumptions and detect possible
  bias.
\end{enumerate}

Throughout this chapter, \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\) denotes a finite
vocabulary, \(d=|V|\) is the vocabulary size, and \(m\) is the embedding
dimension, usually with \(m\ll d\).

\section{From symbols to vectors}\label{from-symbols-to-vectors}

A token is a discrete object. If the vocabulary is

\[
V=\{v_1,v_2,\ldots,v_d\},
\]

then a token \(v_j\) can be represented by the one-hot vector

\[
\delta_j=(0,\ldots,0,1,0,\ldots,0)^T\in R^d,
\]

where the \(1\) occurs in position \(j\). This representation is exact
but not semantic. For \(i\neq j\),

\[
\delta_i^T\delta_j=0.
\]

Thus every pair of distinct words is equally dissimilar. The words
``cat'' and ``dog'' are no closer than ``cat'' and ``gradient''.

A word embedding replaces the one-hot representation with a dense
vector:

\[
e:V\longrightarrow R^m,
\qquad
v_j\longmapsto e_j.
\]

Equivalently, the embedding is stored in a matrix

\[
E=\begin{bmatrix}
--- & e_1^T & ---\\
--- & e_2^T & ---\\
& \vdots & \\
--- & e_d^T & ---
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{d\times m}.
\]

The embedding of token \(v_j\) is the \(j\)th row of \(E\):

\[
e_j=E_{j:}\in R^m.
\]

If a token is encoded as a one-hot vector \(\delta_j\), then the lookup
operation can be written as matrix multiplication:

\[
\delta_j^T E=e_j^T.
\]

\textbf{Embedding lookup.} A word embedding matrix
\(E\in R^{d\times m}\) converts a one-hot token vector into a dense
vector:

\[
\delta_j^TE=e_j^T.
\]

This is why an embedding layer in a neural network is mathematically a
trainable matrix lookup.

\section{Why dense embeddings are
useful}\label{why-dense-embeddings-are-useful}

One-hot vectors live in a high-dimensional coordinate system where each
coordinate is an arbitrary vocabulary index. Dense embeddings live in a
lower-dimensional representation space in which geometry is learned from
data.

The central hope is that semantic or syntactic relationships become
geometric relationships:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  similar words have small distance or large cosine similarity;
\item
  related categories form clusters;
\item
  some relationships correspond approximately to directions;
\item
  analogy tasks can be expressed using vector arithmetic;
\item
  downstream models can use continuous features rather than sparse
  symbolic indicators.
\end{itemize}

This does not mean that embeddings contain ``true meaning.'' It means
that the training objective forces words with similar statistical
behavior to receive related vectors.

\section{The distributional
hypothesis}\label{the-distributional-hypothesis}

The guiding principle behind many word embedding methods is the
\textbf{distributional hypothesis}:

\begin{quote}
Words that occur in similar contexts tend to have related meanings.
\end{quote}

Mathematically, each word \(w\in V\) can be described by a context
distribution

\[
P(C=c\mid W=w),
\]

where \(C\) is a random context word. If two words \(w\) and \(w'\) have
similar conditional context distributions, then they should have nearby
representations.

One way to state this is:

\[
P(C=\cdot\mid W=w)\approx P(C=\cdot\mid W=w')
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
e(w)\approx e(w').
\]

This is a statistical assumption, not a theorem. It is often useful, but
it can fail when words have multiple meanings, when corpora are biased,
or when context alone is not enough.

\textbf{Distributional semantics.} A word embedding is a
finite-dimensional summary of a word's empirical context distribution.
The geometry of the embedding space reflects statistical regularities in
the corpus.

\section{Co-occurrence matrices}\label{co-occurrence-matrices}

Let a corpus be represented as a token sequence

\[
w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T,
\qquad w_t\in V.
\]

Choose a context window size \(h\geq 1\). For each position \(t\), the
context of \(w_t\) is the set of nearby positions

\[
\{s:1\leq s\leq T,\ 0<|s-t|\leq h\}.
\]

The word-context co-occurrence matrix is

\[
C\in R_{\geq 0}^{d\times d},
\]

where

\[
C_{ij}=\#\{(t,s):w_t=v_i,\ w_s=v_j,\ 0<|s-t|\leq h\}.
\]

Rows correspond to center words, and columns correspond to context
words. The row

\[
C_{i:}
\]

is a count-based description of the contexts in which word \(v_i\)
appears.

The simplest possible word representation is to use the row vector
\(C_{i:}\) itself. This is usually high-dimensional and sparse.
Embedding methods compress or transform this information into
lower-dimensional vectors.

\section{Empirical probabilities}\label{empirical-probabilities}

Let

\[
N=\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^d C_{ij}
\]

be the total number of observed word-context pairs. The empirical joint
distribution is

\[
\widehat P(W=v_i,C=v_j)=\frac{C_{ij}}{N}.
\]

The marginal distributions are

\[
\widehat P(W=v_i)=\frac{\sum_j C_{ij}}{N},
\qquad
\widehat P(C=v_j)=\frac{\sum_i C_{ij}}{N}.
\]

The empirical conditional distribution of contexts given a word is

\[
\widehat P(C=v_j\mid W=v_i)
=
\frac{C_{ij}}{\sum_{k=1}^d C_{ik}}.
\]

This conditional distribution is the probabilistic object that the
embedding should summarize.

\section{PMI and PPMI}\label{pmi-and-ppmi}

A raw co-occurrence count is not enough. Common words such as ``the'' or
``and'' co-occur with many words simply because they are frequent.
Pointwise mutual information corrects for marginal frequency.

The empirical pointwise mutual information of a word-context pair is

\[
\operatorname{PMI}(v_i,v_j)
=
\log\frac{\widehat P(W=v_i,C=v_j)}
{\widehat P(W=v_i)\widehat P(C=v_j)}.
\]

Equivalently, using counts,

\[
\operatorname{PMI}(v_i,v_j)
=
\log\frac{C_{ij}N}{\left(\sum_k C_{ik}\right)\left(\sum_k C_{kj}\right)},
\]

when \(C_{ij}>0\).

Positive PMI keeps only positive association:

\[
\operatorname{PPMI}(v_i,v_j)=\max\{\operatorname{PMI}(v_i,v_j),0\}.
\]

A positive PMI value means that the pair occurs more often than expected
under independence. A negative PMI value means that the pair occurs less
often than expected under independence.

\textbf{PMI compares joint occurrence with independence.}

\[
\operatorname{PMI}(w,c)=\log\frac{P(w,c)}{P(w)P(c)}.
\]

If \(W\) and \(C\) were independent, then \(P(w,c)=P(w)P(c)\) and the
PMI would be \(0\).

\section{Matrix factorization
viewpoint}\label{matrix-factorization-viewpoint}

Let \(M\in R^{d\times d}\) be a transformed co-occurrence matrix, such
as a PPMI matrix. A low-rank embedding seeks matrices

\[
E\in R^{d\times m},
\qquad
F\in R^{d\times m},
\]

such that

\[
M\approx EF^T.
\]

Here \(E\) contains word embeddings and \(F\) contains context
embeddings. The approximation says

\[
M_{ij}\approx e_i^Tf_j.
\]

Thus the inner product between a word vector and a context vector
approximates a transformed co-occurrence statistic.

A classical way to obtain such embeddings is the singular value
decomposition. Suppose

\[
M=U\Sigma V^T.
\]

The rank-\(m\) approximation is

\[
M_m=U_m\Sigma_m V_m^T.
\]

A common embedding choice is

\[
E=U_m\Sigma_m^{1/2},
\qquad
F=V_m\Sigma_m^{1/2}.
\]

Then

\[
EF^T=U_m\Sigma_mV_m^T=M_m.
\]

This directly connects word embeddings to the SVD theory from Chapter 7.

\section{Prediction viewpoint}\label{prediction-viewpoint}

Matrix factorization is one route to embeddings. Neural prediction is
another. In the prediction viewpoint, embeddings are learned because
they help predict nearby words.

Let \(w\) be a center word and \(c\) be a context word. The skip-gram
model assigns

\[
P_\theta(c\mid w)=
\frac{\exp(u_c^Tv_w)}
{\sum_{c'\in V}\exp(u_{c'}^Tv_w)},
\]

where

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(v_w\in R^m\) is the input embedding of the center word;
\item
  \(u_c\in R^m\) is the output embedding of the context word;
\item
  \(\theta\) denotes all embedding parameters.
\end{itemize}

Given observed word-context pairs \(D=\{(w_\ell,c_\ell)\}_{\ell=1}^N\),
the negative log-likelihood is

\[
L(\theta)
=-\sum_{\ell=1}^N \log P_\theta(c_\ell\mid w_\ell).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
L(\theta)
=\sum_{\ell=1}^N
\left[
- u_{c_\ell}^Tv_{w_\ell}
+\log\sum_{c'\in V}\exp(u_{c'}^Tv_{w_\ell})
\right].
\]

This is a multiclass cross-entropy objective.

\section{Gradient of the skip-gram softmax
loss}\label{gradient-of-the-skip-gram-softmax-loss}

For one observed pair \((w,c)\), define scores

\[
z_k=u_k^Tv_w,
\qquad k=1,\ldots,d,
\]

and probabilities

\[
p_k=\frac{\exp(z_k)}{\sum_{r=1}^d\exp(z_r)}.
\]

The single-pair loss is

\[
\ell(w,c)=-\log p_c.
\]

The gradient with respect to a score is

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_k}=p_k-1_{\{k=c\}}.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial v_w}
=\sum_{k=1}^d (p_k-1_{\{k=c\}})u_k,
\]

and

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial u_k}
=(p_k-1_{\{k=c\}})v_w.
\]

This formula shows the learning mechanism:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the true context vector \(u_c\) is pulled closer to \(v_w\);
\item
  all other context vectors are pushed away in proportion to their
  predicted probabilities;
\item
  the update is global because the softmax denominator sums over the
  whole vocabulary.
\end{itemize}

\section{Negative sampling}\label{negative-sampling}

The full softmax is expensive when \(d\) is large. Negative sampling
replaces the multiclass softmax problem by several binary classification
problems.

For an observed positive pair \((w,c)\) and negative samples
\(n_1,\ldots,n_K\), the negative-sampling objective for one pair is
often written as

\[
\ell_{\text{NS}}(w,c)
= -\log\sigma(u_c^Tv_w)
-\sum_{r=1}^K\log\sigma(-u_{n_r}^Tv_w),
\]

where

\[
\sigma(x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}.
\]

The positive pair is encouraged to have a large inner product, while
sampled negative pairs are encouraged to have small inner products.

Negative sampling changes the training objective. It is not merely a
computational trick for the same loss. It learns vectors by asking
whether a word-context pair came from the corpus or from a noise
distribution.

\section{GloVe as weighted least
squares}\label{glove-as-weighted-least-squares}

GloVe is another influential embedding method. It begins with a
co-occurrence matrix \(C\) and learns word vectors \(v_i\), context
vectors \(u_j\), and biases \(a_i,b_j\) by minimizing

\[
J=
\sum_{i=1}^d\sum_{j=1}^d
f(C_{ij})
\left(v_i^Tu_j+a_i+b_j-\log C_{ij}\right)^2.
\]

The weight function \(f(C_{ij})\) reduces the influence of rare and
extremely frequent pairs. The model tries to make inner products
approximate log co-occurrence counts, up to additive word and context
biases.

The mathematical form is a weighted matrix approximation problem. Unlike
ordinary SVD, it does not assign equal weight to every matrix entry.

\section{Embedding geometry}\label{embedding-geometry}

Once words have vectors, we can analyze them geometrically. The most
common similarity measure is cosine similarity:

\[
\operatorname{cos}(e_i,e_j)
=
\frac{e_i^Te_j}{\lVert e_i\rVert_2\lVert e_j\rVert_2}.
\]

Nearest-neighbor search asks for

\[
\operatorname{NN}(w)=\arg\max_{v\in V,\ v\neq w}\operatorname{cos}(e(w),e(v)).
\]

Analogy tasks use vector arithmetic. Given words \(a,b,c\), the
classical query

\[
a:b\approx c:?
\]

is approximated by

\[
\hat d
=
\arg\max_{w\in V\setminus\{a,b,c\}}
\operatorname{cos}\left(e(w),e(b)-e(a)+e(c)\right).
\]

A famous informal example is

\[
e(\text{king})-e(\text{man})+e(\text{woman})\approx e(\text{queen}).
\]

This behavior is not guaranteed by the definition of an embedding. It
emerges only when the training data and objective organize certain
relationships approximately as linear directions.

\section{What embeddings do not
solve}\label{what-embeddings-do-not-solve}

Word embeddings are powerful, but they have limitations.

First, a single vector per word cannot represent different meanings of
the same word. The word ``bank'' may refer to a financial institution or
the side of a river. A static embedding averages across contexts.

Second, embeddings can encode social and historical biases present in
the training corpus. Similarity in the embedding space reflects patterns
in data, not moral or factual correctness.

Third, nearest neighbors can be unstable in high dimensions. Very
frequent words, anisotropy, and hubness can distort neighborhood
structure.

Fourth, word embeddings alone do not model word order. They represent
tokens, not full contextual syntax.

These limitations motivate contextual embeddings and transformers in
later chapters.

\chapter{Python examples}\label{python-examples}

We now build a small embedding pipeline from scratch. The examples are
intentionally small so that every mathematical object is visible.

\section{Word-context pairs}\label{word-context-pairs}

The following function constructs center-context pairs using a symmetric
window of radius \(h\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ make\_pairs(tokenized\_docs, window}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    pairs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized\_docs:}
\NormalTok{        ids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [word\_to\_id[w] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc]}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ t, center }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(ids):}
\NormalTok{            left }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, t }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ window)}
\NormalTok{            right }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(ids), t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ window }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
            \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ s }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(left, right):}
                \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ s }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ t:}
\NormalTok{                    pairs.append((center, ids[s]))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pairs}

\NormalTok{pairs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ make\_pairs(tokenized, window}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"number of word{-}context pairs:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(pairs))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{([(id\_to\_word[i], id\_to\_word[j]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ pairs[:}\DecValTok{12}\NormalTok{]])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cooccurrence\_matrix(pairs, d):}
\NormalTok{    C }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((d, d), dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ pairs:}
\NormalTok{        C[i, j] }\OperatorTok{+=} \FloatTok{1.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ C}

\NormalTok{C }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ cooccurrence\_matrix(pairs, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}

\NormalTok{C\_df.iloc[:}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, :}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{]}

\section{PPMI matrix}\label{ppmi-matrix}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ ppmi\_matrix(C, eps}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    total }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ C.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\NormalTok{    row\_sum }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ C.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    col\_sum }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ C.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    expected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_sum }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ col\_sum }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(total, eps)}
    \ControlFlowTok{with}\NormalTok{ np.errstate(divide}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"ignore"}\NormalTok{, invalid}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"ignore"}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{        pmi }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log((C }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ total }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ eps) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (row\_sum }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ col\_sum }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ eps))}
\NormalTok{    pmi[C }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(pmi, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{M }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ppmi\_matrix(C)}
\NormalTok{M\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(M, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab)}
\NormalTok{M\_df.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{).iloc[:}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, :}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{]}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{SVD embeddings from PPMI}\label{svd-embeddings-from-ppmi}

We factor the PPMI matrix and keep the first \(m\) singular directions.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ svd\_embeddings(M, m}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    U, s, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(M, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U[:, :m] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(s[:m])}
\NormalTok{    F }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Vt[:m, :].T }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(s[:m])}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ E, F, s}

\NormalTok{E2, F2, singular\_values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ svd\_embeddings(M, m}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{emb\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(E2, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\StringTok{"z1"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"z2"}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{emb\_df.head()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Nearest neighbors}\label{nearest-neighbors}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ row\_normalize(X, eps}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    norms }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(norms, eps)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ nearest\_neighbors(word, E, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    idx }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ word\_to\_id[word]}
\NormalTok{    En }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_normalize(E)}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ En }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ En[idx]}
\NormalTok{    order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{scores)}
\NormalTok{    rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ order:}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ j }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ idx:}
\NormalTok{            rows.append((id\_to\_word[j], }\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(scores[j])))}
        \ControlFlowTok{if} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(rows) }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ k:}
            \ControlFlowTok{break}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(rows, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cosine\_similarity"}\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{nearest\_neighbors(}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, E2, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Neighbors from raw co{-}occurrence rows"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{display(nearest\_neighbors(}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, E2, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{))}

Raw co-occurrence and PPMI-SVD embeddings can give different neighbors
because they encode different geometry. Raw counts emphasize frequency;
PPMI emphasizes association beyond chance; SVD compresses the result
into a low-dimensional subspace.

\section{A tiny skip-gram softmax
calculation}\label{a-tiny-skip-gram-softmax-calculation}

The next code implements the skip-gram probability for one center word.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{m }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4}

\NormalTok{V\_in }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_out }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, m))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(z):}
\NormalTok{    z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(z)}
\NormalTok{    ez }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(z)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ ez }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ ez.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ skipgram\_probs(center\_word):}
\NormalTok{    i }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ word\_to\_id[center\_word]}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U\_out }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V\_in[i]}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(scores)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{: vocab, }\StringTok{"probability"}\NormalTok{: probs\}).sort\_values(}
        \StringTok{"probability"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}
\NormalTok{    )}

\NormalTok{skipgram\_probs(}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{).head(}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}

& word & probability \\

\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

At initialization, the probabilities are almost uniform because the
random inner products are small. Training changes the vectors so
observed context words receive higher probability.

\section{One negative-sampling
update}\label{one-negative-sampling-update}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(x):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \FloatTok{1.0} \OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\FloatTok{1.0} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.exp(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ negative\_sampling\_step(V\_in, U\_out, center, positive, negatives, lr}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    i }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ word\_to\_id[center]}
\NormalTok{    j }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ word\_to\_id[positive]}
\NormalTok{    neg\_ids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [word\_to\_id[w] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ negatives]}

\NormalTok{    v }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ V\_in[i].copy()}

    \CommentTok{\# Positive pair gradient for {-}log sigmoid(u\_j\^{}T v)}
\NormalTok{    score\_pos }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U\_out[j] }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ v}
\NormalTok{    grad\_v }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (sigmoid(score\_pos) }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ U\_out[j]}
\NormalTok{    grad\_u\_pos }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (sigmoid(score\_pos) }\OperatorTok{{-}} \FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ v}

    \CommentTok{\# Negative pair gradients for {-}log sigmoid({-}u\_n\^{}T v)}
\NormalTok{    grad\_u\_negs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ n }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ neg\_ids:}
\NormalTok{        score\_neg }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U\_out[n] }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ v}
\NormalTok{        grad\_v }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(score\_neg) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ U\_out[n]}
\NormalTok{        grad\_u\_negs.append((n, sigmoid(score\_neg) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ v))}

\NormalTok{    V\_in[i] }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_v}
\NormalTok{    U\_out[j] }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_u\_pos}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ n, grad\_u }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ grad\_u\_negs:}
\NormalTok{        U\_out[n] }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_u}

    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ V\_in, U\_out}

\NormalTok{center }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"language"}
\NormalTok{positive }\OperatorTok{=} \StringTok{"models"}
\NormalTok{negatives }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"algebra"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"matrices"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"singular"}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{before }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U\_out[word\_to\_id[positive]] }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V\_in[word\_to\_id[center]]}
\NormalTok{V\_in, U\_out }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ negative\_sampling\_step(V\_in, U\_out, center, positive, negatives)}
\NormalTok{after }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ U\_out[word\_to\_id[positive]] }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V\_in[word\_to\_id[center]]}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"positive inner product before:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(before), }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"positive inner product after: "}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(after), }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
positive inner product before: -0.0051
positive inner product after:  -0.0043
\end{verbatim}

The update tends to increase the inner product of the observed pair and
decrease the inner products of sampled negative pairs.

\chapter{Interactive HTML: embedding analogy
explorer}\label{interactive-html-embedding-analogy-explorer}

Now define a target vector depending on a scalar \(\alpha\):

\[
z(\alpha)=e(\text{king})-\alpha e(\text{man})+\alpha e(\text{woman}).
\]

When \(\alpha=1\), this is the classical analogy vector

\[
e(\text{king})-e(\text{man})+e(\text{woman}).
\]

This interactive is deliberately idealized. Real embeddings are
high-dimensional, noisy, and trained from data. Nevertheless, the same
vector operation and cosine nearest-neighbor rule are used.

\chapter{Worked example: PPMI by
hand}\label{worked-example-ppmi-by-hand}

Suppose a tiny corpus produces the following co-occurrence counts:

\[
C=
\begin{bmatrix}
10 & 2\\
1 & 7
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The total count is

\[
N=10+2+1+7=20.
\]

For entry \((1,1)\),

\[
P(W=1,C=1)=\frac{10}{20}=0.5,
\]

while

\[
P(W=1)=\frac{12}{20}=0.6,
\qquad
P(C=1)=\frac{11}{20}=0.55.
\]

Thus

\[
\operatorname{PMI}(1,1)
=\log\frac{0.5}{0.6\cdot 0.55}
=\log(1.515\ldots)>0.
\]

The pair \((1,1)\) occurs more often than expected under independence.

For entry \((1,2)\),

\[
P(W=1,C=2)=\frac{2}{20}=0.1,
\]

while

\[
P(W=1)P(C=2)=\frac{12}{20}\cdot\frac{9}{20}=0.27.
\]

Therefore

\[
\operatorname{PMI}(1,2)=\log\frac{0.1}{0.27}<0,
\]

and the PPMI value is set to zero.

\chapter{AI-assisted learning
components}\label{ai-assisted-learning-components}

AI tools can help students explore word embeddings, but they should be
used as mathematical assistants rather than authorities.

\section{Prompt 1: explain an embedding method
mathematically}\label{prompt-1-explain-an-embedding-method-mathematically}

Use an AI assistant to answer:

\begin{quote}
Explain the skip-gram model as a maximum likelihood problem. Define the
vocabulary, the input embedding matrix, the output embedding matrix, the
softmax probability, and the negative log-likelihood. Avoid
implementation details until the mathematical objective is clear.
\end{quote}

Then check whether the answer includes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a conditional probability \(P(c\mid w)\);
\item
  inner products between word and context vectors;
\item
  a softmax denominator over the vocabulary;
\item
  a sum over observed word-context pairs;
\item
  a clear distinction between input and output embeddings.
\end{itemize}

\section{Prompt 2: audit a nearest-neighbor
result}\label{prompt-2-audit-a-nearest-neighbor-result}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
I trained word embeddings and found the nearest neighbors of the word
``model''. How can I tell whether the neighbors reflect semantics,
syntax, frequency effects, or corpus bias? Give a mathematical
checklist.
\end{quote}

A good answer should mention cosine similarity, vector norms, word
frequency, training corpus, context window, and the difference between
association and truth.

\section{Prompt 3: derive the
gradient}\label{prompt-3-derive-the-gradient}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
For the skip-gram softmax loss \(\ell(w,c)=-\log P(c\mid w)\), derive
\(\partial \ell/\partial v_w\) and explain the sign of the update.
\end{quote}

Then compare the result with the gradient derived earlier in this
chapter.

\section{Prompt 4: detect hidden
assumptions}\label{prompt-4-detect-hidden-assumptions}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
What assumptions are hidden in the distributional hypothesis? Give
examples where words appear in similar contexts but should not be
considered semantically equivalent.
\end{quote}

This encourages students to connect mathematical modeling assumptions
with linguistic and social limitations.

\chapter{Exercises}\label{exercises-7}

\section{Conceptual exercises}\label{conceptual-exercises-5}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Explain why one-hot vectors do not encode semantic similarity.
\item
  What information is contained in a row of a co-occurrence matrix?
\item
  Why does PMI correct for word frequency better than raw co-occurrence
  counts?
\item
  What is the difference between a word embedding matrix and a context
  embedding matrix?
\item
  In what sense is GloVe a matrix approximation method?
\item
  Why can static word embeddings struggle with polysemy?
\item
  Why might cosine similarity be preferred over Euclidean distance for
  word embeddings?
\item
  What does it mean for an analogy to be represented by a linear
  direction?
\end{enumerate}

\section{Mathematical exercises}\label{mathematical-exercises-4}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Let \(E\in R^{d\times m}\) and \(\delta_j\in R^d\) be the \(j\)th
  one-hot vector. Prove that \(\delta_j^TE\) returns the \(j\)th row of
  \(E\).
\item
  Let \(C\) be a co-occurrence matrix. Derive the empirical joint and
  marginal distributions from \(C\).
\item
  Show that \(\operatorname{PMI}(w,c)=0\) when \(W\) and \(C\) are
  independent.
\item
  Let \(M=U\Sigma V^T\) and define \(E=U_m\Sigma_m^{1/2}\) and
  \(F=V_m\Sigma_m^{1/2}\). Show that \(EF^T\) equals the rank-\(m\)
  truncated SVD approximation.
\item
  Derive the gradient of the skip-gram softmax loss with respect to the
  center-word embedding.
\item
  For the negative-sampling loss, compute the derivative of
  \(-\log\sigma(u_c^Tv_w)\) with respect to \(v_w\).
\item
  Let \(x,y\in R^m\) be nonzero. Prove that cosine similarity is
  invariant under positive rescaling of either vector.
\item
  Suppose \(e(b)-e(a)\approx e(d)-e(c)\). Explain why this supports the
  analogy \(a:b\approx c:d\).
\end{enumerate}

\section{Computational exercises}\label{computational-exercises-2}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Change the context window size in the Python code from \(h=2\) to
  \(h=1\) and \(h=3\). Compare the co-occurrence matrices.
\item
  Compute PPMI embeddings with dimensions \(m=2,3,5\). How do nearest

\item

  geometry.
\item
  Implement a function that returns the top \(k\) word pairs with

\item
  Train the toy negative-sampling model for several epochs over all

\item
  Use a larger text sample and compare embeddings trained from different

\item
  Investigate whether frequent words have larger embedding norms in your

\item
  Create a Plotly visualization that lets the user choose a word and

\end{enumerate}

\chapter{Mini-project: build and audit toy word
embeddings}\label{mini-project-build-and-audit-toy-word-embeddings}

Choose a small corpus related to one domain, such as mathematics course
descriptions, university advising pages, research abstracts, or textbook
chapter summaries. Build word embeddings from scratch using the
following pipeline:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  tokenize the corpus;
\item
  build a vocabulary;
\item
  construct a word-context co-occurrence matrix;
\item
  compute a PPMI matrix;
\item
  compute SVD embeddings;
\item
  find nearest neighbors for selected words;
\item
  visualize embeddings in two dimensions;
\item
  write a short mathematical audit of the results.
\end{enumerate}

Your audit should answer:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  What does a row of the co-occurrence matrix mean?
\item
  What does PMI emphasize?
\item
  How much information is lost when projecting to two dimensions?
\item
  Which nearest neighbors are sensible?
\item
  Which nearest neighbors are artifacts of the corpus?
\item
  What would change if the corpus were larger?
\end{itemize}

\chapter{Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-4}

The computer lab for this chapter should guide students through a
complete word-embedding workflow:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  build co-occurrence matrices;
\item
  compute empirical probabilities;
\item
  compute PMI and PPMI;
\item
  obtain SVD embeddings;
\item
  implement nearest-neighbor search;
\item

\chapter{Summary}\label{summary}

Word embeddings transform discrete tokens into continuous vectors.
Mathematically, an embedding is a map

\[
e:V\to R^m.
\]

Count-based methods begin with co-occurrence matrices and transform them
using PMI, PPMI, and matrix factorization. Prediction-based methods
learn embeddings by optimizing objectives such as skip-gram softmax or
negative sampling. In both cases, the resulting vectors encode
statistical regularities from the corpus.

The central message is:

\begin{quote}
Word meaning is not inserted into the vectors by hand. It is induced
from patterns of co-occurrence, prediction, and optimization.
\end{quote}

This chapter completes the bridge from classical vector-space models to
modern neural NLP. The next chapter studies the geometry of embedding
spaces more systematically, including clustering, visualization,
anisotropy, and bias.

\chapter{Geometry of Embedding
Spaces}\label{geometry-of-embedding-spaces}

Similarity, dimension reduction, clustering, and high-dimensional
caution

\hfill\break

Word embeddings turn tokens into points in a vector space. Once language
objects become vectors, NLP inherits the language of \textbf{geometry}:
distances, angles, projections, subspaces, neighborhoods, clusters, and
directions. This chapter develops the geometry of embedding spaces
carefully, with emphasis on the mathematical assumptions behind
similarity search and visualization.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-8}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Treat a collection of word or sentence embeddings as a point cloud
  \(X \in R^{n \times m}\).
\item
  Compare inner-product similarity, cosine similarity, and Euclidean
  distance.
\item
  Explain why nearest-neighbor lists depend on normalization and metric
  choice.
\item
  Derive PCA from the singular value decomposition of a centered
  embedding matrix.
\item
  Interpret low-dimensional embedding visualizations responsibly.
\item
  State the \(k\)-means objective and understand clustering as an
  optimization problem.
\item
  Describe anisotropy, hubness, and distance concentration in
  high-dimensional spaces.
\item
  Use linear directions to study interpretable attributes and possible
  bias in embeddings.
\end{itemize}

\section{9.1 Why geometry matters in
NLP}\label{why-geometry-matters-in-nlp}

In earlier chapters, a word embedding was introduced as a map

\[
E:V \longrightarrow R^m,
\]

where \(V\) is a vocabulary and \(m\) is the embedding dimension. For a
token \(w \in V\), the vector \(E(w)\) is often written as
\(e_w \in R^m\).

If \(V = \{w_1,\dots,w_n\}\), the embedding model produces a matrix

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
- & e_{w_1}^T & -\\
- & e_{w_2}^T & -\\
& \vdots & \\
- & e_{w_n}^T & -
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{n\times m}.
\]

The rows of \(X\) form a finite point cloud in \(R^m\). Many NLP
operations can then be written geometrically.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 2\tabcolsep) * \real{0.5000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
NLP question
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Geometric formulation
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Which words are similar to \texttt{king}? & Find nearest neighbors of
\(e_{king}\). \\
Which documents match a query? & Find vectors with large inner product
or cosine similarity to the query vector. \\
Are topics separated? & Look for clusters or low-dimensional
structure. \\
What direction represents an attribute? & Estimate a vector direction
\(b\) and project embeddings onto \(b\). \\
Can we visualize embeddings? & Project \(R^m\) to \(R^2\) using PCA,
SVD, or another map. \\
\end{longtable}
}

The important point is that geometry is not merely a visualization tool.
It is part of the model. A statement such as ``these words are close''
is incomplete until we specify the representation, the metric, and any
preprocessing such as centering or normalization.

\textbf{Core viewpoint.} An embedding space is a finite metric or
inner-product structure induced by a representation map. The geometry we
observe is not intrinsic to language alone; it depends on the
construction of \(E\), the training data, the loss function, and the
similarity measure.

\section{9.2 Similarity measures}\label{similarity-measures}

Let \(x,y \in R^m\) be two embedding vectors.

\subsection{Inner product}\label{inner-product}

The inner product is

\[
\langle x,y\rangle = x^T y = \sum_{j=1}^m x_j y_j.
\]

Large inner products favor vectors that point in similar directions and
also have large norms. Therefore inner-product retrieval is sensitive to
vector length.

\subsection{Euclidean distance}\label{euclidean-distance}

The Euclidean distance is

\[
d_2(x,y)=\|x-y\|_2=
\left(\sum_{j=1}^m (x_j-y_j)^2\right)^{1/2}.
\]

Small Euclidean distance means that the vectors are close as points in
\(R^m\). It uses both direction and length.

\subsection{Cosine similarity}\label{cosine-similarity-1}

The cosine similarity is

\[
\cos(x,y)=\frac{x^T y}{\|x\|_2\|y\|_2},
\qquad x\ne 0,\ y\ne 0.
\]

Cosine similarity depends only on the angle between \(x\) and \(y\). It
is invariant under positive rescaling:

\[
\cos(cx,dy)=\cos(x,y),
\qquad c>0,\ d>0.
\]

This is useful when vector length is less meaningful than direction. In
many word and document embedding applications, cosine similarity is
preferred for nearest-neighbor search.

\subsection{Relationship after
normalization}\label{relationship-after-normalization}

Define the normalized vectors

\[
\hat{x}=\frac{x}{\|x\|_2},
\qquad
\hat{y}=\frac{y}{\|y\|_2}.
\]

Then

\[
\|\hat{x}-\hat{y}\|_2^2
=
\|\hat{x}\|_2^2+
\|\hat{y}\|_2^2-2\hat{x}^T\hat{y}
=2-2\cos(x,y).
\]

Thus, for normalized embeddings, minimizing Euclidean distance is
equivalent to maximizing cosine similarity.

\textbf{Metric choice matters.} The nearest neighbors of a word can
change when we switch from inner product to cosine similarity or
Euclidean distance. This is not a numerical accident. It reflects
different mathematical assumptions about whether vector length carries
semantic information.

\section{9.3 Nearest neighbors as an optimization
problem}\label{nearest-neighbors-as-an-optimization-problem}

Given embeddings \(e_1,\dots,e_n \in R^m\) and a query vector
\(q \in R^m\), nearest-neighbor search solves

\[
\operatorname{NN}_s(q)
=
\arg\max_{1\le i\le n} s(q,e_i),
\]

where \(s\) is a similarity function such as inner product or cosine
similarity. Equivalently, using a distance \(d\),

\[
\operatorname{NN}_d(q)
=
\arg\min_{1\le i\le n} d(q,e_i).
\]

For top-\(k\) retrieval, we return the \(k\) largest scores or the \(k\)
smallest distances.

In matrix form, if \(X\in R^{n\times m}\) stores the candidate
embeddings as rows, inner-product scores are

\[
s = Xq \in R^n.
\]

For cosine similarity, define a row-normalized matrix \(\widehat X\) and
normalized query \(\hat q\). Then

\[
s = \widehat X \hat q.
\]

This simple matrix-vector multiplication is one reason embedding
retrieval is computationally attractive.

\section{9.4 A small geometric example}\label{a-small-geometric-example}

Suppose an embedding model gives the following two-dimensional vectors:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
token & \(x_1\) & \(x_2\) \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
\texttt{cat} & 1.0 & 0.9 \\
\texttt{dog} & 1.1 & 0.8 \\
\texttt{lion} & 1.4 & 1.1 \\
\texttt{car} & -1.0 & -0.8 \\
\texttt{truck} & -1.2 & -0.9 \\
\texttt{bus} & -0.9 & -1.1 \\
\texttt{king} & 0.2 & 1.8 \\
\texttt{queen} & 0.1 & 1.7 \\
\end{longtable}
}

This toy space has three visible regions: animals, vehicles, and
royalty. But even in this simple example, a nearest-neighbor query
depends on whether we use cosine similarity or Euclidean distance. If
two points have similar directions but different magnitudes, cosine and
Euclidean rankings can disagree.

The next interactive example lets you explore this dependence directly.
