\section{9.6 Python example: nearest neighbors from
scratch}\label{python-example-nearest-neighbors-from-scratch}

The following example implements nearest-neighbor search without a
machine learning library. This is useful because it makes the metric
choice explicit.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch09-nearest-neighbors}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{words }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"cat"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"dog"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"lion"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"car"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"truck"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"bus"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"king"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"queen"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.00}\NormalTok{,  }\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.10}\NormalTok{,  }\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.45}\NormalTok{,  }\FloatTok{1.10}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1.00}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1.25}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1.15}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{,  }\FloatTok{1.85}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{,  }\FloatTok{1.70}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cosine\_scores(X, q):}
\NormalTok{    X\_norm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    q\_norm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(q)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ X\_norm }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q\_norm}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ euclidean\_distances(X, q):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ q, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ nearest\_neighbors(query\_word, metric}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"cosine"}\NormalTok{, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    idx }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ words.index(query\_word)}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X[idx]}

    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ metric }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"cosine"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ cosine\_scores(X, q)}
\NormalTok{        order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{values)}
    \ControlFlowTok{elif}\NormalTok{ metric }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"inner"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q}
\NormalTok{        order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{values)}
    \ControlFlowTok{elif}\NormalTok{ metric }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"euclidean"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ euclidean\_distances(X, q)}
\NormalTok{        order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(values)}
    \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{raise} \PreprocessorTok{ValueError}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"metric must be cosine, inner, or euclidean"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{    result }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ order:}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ j }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ idx:}
\NormalTok{            result.append((words[j], }\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(values[j])))}
        \ControlFlowTok{if} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(result) }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ k:}
            \ControlFlowTok{break}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ result}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"cosine:"}\NormalTok{, nearest\_neighbors(}\StringTok{"cat"}\NormalTok{, metric}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"cosine"}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"inner product:"}\NormalTok{, nearest\_neighbors(}\StringTok{"cat"}\NormalTok{, metric}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"inner"}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"euclidean:"}\NormalTok{, nearest\_neighbors(}\StringTok{"cat"}\NormalTok{, metric}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"euclidean"}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
cosine: [('lion', 0.9964891983367161), ('dog', 0.9945949192045226), ('king', 0.7449800754669957)]
inner product: [('lion', 2.44), ('king', 1.8650000000000002), ('dog', 1.82)]
euclidean: [('dog', 0.14142135623730953), ('lion', 0.49244289008980524), ('king', 1.241974234837422)]
\end{verbatim}

The same vectors can produce different neighbor rankings. In a real
embedding model, such differences can affect search results, clustering
results, and qualitative interpretations.

\section{9.7 Centering, normalization, and
anisotropy}\label{centering-normalization-and-anisotropy}

Embedding spaces often have strong global directions. For example, many
vectors may share a large common component. This can make most pairwise
cosine similarities positive and reduce the contrast between meaningful
neighbors and unrelated words.

Let the rows of \(X\in R^{n\times m}\) be embeddings. The sample mean
vector is

\[
\bar{x}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i.
\]

The centered embedding matrix is

\[
X_c = X - {\bf 1}\bar{x}^T,
\]

where \({\bf 1}\in R^n\) is the vector of all ones. Centering removes
the global mean direction.

Row normalization gives

\[
\tilde{x}_i=\frac{x_i}{\|x_i\|_2}.
\]

Depending on the task, one may use raw vectors, centered vectors,
normalized vectors, or centered-and-normalized vectors. These choices
change the geometry.

\textbf{Anisotropy.} A point cloud is anisotropic when its variance is
much larger in some directions than in others. In embedding spaces,
anisotropy can cause a few dominant directions to affect many similarity
computations.

A simple diagnostic is to inspect the singular values of the centered
matrix. If the first few singular values dominate, then much of the
variation lies in a low-dimensional subspace.

\section{9.8 PCA for embedding spaces}\label{pca-for-embedding-spaces}

PCA is a standard method for projecting high-dimensional embeddings to a
lower-dimensional space. It should be understood as a
variance-preserving linear projection, not as a perfect map of semantic
meaning.

Let \(X\in R^{n\times m}\) be the embedding matrix, and let

\[
X_c = X - {\bf 1}\bar{x}^T
\]

be the centered matrix. The sample covariance matrix is

\[
S=\frac{1}{n-1}X_c^T X_c \in R^{m\times m}.
\]

PCA finds orthonormal directions \(v_1,\dots,v_r\) solving

\[
v_1 = \arg\max_{\|v\|_2=1} v^T S v,
\]

and, for \(j>1\),

\[
v_j = \arg\max_{\|v\|_2=1,\ v\perp v_1,\dots,v_{j-1}} v^T S v.
\]

The solutions are eigenvectors of \(S\):

\[
S v_j = \lambda_j v_j,
\qquad
\lambda_1\ge \lambda_2\ge \cdots \ge 0.
\]

Equivalently, use the singular value decomposition

\[
X_c = U\Sigma V^T.
\]

The columns of \(V\) are the principal directions, and the
low-dimensional PCA coordinates are

\[
Z_k = X_c V_k \in R^{n\times k},
\]

where \(V_k=[v_1,\dots,v_k]\).

The fraction of variance explained by the first \(k\) components is

\[
\frac{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_k}{\lambda_1+\cdots+\lambda_m}
=
\frac{\sigma_1^2+\cdots+\sigma_k^2}{\sigma_1^2+\cdots+\sigma_r^2}.
\]

\subsection{PCA is useful but limited}\label{pca-is-useful-but-limited}

PCA preserves large-variance linear structure. It does not necessarily
preserve all nearest-neighbor relationships, clusters, or nonlinear
geometry. A two-dimensional PCA plot is a useful diagnostic, but it
should not be treated as the embedding space itself.

\section{9.9 Python example: PCA by
SVD}\label{python-example-pca-by-svd}

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch09-pca-svd}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\CommentTok{\# Center the toy embedding matrix.}
\NormalTok{X\_centered }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ X.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Singular value decomposition.}
\NormalTok{U, singular\_values, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(X\_centered, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Two{-}dimensional PCA coordinates.}
\NormalTok{Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X\_centered }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Vt[:}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{].T}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Singular values:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(singular\_values, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"PCA coordinates:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, z }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(words, Z):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{word}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}6s\}}\SpecialStringTok{: (}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{z[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{, }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{z[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{)"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Singular values: [3.946 1.522]
PCA coordinates:
   cat: (-0.941, -0.415)
   dog: (-0.928, -0.556)
  lion: (-1.382, -0.635)
   car: ( 1.643,  0.048)
 truck: ( 1.879,  0.177)
   bus: ( 1.849, -0.252)
  king: (-1.166,  0.806)
 queen: (-0.955,  0.827)
\end{verbatim}

For this toy example, the original vectors are already two-dimensional.
In a real embedding model, \(m\) might be 100, 300, 768, or larger. PCA
gives a low-dimensional view of this higher-dimensional structure.

\section{9.10 Clustering embeddings}\label{clustering-embeddings}

Clustering asks whether embedding vectors can be partitioned into groups
with similar geometry. A common model is \(k\)-means clustering.

Given embeddings \(x_1,\dots,x_n\in R^m\), the \(k\)-means objective is

\[
\min_{C_1,\dots,C_k,\ \mu_1,\dots,\mu_k}
\sum_{r=1}^k \sum_{i\in C_r} \|x_i-\mu_r\|_2^2,
\]

where \(C_1,\dots,C_k\) partition \(\{1,
\dots,n\}\) and \(\mu_r\in R^m\) is the centroid of cluster \(r\).

For fixed clusters, the optimal centroid is the sample mean:

\[
\mu_r = \frac{1}{|C_r|}\sum_{i\in C_r} x_i.
\]

The standard \(k\)-means algorithm alternates between two steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Assign each point to the nearest centroid.
\item
  Replace each centroid by the mean of the points assigned to it.
\end{enumerate}

This decreases the objective at every iteration, but it can converge to
a local minimum.

\subsection{Spherical clustering}\label{spherical-clustering}

If cosine similarity is the desired geometry, it is common to normalize
vectors before clustering. Applying \(k\)-means to normalized vectors is
related to spherical clustering, where direction matters more than
length.

\section{\texorpdfstring{9.11 Python example: small \(k\)-means
implementation}{9.11 Python example: small k-means implementation}}\label{python-example-small-k-means-implementation}

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch09-kmeans-from-scratch}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ kmeans(X, k, n\_iter}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{\# Choose initial centroids from the data.}
\NormalTok{    initial }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.choice(X.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{k, replace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    centroids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X[initial].copy()}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n\_iter):}
\NormalTok{        distances }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(X[:, }\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ centroids[}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :, :], axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        labels }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argmin(distances, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{        new\_centroids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ centroids.copy()}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ r }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(k):}
            \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{any}\NormalTok{(labels }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ r):}
\NormalTok{                new\_centroids[r] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X[labels }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ r].mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        centroids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ new\_centroids}

    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ labels, centroids}

\NormalTok{labels, centroids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ kmeans(X, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, n\_iter}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ r }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    cluster\_words }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [w }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w, lab }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(words, labels) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ lab }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ r]}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"cluster }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{r}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{:"}\NormalTok{, cluster\_words)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
cluster 0: ['cat', 'dog', 'lion', 'king', 'queen']
cluster 1: ['car', 'truck']
cluster 2: ['bus']
\end{verbatim}

This example is intentionally small. The goal is not to obtain a perfect
clustering, but to see the mathematical objective behind the algorithm.

\section{9.12 High-dimensional caution: distance
concentration}\label{high-dimensional-caution-distance-concentration}

Embedding spaces used in NLP are often high-dimensional.
High-dimensional geometry can differ sharply from low-dimensional
intuition.

Suppose \(x,y\in R^m\) have independent standard normal coordinates.
Then

\[
\|x-y\|_2^2 = \sum_{j=1}^m (x_j-y_j)^2.
\]

Since \(x_j-y_j\sim N(0,2)\), the expected squared distance is

\[
E\|x-y\|_2^2 = 2m.
\]

As \(m\) grows, distances between random points become increasingly
concentrated around their mean. This can make nearest-neighbor structure
unstable unless the embedding space has meaningful low-dimensional or
clustered structure.

Another related issue is \textbf{hubness}: some points appear as nearest
neighbors of many other points. In embedding spaces, hubs may arise
because of frequency effects, anisotropy, or dominant common directions.

\section{9.13 Python example: distance
concentration}\label{python-example-distance-concentration}

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch09-distance-concentration}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{9}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ distance\_summary(dim, n\_pairs}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{5000}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(n\_pairs, dim))}
\NormalTok{    B }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(n\_pairs, dim))}
\NormalTok{    distances }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(A }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ B, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ distances.mean(), distances.std(), distances.std() }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ distances.mean()}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ dim }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{50}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{300}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{768}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    mean\_d, std\_d, cv }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ distance\_summary(dim)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"dim=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{dim}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}3d\}}\SpecialStringTok{: mean=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{mean\_d}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{, std=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{std\_d}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{, coefficient of variation=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{cv}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
dim=  2: mean=1.788, std=0.928, coefficient of variation=0.519
dim= 10: mean=4.367, std=0.987, coefficient of variation=0.226
dim= 50: mean=9.941, std=1.005, coefficient of variation=0.101
dim=100: mean=14.122, std=0.989, coefficient of variation=0.070
dim=300: mean=24.472, std=0.998, coefficient of variation=0.041
dim=768: mean=39.178, std=0.999, coefficient of variation=0.025
\end{verbatim}

The coefficient of variation decreases as dimension increases. This does
not mean all high-dimensional embeddings are useless. It means that
meaningful structure must come from learned correlations, training
objectives, and data geometry rather than from random high-dimensional
distance alone.

\section{9.14 Semantic directions and analogy
geometry}\label{semantic-directions-and-analogy-geometry}

Embedding spaces often encode attributes as approximate directions. For
example, the analogy pattern

\[
e_{king}-e_{man}+e_{woman}\approx e_{queen}
\]

suggests that the difference vector

\[
b = e_{woman}-e_{man}
\]

may represent a gender-related direction in that embedding space.

More generally, if we have paired examples \((a_i,b_i)\) representing an
attribute change, we can estimate a direction

\[
d = \frac{1}{r}\sum_{i=1}^r (e_{b_i}-e_{a_i}).
\]

Then the scalar projection of a word vector \(x\) onto this direction is

\[
\operatorname{score}_d(x)=\frac{x^T d}{\|d\|_2}.
\]

This score measures how far \(x\) lies along the direction \(d\). Such
directions can be useful for interpretation, but they must be used
carefully: a direction learned from a small set of examples may reflect
social bias, corpus artifacts, or confounding variables.

\textbf{Bias as geometry.} If an embedding space encodes an undesirable
association as a direction or subspace, then downstream models that use
the embeddings may inherit that association. Geometric analysis can
reveal such structure, but it does not automatically solve the ethical
or statistical problem.

\section{9.15 Python example: a toy attribute
direction}\label{python-example-a-toy-attribute-direction}

The example below constructs a toy \textbf{singular-to-plural} direction
and projects each word onto it. This avoids making a social claim and
lets us focus on the linear algebra.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch09-attribute-direction}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{morph\_words }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"cat"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cats"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"dog"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"dogs"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"car"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cars"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"book"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"books"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"city"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cities"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# cat}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# cats}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# dog}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{],   }\CommentTok{\# dogs}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{],  }\CommentTok{\# car}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.85}\NormalTok{],  }\CommentTok{\# cars}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{],  }\CommentTok{\# book}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{],  }\CommentTok{\# books}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.70}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{], }\CommentTok{\# city}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.70}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{], }\CommentTok{\# cities}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{pairs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [(}\StringTok{"cat"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cats"}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{"dog"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"dogs"}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{"car"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cars"}\NormalTok{), (}\StringTok{"book"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"books"}\NormalTok{)]}
\NormalTok{plural\_direction }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(Y.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ singular, plural }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ pairs:}
\NormalTok{    plural\_direction }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ Y[morph\_words.index(plural)] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Y[morph\_words.index(singular)]}
\NormalTok{plural\_direction }\OperatorTok{/=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(pairs)}
\NormalTok{plural\_direction }\OperatorTok{/=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(plural\_direction)}

\NormalTok{scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Y }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ plural\_direction}
\NormalTok{order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{scores)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Projection onto the toy singular{-}to{-}plural direction:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ order:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{morph\_words[j]}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}6s\}}\SpecialStringTok{: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{scores[j]}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Projection onto the toy singular-to-plural direction:
  dogs:  1.003
  cats:  0.958
 books:  0.957
cities:  0.890
  cars:  0.806
  book:  0.106
   dog:  0.101
   cat:  0.057
  city:  0.039
   car: -0.046
\end{verbatim}

In real applications, one should estimate directions from multiple
pairs, test sensitivity to the choice of pairs, and evaluate whether the
direction is stable across corpora and model families.

\section{9.16 Debiasing as projection: a mathematical
sketch}\label{debiasing-as-projection-a-mathematical-sketch}

A simple geometric debiasing operation removes the component of a vector
along a direction \(b\ne 0\).

The projection of \(x\) onto the span of \(b\) is

\[
\operatorname{proj}_b(x)=\frac{x^T b}{b^T b}b.
\]

The component orthogonal to \(b\) is

\[
x_{\perp}=x-\operatorname{proj}_b(x).
\]

This operation guarantees

\[
x_{\perp}^T b = 0.
\]

However, this does not guarantee that all bias has been removed. Bias
may live in a higher-dimensional subspace, in nonlinear structure, or in
downstream training data. Projection is a useful mathematical tool, but
it is not a complete social or statistical solution.

\section{9.17 Static versus contextual embedding
geometry}\label{static-versus-contextual-embedding-geometry}

The previous chapter focused mostly on static embeddings, where each
word type has one vector:

\[
E:V\to R^m.
\]

Modern transformer models produce contextual embeddings. A token's
vector depends on the full input sequence:

\[
H_t = F_t(w_1,\dots,w_T) \in R^m.
\]

Thus the same word can have different vectors in different contexts. For
example, \texttt{bank} in ``river bank'' and \texttt{bank} in ``savings
bank'' may have different contextual embeddings.

The geometry of contextual embeddings is therefore a geometry of token
occurrences rather than only word types. The data matrix may contain
many rows for the same word in different contexts:

\[
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
- & H_{t_1}^{(1)T} & -\\
- & H_{t_2}^{(2)T} & -\\
& \vdots & \\
- & H_{t_n}^{(n)T} & -
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

This shift is important. Static embedding geometry asks: ``Where is the
word type?'' Contextual embedding geometry asks: ``Where is this
occurrence of the word in this sentence?''

\section{9.18 What can go wrong in embedding
visualization?}\label{what-can-go-wrong-in-embedding-visualization}

Low-dimensional plots are useful, but they can be misleading. Common
issues include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Projection distortion:} points close in \(R^2\) may not be
  close in \(R^m\).
\item
  \textbf{Lost variance:} a two-dimensional PCA plot may explain only a
  small fraction of total variance.
\item
  \textbf{Metric mismatch:} visualization may use Euclidean distance
  while retrieval uses cosine similarity.
\item
  \textbf{Crowding:} many points in high dimension must be packed into a
  small two-dimensional region.
\item
  \textbf{Overinterpretation:} visible clusters may be artifacts of
  projection, preprocessing, or selected examples.
\end{itemize}

A responsible visualization should report the preprocessing, projection
method, metric, and explained variance when applicable.

\section{9.19 AI-assisted learning
component}\label{ai-assisted-learning-component-3}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic, not as an authority. The
goal is to force precise statements.

\subsection{Prompt 1: metric audit}\label{prompt-1-metric-audit}

\begin{quote}
I have a word embedding matrix \(X\in R^{n\times m}\). I used cosine
similarity to find nearest neighbors. Ask me five mathematical questions
that check whether this choice is appropriate. Focus on normalization,
vector norms, anisotropy, and downstream task goals.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Prompt 2: PCA interpretation
critique}\label{prompt-2-pca-interpretation-critique}

\begin{quote}
I plotted word embeddings using the first two principal components. Give
a careful explanation of what this plot preserves and what it may
distort. Include the formulas for centering, covariance, and explained
variance.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Prompt 3: bias direction
analysis}\label{prompt-3-bias-direction-analysis}

\begin{quote}
Suppose I define a direction \(d\) by averaging difference vectors
\(e_{b_i}-e_{a_i}\). Explain how to test whether this direction is
stable and how projection onto this direction should be interpreted
statistically.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Prompt 4: nearest-neighbor
debugging}\label{prompt-4-nearest-neighbor-debugging}

\begin{quote}
My embedding nearest-neighbor results are dominated by frequent or
generic words. Give possible geometric explanations and suggest
mathematical diagnostics.
\end{quote}

After using an AI assistant, verify all formulas and test claims with a
small numerical example.

\section{9.20 Worked calculation}\label{worked-calculation}

Let

\[
x=(2,1),
\qquad
 y=(4,2),
\qquad
 z=(1,2).
\]

Then

\[
\cos(x,y)=\frac{2\cdot 4+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{2^2+1^2}\sqrt{4^2+2^2}}
=\frac{10}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{20}}
=1.
\]

So \(x\) and \(y\) have exactly the same direction. Their Euclidean
distance is

\[
\|x-y\|_2=\sqrt{(2-4)^2+(1-2)^2}=\sqrt{5}.
\]

For \(z\),

\[
\cos(x,z)=\frac{2\cdot 1+1\cdot 2}{\sqrt{5}\sqrt{5}}=\frac{4}{5}=0.8,
\]

while

\[
\|x-z\|_2=\sqrt{(2-1)^2+(1-2)^2}=\sqrt{2}.
\]

Thus \(y\) is more similar to \(x\) by cosine similarity, but \(z\) is
closer to \(x\) by Euclidean distance. This illustrates why metric
choice changes nearest-neighbor rankings.

\section{9.21 Mini-project: metric sensitivity of
embeddings}\label{mini-project-metric-sensitivity-of-embeddings}

Choose a small embedding set. You may use word embeddings, sentence
embeddings, or vectors constructed from TF-IDF and SVD.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Select 20 query words or sentences.
\item
  Compute top-5 neighbors under cosine similarity, inner product, and
  Euclidean distance.
\item
  Compare the overlap between the three neighbor lists.
\item
  Compute vector norms and examine whether high-norm vectors dominate
  inner-product retrieval.
\item
  Center the embeddings and repeat the analysis.
\item
  Write a short mathematical report explaining how preprocessing changed
  the geometry.
\end{enumerate}

A useful overlap statistic for two top-\(k\) neighbor sets \(A\) and
\(B\) is the Jaccard index

\[
J(A,B)=\frac{|A\cap B|}{|A\cup B|}.
\]

\section{9.22 Exercises}\label{exercises-8}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Cosine and Euclidean distance.} Prove that for nonzero
  \(x,y\in R^m\), \[
  \left\|\frac{x}{\|x\|_2}-\frac{y}{\|y\|_2}\right\|_2^2
  =2-2\cos(x,y).
  \]
\item
  \textbf{Nearest-neighbor matrix form.} Let \(X\in R^{n\times m}\)
  contain row-normalized embeddings. Show that the vector \(Xq\) gives
  cosine similarities to a normalized query \(q\).
\item
  \textbf{PCA derivation.} Let \(S\) be a symmetric positive
  semidefinite covariance matrix. Show that maximizing \(v^T S v\)
  subject to \(\|v\|_2=1\) leads to the eigenvalue equation
  \(Sv=\lambda v\).
\item
  \textbf{Explained variance.} Given singular values
  \(\sigma_1\ge\cdots\ge\sigma_r>0\), write the fraction of variance
  explained by the first \(k\) principal components.
\item
  \textbf{\(k\)-means centroid.} For a fixed cluster \(C\), prove that
  \[
  \mu=\frac{1}{|C|}\sum_{i\in C}x_i
  \] minimizes \(\sum_{i\in C}\|x_i-\mu\|_2^2\).
\item
  \textbf{Projection removal.} Let \(b\ne 0\) and define \[
  x_{\perp}=x-\frac{x^T b}{b^T b}b.
  \] Prove that \(x_{\perp}^T b=0\).
\item
  \textbf{Distance concentration simulation.} Simulate random Gaussian
  points in dimensions \(m=2,10,100,1000\). Plot the distribution of
  pairwise distances. Describe what changes as \(m\) increases.
\item
  \textbf{Contextual embeddings.} Explain why the geometry of contextual
  embeddings is a geometry of token occurrences rather than word types.
\item
  \textbf{AI critique.} Ask an AI assistant to explain why a
  two-dimensional embedding plot can be misleading. Identify at least
  two statements that need mathematical qualification.
\end{enumerate}

\section{9.24 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-1}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Embedding geometry depends on the representation, preprocessing, and
  metric.
\item
  Cosine similarity compares directions; Euclidean distance compares
  positions; inner products also reward large norms.
\item
  PCA is a linear variance-preserving projection, not a perfect picture
  of semantic space.
\item
  Clustering embeddings means optimizing a geometric objective, not
  discovering guaranteed natural categories.
\item
  High-dimensional spaces can exhibit distance concentration, hubness,
  and anisotropy.
\item
  Linear directions can be useful for interpretation, but they can also
  reveal or amplify bias.
\item
  Contextual embeddings move from word-type geometry to token-occurrence
  geometry.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-4}

This chapter builds on vector space models and word embeddings from
Chapters 7 and 8. Classical background on distributional representations
appears in Manning and Schuetze (1999) and Manning et al. (2008). Modern
word embedding models include Mikolov, Chen, et al. (2013) and
Pennington et al. (2014). The broader NLP context is developed in
Jurafsky and Martin (2024).

\part{Part IV. Neural Networks for Sequences}

\chapter{Neural Networks for Text}\label{neural-networks-for-text}

Embeddings, softmax classifiers, and trainable nonlinear maps

\hfill\break

Classical text models often use a fixed representation such as a count
vector, TF--IDF vector, or SVD coordinate. A \textbf{neural network for
text} replaces part of this representation pipeline by a trainable map.
Tokens become vectors, vectors are combined into a document or sequence
representation, and the resulting representation is sent through
nonlinear maps and a softmax output layer.

The goal of this chapter is not to treat neural networks as black boxes.
The goal is to write down the maps, dimensions, losses, and gradients
clearly enough that the model becomes a familiar object from linear
algebra, probability, and optimization.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-9}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  describe a neural text classifier as a composition of maps;
\item
  distinguish fixed text features from trainable embeddings;
\item
  compute softmax probabilities and cross-entropy loss;
\item
  derive the gradient of softmax cross-entropy with respect to logits;
\item
  explain how an embedding layer receives gradients from a
  sentence-level loss;
\item
  implement a small neural text classifier from scratch in Python;
\item
  interpret regularization, temperature, and calibration for neural text
  models.
\end{enumerate}

\section{10.1 The modeling pipeline}\label{the-modeling-pipeline}

A simple neural text classifier has four conceptual steps.

\[
\text{text}
\longrightarrow
\text{token indices}
\longrightarrow
\text{token embeddings}
\longrightarrow
\text{text representation}
\longrightarrow
\text{class probabilities}.
\]

Let \(V = \{1,\ldots,d\}\) be a finite vocabulary. A document or
sentence is represented as a token sequence

\[
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_T) \in V^T.
\]

A neural model is a parameterized function

\[
f_\theta: V^T \to \Delta^{K-1},
\]

where \(K\) is the number of classes and

\[
\Delta^{K-1}
=
\left\{p \in \mathbb R^K: p_k \ge 0,\ \sum_{k=1}^K p_k=1\right\}
\]

is the probability simplex. The output \(f_\theta(x)\) is interpreted as
a conditional distribution over labels:

\[
f_\theta(x)_k \approx P(Y=k\mid X=x).
\]

A minimal neural text classifier can be written as

\[
\begin{aligned}
e_i &= E_{x_i} \in \mathbb R^m, \qquad i=1,\ldots,T,\\
h(x) &= \frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^T e_i \in \mathbb R^m,\\
r(x) &= \sigma(Ah(x)+a) \in \mathbb R^q,\\
z(x) &= Wr(x)+b \in \mathbb R^K,\\
f_\theta(x) &= \operatorname{softmax}(z(x)).
\end{aligned}
\]

Here:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(E\in \mathbb R^{d\times m}\) is an \textbf{embedding matrix};
\item
  \(E_j\) is the row vector representing token \(j\);
\item
  \(h(x)\) is an averaged sentence representation;
\item
  \(A\in \mathbb R^{q\times m}\) and \(a\in \mathbb R^q\) define a
  hidden layer;
\item
  \(\sigma\) is a nonlinear activation such as ReLU or tanh;
\item
  \(W\in \mathbb R^{K\times q}\) and \(b\in \mathbb R^K\) define the
  output logits;
\item
  \(\theta=(E,A,a,W,b)\) denotes all trainable parameters.
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Core idea.} A neural text classifier is a composition of a
discrete lookup map, vector averaging or sequence aggregation, nonlinear
transformations, and a probabilistic output map.

\section{10.2 From fixed features to trainable
features}\label{from-fixed-features-to-trainable-features}

Earlier chapters studied fixed representation maps such as

\[
\phi(x) \in \mathbb R^d,
\]

where \(\phi(x)\) may be a count vector, a TF--IDF vector, or an SVD
coordinate. A linear classifier then uses

\[
z(x)=W\phi(x)+b.
\]

In a neural model, part of \(\phi\) is learned from data. For example,
an embedding layer defines

\[
\phi_E(x)
=
\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^T E_{x_i}.
\]

The representation depends on trainable parameters \(E\). Therefore
training changes not only the classifier weights, but also the geometry
in which tokens are represented.

This is the main mathematical shift:

\[
\text{fixed representation } \phi
\quad \longrightarrow \quad
\text{trainable representation } \phi_\theta.
\]

The statistical question also changes. We are no longer only estimating
class probabilities after selecting features. We are jointly estimating
a feature map and a classifier.

\section{10.3 The embedding layer as a matrix
lookup}\label{the-embedding-layer-as-a-matrix-lookup}

Let \(E\in \mathbb R^{d\times m}\). If token \(j\in V\) is represented
by the one-hot vector \(u_j\in \mathbb R^d\), then its embedding is

\[
E^T u_j \in \mathbb R^m.
\]

Equivalently, if \(E_j\) denotes the \(j\)th row of \(E\), then

\[
E^T u_j = E_j^T.
\]

Thus an embedding layer is just a matrix multiplication by a one-hot
vector, implemented efficiently as a row lookup.

For a sequence \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\), the embedding layer produces a
matrix

\[
M(x)
=
\begin{bmatrix}
E_{x_1}\\
E_{x_2}\\
\vdots\\
E_{x_T}
\end{bmatrix}
\in \mathbb R^{T\times m}.
\]

A simple sentence representation is average pooling:

\[
h(x)=\frac{1}{T}\mathbf 1_T^T M(x).
\]

This representation is permutation-invariant. It ignores word order.
That is a serious limitation for some language tasks, but it is a useful
first model because its mathematics is transparent.

\textbf{Dimension check.} If \(E\in \mathbb R^{d\times m}\) and
\(M(x)\in \mathbb R^{T\times m}\), then average pooling gives
\(h(x)\in \mathbb R^m\). If the hidden layer has width \(q\) and there
are \(K\) classes, then \(A\in \mathbb R^{q\times m}\) and
\(W\in \mathbb R^{K\times q}\).

\section{10.4 Activations and nonlinear
maps}\label{activations-and-nonlinear-maps}

A neural network becomes more than a linear classifier because of
nonlinear activation functions. Common choices include

\[
\operatorname{ReLU}(t)=\max\{0,t\},
\]

\[
\tanh(t)=\frac{e^t-e^{-t}}{e^t+e^{-t}},
\]

and the logistic sigmoid

\[
\sigma(t)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-t}}.
\]

Applied coordinatewise, an activation maps vectors to vectors:

\[
\sigma(v)=(\sigma(v_1),\ldots,\sigma(v_q)).
\]

A one-hidden-layer classifier is

\[
z(x)=W\sigma(Ah(x)+a)+b.
\]

Without the activation, this collapses to another affine map:

\[
W(Ah+a)+b=(WA)h+(Wa+b).
\]

Therefore the activation is what allows the model to represent nonlinear
decision boundaries in the representation space.

\section{10.5 Softmax output and class
probabilities}\label{softmax-output-and-class-probabilities}

For \(K\) classes, the model produces logits

\[
z=(z_1,\ldots,z_K)\in \mathbb R^K.
\]

The softmax function maps logits to probabilities:

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(z)_k
=
\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K e^{z_\ell}}.
\]

Softmax is invariant under adding a constant to all logits:

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(z+c\mathbf 1)=\operatorname{softmax}(z).
\]

This identity is important for numerical stability. In computation, we
usually evaluate

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(z)
=
\operatorname{softmax}(z-\max_j z_j\mathbf 1).
\]

For binary classification with classes \(0\) and \(1\), the two-class
softmax is equivalent to logistic regression. If

\[
z_1-z_0=s,
\]

then

\[
P(Y=1\mid x)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-s}}.
\]

Thus a neural binary classifier can be interpreted as logistic
regression applied after a learned nonlinear representation.

\section{10.6 Cross-entropy and maximum
likelihood}\label{cross-entropy-and-maximum-likelihood}

Suppose the training data are

\[
\mathcal D_n=\{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n,
\]

where \(y_i\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\). Let \(p_\theta(x_i)=f_\theta(x_i)\). The
model assigns probability

\[
p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i)=p_\theta(x_i)_{y_i}.
\]

The conditional likelihood is

\[
L(\theta)
=
\prod_{i=1}^n p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i).
\]

Maximizing likelihood is equivalent to minimizing negative
log-likelihood:

\[
\ell(\theta)
=
-
\sum_{i=1}^n \log p_\theta(y_i\mid x_i).
\]

If \(e_{y_i}\in\mathbb R^K\) is the one-hot vector for the true label,
the per-example loss is

\[
\ell_i(\theta)
=
-
\sum_{k=1}^K (e_{y_i})_k \log p_\theta(x_i)_k.
\]

This is the cross-entropy between the empirical one-hot label
distribution and the model's predicted distribution.

For empirical risk minimization, we usually minimize the average loss:

\[
\widehat R_n(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell_i(\theta).
\]

\section{10.7 The key gradient: softmax plus
cross-entropy}\label{the-key-gradient-softmax-plus-cross-entropy}

The softmax cross-entropy gradient has a remarkably simple form. Let

\[
p=\operatorname{softmax}(z),
\qquad
\ell(z,y)=-\log p_y.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_k}=p_k-\mathbf 1\{k=y\}.
\]

In vector notation,

\[
\nabla_z \ell=p-e_y.
\]

This formula is one reason softmax cross-entropy is convenient for
classification.

\subsection{Derivation}\label{derivation-1}

First note that

\[
\log p_y
=
\log\left(\frac{e^{z_y}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K e^{z_\ell}}\right)
=
z_y-
\log\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^K e^{z_\ell}\right).
\]

Thus

\[
\ell(z,y)
=
-z_y+
\log\left(\sum_{\ell=1}^K e^{z_\ell}\right).
\]

Differentiating with respect to \(z_k\) gives

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_k}
=
-\mathbf 1\{k=y\}
+
\frac{e^{z_k}}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K e^{z_\ell}}
=
p_k-\mathbf 1\{k=y\}.
\]

\textbf{Statistical interpretation.} The vector \(p-e_y\) is the
difference between the predicted class distribution and the empirical
one-hot class distribution. Gradient descent pushes predicted
probabilities toward the observed labels.

\section{10.8 Backpropagation through an averaged embedding
model}\label{backpropagation-through-an-averaged-embedding-model}

Consider the simple model

\[
h=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^T E_{x_i},
\qquad
z=Wh+b,
\qquad
p=\operatorname{softmax}(z),
\qquad
\ell=-\log p_y.
\]

Let

\[
g_z=\nabla_z\ell=p-e_y.
\]

Then the gradients are

\[
\nabla_W\ell=g_z h^T,
\]

\[
\nabla_b\ell=g_z,
\]

and

\[
g_h=\nabla_h\ell=W^Tg_z.
\]

Since

\[
h=\frac{1}{T}\sum_{i=1}^T E_{x_i},
\]

each token embedding in the document receives the gradient

\[
\nabla_{E_{x_i}}\ell = \frac{1}{T}g_h.
\]

If the same token appears multiple times, its row in \(E\) accumulates
multiple contributions. This is why embedding layers are trainable even
though token indices are discrete: the gradient flows into the
continuous row vectors selected by the indices.

\section{10.9 Optimization and
regularization}\label{optimization-and-regularization}

Neural text models are usually trained with stochastic optimization. For
a mini-batch \(B\subset\{1,\ldots,n\}\), define

\[
\widehat R_B(\theta)
=
\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{i\in B}\ell_i(\theta).
\]

A stochastic gradient descent update is

\[
\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta_t\nabla_\theta \widehat R_B(\theta_t),
\]

where \(\eta_t>0\) is a learning rate.

A regularized objective may be written as

\[
J(\theta)=\widehat R_n(\theta)+\lambda\|\theta\|_2^2.
\]

In practice, one often regularizes only selected parameters, such as
\(A\) and \(W\), not necessarily the embedding matrix. Dropout, early
stopping, and weight decay are also commonly used.

From a statistical perspective, regularization is important because
neural models often have many more parameters than training examples.
Without regularization or inductive bias, empirical loss alone may not
control generalization.

\section{10.10 Temperature, confidence, and
calibration}\label{temperature-confidence-and-calibration}

For logits \(z\), define temperature-scaled softmax by

\[
p_k(\tau)
=
\frac{\exp(z_k/\tau)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^K\exp(z_\ell/\tau)},
\qquad \tau>0.
\]

Small \(\tau\) makes the distribution sharper. Large \(\tau\) makes it
flatter. Temperature does not change the ranking of logits, but it
changes the confidence assigned to predictions.

This distinction matters in NLP because a model can be accurate but
poorly calibrated. Calibration asks whether predicted probabilities
match empirical frequencies. For example, among all examples to which a
model assigns confidence near \(0.8\), approximately \(80\%\) should be
correct if the model is calibrated.

\section{10.11 Interactive: Softmax classifier and
temperature}\label{interactive-softmax-classifier-and-temperature}

The following interactive illustrates a binary softmax classifier in a
two-feature representation space. Think of the horizontal coordinate as
the strength of evidence for technical or mathematical language and the
vertical coordinate as the strength of evidence for casual or
nontechnical language. The sliders control the logit difference

\[
s(x)=w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b,
\]

and the model probability

\[
P(Y=1\mid x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-s(x)/\tau)}.
\]

The HTML version of this chapter contains an interactive Plotly.js
visualization of a two-feature softmax classifier. In PDF format, the
same mathematical object is

\[
P(Y=1\mid x)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b)/\tau)}.
\]

The decision boundary is the line \(w_1x_1+w_2x_2+b=0\). Temperature
\(\tau\) changes confidence but not the boundary.

\section{10.12 Python example: data, tokenization, and
vocabulary}\label{python-example-data-tokenization-and-vocabulary}

The following example builds a tiny text classification dataset. The
goal is not high performance. The goal is to expose every mathematical
object in a neural text classifier.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ re}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter}

\NormalTok{texts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"linear algebra and probability are useful for machine learning"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"statistics studies uncertainty and data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"neural networks learn representations from data"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"the theorem gives a clean mathematical proof"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"the movie was funny and enjoyable"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"the dinner was tasty and relaxing"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"music and stories made the evening fun"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"the game was exciting and easy to watch"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\CommentTok{\# 1 = mathematical/technical, 0 = casual/nontechnical}
\NormalTok{labels }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ re.findall(}\VerbatimStringTok{r"}\PreprocessorTok{[a{-}z]}\OperatorTok{+}\VerbatimStringTok{"}\NormalTok{, text.lower())}

\NormalTok{tokenized }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [tokenize(t) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ t }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ texts]}
\NormalTok{counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(tok }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc)}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{tok: j }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, (tok, \_) }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(counts.most\_common())\}}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Vocabulary size:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"First 10 vocabulary items:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(vocab.items())[:}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"First document tokens:"}\NormalTok{, tokenized[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Vocabulary size: 42
First 10 vocabulary items: [('and', 0), ('the', 1), ('was', 2), ('data', 3), ('linear', 4), ('algebra', 5), ('probability', 6), ('are', 7), ('useful', 8), ('for', 9)]
First document tokens: ['linear', 'algebra', 'and', 'probability', 'are', 'useful', 'for', 'machine', 'learning']
\end{verbatim}

Convert each document to a list of token indices.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{indexed }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [[vocab[tok] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized]}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(indexed[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[4, 5, 0, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11]
\end{verbatim}

\section{10.13 Python example: softmax and
cross-entropy}\label{python-example-softmax-and-cross-entropy}

A numerically stable softmax subtracts the largest logit.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(Z):}
\NormalTok{    Z\_shift }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Z.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    expZ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(Z\_shift)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ expZ }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ expZ.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cross\_entropy(P, y):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(y)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.mean(np.log(P[np.arange(n), y] }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([[}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.7}\NormalTok{]])}
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(Z)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(P)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"loss:"}\NormalTok{, cross\_entropy(P, np.array([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[[0.81757448 0.18242552]
 [0.18242552 0.81757448]]
loss: 0.2014132779815293
\end{verbatim}

\section{10.14 Python example: averaged embedding classifier from
scratch}\label{python-example-averaged-embedding-classifier-from-scratch}

We now train the model

\[
h_i=\frac{1}{T_i}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}E_{x_{it}},
\qquad
z_i=h_iW+b,
\qquad
p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(z_i).
\]

Here \(E\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}\) and \(W\in\mathbb R^{m\times K}\).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Model dimensions}
\NormalTok{D }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{m }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(indexed)}

\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array(labels, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{E }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.05} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(D, m))}
\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.05} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(m, K))}
\NormalTok{b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(K)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ forward(indexed\_docs, E, W, b):}
\NormalTok{    H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(indexed\_docs), E.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]))}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, doc }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(indexed\_docs):}
\NormalTok{        H[i] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E[doc].mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ H }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b}
\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(Z)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ H, Z, P}

\NormalTok{H, Z, P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ forward(indexed, E, W, b)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"H shape:"}\NormalTok{, H.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Z shape:"}\NormalTok{, Z.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Initial loss:"}\NormalTok{, cross\_entropy(P, y))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
H shape: (8, 6)
Z shape: (8, 2)
Initial loss: 0.6922852483744657
\end{verbatim}

Training by full-batch gradient descent.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{lr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1.0}
\NormalTok{history }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ epoch }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{300}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    H, Z, P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ forward(indexed, E, W, b)}
\NormalTok{    loss }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ cross\_entropy(P, y)}
\NormalTok{    history.append(loss)}

    \CommentTok{\# Gradient of average cross{-}entropy with respect to logits}
\NormalTok{    Gz }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P.copy()}
\NormalTok{    Gz[np.arange(n), y] }\OperatorTok{{-}=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{    Gz }\OperatorTok{/=}\NormalTok{ n}

    \CommentTok{\# Gradients for W and b}
\NormalTok{    grad\_W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ H.T }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Gz}
\NormalTok{    grad\_b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Gz.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}

    \CommentTok{\# Gradient with respect to averaged document representations}
\NormalTok{    grad\_H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Gz }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W.T}

    \CommentTok{\# Gradient for embedding matrix}
\NormalTok{    grad\_E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(E)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, doc }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(indexed):}
\NormalTok{        contribution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grad\_H[i] }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(doc)}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token\_id }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc:}
\NormalTok{            grad\_E[token\_id] }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ contribution}

\NormalTok{    E }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_E}
\NormalTok{    W }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_W}
\NormalTok{    b }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_b}

\NormalTok{H, Z, P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ forward(indexed, E, W, b)}
\NormalTok{pred }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P.argmax(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final loss:"}\NormalTok{, cross\_entropy(P, y))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Predictions:"}\NormalTok{, pred.tolist())}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Training accuracy:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.mean(pred }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ y)))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"First five losses:"}\NormalTok{, [}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(v, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{)) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ v }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ history[:}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{]])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Last five losses:"}\NormalTok{, [}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(v, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{)) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ v }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ history[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{:]])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Final loss: 0.0019680287531346615
Predictions: [1, 1, 1, 1, 0, 0, 0, 0]
Training accuracy: 1.0
First five losses: [0.6923, 0.6919, 0.6915, 0.691, 0.6904]
Last five losses: [0.002, 0.002, 0.002, 0.002, 0.002]
\end{verbatim}

Plot the loss curve.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}

\NormalTok{plt.figure(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{plt.plot(history)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"epoch"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"cross{-}entropy loss"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.title(}\StringTok{"Training loss for an averaged{-}embedding classifier"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{chapters/chapter-10-neural-networks-for-text_files/figure-pdf/cell-7-output-1.pdf}}

\section{10.15 Python example: inspecting learned token
directions}\label{python-example-inspecting-learned-token-directions}

For binary classification, the difference between the two output weight
columns gives a direction in embedding space:

\[
v=W_{:,1}-W_{:,0}.
\]

For an embedded token \(E_j\), the score

\[
E_j^T v
\]

measures how much that token pushes the classifier toward class \(1\)
rather than class \(0\), at least in the averaged linear model.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{direction }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W[:, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ W[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ direction}
\NormalTok{id\_to\_token }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{j: tok }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok, j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ vocab.items()\}}

\NormalTok{ranked }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{([(id\_to\_token[j], scores[j]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(D)], key}\OperatorTok{=}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ t: t[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], reverse}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Most class{-}1{-}associated tokens:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok, score }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ ranked[:}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{]:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{tok}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}15s\}}\SpecialStringTok{  }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{score}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Most class{-}0{-}associated tokens:"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok, score }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ ranked[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{:]:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{tok}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}15s\}}\SpecialStringTok{  }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{score}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Most class-1-associated tokens:
           data   11.539
        theorem   8.061
   mathematical   7.781
          gives   7.360
          proof   7.333
    uncertainty   7.122
     statistics   6.976
        studies   6.951

Most class-0-associated tokens:
           made  -5.794
        stories  -6.040
          music  -6.161
        evening  -6.299
            fun  -6.635
            and  -7.697
            the  -13.089
            was  -13.491
\end{verbatim}

This kind of inspection is limited but useful. It helps students see
that a trainable embedding model still has interpretable linear algebra
inside it.

\section{10.16 Python example: adding one hidden ReLU
layer}\label{python-example-adding-one-hidden-relu-layer}

A one-hidden-layer model uses

\[
r_i=\operatorname{ReLU}(h_iA+a),
\qquad
z_i=r_iW+b.
\]

The additional nonlinear layer can represent more complicated decision
regions in \(h\)-space.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ relu(U):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(U, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ relu\_grad(U):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ (U }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{).astype(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{q }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{8}
\NormalTok{E2 }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.05} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(D, m))}
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.05} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(m, q))}
\NormalTok{a }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(q)}
\NormalTok{W2 }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.05} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(q, K))}
\NormalTok{b2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(K)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ forward\_relu(indexed\_docs, E, A, a, W, b):}
\NormalTok{    H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(indexed\_docs), E.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]))}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, doc }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(indexed\_docs):}
\NormalTok{        H[i] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E[doc].mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    U }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ H }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ a}
\NormalTok{    R }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ relu(U)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ R }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b}
\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(Z)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ H, U, R, Z, P}

\NormalTok{history\_relu }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{lr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.8}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ epoch }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{400}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    H, U, R, Z, P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ forward\_relu(indexed, E2, A, a, W2, b2)}
\NormalTok{    loss }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ cross\_entropy(P, y)}
\NormalTok{    history\_relu.append(loss)}

\NormalTok{    Gz }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P.copy()}
\NormalTok{    Gz[np.arange(n), y] }\OperatorTok{{-}=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{    Gz }\OperatorTok{/=}\NormalTok{ n}

\NormalTok{    grad\_W2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ R.T }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Gz}
\NormalTok{    grad\_b2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Gz.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    grad\_R }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Gz }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W2.T}
\NormalTok{    grad\_U }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grad\_R }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ relu\_grad(U)}
\NormalTok{    grad\_A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ H.T }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ grad\_U}
\NormalTok{    grad\_a }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grad\_U.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    grad\_H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grad\_U }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ A.T}

\NormalTok{    grad\_E2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(E2)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, doc }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(indexed):}
\NormalTok{        contribution }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grad\_H[i] }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(doc)}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token\_id }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc:}
\NormalTok{            grad\_E2[token\_id] }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ contribution}

\NormalTok{    E2 }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_E2}
\NormalTok{    A }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_A}
\NormalTok{    a }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_a}
\NormalTok{    W2 }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_W2}
\NormalTok{    b2 }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_b2}

\NormalTok{H, U, R, Z, P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ forward\_relu(indexed, E2, A, a, W2, b2)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final ReLU{-}model loss:"}\NormalTok{, cross\_entropy(P, y))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Training accuracy:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.mean(P.argmax(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ y)))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Final ReLU-model loss: 0.0005048229998677652
Training accuracy: 1.0
\end{verbatim}

\section{10.17 Worked calculation: one softmax
gradient}\label{worked-calculation-one-softmax-gradient}

Suppose a three-class model gives logits

\[
z=(2,1,0).
\]

Then

\[
p=\operatorname{softmax}(z)
=\frac{1}{e^2+e+1}(e^2,e,1).
\]

If the true class is \(1\) using zero-based indexing, then
\(e_y=(0,1,0)\) and

\[
\nabla_z\ell=p-e_y.
\]

Using approximate values,

\[
p\approx(0.665,0.245,0.090),
\]

so

\[
\nabla_z\ell\approx(0.665,-0.755,0.090).
\]

The negative entry for the true class means gradient descent will
increase the true-class logit. The positive entries for the other
classes mean gradient descent will decrease the competing logits.

\section{10.18 Neural networks versus classical text
classifiers}\label{neural-networks-versus-classical-text-classifiers}

The table summarizes important contrasts.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2000}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Model
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Representation
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Decision function
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Strength
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Limitation
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Naive Bayes & counts & log posterior score & simple probabilistic model
& strong independence assumption \\
Logistic regression & fixed feature vector & linear logits &
interpretable and convex & depends on chosen features \\
Averaged embeddings & trainable token vectors & linear or nonlinear
logits & learns representation & weak treatment of word order \\
RNN/LSTM & sequence of embeddings & recurrent hidden state & uses order
& harder to parallelize \\
Transformer & sequence of contextual embeddings & attention-based maps &
long-range interactions & expensive and data-hungry \\
\end{longtable}
}

This chapter studies the third row. The next two chapters develop
recurrent models that use word order more explicitly.

\section{10.19 AI component: using AI to audit a neural text
model}\label{ai-component-using-ai-to-audit-a-neural-text-model}

Modern AI tools can help students debug, explain, and critique models,
but they should not replace mathematical verification. Use AI as a
structured reviewer.

\subsection{Prompt 1: dimension
checking}\label{prompt-1-dimension-checking}

\begin{quote}
I have a vocabulary of size \(d\), embedding dimension \(m\), hidden
width \(q\), and \(K\) classes. My model is \(E\in R^{d\times m}\),
\(h\) is the average of token embeddings,
\(r=\operatorname{ReLU}(Ah+a)\), and \(z=Wr+b\). Check all dimensions
and tell me which convention I am using for row versus column vectors.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Prompt 2: gradient
auditing}\label{prompt-2-gradient-auditing}

\begin{quote}
For the averaged embedding classifier \(h=T^{-1}\sum_i E_{x_i}\),
\(z=Wh+b\), and \(\ell=-\log\operatorname{softmax}(z)_y\), derive the
gradients with respect to \(W\), \(b\), \(h\), and each selected
embedding row. State every shape.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Prompt 3: modeling
critique}\label{prompt-3-modeling-critique}

\begin{quote}
I trained an averaged-embedding sentiment classifier. It performs well
on short reviews but fails on sentences with negation, such as ``not
good''. Explain mathematically why averaging embeddings may fail and
suggest a model class that can represent word order.
\end{quote}

\subsection{Prompt 4: statistical
caution}\label{prompt-4-statistical-caution}

\begin{quote}
My neural text classifier achieves perfect training accuracy on 40
examples. List possible statistical explanations and propose validation
diagnostics.
\end{quote}

The best use of AI is to ask it for checks that you can verify. In this
book, every AI-generated explanation should be reduced to mathematical
objects: maps, losses, gradients, distributions, and evaluation metrics.

\section{10.20 Common pitfalls}\label{common-pitfalls-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing tokens and embeddings.} Token indices are discrete.
  Embeddings are continuous row vectors.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring dimensions.} Many implementation errors are shape
  errors disguised as conceptual errors.
\item
  \textbf{Interpreting softmax scores as calibrated probabilities
  without checking calibration.}
\item
  \textbf{Believing that more nonlinear layers always improve
  generalization.} Larger models can overfit small text datasets.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting word order.} Averaging embeddings is simple but
  cannot distinguish many different sequences.
\item
  \textbf{Reading too much into learned embedding coordinates.}
  Individual coordinates are usually not uniquely meaningful because
  rotations or reparameterizations can preserve predictions.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Conceptual exercises}\label{conceptual-exercises-6}

\begin{enumerate}

\item
  Let \(E\in\mathbb R^{d\times m}\) and \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_T)\). Write

\item

  \(\mathbf 1\) to the logits.
\item

  the logit difference.
\item
  Explain why an averaged-embedding classifier is invariant under
  permutations of the input tokens.

  averaged embedding representation.

\subsection{Computational exercises}\label{computational-exercises-3}

\begin{enumerate}

\subsection{Mathematical exercises}\label{mathematical-exercises-5}

\begin{enumerate}

  Derive the gradient of the regularized loss \[
  \widehat R_n(W)+\lambda\|W\|_F^2
  \] with respect to \(W\).
