\section{10.24 Chapter summary}\label{chapter-summary-3}

A neural text classifier is a trainable composition of maps:

\[
V^T \to \mathbb R^{T\times m} \to \mathbb R^m \to \mathbb R^q \to \mathbb R^K \to \Delta^{K-1}.
\]

The embedding layer is a matrix lookup. Pooling turns token embeddings
into a document representation. Hidden layers apply nonlinear
transformations. Softmax turns logits into class probabilities.
Cross-entropy corresponds to negative conditional log-likelihood. The
gradient \(p-e_y\) links probabilistic prediction to optimization.

The model in this chapter is intentionally simple. It is powerful enough
to introduce trainable representations, but simple enough to analyze by
hand. The next chapters explain how recurrent models and gated models
add explicit sequence dependence.

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-5}

This chapter connects classical neural network ideas with text
classification. Useful background sources include Goodfellow et al.
(2016a) for neural networks, Bishop (2006a) for probabilistic
classification and optimization, Jurafsky and Martin (2024) for NLP
context, and Manning et al. (2008) for text representations and
classification.

\chapter{Recurrent Neural Networks}\label{recurrent-neural-networks}

Dynamical systems, sequence likelihood, and backpropagation through time

\hfill\break

A bag-of-words classifier treats a sentence as an unordered collection
of tokens. A recurrent neural network treats a sentence as an ordered
sequence. At each time step, the model reads one token, updates an
internal state, and uses that state to make predictions.

Mathematically, an RNN is a parameterized discrete-time dynamical system
driven by a sequence of input vectors. This viewpoint makes the model
easier to understand: hidden states are states of a dynamical system,
recurrent weights control memory and stability, and backpropagation
through time is differentiation through repeated function composition.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-10}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  explain why order-sensitive language tasks require sequence models
  rather than pure bag-of-words models;
\item
  write a vanilla RNN as a nonlinear recurrence;
\item
  interpret hidden states as summaries of past tokens;
\item
  formulate RNNs for sequence classification and language modeling;
\item
  derive the negative log-likelihood for an RNN language model;
\item
  explain backpropagation through time using products of Jacobian
  matrices;
\item
  connect vanishing and exploding gradients to spectral radius and
  nonlinear saturation;
\item
  implement a small RNN forward pass and training loop in Python;
\item
  use an interactive visualization to study recurrent memory and
  stability.
\end{enumerate}

\section{11.1 Why recurrence?}\label{why-recurrence}

Consider the two short sentences:

\[
\text{not good}
\qquad \text{and} \qquad
\text{good not}.
\]

A bag-of-words representation records the same two tokens in both cases.
Therefore a bag-of-words model cannot distinguish them. More generally,
count vectors ignore the order of tokens, so they cannot directly
represent syntax, negation scope, local dependencies, or temporal
structure.

Let \(V\) be a vocabulary. A sentence of length \(T\) is an ordered
sequence

\[
x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T) \in V^T.
\]

A sequence model should process the tokens in order. Instead of mapping
the full sequence immediately to one fixed vector, it constructs a
sequence of hidden states

\[
h_1,h_2,\ldots,h_T,
\]

where \(h_t\) is intended to summarize the prefix

\[
(x_1,\ldots,x_t).
\]

The key modeling idea is recursive summarization:

\[
\text{new summary}
=\text{update}(\text{old summary},\text{new token}).
\]

This is exactly the mathematical structure of a discrete-time dynamical
system with external input.

\section{11.2 The vanilla RNN as a nonlinear
recurrence}\label{the-vanilla-rnn-as-a-nonlinear-recurrence}

Let each token \(x_t \in V\) be mapped to an embedding vector

\[
e_t = E_{x_t} \in \mathbb R^m,
\]

where \(E\in \mathbb R^{d\times m}\) is an embedding matrix and
\(d=|V|\).

A vanilla RNN defines hidden states \(h_t\in \mathbb R^r\) by

\[
h_t = \phi(W_h h_{t-1}+W_x e_t+b_h),
\qquad t=1,\ldots,T.
\]

Here:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(h_0\in \mathbb R^r\) is an initial state, often the zero vector;
\item
  \(W_h\in \mathbb R^{r\times r}\) is the recurrent weight matrix;
\item
  \(W_x\in \mathbb R^{r\times m}\) maps token embeddings into hidden
  space;
\item
  \(b_h\in \mathbb R^r\) is a bias vector;
\item
  \(\phi\) is a coordinatewise nonlinearity such as \(\tanh\) or ReLU.
\end{itemize}

A common choice is

\[
\phi(u)=\tanh(u),
\]

applied coordinatewise. Then every coordinate of \(h_t\) lies between
\(-1\) and \(1\).

\textbf{Dimension check.} If \(h_{t-1}\in \mathbb R^r\),
\(e_t\in \mathbb R^m\), \(W_h\in \mathbb R^{r\times r}\), and
\(W_x\in \mathbb R^{r\times m}\), then

\[
W_hh_{t-1}+W_xe_t+b_h\in \mathbb R^r.
\]

Therefore \(h_t\in \mathbb R^r\).

The same update rule is applied at every time step. This
\textbf{parameter sharing across time} is essential. It allows the model
to process sequences of different lengths and keeps the number of
parameters independent of \(T\).

\section{11.3 The state-space
viewpoint}\label{the-state-space-viewpoint}

The RNN recurrence can be written as

\[
h_t = F_\theta(h_{t-1},e_t),
\]

where

\[
F_\theta(h,e)=\phi(W_hh+W_xe+b_h).
\]

This is a controlled dynamical system. The input sequence
\(e_1,e_2,\ldots,e_T\) drives the state trajectory

\[
h_0 \to h_1 \to h_2 \to \cdots \to h_T.
\]

For language, the hidden state has an information-processing
interpretation:

\[
h_t \approx \text{a vector summary of the prefix } (x_1,\ldots,x_t).
\]

The hidden state is not guaranteed to contain all information about the
prefix. It is a compressed representation of a possibly long discrete
sequence. The quality of this compression depends on the hidden
dimension \(r\), the parameters, the nonlinearity, the training data,
and the task.

\textbf{RNN as learned sufficient statistic.} In ideal probabilistic
modeling, one might want a statistic \(S_t=S(x_1,\ldots,x_t)\) such that
the future depends on the past only through \(S_t\). An RNN attempts to
learn a finite-dimensional vector \(h_t\) that plays this role for a
prediction task.

\section{11.4 Output maps: many-to-one and many-to-many
models}\label{output-maps-many-to-one-and-many-to-many-models}

The hidden states can be used in different ways.

\subsection{Sequence classification}\label{sequence-classification}

For sentiment classification, topic classification, or spam detection,
the input is a sequence and the output is one label. A common model uses
only the final hidden state:

\[
z = W_o h_T+b_o,
\]

\[
\widehat p(y\mid x)=\operatorname{softmax}(z).
\]

This is called a \textbf{many-to-one} model because many input tokens
produce one output label.

The loss for one training example \((x,y)\) is cross-entropy:

\[
\ell(\theta;x,y)
= -\log \widehat p(y\mid x).
\]

\subsection{Sequence labeling}\label{sequence-labeling-1}

For part-of-speech tagging or named-entity recognition, the model
predicts a label at each time step:

\[
z_t = W_o h_t+b_o,
\]

\[
\widehat p(y_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_t)=\operatorname{softmax}(z_t).
\]

This is a \textbf{many-to-many} model.

\subsection{Language modeling}\label{language-modeling-1}

For next-token prediction, the model uses the prefix hidden state to
predict the next token:

\[
\widehat p(x_{t+1}=j\mid x_1,\ldots,x_t)
= \operatorname{softmax}(W_o h_t+b_o)_j.
\]

The RNN language model estimates the conditional distribution

\[
P(X_{t+1}\mid X_1,\ldots,X_t).
\]

This is the recurrent analogue of the \(n\)-gram models from Chapter 5.
An \(n\)-gram model keeps a finite symbolic context. An RNN keeps a
finite-dimensional learned vector context.

\section{11.5 RNN language-model
likelihood}\label{rnn-language-model-likelihood}

Let a training sequence be

\[
x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T).
\]

A language model assigns probability using the chain rule:

\[
P_\theta(x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=\prod_{t=1}^T P_\theta(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}).
\]

In an RNN language model, the conditional probability is computed from
the previous hidden state:

\[
p_t=\operatorname{softmax}(W_oh_{t-1}+b_o),
\]

\[
P_\theta(x_t=j\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1})=(p_t)_j.
\]

The hidden state is then updated using the observed token \(x_t\):

\[
h_t=\phi(W_hh_{t-1}+W_xE_{x_t}+b_h).
\]

The negative log-likelihood is

\[
L(\theta;x)
=
-\sum_{t=1}^T \log (p_t)_{x_t}.
\]

The average token-level cross-entropy is

\[
\operatorname{CE}(\theta;x)
=\frac{1}{T}L(\theta;x),
\]

and the perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{PPL}(\theta;x)
=\exp(\operatorname{CE}(\theta;x)).
\]

Thus training an RNN language model is maximum likelihood estimation, or
equivalently empirical risk minimization with cross-entropy loss.

\section{11.6 Unrolling the recurrence}\label{unrolling-the-recurrence}

For a fixed sequence length \(T\), the recurrent computation can be
unrolled into a deep feedforward network with shared weights.

For example,

\[
h_1=F_\theta(h_0,e_1),
\]

\[
h_2=F_\theta(h_1,e_2)=F_\theta(F_\theta(h_0,e_1),e_2),
\]

and so on. Therefore

\[
h_T=F_\theta(F_\theta(\cdots F_\theta(h_0,e_1)\cdots,e_{T-1}),e_T).
\]

The same parameters occur at every layer of this unrolled network. This
is why training RNNs is similar to training deep networks, but with
additional weight sharing.

For sequence classification, the loss may depend only on \(h_T\). For
language modeling, the loss depends on many hidden states:

\[
L=\sum_{t=1}^T \ell_t(h_{t-1}).
\]

In both cases, gradients must flow backward through the entire chain of
recurrent updates.

\section{11.7 Backpropagation through
time}\label{backpropagation-through-time}

Backpropagation through time, or \textbf{BPTT}, is ordinary
backpropagation applied to the unrolled recurrent computation graph.

To see the main issue, consider how the final state depends on an
earlier state. By the chain rule,

\[
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t}
=
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_{T-1}}
\frac{\partial h_{T-1}}{\partial h_{T-2}}
\cdots
\frac{\partial h_{t+1}}{\partial h_t}.
\]

For the vanilla RNN,

\[
h_s=\phi(a_s),
\qquad
 a_s=W_hh_{s-1}+W_xe_s+b_h.
\]

The one-step Jacobian is

\[
J_s
=
\frac{\partial h_s}{\partial h_{s-1}}
=
D_s W_h,
\]

where

\[
D_s=\operatorname{diag}(\phi'(a_s)).
\]

Therefore

\[
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_t}
=
J_TJ_{T-1}\cdots J_{t+1}.
\]

This product of many matrices is the central mathematical source of
vanishing and exploding gradients.

\textbf{Gradient stability.} If the norms of the Jacobians are typically
less than \(1\), products shrink rapidly. If they are typically greater
than \(1\), products may grow rapidly. Long-range learning in vanilla
RNNs is difficult because gradients involve long products of Jacobian
matrices.

\section{11.8 Vanishing and exploding
gradients}\label{vanishing-and-exploding-gradients}

Suppose, as a simplified model, that the nonlinear derivative is
approximately constant and

\[
J_s \approx J.
\]

Then

\[
J_TJ_{T-1}\cdots J_{t+1}\approx J^{T-t}.
\]

If \(J\) has eigenvalues with magnitudes smaller than \(1\), then
\(J^k\) tends to shrink directions as \(k\) increases. If \(J\) has
eigenvalues with magnitudes larger than \(1\), then \(J^k\) may grow
rapidly in some directions.

For a linear recurrence

\[
h_t=W_hh_{t-1},
\]

the state is

\[
h_T=W_h^T h_0.
\]

If \(W_h\) is diagonalizable as \(W_h=Q\Lambda Q^{-1}\), then

\[
W_h^T=Q\Lambda^TQ^{-1}.
\]

The powers of the eigenvalues determine the long-run behavior. This
connects RNN stability to familiar ideas from linear algebra and
dynamical systems.

For \$ anh\$ RNNs, saturation introduces another source of gradient
shrinkage. Since

\[
\frac{d}{du}\tanh(u)=1-\tanh^2(u),
\]

large values of \(|u|\) produce derivatives close to zero. Even if
\(W_h\) is not small, saturated nonlinearities can make \(D_s\) small.

\section{11.9 Truncated BPTT and gradient
clipping}\label{truncated-bptt-and-gradient-clipping}

For long sequences, full BPTT can be expensive and unstable. Two
practical techniques are common.

\subsection{Truncated backpropagation through
time}\label{truncated-backpropagation-through-time}

Instead of backpropagating through the entire history, one
backpropagates only through a window of length \(K\):

\[
\frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-K}}.
\]

This reduces computation and memory cost, but limits how directly the
model learns very long-range dependencies.

\subsection{Gradient clipping}\label{gradient-clipping}

When gradients explode, one can rescale the gradient vector \(g\) before
the optimizer update:

\[
g \leftarrow g\cdot \min\left\{1,\frac{c}{\|g\|}\right\}.
\]

Here \(c>0\) is a clipping threshold. Gradient clipping does not solve
all long-memory problems, but it prevents extremely large updates from
destabilizing training.

\section{\texorpdfstring{11.10 RNNs versus \(n\)-gram
models}{11.10 RNNs versus n-gram models}}\label{rnns-versus-n-gram-models}

An \(n\)-gram model approximates

\[
P(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1})
\approx
P(x_t\mid x_{t-n+1},\ldots,x_{t-1}).
\]

It stores a discrete context of length \(n-1\). An RNN approximates

\[
P(x_t\mid x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1})
\approx
P(x_t\mid h_{t-1}),
\]

where \(h_{t-1}\) is a learned continuous summary of the prefix.

This has advantages and disadvantages.

  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}

\(n\)-gram & last \(n-1\) tokens & transparent counts & sparse for large
\(n\) \\

through vectors & difficult long-range optimization \\
\end{longtable}
}

The RNN is more flexible because similar contexts can produce similar
hidden states. However, this flexibility comes from nonlinear
optimization, so the model is harder to analyze and train.

\section{11.11 Worked example: scalar linear
RNN}\label{worked-example-scalar-linear-rnn}

A scalar linear RNN is

\[
h_t=ah_{t-1}+bu_t,
\]

where \(u_t\) is a scalar input. Starting from \(h_0=0\), we obtain

\[
h_1=bu_1,
\]

\[
h_2=abu_1+bu_2,
\]

\[
h_3=a^2bu_1+abu_2+bu_3.
\]

By induction,

\[
h_T=\sum_{s=1}^T a^{T-s}b u_s.
\]

Thus the input from time \(s\) receives weight \(a^{T-s}\). If
\(|a|<1\), older inputs decay. If \(|a|>1\), older inputs may be
amplified. If \(a\approx 1\), the model can maintain information for a
longer time.

This simple formula is one of the cleanest mathematical explanations of
recurrent memory.

\section{11.12 Interactive: recurrent memory and
stability}\label{interactive-recurrent-memory-and-stability}

The following interactive studies the scalar recurrence

\[
h_t = \tanh(a h_{t-1}+b u_t).
\]

The parameter \(a\) plays the role of a recurrent weight. The parameter
\(b\) controls input strength. The input sequence has a pulse near the
beginning, followed by smaller oscillating inputs. Move the sliders to
see how memory, saturation, and stability change.

The HTML version of this chapter contains an interactive Plotly
visualization of the scalar recurrence \(h_t=\tanh(ah_{t-1}+bu_t)\).

\section{11.13 Python example: RNN forward pass from
scratch}\label{python-example-rnn-forward-pass-from-scratch}

The following code implements a small vanilla RNN forward pass for
sequence classification. It is intentionally written with NumPy rather
than a deep learning framework so the linear algebra is visible.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch11-rnn-forward}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\CommentTok{\# Tiny vocabulary and sequence}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"not"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"very"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"bad"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"movie"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{sequence }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"not"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"very"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"movie"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([vocab[w] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ sequence])}

\CommentTok{\# Dimensions}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)   }\CommentTok{\# vocabulary size}
\NormalTok{m }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4}            \CommentTok{\# embedding dimension}
\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}            \CommentTok{\# hidden dimension}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}            \CommentTok{\# number of classes}

\CommentTok{\# Parameters}
\NormalTok{E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, m))}
\NormalTok{W\_h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{W\_x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{b\_h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{W\_o }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(K, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_o }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(K)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(z):}
\NormalTok{    z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(z)}
\NormalTok{    ez }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(z)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ ez }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ ez.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ rnn\_forward(x):}
\NormalTok{    h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{    states }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token\_id }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ x:}
\NormalTok{        e }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E[token\_id]}
\NormalTok{        h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.tanh(W\_h }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ W\_x }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_h)}
\NormalTok{        states.append(h.copy())}
\NormalTok{    logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W\_o }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_o}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ probs, np.array(states)}

\NormalTok{probs, states }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rnn\_forward(x)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Sequence:"}\NormalTok{, sequence)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Hidden{-}state matrix shape:"}\NormalTok{, states.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Class probabilities:"}\NormalTok{, probs)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Sequence: ['not', 'very', 'good', 'movie']
Hidden-state matrix shape: (4, 5)
Class probabilities: [0.4960052 0.5039948]
\end{verbatim}

The hidden-state matrix has shape \(T\times r\). Each row is the hidden
state after reading one more token.

\section{11.14 Python example: visualizing hidden-state
trajectories}\label{python-example-visualizing-hidden-state-trajectories}

A hidden-state sequence is a trajectory in \(\mathbb R^r\). We can
project it to two dimensions with SVD to visualize how the RNN state
changes over time.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}

\CommentTok{\# Center the hidden states and compute a 2D SVD projection}
\NormalTok{H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ states }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ states.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{U, S, Vt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.svd(H, full\_matrices}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{coords }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ H }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Vt[:}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{].T}

\NormalTok{plt.figure(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{plt.plot(coords[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], coords[:, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], marker}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"o"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, token }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(sequence):}
\NormalTok{    plt.text(coords[i, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], coords[i, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], token)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"first SVD direction"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"second SVD direction"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.title(}\StringTok{"Hidden{-}state trajectory of a toy RNN"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.grid(}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{chapters/chapter-11-recurrent-neural-networks_files/figure-pdf/ch11-hidden-trajectory-output-1.pdf}}

The plot should not be overinterpreted. This is only a two-dimensional
projection of a higher-dimensional trajectory. Still, it provides useful
intuition: recurrent models convert a token sequence into a path through
representation space.

\section{11.15 Python example: RNN language-model
probabilities}\label{python-example-rnn-language-model-probabilities}

Now we implement the likelihood for a tiny RNN language model. The model
predicts the next token from the previous hidden state.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch11-rnn-language-model}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7339}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"math students learn probability"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"statistics students learn inference"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language models learn probability"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"students study language models"}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{tokens }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{" "}\NormalTok{.join(corpus).split()))}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{w: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(tokens)\}}
\NormalTok{id\_to\_word }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{i: w }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w, i }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ vocab.items()\}}
\NormalTok{encoded }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [[vocab[w] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ sent.split()] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ sent }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ corpus]}

\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{m }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}
\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{8}

\NormalTok{E\_lm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, m))}
\NormalTok{W\_h\_lm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{W\_x\_lm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{b\_h\_lm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{W\_o\_lm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_o\_lm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(d)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ lm\_sequence\_nll(seq):}
\NormalTok{    h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{    nll }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{    count }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token\_id }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ seq:}
\NormalTok{        logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W\_o\_lm }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_o\_lm}
\NormalTok{        p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits)}
\NormalTok{        nll }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ np.log(p[token\_id] }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        count }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{        e }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E\_lm[token\_id]}
\NormalTok{        h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.tanh(W\_h\_lm }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ W\_x\_lm }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_h\_lm)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ nll, count}

\NormalTok{total\_nll }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{total\_tokens }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ seq }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ encoded:}
\NormalTok{    nll, count }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ lm\_sequence\_nll(seq)}
\NormalTok{    total\_nll }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ nll}
\NormalTok{    total\_tokens }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ count}

\NormalTok{cross\_entropy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ total\_nll }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ total\_tokens}
\NormalTok{perplexity }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(cross\_entropy)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Vocabulary:"}\NormalTok{, tokens)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Average cross{-}entropy:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(cross\_entropy, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Perplexity:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(perplexity, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Vocabulary: ['inference', 'language', 'learn', 'math', 'models', 'probability', 'statistics', 'students', 'study']
Average cross-entropy: 2.232
Perplexity: 9.315
\end{verbatim}

The parameters above are random, so the model is not expected to be
good. The purpose is to show the exact computation of likelihood,
cross-entropy, and perplexity.

\section{11.16 Python example: one training step by finite
differences}\label{python-example-one-training-step-by-finite-differences}

Full BPTT is lengthy to implement from scratch. To check our
understanding, we can examine a one-parameter finite-difference
derivative for the recurrent weight matrix.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch11-finite-difference-gradient}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Use one sequence and one entry of W\_h\_lm.}
\NormalTok{seq }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ encoded[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ loss\_with\_current\_params():}
\NormalTok{    nll, \_ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ lm\_sequence\_nll(seq)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ nll}

\NormalTok{base\_loss }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_with\_current\_params()}

\NormalTok{i, j }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}
\NormalTok{eps }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1e{-}5}
\NormalTok{old\_value }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W\_h\_lm[i, j]}

\NormalTok{W\_h\_lm[i, j] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ old\_value }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ eps}
\NormalTok{loss\_plus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_with\_current\_params()}

\NormalTok{W\_h\_lm[i, j] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ old\_value }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ eps}
\NormalTok{loss\_minus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_with\_current\_params()}

\NormalTok{W\_h\_lm[i, j] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ old\_value}
\NormalTok{finite\_difference }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (loss\_plus }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ loss\_minus) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ eps)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Base loss:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(base\_loss, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Finite{-}difference derivative for W\_h[0,0]:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(finite\_difference, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Base loss: 8.8042
Finite-difference derivative for W_h[0,0]: 0.0139
\end{verbatim}

Finite differences are too slow for training real RNNs, but they are
useful for verifying gradient code. BPTT computes all such derivatives
efficiently by reusing intermediate Jacobian-vector products.

\section{11.17 Python example: gradient norm through
time}\label{python-example-gradient-norm-through-time}

The following simulation illustrates the product-of-Jacobians phenomenon
in a linear recurrence. We compute powers of a recurrent matrix and
observe how their norms behave.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch11-gradient-norm-simulation}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{2026}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\CommentTok{\# Normalize A and create versions with different spectral scales.}
\NormalTok{eig\_max }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.eigvals(A)))}
\NormalTok{A\_base }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ eig\_max}

\NormalTok{scales }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{steps }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{31}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{norms }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{\}}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ scale }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ scales:}
\NormalTok{    M }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scale }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ A\_base}
\NormalTok{    values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.eye(r)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ steps:}
\NormalTok{        P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ M }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ P}
\NormalTok{        values.append(np.linalg.norm(P, }\BuiltInTok{ord}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    norms[scale] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ values}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ scale, values }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ norms.items():}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"scale"}\NormalTok{, scale, }\StringTok{"first norm"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(values[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{"last norm"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(values[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
scale 0.7 first norm 1.118 last norm 0.0
scale 0.95 first norm 1.517 last norm 0.264
scale 1.1 first norm 1.757 last norm 21.454
\end{verbatim}

When the effective recurrent scale is below \(1\), powers tend to
shrink. When it is above \(1\), powers may grow. Nonlinearities and
data-dependent Jacobians complicate this picture, but the linear example
captures the core phenomenon.

\section{11.18 AI-assisted learning
component}\label{ai-assisted-learning-component-4}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic rather than as a
replacement for derivation. Good prompts include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Dimension audit.} ``Given the RNN equations
  \(h_t=\tanh(W_hh_{t-1}+W_xe_t+b_h)\) and \(z_t=W_oh_t+b_o\), check
  every matrix dimension and identify possible shape errors.''
\item
  \textbf{Gradient explanation.} ``Explain why products of Jacobian
  matrices can cause vanishing gradients in vanilla RNNs. Use a
  two-dimensional linear example.''
\item
  \textbf{Model comparison.} ``Compare an \(n\)-gram model and an RNN
  language model using conditional probability notation.''
\item
  \textbf{Code review.} ``Review this NumPy RNN forward pass and
  identify whether the hidden state is updated before or after
  next-token prediction.''
\item
  \textbf{Interpretability caution.} ``Give three reasons why a
  two-dimensional projection of hidden states should not be interpreted
  as the true geometry of the RNN.''
\end{enumerate}

The student should verify every answer by checking equations,
dimensions, and small numerical examples.

\section{11.19 Common pitfalls}\label{common-pitfalls-2}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing token embeddings with hidden states.} The embedding
  \(e_t\) represents the current token. The hidden state \(h_t\)
  represents the prefix up to time \(t\).
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting parameter sharing.} The same recurrent weights are
  used at every time step.
\item
  \textbf{Updating in the wrong order for language modeling.} To predict
  \(x_t\), the model should use information from \(x_1,\ldots,x_{t-1}\),
  not from \(x_t\) itself.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring gradient products.} Long-range learning depends on
  products of Jacobians.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming RNNs solve all sequence problems.} Vanilla RNNs often
  struggle with long dependencies. LSTM, GRU, and attention mechanisms
  were developed partly to address this problem.
\end{enumerate}

\section{11.20 Summary}\label{summary-1}

A recurrent neural network is a sequence model built from a repeated
update rule

\[
h_t=\phi(W_hh_{t-1}+W_xe_t+b_h).
\]

The hidden state is a learned continuous summary of the prefix. For
classification, the final state can feed a softmax classifier. For
language modeling, each hidden state predicts the next token
distribution.

The central mathematical challenge is that training requires
differentiating through many repeated compositions. Gradients contain
products of Jacobian matrices, which can vanish or explode. This
explains why vanilla RNNs are historically important but limited for
long-context language tasks. The next chapter studies gated recurrent
models, which modify the recurrence to control memory more explicitly.

\section{Exercises}\label{exercises-10}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Dimension check.} Let \(E\in \mathbb R^{10000\times 128}\),
  \(W_h\in \mathbb R^{256\times 256}\), and
  \(W_x\in \mathbb R^{256\times 128}\). What is the dimension of
  \(h_t\)? What is the dimension of \(W_xE_{x_t}\)?
\item
  \textbf{Bag-of-words failure.} Construct two sentences with the same
  bag-of-words vector but different meanings. Explain why a recurrent
  model can distinguish them in principle.
\item
  \textbf{Scalar recurrence.} For \(h_t=ah_{t-1}+bu_t\) with \(h_0=0\),
  prove that \[
  h_T=\sum_{s=1}^T a^{T-s}bu_s.
  \]
\item

  for the sequence \((x_1,x_2,x_3,x_4)\) under an RNN language model.
\item

\item

The accompanying lab for this chapter should guide students through:

\item

\chapter{LSTM and GRU Models}\label{lstm-and-gru-models}

Gated recurrences, memory paths, and long-range dependence

\hfill\break

A vanilla recurrent neural network updates its hidden state by
repeatedly applying the same nonlinear map. This gives a clean
dynamical-system model for sequences, but it also creates a mathematical
difficulty: gradients must pass through long products of Jacobian
matrices. These products may shrink or explode.

Long short-term memory networks and gated recurrent units modify the
recurrence by adding \textbf{gates}. A gate is a vector with coordinates
between \(0\) and \(1\). It controls how much information is kept,
forgotten, written, or revealed. From a mathematical point of view,
gated recurrent models are controlled nonlinear dynamical systems with
coordinatewise interpolation. Their main purpose is to create more
stable paths for information and gradients across long sequences.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-11}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  explain why vanilla RNNs have difficulty learning long-range
  dependencies;
\item
  define sigmoid gates and interpret them as coordinatewise
  interpolation weights;
\item
  write the LSTM equations and check all dimensions;
\item
  interpret the LSTM cell state as a controlled memory variable;
\item
  explain how forget gates create a direct memory path through time;
\item
  write the GRU equations and compare them with LSTM equations;
\item
  connect gate values to gradient flow and effective memory length;
\item
  implement LSTM and GRU forward passes from scratch in Python;
\item
  use an interactive visualization to compare ungated and gated memory.
\end{enumerate}

\section{12.1 The limitation of a vanilla
RNN}\label{the-limitation-of-a-vanilla-rnn}

In Chapter 11, a vanilla RNN was written as

\[
h_t = \phi(W_hh_{t-1}+W_xe_t+b_h),
\]

where \(e_t\) is the embedding of token \(x_t\) and \(h_t\) is the
hidden state. This recurrence is mathematically natural, but it has a
difficult optimization structure.

To see the issue, consider a scalar linearized recurrence

\[
h_t = a h_{t-1} + b u_t.
\]

Starting from \(h_0=0\), we have

\[
h_T = \sum_{s=1}^T a^{T-s}b u_s.
\]

The contribution of an earlier input \(u_s\) to the final state \(h_T\)
is multiplied by \(a^{T-s}\). Therefore:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  if \(|a|<1\), old information decays exponentially;
\item
  if \(|a|>1\), old information may explode;
\item
  if \(|a|\approx 1\), old information may persist.
\end{itemize}

The same idea appears in nonlinear vector RNNs. Differentiating through
time gives products of Jacobians. A typical factor has the form

\[
J_t = \frac{\partial h_t}{\partial h_{t-1}}.
\]

The derivative from time \(s\) to time \(T\) contains a product

\[
\frac{\partial h_T}{\partial h_s}
= J_TJ_{T-1}\cdots J_{s+1}.
\]

Long products of matrices are numerically delicate. Their norms can
become very small or very large. This is the mathematical source of the
vanishing and exploding gradient problem.

\textbf{Core difficulty.} A vanilla RNN asks one nonlinear state vector
\(h_t\) to do two jobs at once:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  represent the current useful summary of the prefix;
\item
  carry information and gradients across many time steps.
\end{enumerate}

LSTM and GRU models separate these roles more carefully by using gates.

\section{12.2 Gates as coordinatewise control
variables}\label{gates-as-coordinatewise-control-variables}

The basic mathematical object in an LSTM or GRU is a \textbf{gate}. A
gate is a vector

\[
g_t \in (0,1)^r
\]

computed from the current input and previous hidden state:

\[
g_t = \sigma(W_ge_t+U_gh_{t-1}+b_g).
\]

Here:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(e_t\in R^m\) is the input embedding;
\item
  \(h_{t-1}\in R^r\) is the previous hidden state;
\item
  \(W_g\in R^{r\times m}\);
\item
  \(U_g\in R^{r\times r}\);
\item
  \(b_g\in R^r\);
\item
  \(\sigma\) is the logistic sigmoid function applied coordinatewise.
\end{itemize}

The sigmoid function is

\[
\sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}}.
\]

Thus every coordinate satisfies

\[
0 < (g_t)_j < 1.
\]

This makes a gate useful for interpolation. For two vectors
\(a,b\in R^r\), the expression

\[
g_t\odot a + (1-g_t)\odot b
\]

is a coordinatewise convex combination of \(a\) and \(b\). The symbol
\(\odot\) denotes coordinatewise multiplication.

\textbf{Gate interpretation.} In coordinate \(j\),

\[
(g_t)_j a_j + (1-(g_t)_j)b_j
\]

lies between \(a_j\) and \(b_j\). If \((g_t)_j\approx 1\), the
coordinate mostly chooses \(a_j\). If \((g_t)_j\approx 0\), it mostly
chooses \(b_j\).

This simple interpolation idea is the mathematical heart of gated
recurrent networks.

\section{12.3 A minimal gated-memory
recurrence}\label{a-minimal-gated-memory-recurrence}

Before writing the full LSTM, consider a simplified memory recurrence:

\[
c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1} + i_t\odot \widetilde c_t.
\]

Here:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(c_t\in R^r\) is a memory state;
\item
  \(f_t\in (0,1)^r\) is a forget gate;
\item
  \(i_t\in (0,1)^r\) is an input gate;
\item
  \(\widetilde c_t\in R^r\) is a candidate update.
\end{itemize}

The recurrence has two terms:

\[
\text{old memory kept} = f_t\odot c_{t-1},
\]

\[
\text{new information written} = i_t\odot \widetilde c_t.
\]

If a coordinate of \(f_t\) is close to \(1\), then the corresponding
coordinate of \(c_{t-1}\) is copied forward almost unchanged. If it is
close to \(0\), that coordinate is mostly erased.

Suppose for a moment that \(f_t=f\) is a constant scalar and the
candidate update is zero after time \(s\). Then the memory contribution
from time \(s\) to time \(T\) is multiplied by

\[
f^{T-s}.
\]

This resembles the scalar RNN factor \(a^{T-s}\), but with an important
difference: the model learns the value of \(f_t\) dynamically from the
data. It can choose long memory for some coordinates and short memory
for others.

More generally, the direct derivative of the cell state with respect to
the previous cell state is approximately

\[
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(f_t),
\]

when we focus on the direct path and ignore indirect dependence of the
gates on earlier states. Therefore the memory path from time \(s\) to
time \(T\) contains factors

\[
\operatorname{diag}(f_T)\operatorname{diag}(f_{T-1})\cdots \operatorname{diag}(f_{s+1}).
\]

Coordinatewise, this is a product of forget-gate values. This is much
easier to interpret than a product of arbitrary recurrent Jacobian
matrices.

\section{12.4 The LSTM equations}\label{the-lstm-equations}

An LSTM has two state vectors:

\[
h_t\in R^r,
\qquad
c_t\in R^r.
\]

The vector \(h_t\) is the hidden state exposed to the output layer. The
vector \(c_t\) is the memory cell state.

Given input embedding \(e_t\in R^m\), previous hidden state
\(h_{t-1}\in R^r\), and previous cell state \(c_{t-1}\in R^r\), the LSTM
computes

\[
f_t = \sigma(W_fe_t+U_fh_{t-1}+b_f),
\]

\[
i_t = \sigma(W_ie_t+U_ih_{t-1}+b_i),
\]

\[
o_t = \sigma(W_oe_t+U_oh_{t-1}+b_o),
\]

\[
\widetilde c_t = \tanh(W_ce_t+U_ch_{t-1}+b_c).
\]

Then it updates

\[
c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1} + i_t\odot \widetilde c_t,
\]

and exposes

\[
h_t = o_t\odot \tanh(c_t).
\]

The three gates have standard names:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
Gate & Formula & Main role \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
forget gate & \(f_t\) & how much previous memory to keep \\
input gate & \(i_t\) & how much new candidate memory to write \\
output gate & \(o_t\) & how much memory to reveal as hidden state \\
\end{longtable}
}

The candidate \(\widetilde c_t\) proposes new content. The input gate
decides how much of that content enters memory.

\section{12.5 Dimension check for LSTM}\label{dimension-check-for-lstm}

Let:

\[
e_t\in R^m,
\qquad
h_t,c_t\in R^r.
\]

For each gate \(g\in\{f,i,o\}\), the parameters satisfy

\[
W_g\in R^{r\times m},
\qquad
U_g\in R^{r\times r},
\qquad
b_g\in R^r.
\]

For the candidate memory,

\[
W_c\in R^{r\times m},
\qquad
U_c\in R^{r\times r},
\qquad
b_c\in R^r.
\]

Therefore

\[
W_ge_t+U_gh_{t-1}+b_g\in R^r,
\]

so each gate is in \(R^r\). The update

\[
c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot \widetilde c_t
\]

is a sum of two vectors in \(R^r\). Hence \(c_t\in R^r\). Finally,

\[
h_t=o_t\odot \tanh(c_t)\in R^r.
\]

\textbf{Parameter count.} Each of the four affine maps has \(rm+r^2+r\)
parameters. Therefore one LSTM layer has

\[
4(rm+r^2+r)
\]

recurrent parameters, not counting the token embedding matrix and output
layer.

\section{12.6 Why the LSTM helps gradient
flow}\label{why-the-lstm-helps-gradient-flow}

The important mathematical feature is the additive cell-state update

\[
c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot \widetilde c_t.
\]

This creates a direct path from \(c_{t-1}\) to \(c_t\). Along this path,
the derivative is governed by the forget gate:

\[
\frac{\partial c_t}{\partial c_{t-1}} \approx \operatorname{diag}(f_t).
\]

Therefore, for coordinate \(j\), the direct memory derivative from time
\(s\) to time \(T\) is approximately

\[
\prod_{t=s+1}^T (f_t)_j.
\]

This formula gives a clean interpretation of memory length.

If \((f_t)_j\approx 0.5\), then memory decays quickly:

\[
0.5^{20}\approx 9.5\times 10^{-7}.
\]

If \((f_t)_j\approx 0.95\), then memory decays slowly:

\[
0.95^{20}\approx 0.36.
\]

So a gate coordinate near \(1\) can preserve information over many
steps. A gate coordinate near \(0\) can deliberately forget.

\textbf{Effective memory length.} If the forget gate is approximately
constant with value \(f\in(0,1)\), then the contribution after \(k\)
steps is roughly \(f^k\). The half-life \(k_{1/2}\) solves

\[
f^{k_{1/2}}=\frac12.
\]

Thus

\[
k_{1/2}=\frac{\log(1/2)}{\log f}.
\]

For \(f=0.9\), the half-life is about \(6.58\) steps. For \(f=0.99\), it
is about \(68.97\) steps.

\section{12.7 Statistical view: adaptive state-space
modeling}\label{statistical-view-adaptive-state-space-modeling}

A gated recurrent model can be viewed as a parameterized state-space
model for sequences. At time \(t\), it computes latent states

\[
(h_t,c_t)=F_\theta(h_{t-1},c_{t-1},e_t).
\]

For classification, it defines

\[
\widehat p_\theta(y\mid x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=\operatorname{softmax}(W_yh_T+b_y).
\]

For language modeling, it defines

\[
\widehat p_\theta(x_{t+1}\mid x_1,
\ldots,x_t)
=\operatorname{softmax}(W_yh_t+b_y).
\]

Given a training set

\[
D=\{(x^{(n)},y^{(n)})\}_{n=1}^N,
\]

a sequence classifier is usually trained by minimizing empirical
cross-entropy:

\[
\widehat R(\theta)
=\frac1N\sum_{n=1}^N
\left[-\log \widehat p_\theta(y^{(n)}\mid x^{(n)})\right].
\]

For language modeling, the negative log-likelihood is

\[
L(\theta)
= -\sum_{n=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^{T_n}
\log \widehat p_\theta(x_t^{(n)}\mid x_1^{(n)},\ldots,x_{t-1}^{(n)}).
\]

Thus LSTM and GRU models are not mysterious from a statistical point of
view. They are flexible parameterized conditional probability models.
The gates are part of the parameterized representation map.

\section{12.8 The GRU equations}\label{the-gru-equations}

A gated recurrent unit is a simpler gated model. It uses one state
vector \(h_t\in R^r\) rather than separate hidden and cell states.

Given input embedding \(e_t\in R^m\) and previous state
\(h_{t-1}\in R^r\), a GRU computes

\[
z_t = \sigma(W_ze_t+U_zh_{t-1}+b_z),
\]

\[
r_t = \sigma(W_re_t+U_rh_{t-1}+b_r),
\]

\[
\widetilde h_t = \tanh(W_he_t+U_h(r_t\odot h_{t-1})+b_h).
\]

Then it updates

\[
h_t = (1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1}+z_t\odot \widetilde h_t.
\]

The two gates are:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Gate
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Formula
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Main role
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
update gate & \(z_t\) & controls interpolation between old state and
candidate state \\
reset gate & \(r_t\) & controls how much old state is used in the
candidate \\
\end{longtable}
}

The update gate \(z_t\) is especially important. If
\((z_t)_j\approx 0\), then

\[
(h_t)_j\approx (h_{t-1})_j.
\]

If \((z_t)_j\approx 1\), then

\[
(h_t)_j\approx (\widetilde h_t)_j.
\]

Thus the GRU also creates a direct copying path through time.

\section{12.9 LSTM versus GRU}\label{lstm-versus-gru}

The LSTM has a separate memory cell \(c_t\) and hidden state \(h_t\).
The GRU combines memory and hidden state into one vector \(h_t\).

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2143}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2857}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2143}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Model
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
States
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
Gates
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Main memory path
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
vanilla RNN & \(h_t\) & none & nonlinear recurrence \\
LSTM & \(h_t,c_t\) & forget, input, output & cell-state update
\(c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\widetilde c_t\) \\
GRU & \(h_t\) & update, reset & interpolation
\(h_t=(1-z_t)\odot h_{t-1}+z_t\odot\widetilde h_t\) \\
\end{longtable}
}

There is no universal rule that one is always better. The LSTM is more
expressive and exposes a separate memory state. The GRU has fewer gates
and often fewer parameters, which can make it easier to train on smaller
data. Both are mathematically designed to improve long-range credit
assignment relative to a vanilla RNN.

\section{12.10 Worked example: memory
half-life}\label{worked-example-memory-half-life}

Suppose a scalar LSTM memory coordinate follows

\[
c_t=f c_{t-1}
\]

with no new input after time \(0\). If \(c_0=1\), then

\[
c_t=f^t.
\]

The half-life is the number of steps until \(c_t=1/2\):

\[
f^t=\frac12.
\]

Taking logs gives

\[
t=\frac{\log(1/2)}{\log f}.
\]

For \(f=0.8\),

\[
t\approx \frac{-0.6931}{-0.2231}\approx 3.11.
\]

For \(f=0.95\),

\[
t\approx \frac{-0.6931}{-0.0513}\approx 13.51.
\]

For \(f=0.99\),

\[
t\approx \frac{-0.6931}{-0.01005}\approx 68.97.
\]

This calculation gives an intuitive numerical meaning to the forget
gate.

\section{12.11 Interactive: gated memory versus vanilla
recurrence}\label{interactive-gated-memory-versus-vanilla-recurrence}

The following interactive compares a scalar vanilla recurrence with a
simplified scalar LSTM memory recurrence.

Vanilla recurrence:

\[
h_t=\tanh(a h_{t-1}+b u_t).
\]

Gated memory recurrence:

\[
c_t=f c_{t-1}+i\tanh(bu_t),
\qquad
h_t=o\tanh(c_t).
\]

Move the sliders to see how the forget gate \(f\) controls memory
persistence.

The HTML version of this chapter contains an interactive Plotly
visualization comparing a scalar vanilla recurrence with a simplified
scalar LSTM memory cell.

\section{12.12 Python example: LSTM forward pass from
scratch}\label{python-example-lstm-forward-pass-from-scratch}

The following NumPy example implements one LSTM layer for a short token
sequence. The goal is not to build a production model. The goal is to
make every matrix and vector visible.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch12-lstm-forward}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"the"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"movie"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"was"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"not"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"very"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{sequence }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"the"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"movie"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"was"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"not"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"very"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"good"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([vocab[w] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ sequence])}

\CommentTok{\# Dimensions}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)   }\CommentTok{\# vocabulary size}
\NormalTok{m }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4}            \CommentTok{\# embedding dimension}
\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}            \CommentTok{\# hidden/cell dimension}

\CommentTok{\# Embedding matrix}
\NormalTok{E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, m))}

\CommentTok{\# LSTM parameters}
\NormalTok{W\_f }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_f }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_f }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.ones(r) }\OperatorTok{*} \FloatTok{0.5}       \CommentTok{\# positive forget bias encourages memory early in training}

\NormalTok{W\_i }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_i }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_i }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}

\NormalTok{W\_o }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_o }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_o }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}

\NormalTok{W\_c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(z):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.exp(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{z))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ lstm\_step(e\_t, h\_prev, c\_prev):}
\NormalTok{    f\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(W\_f }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_f }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_f)}
\NormalTok{    i\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(W\_i }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_i }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_i)}
\NormalTok{    o\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(W\_o }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_o }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_o)}
\NormalTok{    c\_tilde }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.tanh(W\_c }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_c }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_c)}
\NormalTok{    c\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ f\_t }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ c\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ i\_t }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ c\_tilde}
\NormalTok{    h\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ o\_t }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.tanh(c\_t)}
\NormalTok{    cache }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"f"}\NormalTok{: f\_t, }\StringTok{"i"}\NormalTok{: i\_t, }\StringTok{"o"}\NormalTok{: o\_t, }\StringTok{"c\_tilde"}\NormalTok{: c\_tilde, }\StringTok{"c"}\NormalTok{: c\_t, }\StringTok{"h"}\NormalTok{: h\_t\}}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ h\_t, c\_t, cache}

\NormalTok{h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{c }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{history }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token\_id }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ x:}
\NormalTok{    e\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E[token\_id]}
\NormalTok{    h, c, cache }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ lstm\_step(e\_t, h, c)}
\NormalTok{    history.append(cache)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Sequence:"}\NormalTok{, sequence)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final hidden state shape:"}\NormalTok{, h.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final cell state shape:"}\NormalTok{, c.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final hidden state:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(h, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final forget gate:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(history[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][}\StringTok{"f"}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}

\CommentTok{\# Save the final LSTM states for later examples.}
\NormalTok{h\_lstm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ h.copy()}
\NormalTok{c\_lstm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ c.copy()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Sequence: ['the', 'movie', 'was', 'not', 'very', 'good']
Final hidden state shape: (5,)
Final cell state shape: (5,)
Final hidden state: [ 0.081  0.012  0.006  0.043 -0.037]
Final forget gate: [0.618 0.655 0.649 0.638 0.624]
\end{verbatim}

The forget bias was initialized to a positive value. This is common
because at the beginning of training it encourages the model not to
erase memory too aggressively.

\section{12.13 Python example: gate products and effective
memory}\label{python-example-gate-products-and-effective-memory}

The direct LSTM memory path is controlled by products of forget gates.
The following example simulates several constant forget-gate values and
plots the decay curves.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{80}
\NormalTok{steps }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(T }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{forget\_values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.70}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.85}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.99}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{plt.figure(figsize}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ f }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ forget\_values:}
\NormalTok{    weights }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ f }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ steps}
\NormalTok{    half\_life }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log(}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.log(f)}
\NormalTok{    plt.plot(steps, weights, label}\OperatorTok{=}\SpecialStringTok{f"f=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{f}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{, half{-}life=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{half\_life}\SpecialCharTok{:.1f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{plt.axhline(}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, linestyle}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"{-}{-}"}\NormalTok{, linewidth}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.xlabel(}\StringTok{"number of steps k"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.ylabel(}\StringTok{"memory weight f\^{}k"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.title(}\StringTok{"Direct memory decay controlled by the forget gate"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{plt.legend()}
\NormalTok{plt.show()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\pandocbounded{\includegraphics[keepaspectratio]{chapters/chapter-12-lstm-gru-models_files/figure-pdf/ch12-forget-products-output-1.pdf}}

This plot gives a concrete mathematical interpretation of gate values. A
change from \(0.95\) to \(0.99\) has a large effect on long-range
memory.

\section{12.14 Python example: GRU forward pass from
scratch}\label{python-example-gru-forward-pass-from-scratch}

The GRU is similar in spirit but uses fewer state variables. The
following code implements a GRU forward pass.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch12-gru-forward}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7339}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"need"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"memory"}\NormalTok{: }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{\}}
\NormalTok{sequence }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"need"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"memory"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([vocab[w] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ sequence])}

\CommentTok{\# Dimensions}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{m }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4}
\NormalTok{r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}

\NormalTok{E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, m))}

\NormalTok{W\_z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}

\NormalTok{W\_r }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_r }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_r }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}

\NormalTok{W\_h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, m))}
\NormalTok{U\_h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, r))}
\NormalTok{b\_h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(z):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.exp(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{z))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ gru\_step(e\_t, h\_prev):}
\NormalTok{    z\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(W\_z }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_z }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_z)}
\NormalTok{    r\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(W\_r }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_r }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_r)}
\NormalTok{    h\_tilde }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.tanh(W\_h }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ e\_t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ U\_h }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ (r\_t }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ h\_prev) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_h)}
\NormalTok{    h\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ z\_t) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ h\_prev }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ z\_t }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ h\_tilde}
\NormalTok{    cache }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"z"}\NormalTok{: z\_t, }\StringTok{"r"}\NormalTok{: r\_t, }\StringTok{"h\_tilde"}\NormalTok{: h\_tilde, }\StringTok{"h"}\NormalTok{: h\_t\}}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ h\_t, cache}

\NormalTok{h }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(r)}
\NormalTok{states }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{gates }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token\_id }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ x:}
\NormalTok{    e\_t }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E[token\_id]}
\NormalTok{    h, cache }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ gru\_step(e\_t, h)}
\NormalTok{    states.append(h.copy())}
\NormalTok{    gates.append(cache)}

\NormalTok{states }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array(states)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Sequence:"}\NormalTok{, sequence)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Hidden{-}state trajectory shape:"}\NormalTok{, states.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final update gate:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(gates[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][}\StringTok{"z"}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Final reset gate:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(gates[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][}\StringTok{"r"}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Sequence: ['language', 'models', 'need', 'long', 'memory']
Hidden-state trajectory shape: (5, 5)
Final update gate: [0.489 0.517 0.502 0.449 0.454]
Final reset gate: [0.506 0.508 0.52  0.481 0.498]
\end{verbatim}

The update gate \(z_t\) controls how much the state changes. Small
update-gate values preserve the old hidden state, while large values
overwrite it with the candidate state.

\section{12.15 Python example: LSTM output layer for
classification}\label{python-example-lstm-output-layer-for-classification}

After reading a full sequence, an LSTM can feed \(h_T\) into a
classifier:

\[
z = W_yh_T+b_y,
\qquad
p=\operatorname{softmax}(z).
\]

The following code uses the final LSTM hidden state saved from the
earlier forward pass and computes class probabilities.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch12-lstm-classifier-head}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{hidden\_dim }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ h\_lstm.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{W\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(K, hidden\_dim))}
\NormalTok{b\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(K)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(z):}
\NormalTok{    z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(z)}
\NormalTok{    exp\_z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(z)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ exp\_z }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ exp\_z.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\NormalTok{logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W\_y }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ h\_lstm }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b\_y}
\NormalTok{probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits)}
\NormalTok{y\_true }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{loss }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.log(probs[y\_true])}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Logits:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(logits, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Class probabilities:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(probs, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Cross{-}entropy loss:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(loss), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Logits: [-0.063 -0.025]
Class probabilities: [0.49 0.51]
Cross-entropy loss: 0.674
\end{verbatim}

The recurrent layer constructs the representation. The softmax layer
converts the representation into a conditional probability distribution.

\section{12.17 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-2}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  A gate is a vector in \((0,1)^r\) computed by a sigmoid affine map.
\item
  Gates create coordinatewise interpolation between old information and
  new information.
\item
  The LSTM cell state follows
\end{enumerate}

\[
c_t=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot\widetilde c_t.
\]

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{3}
\tightlist
\item
  The direct LSTM memory path is governed by products of forget-gate
  coordinates.
\item
  A GRU uses an update gate to interpolate between the old hidden state
  and a candidate hidden state.
\item
  LSTM and GRU models are conditional probability models trained by
  cross-entropy or negative log-likelihood.
\item
  The mathematical advantage of gates is not magic memory; it is a more
  stable differentiable path through time.
\end{enumerate}

\section{12.18 Exercises}\label{exercises-11}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Gate range.} Prove that every coordinate of
  \(g_t=\sigma(W_ge_t+U_gh_{t-1}+b_g)\) lies strictly between \(0\) and
  \(1\).
\item
  \textbf{Dimension check.} Suppose \(e_t\in R^{20}\) and
  \(h_t,c_t\in R^{64}\). Give the dimensions of all LSTM matrices
  \(W_f,U_f,W_i,U_i,W_o,U_o,W_c,U_c\) and all biases.
\item
  \textbf{Parameter count.} For \(m=100\) and \(r=256\), compute the
  number of recurrent parameters in one LSTM layer. Do the same for one
  GRU layer.
\item
  \textbf{Memory half-life.} Compute the memory half-life for \(f=0.8\),
  \(0.9\), \(0.95\), and \(0.99\). Interpret the result.
\item
  \textbf{Scalar LSTM.} Let \(c_t=0.9c_{t-1}+0.5\tanh(u_t)\) and
  \(h_t=\tanh(c_t)\). Compute \(c_1,c_2,c_3\) for \(c_0=0\) and inputs
  \(u_1=1\), \(u_2=0\), \(u_3=0\).
\item
  \textbf{GRU interpolation.} For scalar
  \(h_t=(1-z)h_{t-1}+z\widetilde h_t\), show that \(h_t\) lies between
  \(h_{t-1}\) and \(\widetilde h_t\) whenever \(0\le z\le 1\).
\item
  \textbf{Gradient path.} For constant scalar forget gate \(f\), derive
  \(\partial c_T/\partial c_s=f^{T-s}\).
\item
  \textbf{Model comparison.} Explain why the LSTM has more parameters
  than the GRU for the same input and hidden dimensions.
\item
  \textbf{Language modeling.} Write the negative log-likelihood for an
  LSTM language model on a corpus of variable-length token sequences.
\item
  \textbf{Critical thinking.} Give one situation in which a gated RNN
  might still fail to capture long-range structure. Explain whether the
  issue is representation, optimization, data, or evaluation.
\end{enumerate}

\section{12.19 Mini-project}\label{mini-project}

Build a small NumPy experiment comparing a scalar vanilla recurrence and
a scalar gated memory recurrence on a delayed-signal task.

A possible task is:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Generate sequences of length \(T\).
\item
  Put a binary signal at time \(1\).
\item
  Ask the model to predict the signal at time \(T\).
\item
  Compare how the memory weight changes with \(a\) in the vanilla
  recurrence and \(f\) in the gated recurrence.
\item
  Plot the final memory strength as a function of \(T\).
\end{enumerate}

The goal is not to train a large neural network. The goal is to
understand how recurrence parameters control memory mathematically.
