\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-6}

The LSTM was introduced by Hochreiter and Schmidhuber, and the GRU was
introduced as a simpler gated recurrent architecture in neural machine
translation research. This chapter emphasizes the mathematical structure
of gated recurrence: coordinatewise gates, additive memory updates, and
gradient paths. For broader NLP context, see Jurafsky and Martin (2024)
and Goldberg (2017). For deep learning background, see Goodfellow et al.
(2016a).

\part{Part V. Attention and Transformers}

\chapter{Attention Mechanisms}\label{attention-mechanisms}

Queries, keys, values, and weighted information flow

\hfill\break

Attention is the mathematical operation that allows a model to decide,
at each token position, which other token positions are most relevant.
Instead of compressing a whole prefix into a single recurrent state,
attention forms many pairwise comparisons between tokens. These
comparisons become nonnegative weights, and the output at each position
is a weighted average of value vectors.

This chapter develops attention from first principles. The central
object is the matrix formula

\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.
\]

The goal is not to memorize the formula, but to understand what each
matrix means, why the scaling factor appears, why the rows of the
attention matrix are probability vectors, and how masking changes the
conditional structure of the model.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-12}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  explain the role of queries, keys, and values in an attention layer;
\item
  check the dimensions in the scaled dot-product attention formula;
\item
  interpret the attention matrix as a row-stochastic matrix;
\item
  explain why attention outputs are weighted averages of value vectors;
\item
  compare hard lookup, nearest-neighbor search, kernel smoothing, and
  attention;
\item
  implement attention from scratch in NumPy;
\item
  apply padding masks and causal masks correctly;
\item
  use attention weights to inspect token-token interactions;
\item
  explain why attention is useful for NLP sequence modeling.
\end{enumerate}

\section{13.1 From sequential memory to pairwise
interaction}\label{from-sequential-memory-to-pairwise-interaction}

In a recurrent neural network, information flows through a hidden-state
recurrence

\[
h_t = F(h_{t-1},x_t).
\]

The representation of token \(t\) depends on earlier tokens through
repeated application of \(F\). This is a natural model for ordered data,
but it creates a narrow information path. If token \(t\) needs
information from token \(s\) with \(s\ll t\), the information must pass
through all intermediate updates.

Attention uses a different idea. Given token representations

\[
x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T \in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}},
\]

attention lets every position compare itself directly with every other
position. Position \(i\) asks a question, position \(j\) offers a key,
and the similarity between the question and the key determines how much
information flows from \(j\) to \(i\).

In one sentence:

\textbf{Attention is adaptive weighted averaging.} For each output
position \(i\), attention computes weights \(a_{ij}\ge 0\) with
\(\sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}=1\), then returns

\[
z_i = \sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}v_j.
\]

The weights are not fixed in advance. They are computed from the current
sequence.

\section{13.2 Input matrix and token
representations}\label{input-matrix-and-token-representations}

Suppose a sequence has length \(T\). Let

\[
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
- & x_1^T & - \\
- & x_2^T & - \\
& \vdots & \\
- & x_T^T & -
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
\]

The row \(x_i^T\) is the representation of token position \(i\). This
representation may combine token embedding, positional information, and
earlier neural transformations.

Attention does not use \(X\) directly. It first produces three
transformed views of the same sequence:

\[
Q = XW_Q,\qquad K = XW_K,\qquad V = XW_V.
\]

Here

\[
W_Q\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_k},\qquad
W_K\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_k},\qquad
W_V\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_v}.
\]

Therefore

\[
Q,K\in R^{T\times d_k},\qquad V\in R^{T\times d_v}.
\]

The rows are denoted

\[
q_i^T = \text{row } i \text{ of } Q,\qquad
k_j^T = \text{row } j \text{ of } K,\qquad
v_j^T = \text{row } j \text{ of } V.
\]

Interpretation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(q_i\) is the query at output position \(i\);
\item
  \(k_j\) is the key advertised by input position \(j\);
\item
  \(v_j\) is the information carried by input position \(j\).
\end{itemize}

The query and key live in the same space \(R^{d_k}\) so that their dot
product is meaningful. The value vector may live in a different space
\(R^{d_v}\).

\section{13.3 Scores as pairwise
similarities}\label{scores-as-pairwise-similarities}

For each pair of positions \((i,j)\), define the raw attention score

\[
s_{ij}=q_i^T k_j.
\]

In matrix form,

\[
S = QK^T \in R^{T\times T}.
\]

The entry \(S_{ij}\) compares the query at position \(i\) with the key
at position \(j\).

A large positive score means that token \(i\) strongly attends to token
\(j\). A large negative score means that token \(j\) is unlikely to
receive much attention from token \(i\) after the softmax step.

\subsection{\texorpdfstring{Why divide by
\(\sqrt{d_k}\)?}{Why divide by \textbackslash sqrt\{d\_k\}?}}\label{why-divide-by-sqrtd_k}

Assume for intuition that the coordinates of \(q_i\) and \(k_j\) are
independent random variables with mean \(0\) and variance \(1\). Then

\[
q_i^T k_j = \sum_{r=1}^{d_k} q_{ir}k_{jr}.
\]

Each product has mean \(0\) and variance approximately \(1\), so the sum
has variance approximately \(d_k\). Thus the typical size of
\(q_i^Tk_j\) grows like \(\sqrt{d_k}\).

If \(d_k\) is large, the unscaled scores may be too large in magnitude.
The softmax then becomes nearly one-hot, which can produce unstable
gradients. The scaled score is

\[
\tilde{s}_{ij}=\frac{q_i^Tk_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}.
\]

The scaling keeps the variance of scores more stable as \(d_k\) changes.

\section{13.4 Row-wise softmax and the attention
matrix}\label{row-wise-softmax-and-the-attention-matrix}

Given scaled scores

\[
\tilde{S}=\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}},
\]

define the attention weights row by row:

\[
a_{ij}
=
\frac{\exp(\tilde{s}_{ij})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^T \exp(\tilde{s}_{i\ell})}.
\]

Let

\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(\tilde{S}).
\]

Then \(A\in R^{T\times T}\) and every row of \(A\) is a probability
vector:

\[
a_{ij}\ge 0,
\qquad
\sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}=1.
\]

Thus attention turns arbitrary real-valued similarity scores into a
row-stochastic matrix.

\textbf{Attention as a Markov-style matrix.} The matrix \(A\) is
row-stochastic, like a transition matrix in a Markov chain. However,
\(A\) is not fixed. It is computed from \(X\) and therefore changes from
sequence to sequence.

\section{13.5 Weighted averages of
values}\label{weighted-averages-of-values}

The output of attention is

\[
Z=AV.
\]

Because \(A\in R^{T\times T}\) and \(V\in R^{T\times d_v}\), the output
satisfies

\[
Z\in R^{T\times d_v}.
\]

Row \(i\) is

\[
z_i = \sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}v_j.
\]

Since \(a_{ij}\ge 0\) and \(\sum_j a_{ij}=1\), each output vector
\(z_i\) is a convex combination of the value vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_T\).

This is the basic mechanism by which token representations exchange
information. Token \(i\) receives a weighted summary of all value
vectors, with weights determined by the similarity between \(q_i\) and
the keys.

\section{13.6 Attention as adaptive kernel
smoothing}\label{attention-as-adaptive-kernel-smoothing}

Students with a statistics background may find the following analogy
helpful. In kernel smoothing, an estimate at a point \(x\) often has the
form

\[
\hat{m}(x)=\sum_{j=1}^n w_j(x)y_j,
\]

where \(w_j(x)\ge 0\) and \(\sum_j w_j(x)=1\). The weights depend on the
similarity between \(x\) and training points \(x_j\).

Attention has the same weighted-average form:

\[
z_i = \sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}v_j.
\]

The difference is that the similarity function is learned. Instead of
choosing a fixed kernel, the model learns \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\), and
therefore learns how to compare tokens.

This viewpoint is useful:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(q_i\) is the location where the model wants information;
\item
  \(k_j\) determines how relevant position \(j\) is to that location;
\item
  \(v_j\) is the response or information to be averaged;
\item
  \(a_{ij}\) is a data-dependent weight.
\end{itemize}

\section{13.7 Masking}\label{masking}

Not every token should always attend to every other token. A mask is a
matrix \(M\in R^{T\times T}\) added to the scaled scores before the
softmax:

\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right).
\]

Allowed positions have mask value \(0\). Disallowed positions receive a
very negative number, such as \(-10^9\):

\[
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0, & \text{if position } j \text{ is allowed for query } i,\\
-10^9, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{cases}
\]

After the softmax, masked positions receive attention weight
approximately \(0\).

\subsection{Padding mask}\label{padding-mask}

Sequences in a batch often have different lengths. Shorter sequences are
padded with artificial tokens. A padding mask prevents real tokens from
attending to padding positions.

\subsection{Causal mask}\label{causal-mask}

In autoregressive language modeling, token \(i\) should not attend to
future tokens \(j>i\). The causal mask is

\[
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0, & j\le i,\\
-10^9, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\]

This makes the attention matrix lower triangular after the softmax, up
to numerical precision.

\section{13.8 Numerical stability}\label{numerical-stability}

The softmax should be computed using the stable formula

\[
\operatorname{softmax}(r)_j
=
\frac{\exp(r_j-c)}{\sum_{\ell}\exp(r_{\ell}-c)},
\qquad
c=\max_{\ell} r_{\ell}.
\]

Subtracting \(c\) does not change the softmax because it multiplies
numerator and denominator by the same constant. It prevents overflow
when some scores are large.

For a score row \(r\in R^T\), the Jacobian of the softmax is

\[
\frac{\partial a_j}{\partial r_\ell}
= a_j(\delta_{j\ell}-a_\ell).
\]

This formula shows why extremely peaked attention can make learning
difficult: when one \(a_j\) is almost \(1\) and the rest are almost
\(0\), many derivatives are close to \(0\).

\section{13.9 Worked example}\label{worked-example}

Suppose a sequence has \(T=3\) positions and \(d_k=2\). Let

\[
Q=K=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0\\
0 & 1\\
1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Then

\[
QK^T
=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1\\
0 & 1 & 1\\
1 & 1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Since \(d_k=2\), the scaled score matrix is

\[
\tilde{S}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 1\\
0 & 1 & 1\\
1 & 1 & 2
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The first row assigns equal raw similarity to positions \(1\) and \(3\),
and lower similarity to position \(2\). After the row-wise softmax, the
first output vector becomes a weighted average of \(v_1\), \(v_2\), and
\(v_3\), with larger weights on \(v_1\) and \(v_3\).

This example illustrates a key point: attention is not simply copying
one token. Unless the softmax is very sharp, attention blends
information from multiple positions.

\section{13.10 Python: scaled dot-product attention from
scratch}\label{python-scaled-dot-product-attention-from-scratch}

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch13-scaled-dot-product-attention}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\NormalTok{np.set\_printoptions(precision}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, suppress}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ row\_softmax(S):}
    \CommentTok{"""Stable row{-}wise softmax."""}
\NormalTok{    S\_shifted }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ S }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ S.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(S\_shifted)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ E }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ E.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ attention(Q, K, V, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{"""Scaled dot{-}product attention.}

\CommentTok{    Q: shape (T\_q, d\_k)}
\CommentTok{    K: shape (T\_k, d\_k)}
\CommentTok{    V: shape (T\_k, d\_v)}
\CommentTok{    mask: optional shape (T\_q, T\_k), added to scores before softmax}
\CommentTok{    """}
\NormalTok{    d\_k }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ K.T }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(d\_k)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ mask }\KeywordTok{is} \KeywordTok{not} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scores }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ mask}
\NormalTok{    A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_softmax(scores)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z, A, scores}

\NormalTok{Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([[}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{              [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{              [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]])}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q.copy()}
\NormalTok{V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([[}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{              [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{              [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]])}

\NormalTok{Z, A, scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ attention(Q, K, V)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"scaled scores"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(scores)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"attention weights"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(A)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"output"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(Z)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
scaled scores
[[0.707 0.    0.707]
 [0.    0.707 0.707]
 [0.707 0.707 1.414]]
attention weights
[[0.401 0.198 0.401]
 [0.198 0.401 0.401]

[[0.802 0.599]

\section{13.11 Python: attention with learned
projections}\label{python-attention-with-learned-projections}

In a neural network, \(Q\), \(K\), and \(V\) are usually obtained from
an input matrix \(X\) by learned linear maps.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch13-projections}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}
\NormalTok{D\_model }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4}
\NormalTok{d\_k }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{3}
\NormalTok{d\_v }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(T, D\_model))}
\NormalTok{W\_Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(D\_model, d\_k))}
\NormalTok{W\_K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(D\_model, d\_k))}
\NormalTok{W\_V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(D\_model, d\_v))}

\NormalTok{Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_Q}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_K}
\NormalTok{V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_V}

\NormalTok{Z, A, scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ attention(Q, K, V)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"X shape:"}\NormalTok{, X.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Q shape:"}\NormalTok{, Q.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"K shape:"}\NormalTok{, K.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"V shape:"}\NormalTok{, V.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"A shape:"}\NormalTok{, A.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Z shape:"}\NormalTok{, Z.shape)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

K shape: (5, 3)
V shape: (5, 2)
A shape: (5, 5)
Z shape: (5, 2)
\end{verbatim}

Dimension checking is not bookkeeping only. It is the fastest way to
find conceptual mistakes in an attention implementation.

\section{13.12 Python: causal mask}\label{python-causal-mask}

A causal mask prevents position \(i\) from using information at future
positions \(j>i\).

\begin{Shaded}

\section{13.14 Interactive HTML: scaled attention
explorer}\label{interactive-html-scaled-attention-explorer}

The following interactive component lets you vary the scale of the
dot-product scores and choose whether to apply a causal mask. It uses a
local Plotly file from \texttt{assets/plotly.min.js}, so it does not
depend on a CDN.

The slider changes the sharpness of the attention distribution. Low
scale gives diffuse averaging. High scale gives attention weights closer
to hard selection.

\section{13.15 Multi-head attention
preview}\label{multi-head-attention-preview}

A single attention head compares tokens in one learned query-key space.
Multi-head attention uses several heads in parallel:

\[
\operatorname{head}_h
=
\operatorname{Attention}(XW_Q^{(h)},XW_K^{(h)},XW_V^{(h)}).
\]

The heads are concatenated and projected:

\[
\operatorname{MultiHead}(X)
=
\operatorname{Concat}(\operatorname{head}_1,\ldots,\operatorname{head}_H)W_O.
\]

Different heads can learn different comparison rules. One head may
attend to local syntax, another to long-range agreement, and another to
delimiter or position-like patterns. The next chapter studies
self-attention and multi-head attention in more detail.

\section{13.16 AI-assisted learning: attention
audit}\label{ai-assisted-learning-attention-audit}

Use an AI system as a mathematical critic, not as an authority.

\subsection{Prompt 1: dimension
checking}\label{prompt-1-dimension-checking-1}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
I have \(X\in R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\),
\(W_Q,W_K\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_k}\), and
\(W_V\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_v}\). Check every dimension in
scaled dot-product attention and explain the shape of the final output.
\end{quote}

Then verify every matrix product yourself.

\subsection{Prompt 2: interpretation
critique}\label{prompt-2-interpretation-critique}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Explain why attention weights should not automatically be interpreted as
a complete explanation of a transformer model's prediction.
\end{quote}

A good answer should distinguish internal routing from causal
explanation.

\subsection{Prompt 3: mask debugging}\label{prompt-3-mask-debugging}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
I implemented a causal mask for self-attention. What numerical checks
should I run to verify that future positions have zero attention weight?
\end{quote}

You should expect checks involving the upper triangular part of the
attention matrix.

\section{13.17 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-2}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing keys and values.} Keys determine weights; values
  carry the information being averaged.
\item
  \textbf{Applying softmax over the wrong axis.} In standard attention,
  softmax is applied row by row over keys for each query.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting the scaling factor.} Without \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\),
  scores may become too large when \(d_k\) is large.
\item
  \textbf{Using a mask after softmax.} Masks should be applied to scores
  before softmax, followed by renormalization.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring dimensions.} Most attention implementation errors are
  shape errors in disguise.
\end{enumerate}

\section{13.18 Exercises}\label{exercises-12}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Dimension check.} Suppose \(T=12\), \(d_{\mathrm{model}}=64\),
  \(d_k=16\), and \(d_v=20\). Write the shapes of \(X\), \(W_Q\),
  \(W_K\), \(W_V\), \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\), \(QK^T\), \(A\), and \(Z\).
\item
  \textbf{Row-stochastic proof.} Prove that each row of
  \(A=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S)\) sums to \(1\) and has
  nonnegative entries.
\item
  \textbf{Convex combination.} Prove that each attention output \(z_i\)
  lies in the convex hull of the value vectors \(v_1,\ldots,v_T\).
\item
  \textbf{Scaling argument.} Assume the coordinates of \(q\) and \(k\)
  are independent with mean \(0\) and variance \(1\). Compute the mean
  and variance of \(q^Tk\).
\item
  \textbf{Masking.} For \(T=4\), write the causal mask matrix using
  \(0\) and \(-\infty\) notation.
\item
  \textbf{Attention versus kernel smoothing.} Compare attention with
  Nadaraya-Watson kernel regression. What is fixed in kernel regression
  but learned in attention?
\item
  \textbf{Implementation.} Implement attention in NumPy. Verify that the
  attention matrix is row-stochastic before and after applying a causal
  mask.
\item
  \textbf{Interpretation.} Give an example where a token receives high
  attention weight but is not necessarily the sole explanation for the
  model's final prediction.
\end{enumerate}

\section{13.21 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-3}

Attention is a learned, data-dependent weighted-average operator. The
mathematical structure is simple and powerful:

\[
Q=XW_Q,
\qquad
K=XW_K,
\qquad
V=XW_V,
\]

\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right),
\qquad
Z=AV.
\]

The matrix \(A\) determines how information moves among token positions.
Because \(A\) is computed from the sequence itself, attention can adapt
its information flow to each input.

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-7}

Attention was introduced into neural sequence modeling before the
transformer architecture and became central in encoder-decoder models
for machine translation. Scaled dot-product attention and multi-head
attention are the core operations in the transformer architecture.
Useful references include Bahdanau et al. (2015), Vaswani et al. (2017),
Jurafsky and Martin (2024), and Goodfellow et al. (2016b).

\chapter{Self-Attention}\label{self-attention}

Contextual token representations, permutation equivariance, and
multi-head structure

\hfill\break

Self-attention is the operation that made the Transformer architecture
possible. In an RNN, information moves through a time-indexed hidden
state. In self-attention, all token positions in a sequence compare
themselves with all other token positions directly. The result is a new
representation for each token, called a \textbf{contextual embedding},
whose meaning depends on the entire sequence.

The mathematical object in this chapter is the self-attention map

\[
X \mapsto \operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{XW_QW_K^TX^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right)XW_V.
\]

This formula is compact, but it hides several important ideas: learned
pairwise similarity, row-stochastic averaging, masking, positional
information, permutation equivariance, and parallel attention heads. We
study each idea carefully.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-13}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  define self-attention as attention with \(Q,K,V\) all computed from
  the same sequence matrix \(X\);
\item
  check every matrix dimension in a self-attention layer;
\item
  explain why self-attention produces contextual token embeddings;
\item
  prove the permutation equivariance of self-attention without
  positional encodings;
\item
  explain why positional information is necessary for language modeling;
\item
  construct padding masks and causal masks;
\item
  interpret multi-head attention as several learned comparison
  geometries in parallel;
\item
  implement single-head and multi-head self-attention from scratch in
  NumPy;
\item
  use attention heatmaps carefully without over-interpreting them;
\item
  explain the computational cost of self-attention.
\end{enumerate}

\section{14.1 From attention to
self-attention}\label{from-attention-to-self-attention}

In Chapter 13, attention was defined for three matrices

\[
Q\in R^{T_q\times d_k},\qquad K\in R^{T_k\times d_k},\qquad V\in R^{T_k\times d_v},
\]

by

\[
\operatorname{Attention}(Q,K,V)
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.
\]

In \textbf{self-attention}, the queries, keys, and values are all
computed from the same sequence. Let

\[
X\in R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}
\]

be the matrix of token representations for a sequence of length \(T\).
The \(i\)th row \(x_i^T\) represents token position \(i\). A
self-attention head uses learned matrices

\[
W_Q\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_k},\qquad
W_K\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_k},\qquad
W_V\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_v}
\]

to form

\[
Q=XW_Q,
\qquad
K=XW_K,
\qquad
V=XW_V.
\]

Then

\[
Z
=
\operatorname{SelfAttn}(X)
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{XW_QW_K^TX^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)XW_V.
\]

The output \(Z\in R^{T\times d_v}\) has one row for each token position.
Each row is a weighted average of transformed value vectors from the
same sequence.

\textbf{One sentence summary.} Self-attention lets every token position
build a new representation by asking: which other token positions in
this same sequence are relevant to me?

\section{14.2 Token matrices and dimension
bookkeeping}\label{token-matrices-and-dimension-bookkeeping}

A sequence of tokens

\[
w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T
\]

is first mapped to vectors. If \(E\in R^{|V|\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\)
is a token embedding matrix and token \(w_i\) has integer index \(r_i\),
then

\[
e_i=E_{r_i,:}\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
\]

Usually we also add positional information
\(p_i\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}}\):

\[
x_i=e_i+p_i.
\]

Stacking rows gives

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
x_1^T\\
x_2^T\\
\vdots\\
x_T^T
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
\]

For one attention head:

\[
XW_Q\in R^{T\times d_k},
\qquad
XW_K\in R^{T\times d_k},
\qquad
XW_V\in R^{T\times d_v}.
\]

The score matrix is

\[
S=\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\in R^{T\times T}.
\]

The attention matrix is

\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S)\in R^{T\times T}.
\]

The output is

\[
Z=AV\in R^{T\times d_v}.
\]

The row \(z_i^T\) is the new representation of token position \(i\).

\section{14.3 Contextual embeddings}\label{contextual-embeddings}

A static word embedding assigns one vector to each token type. For
example, the word \texttt{bank} might have a single embedding vector.
But the meaning of \texttt{bank} changes in different contexts:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{river\ bank}
\item
  \texttt{bank\ loan}
\item
  \texttt{central\ bank}
\end{itemize}

Self-attention produces \textbf{contextual embeddings}. The output
vector \(z_i\) at position \(i\) depends not only on \(x_i\), but also
on all rows of \(X\) through the attention weights.

Row \(i\) of the output is

\[
z_i
=
\sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}v_j,
\]

where

\[
a_{ij}
=
\frac{\exp(q_i^Tk_j/\sqrt{d_k})}
{\sum_{\ell=1}^T \exp(q_i^Tk_\ell/\sqrt{d_k})}.
\]

Since \(q_i\), \(k_j\), and \(v_j\) are all functions of the input token
representations, the vector \(z_i\) changes when the surrounding
sentence changes.

\textbf{Contextualization.} A token representation is contextual if
changing another token in the same sequence can change the
representation at the original position.

\subsection{A small mathematical test for
contextuality}\label{a-small-mathematical-test-for-contextuality}

Let \(F:R^{T\times d}\to R^{T\times d_v}\) be a sequence model. The
representation at position \(i\) is contextual if there exists some
\(j\ne i\) such that

\[
\frac{\partial F_i(X)}{\partial x_j}\ne 0.
\]

For self-attention, this derivative is usually nonzero because the
scores \(q_i^Tk_j\) and the value \(v_j\) both depend on \(x_j\).

\section{14.4 Self-attention as a learned graph on
tokens}\label{self-attention-as-a-learned-graph-on-tokens}

For a fixed input sequence \(X\), the attention matrix

\[
A(X)\in R^{T\times T}
\]

can be viewed as the weighted adjacency matrix of a directed graph on
token positions. The edge weight from query position \(i\) to key/value
position \(j\) is \(a_{ij}\).

This graph is:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{weighted}, because \(a_{ij}\in[0,1]\);
\item
  \textbf{directed}, because usually \(a_{ij}\ne a_{ji}\);
\item
  \textbf{row-stochastic}, because \(\sum_j a_{ij}=1\);
\item
  \textbf{data-dependent}, because \(A\) changes with \(X\).
\end{itemize}

Self-attention therefore constructs a sequence-specific graph and then
performs a weighted message-passing step:

\[
z_i=\sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}v_j.
\]

This connects self-attention with graph neural networks. The difference
is that the graph is not given externally; it is inferred from learned
similarities inside the sequence.

\section{14.5 Permutation equivariance without positional
information}\label{permutation-equivariance-without-positional-information}

A subtle but important mathematical property of self-attention is
permutation equivariance. Without positional information or masks,
self-attention does not know the order of tokens. It only sees a set of
input rows.

Let \(P\in R^{T\times T}\) be a permutation matrix. The matrix \(PX\) is
obtained by permuting the rows of \(X\). Define one-head self-attention
by

\[
F(X)=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{XW_QW_K^TX^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)XW_V.
\]

Then

\[
F(PX)=PF(X).
\]

This property is called \textbf{permutation equivariance}.

\subsection{Proof}\label{proof}

Let

\[
Q=XW_Q,
\qquad
K=XW_K,
\qquad
V=XW_V.
\]

For the permuted input \(PX\),

\[
Q'=PXW_Q=PQ,
\qquad
K'=PXW_K=PK,
\qquad
V'=PXW_V=PV.
\]

The score matrix becomes

\[
S'
=
\frac{Q'(K')^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
=
\frac{(PQ)(PK)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
=
\frac{P Q K^T P^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
=
P S P^T.
\]

Row-wise softmax commutes with simultaneous row and column permutation,
so

\[
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S')
=
P\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S)P^T
=
PAP^T.
\]

Therefore

\[
F(PX)
=
(PAP^T)(PV)
=PA(P^TP)V
=PAV
=PF(X).
\]

This proves the claim.

\subsection{Why this matters}\label{why-this-matters}

A language model must distinguish

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{student studies model}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

from

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{model studies student}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

because the order changes the meaning. Self-attention without positional
information treats these as row permutations of the same collection of
token vectors. The output rows are permuted in the same way, but the
model has no intrinsic sense of first, second, or third position.

Therefore Transformers add positional information.

\section{14.6 Positional information breaks pure permutation
symmetry}\label{positional-information-breaks-pure-permutation-symmetry}

A common input representation is

\[
x_i=e(w_i)+p_i,
\]

where \(e(w_i)\) is the token embedding and \(p_i\) is a position
vector. The sequence matrix is then

\[
X=
\begin{bmatrix}
(e(w_1)+p_1)^T\\
\cdots\\
(e(w_T)+p_T)^T
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

Now token identity and token position are mixed in each row. The model
can learn different behaviors for early positions, nearby positions, or
relative patterns.

There are several common approaches:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  learned absolute position embeddings;
\item
  sinusoidal position encodings;
\item
  relative position biases;
\item
  rotary position embeddings.
\end{itemize}

Chapter 16 studies these in more detail. For now, the key point is
simple: self-attention provides token-token interaction, but positional
information provides order.

\section{14.7 Masked self-attention}\label{masked-self-attention}

A mask is added to the score matrix before softmax:

\[
A
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}
\left(
\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M
\right).
\]

Allowed entries of \(M\) are \(0\). Disallowed entries are large
negative numbers.

\subsection{Padding mask}\label{padding-mask-1}

A padding mask prevents real tokens from attending to artificial padding
tokens. If token position \(j\) is padding, then set

\[
M_{ij}=-10^9
\]

for every query position \(i\).

\subsection{Causal mask}\label{causal-mask-1}

A causal mask prevents position \(i\) from attending to future positions
\(j>i\):

\[
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0, & j\le i,\\
-10^9, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\]

Causal masking is necessary for autoregressive language modeling. When
predicting token \(w_{t+1}\), the representation at position \(t\) must
not use information from tokens after \(t\).

The causal factorization is

\[
P(w_1,\ldots,w_T)
=
\prod_{t=1}^T P(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}).
\]

Causal self-attention enforces this conditional structure inside the
network.

\section{14.8 Multi-head
self-attention}\label{multi-head-self-attention}

A single attention head uses one learned query-key geometry. Multi-head
attention uses \(H\) such heads in parallel.

For head \(h\), define

\[
Q^{(h)}=XW_Q^{(h)},
\qquad
K^{(h)}=XW_K^{(h)},
\qquad
V^{(h)}=XW_V^{(h)}.
\]

The head output is

\[
Z^{(h)}
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}
\left(
\frac{Q^{(h)}(K^{(h)})^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M
\right)V^{(h)}.
\]

The head outputs are concatenated:

\[
Z_{\mathrm{cat}}
=
\operatorname{Concat}(Z^{(1)},\ldots,Z^{(H)})
\in R^{T\times Hd_v}.
\]

Then an output projection maps back to the model dimension:

\[
\operatorname{MHA}(X)
=
Z_{\mathrm{cat}}W_O,
\qquad
W_O\in R^{Hd_v\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}.
\]

If \(d_v=d_k=d_{\mathrm{model}}/H\), then the concatenated output has
dimension \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\), which is convenient for residual
connections.

\textbf{Multi-head viewpoint.} Each head learns a different similarity
geometry. One head may emphasize nearby tokens, another may emphasize
matching syntax, and another may emphasize semantic roles. The
architecture does not force these roles; they emerge, if useful, from
the training objective.

\section{14.9 Self-attention as matrix-valued feature
construction}\label{self-attention-as-matrix-valued-feature-construction}

From a statistical learning point of view, a self-attention layer is a
data-dependent feature map.

For a fixed parameter collection \(\theta=(W_Q,W_K,W_V)\),

\[
F_\theta(X)=A_\theta(X)XW_V,
\]

where

\[
A_\theta(X)
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}
\left(\frac{XW_QW_K^TX^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right).
\]

This is nonlinear in \(X\) because \(A_\theta(X)\) itself depends on
\(X\). However, conditional on the attention matrix \(A_\theta(X)\), the
output is linear in the values:

\[
Z=A_\theta(X)V.
\]

So self-attention has two layers of structure:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  construct a similarity matrix from \(X\);
\item
  use that matrix to average transformed vectors.
\end{enumerate}

This decomposition is often the cleanest way to understand the
operation.

\section{14.10 Attention entropy and
sharpness}\label{attention-entropy-and-sharpness}

For each query position \(i\), the attention row
\(a_i=(a_{i1},\ldots,a_{iT})\) is a probability vector. Its entropy is

\[
H(a_i)=-\sum_{j=1}^T a_{ij}\log a_{ij}.
\]

Low entropy means the query attends mostly to a few positions. High
entropy means the query averages broadly across the sequence.

If the scores are multiplied by a scale parameter \(\gamma>0\),

\[
a_{ij}(\gamma)
=
\frac{\exp(\gamma s_{ij})}{\sum_{\ell=1}^T \exp(\gamma s_{i\ell})},
\]

then increasing \(\gamma\) usually makes attention sharper. Decreasing
\(\gamma\) makes attention more uniform.

This is one reason the factor \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\) matters: it controls the
typical scale of the scores before the softmax.

\section{14.11 Computational complexity}\label{computational-complexity}

For sequence length \(T\) and key dimension \(d_k\), the score matrix

\[
QK^T
\]

requires roughly \(O(T^2d_k)\) arithmetic operations and stores
\(O(T^2)\) attention weights. The multiplication

\[
AV
\]

requires roughly \(O(T^2d_v)\) operations.

Thus standard full self-attention scales quadratically in sequence
length. This is powerful for moderate sequences but expensive for very
long documents. Many efficient Transformer variants modify the attention
pattern to reduce this cost.

For this book, the main mathematical point is:

The power of full self-attention comes from all-pairs token interaction.
The cost of full self-attention also comes from all-pairs token
interaction.

\section{14.12 Worked example: two query
positions}\label{worked-example-two-query-positions}

Suppose a sequence has three value vectors

\[
v_1=(1,0),\qquad v_2=(0,1),\qquad v_3=(1,1).
\]

Assume that after softmax the first two attention rows are

\[
a_1=(0.7,0.2,0.1),
\qquad
a_2=(0.1,0.3,0.6).
\]

Then

\[
z_1=0.7v_1+0.2v_2+0.1v_3
=(0.8,0.3),
\]

and

\[
z_2=0.1v_1+0.3v_2+0.6v_3
=(0.7,0.9).
\]

The same value vectors produce different contextual embeddings because
the attention rows are different.

\section{14.13 Python example: single-head self-attention from
scratch}\label{python-example-single-head-self-attention-from-scratch}

The next code block implements one self-attention head using NumPy.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{np.set\_printoptions(precision}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, suppress}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ row\_softmax(S):}
\NormalTok{    S\_shifted }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ S }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ S.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(S\_shifted)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ E }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ E.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ self\_attention(X, W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_Q}
\NormalTok{    K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_K}
\NormalTok{    V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_V}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ K.T }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(Q.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ mask }\KeywordTok{is} \KeywordTok{not} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scores }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ mask}
\NormalTok{    A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_softmax(scores)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z, A, scores}

\CommentTok{\# Toy token matrix: T = 4 tokens, d\_model = 3 features.}
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{W\_Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{W\_K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{W\_V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{Z, A, scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ self\_attention(X, W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Attention matrix A:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(A)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Output Z:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(Z)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Row sums of A:"}\NormalTok{, A.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Attention matrix A:
[[0.312 0.277 0.204 0.207]
 [0.292 0.267 0.22  0.222]
 [0.196 0.204 0.299 0.301]
 [0.178 0.192 0.315 0.315]]

Output Z:
[[0.734 0.583]
 [0.713 0.615]
 [0.614 0.776]
 [0.595 0.806]]

Row sums of A: [1. 1. 1. 1.]
\end{verbatim}

Each row of \(A\) sums to \(1\). The output row \(z_i\) is a weighted
average of the rows of \(V=XW_V\).

\section{14.14 Python example: causal
masking}\label{python-example-causal-masking}

The causal mask prevents future attention.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{causal\_mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{causal\_mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.where(causal\_mask }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1e9}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{Z\_causal, A\_causal, scores\_causal }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ self\_attention(}
\NormalTok{    X, W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{causal\_mask}
\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Causal attention matrix:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(A\_causal)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Entries above the diagonal are approximately zero."}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Causal attention matrix:
[[1.    0.    0.    0.   ]
 [0.522 0.478 0.    0.   ]
 [0.28  0.292 0.428 0.   ]
 [0.178 0.192 0.315 0.315]]

Entries above the diagonal are approximately zero.
\end{verbatim}

The first token can attend only to itself. The second token can attend
to positions \(1\) and \(2\). The last token can attend to all previous
positions and itself.

\section{14.15 Python example: multi-head
self-attention}\label{python-example-multi-head-self-attention}

The following implementation uses a list of projection matrices, one set
per head.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ multi\_head\_self\_attention(X, heads, W\_O}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    outputs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{    attentions }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ W\_Q\_h, W\_K\_h, W\_V\_h }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ heads:}
\NormalTok{        Z\_h, A\_h, \_ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ self\_attention(X, W\_Q\_h, W\_K\_h, W\_V\_h, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{mask)}
\NormalTok{        outputs.append(Z\_h)}
\NormalTok{        attentions.append(A\_h)}
\NormalTok{    Z\_cat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.concatenate(outputs, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ W\_O }\KeywordTok{is} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z\_cat, attentions}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z\_cat }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W\_O, attentions}

\NormalTok{heads }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
\NormalTok{    (W\_Q, W\_K, W\_V),}
\NormalTok{    (}
\NormalTok{        np.array([[}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{]]),}
\NormalTok{        np.array([[}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.6}\NormalTok{]]),}
\NormalTok{        np.array([[}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{], [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]]),}
\NormalTok{    ),}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{Z\_multi, A\_heads }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ multi\_head\_self\_attention(X, heads)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Multi{-}head output shape:"}\NormalTok{, Z\_multi.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Head 1 attention:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(A\_heads[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Head 2 attention:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(A\_heads[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Multi-head output shape: (4, 4)
Head 1 attention:
[[0.312 0.277 0.204 0.207]
 [0.292 0.267 0.22  0.222]
 [0.196 0.204 0.299 0.301]
 [0.178 0.192 0.315 0.315]]
Head 2 attention:
[[0.266 0.24  0.222 0.272]
 [0.249 0.232 0.239 0.28 ]
 [0.181 0.19  0.304 0.325]
 [0.194 0.198 0.289 0.32 ]]
\end{verbatim}

The two heads may produce different attention patterns because their
projection matrices define different query-key geometries.

\section{14.16 Python example: attention
entropy}\label{python-example-attention-entropy}

Attention rows are probability vectors, so we can compute row entropies.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ entropy\_rows(A):}
\NormalTok{    A\_safe }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.clip(A, }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{(A\_safe }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.log(A\_safe)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Unmasked row entropies:"}\NormalTok{, entropy\_rows(A))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Causal row entropies:"}\NormalTok{, entropy\_rows(A\_causal))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Unmasked row entropies: [1.369 1.379 1.366 1.352]
Causal row entropies: [0.    0.692 1.079 1.352]
\end{verbatim}

Entropy is not automatically good or bad. It is a diagnostic. The
appropriate sharpness depends on the task, the layer, and the head.

\section{14.17 Interactive HTML: self-attention head
explorer}\label{interactive-html-self-attention-head-explorer}

The following interactive component compares three hand-designed
self-attention heads. It uses the local Plotly file
\texttt{assets/plotly.min.js}, so it should work without a network
connection after the book is rendered.

Use this interactive as a mathematical object, not merely a picture. Ask
how the attention matrix changes when scores are sharpened, when future
tokens are masked, and when the head geometry changes.

\section{14.18 AI-assisted learning: self-attention
audit}\label{ai-assisted-learning-self-attention-audit}

AI systems can help you check your reasoning, but they should not
replace it. Use them as mathematical critics.

\subsection{Prompt 1: dimension audit}\label{prompt-1-dimension-audit-1}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Let \(X\in R^{T\times d_{\mathrm{model}}}\) and let
\(W_Q,W_K\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_k}\),
\(W_V\in R^{d_{\mathrm{model}}\times d_v}\). Check every matrix
dimension in one-head self-attention and explain why the output has
shape \(T\times d_v\).
\end{quote}

Then verify the answer line by line.

\subsection{Prompt 2: proof critique}\label{prompt-2-proof-critique}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
I claim that self-attention without positional encodings is permutation
equivariant. Give a proof using a permutation matrix \(P\), and identify
exactly where row-wise softmax is used.
\end{quote}

Check whether the proof distinguishes invariance from equivariance.

\subsection{Prompt 3: causal-mask
explanation}\label{prompt-3-causal-mask-explanation}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Explain why causal self-attention is needed for autoregressive language
modeling. Connect the mask to the factorization
\(P(w_1,\ldots,w_T)=\prod_t P(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1})\).
\end{quote}

Then write your own explanation in one paragraph.

\section{14.19 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-3}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing attention with explanation.} Attention weights are
  useful diagnostics, but they are not complete causal explanations of a
  model's decision.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting row-wise softmax.} The softmax is applied
  separately to each query row.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring positional information.} Self-attention alone is
  permutation equivariant; language requires order.
\item
  \textbf{Using the wrong mask orientation.} In causal attention, query
  position \(i\) may attend to key position \(j\) only when \(j\le i\).
\item
  \textbf{Confusing token type and token position.} The same word
  appearing twice can have two different contextual embeddings.
\item
  \textbf{Overlooking quadratic cost.} Full attention stores a
  \(T\times T\) matrix for each head.
\end{enumerate}

\section{14.20 Exercises}\label{exercises-13}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Dimension check.} Let \(T=12\), \(d_{\mathrm{model}}=64\),
  \(d_k=16\), and \(d_v=16\). Give the shapes of \(Q,K,V,QK^T,A\), and
  \(Z\) for one attention head.
\item
  \textbf{Contextuality.} Explain why changing token \(x_j\) can change
  output vector \(z_i\) even when \(i\ne j\).
\item
  \textbf{Permutation equivariance.} Prove that one-head self-attention
  without masks and positional embeddings satisfies \(F(PX)=PF(X)\) for
  every permutation matrix \(P\).
\item
  \textbf{Position necessity.} Give two three-token sentences with the
  same words but different order and different meaning. Explain why
  token embeddings alone cannot distinguish them under a
  permutation-equivariant model.
\item
  \textbf{Causal mask.} Write the \(5\times 5\) causal mask pattern
  showing allowed and disallowed entries.
\item
  \textbf{Entropy.} For \(a=(0.7,0.2,0.1)\) and \(b=(1/3,1/3,1/3)\),
  compute \(H(a)\) and \(H(b)\). Which distribution is sharper?
\item
  \textbf{Multi-head dimensions.} Suppose \(d_{\mathrm{model}}=128\),
  \(H=8\), and \(d_v=16\). What is the dimension of the concatenated
  head output? What shape should \(W_O\) have to return to
  \(d_{\mathrm{model}}\)?
\item
  \textbf{Implementation.} Modify the Python function
  \texttt{self\_attention} to return both the unnormalized score matrix
  and the attention matrix.
\item
  \textbf{Mask orientation test.} Construct a toy sequence of length
  \(4\) and verify that your causal mask makes the upper triangular
  entries of \(A\) approximately zero.
\item
  \textbf{Interpretation.} Give one reason an attention heatmap may be
  useful and one reason it may be misleading.
\end{enumerate}

Build a small attention laboratory in Python.

\item

\item

\item
  Write a short report explaining what each head appears to measure.

The goal is not to train a model. The goal is to understand how
different query-key geometries produce different attention patterns.

\section{14.23 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-4}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Self-attention computes \(Q,K,V\) from the same sequence matrix \(X\).
\item
  Each output token representation is a weighted average of value
  vectors from the sequence.
\item
  Attention weights form a row-stochastic matrix.
\item
  Self-attention produces contextual embeddings.
\item
  Without positional information and masks, self-attention is
  permutation equivariant.
\item
  Causal masks enforce the conditional structure of autoregressive
  language modeling.
\item
  Multi-head attention learns several comparison geometries in parallel.
\item
  Full self-attention has quadratic cost in sequence length.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-8}

Self-attention is the central operation in the Transformer architecture.
This chapter connects the attention formula from Chapter 13 to
contextual token representations, symmetry, masking, and multi-head
design. Useful background sources include Vaswani et al. (2017),
Jurafsky and Martin (2024), and Goodfellow et al. (2016b).

\chapter{The Transformer
Architecture}\label{the-transformer-architecture}

Residual nonlinear operators on token sequences

\hfill\break

The Transformer combines the self-attention mechanism from Chapter 14
with residual connections, normalization, and position-wise neural
networks. From a mathematical point of view, a Transformer layer is a
learned nonlinear map

\[
F:R^{T\times d}\to R^{T\times d}
\]

that transforms a matrix of token representations into a new matrix of
contextual token representations. The key architectural idea is not a
single formula, but a carefully organized composition of simple maps:

\[
\text{linear maps}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{softmax attention}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{residual addition}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{normalization}\;\longrightarrow\;\text{position-wise nonlinear maps}.
\]

This chapter studies the Transformer as an operator on sequence
matrices. We emphasize dimensions, probability models, optimization
objectives, and why the architecture is easier to train than a plain
deep stack of nonlinear maps.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-14}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  describe a Transformer layer as a map from \(R^{T\times d}\) to
  \(R^{T\times d}\);
\item
  distinguish encoder blocks, decoder blocks, and encoder-decoder
  blocks;
\item
  write the formulas for multi-head attention, residual connections,
  layer normalization, and feedforward sublayers;
\item
  explain why residual connections help gradient flow;
\item
  explain layer normalization as a row-wise standardization map;
\item
  compute the parameter count of a basic Transformer block;
\item
  connect decoder-only Transformers with autoregressive language
  modeling;
\item
  implement a small Transformer block from scratch in NumPy;
\item
  use a Plotly.js interactive to visualize how attention, residual
  mixing, and nonlinear feedforward maps change token representations;
\item
  describe the main mathematical difference between RNNs and
  Transformers.
\end{enumerate}

\section{15.1 The sequence-matrix
viewpoint}\label{the-sequence-matrix-viewpoint}

Let a token sequence have length \(T\). After token embedding and
positional encoding, the input to a Transformer layer is a matrix

\[
X\in R^{T\times d},
\]

where row \(x_i^T\in R^d\) represents token position \(i\). The
Transformer layer produces another matrix

\[
Y=F(X)\in R^{T\times d}.
\]

The row \(y_i^T\) is a contextual representation of token position
\(i\). The same layer is applied to every example in a batch, but for
mathematical clarity we first ignore the batch dimension.

A simple Transformer encoder layer has the form

\[
\begin{aligned}
H &= \operatorname{LayerNorm}\bigl(X + \operatorname{MHA}(X)\bigr),\\
Y &= \operatorname{LayerNorm}\bigl(H + \operatorname{FFN}(H)\bigr).
\end{aligned}
\]

This is called a \textbf{post-norm} block because layer normalization is
applied after the residual addition. Many modern implementations use a
\textbf{pre-norm} block:

\[
\begin{aligned}
H &= X + \operatorname{MHA}(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(X)),\\
Y &= H + \operatorname{FFN}(\operatorname{LayerNorm}(H)).
\end{aligned}
\]

The two designs use the same basic pieces, but place normalization in
different locations. Pre-norm blocks are often easier to train in very
deep networks because the residual path is more direct.

\textbf{Main mathematical abstraction.} A Transformer is a deep
composition

\[
F_L\circ F_{L-1}\circ\cdots\circ F_1
\]

of sequence-to-sequence maps, where each \(F_\ell\) mixes token
positions by attention and transforms feature coordinates by feedforward
nonlinear maps.

\section{15.2 Multi-head attention inside a Transformer
block}\label{multi-head-attention-inside-a-transformer-block}

A Transformer does not usually use a single attention head. It uses
\(h\) heads in parallel. Let

\[
X\in R^{T\times d}.
\]

For head \(r=1,\ldots,h\), define

\[
Q_r=XW_Q^{(r)},\qquad
K_r=XW_K^{(r)},\qquad
V_r=XW_V^{(r)},
\]

where

\[
W_Q^{(r)},W_K^{(r)}\in R^{d\times d_k},
\qquad
W_V^{(r)}\in R^{d\times d_v}.
\]

The \(r\)th head output is

\[
Z_r=\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{Q_rK_r^T+M}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V_r
\in R^{T\times d_v}.
\]

The matrix \(M\in R^{T\times T}\) is optional. For encoder
self-attention, \(M\) may be a padding mask. For decoder self-attention,
\(M\) also includes a causal mask.

The head outputs are concatenated:

\[
Z=\operatorname{concat}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_h)\in R^{T\times hd_v}.
\]

Then a final output projection gives

\[
\operatorname{MHA}(X)=ZW_O,
\qquad
W_O\in R^{hd_v\times d}.
\]

A common choice is

\[
d_k=d_v=d/h,
\]

so \(hd_v=d\) and the output has the same feature dimension as \(X\).

\subsection{Why multiple heads?}\label{why-multiple-heads}

A single attention head has one learned geometry for comparing tokens.
Multiple heads allow several comparison geometries in parallel. One head
might emphasize local syntactic relations, another might emphasize
long-range dependencies, and another might attend to special tokens or
punctuation. This interpretation should be used carefully: attention
heads are learned numerical objects, not guaranteed linguistic modules.

Mathematically, multi-head attention increases expressiveness by
applying several different bilinear score functions

\[
(x_i,x_j)\mapsto x_i^TW_Q^{(r)}(W_K^{(r)})^Tx_j
\]

and several different value transformations

\[
x_j\mapsto x_j^TW_V^{(r)}.
\]

Thus each head defines a different kernel-like similarity and a
different message representation.

\section{15.3 Residual connections}\label{residual-connections}

A residual connection adds the input of a sublayer to its output. If
\(G:R^{T\times d}\to R^{T\times d}\) is a sublayer, the residual map is

\[
R(X)=X+G(X).
\]

The derivative of this map has the form

\[
DR(X)=I+DG(X),
\]

where \(I\) denotes the identity map on \(R^{T\times d}\). This is the
main mathematical reason residual connections help optimization: even if
\(DG(X)\) has small singular values, the identity term provides a direct
path for gradients.

To see the idea in a scalar example, suppose

\[
y=x+g(x).
\]

Then

\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=1+g'(x).
\]

In a deep non-residual composition, derivatives multiply many factors.
In a residual network, each layer has an identity contribution, so
information and gradients can pass through the network more easily.

\textbf{Residual learning.} A residual block does not need to learn the
entire transformation. It only needs to learn a correction to the
identity map.

\section{15.4 Layer normalization}\label{layer-normalization}

Layer normalization standardizes each token vector across its feature
coordinates. For a row vector

\[
x=(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\in R^d,
\]

define

\[
\mu(x)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^d x_j,
\qquad
\sigma^2(x)=\frac{1}{d}\sum_{j=1}^d (x_j-\mu(x))^2.
\]

Layer normalization maps \(x\) to

\[
\operatorname{LN}(x)_j
=
\gamma_j\frac{x_j-\mu(x)}{\sqrt{\sigma^2(x)+\varepsilon}}+\beta_j,
\qquad j=1,\ldots,d,
\]

where \(\gamma,\beta\in R^d\) are trainable parameters and
\(\varepsilon>0\) is a small constant for numerical stability.

For a sequence matrix \(X\in R^{T\times d}\), layer normalization is
applied row by row:

\[
\operatorname{LN}(X)_{i,:}=\operatorname{LN}(X_{i,:}).
\]

Layer normalization is different from batch normalization. It does not
compute statistics across examples in a batch. Instead, it computes
statistics across the coordinates of one token representation.

\subsection{Geometric interpretation}\label{geometric-interpretation}

Ignoring \(\gamma\) and \(\beta\), layer normalization subtracts the
component in the direction of the all-ones vector and rescales to
approximately fixed length. If

\[
\mathbf{1}=(1,\ldots,1)^T\in R^d,
\]

then centering replaces \(x\) by

\[
x-\mu(x)\mathbf{1}.
\]

This vector lies in the hyperplane

\[
\{z\in R^d: z^T\mathbf{1}=0\}.
\]

Thus layer normalization controls scale and location of token features,
making the optimization problem more stable.

\section{15.5 Position-wise feedforward
networks}\label{position-wise-feedforward-networks}

After attention mixes information across token positions, a Transformer
block applies the same feedforward network to each token position
independently. For one row \(h_i\in R^d\), define

\[
\operatorname{FFN}(h_i)=\sigma(h_iW_1+b_1)W_2+b_2,
\]

where

\[
W_1\in R^{d\times d_{\mathrm{ff}}},
\qquad
W_2\in R^{d_{\mathrm{ff}}\times d}.
\]

The activation \(\sigma\) is applied coordinatewise. Common choices
include ReLU and GELU. In matrix form,

\[
\operatorname{FFN}(H)=\sigma(HW_1+\mathbf{1}b_1^T)W_2+\mathbf{1}b_2^T.
\]

This sublayer does not mix token positions. It transforms the feature
representation at each position. Attention mixes positions; the
feedforward network mixes coordinates.

\textbf{Two kinds of mixing.} In a Transformer block, attention mixes
rows of \(X\), while the feedforward network mixes columns of \(X\).

\section{15.6 Encoder blocks}\label{encoder-blocks}

A Transformer encoder is designed to read an entire input sequence and
produce contextual representations for all positions. An encoder block
uses bidirectional self-attention: every non-padding token may attend to
every other non-padding token.

For an encoder block, a typical post-norm formula is

\[
\begin{aligned}
H &= \operatorname{LN}(X+\operatorname{MHA}_{\text{enc}}(X)),\\
Y &= \operatorname{LN}(H+\operatorname{FFN}(H)).
\end{aligned}
\]

The attention mask usually prevents real tokens from attending to
padding positions. It does not prevent a token from attending to future
positions because the encoder is not generating left-to-right.

Encoder-only architectures are natural for:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  document classification;
\item
  token classification;
\item
  sentence similarity;
\item
  extractive question answering;
\item
  sequence representation.
\end{itemize}

Mathematically, an encoder is a map

\[
F_{\text{enc}}:R^{T\times d}\to R^{T\times d}
\]

that is allowed to use information from the full input sequence at every
output position.

\section{15.7 Decoder blocks}\label{decoder-blocks}

A Transformer decoder is designed for generation. In a decoder-only
language model, token position \(t\) should not use information from
positions \(t+1,t+2,\ldots,T\) when predicting the next token. This is
enforced by a causal mask.

For decoder self-attention, the mask satisfies

\[
M_{ij}=\begin{cases}
0, & j\le i,\\
-\infty, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\]

Then after applying row-wise softmax, all future-position weights are
zero:

\[
a_{ij}=0\qquad\text{for }j>i.
\]

A decoder-only block has the same two main sublayers as an encoder
block, but with causal self-attention:

\[
\begin{aligned}
H &= \operatorname{LN}(X+\operatorname{MHA}_{\text{causal}}(X)),\\
Y &= \operatorname{LN}(H+\operatorname{FFN}(H)).
\end{aligned}
\]

Decoder-only architectures are natural for autoregressive language
modeling:

\[
P(w_1,\ldots,w_T)=\prod_{t=1}^T P(w_t\mid w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1}).
\]

The model predicts a probability distribution for the next token at each
position.

\section{15.8 Encoder-decoder
Transformers}\label{encoder-decoder-transformers}

The original Transformer architecture for machine translation used both
an encoder and a decoder. The encoder reads the source sequence. The
decoder generates the target sequence. The decoder uses two kinds of
attention:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{causal self-attention} over previously generated target
  tokens;
\item
  \textbf{cross-attention} from target positions to source positions.
\end{enumerate}

Let

\[
X_{\text{src}}\in R^{T_s\times d},
\qquad
X_{\text{tgt}}\in R^{T_t\times d}.
\]

The encoder produces

\[
E=F_{\text{enc}}(X_{\text{src}})\in R^{T_s\times d}.
\]

In cross-attention, queries come from the decoder state, while keys and
values come from the encoder output:

\[
Q=HW_Q,
\qquad
K=EW_K,
\qquad
V=EW_V.
\]

The cross-attention output is

\[
\operatorname{CrossAttn}(H,E)
=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V.
\]

This lets each target position decide which source positions are
relevant.

\section{15.9 Output layer and language
modeling}\label{output-layer-and-language-modeling}

For a decoder-only language model, the final Transformer representation
at position \(t\) is a vector

\[
h_t\in R^d.
\]

A linear output layer maps \(h_t\) to vocabulary logits:

\[
z_t=h_tW_U+b_U\in R^{|V|},
\]

where

\[
W_U\in R^{d\times |V|},
\qquad
b_U\in R^{|V|}.
\]

The conditional distribution over the next token is

\[
P_\theta(w_{t+1}=v\mid w_1,\ldots,w_t)
=\frac{\exp(z_{t,v})}{\sum_{u\in V}\exp(z_{t,u})}.
\]

For a training sequence \(w_1,\ldots,w_T\), the negative log-likelihood
is

\[
\mathcal{L}(\theta)
= -\sum_{t=1}^{T-1}\log P_\theta(w_{t+1}\mid w_1,\ldots,w_t).
\]

Dividing by \(T-1\) gives the average cross-entropy loss. Exponentiating
average cross-entropy gives perplexity.

\section{15.10 Parameter count of a basic
block}\label{parameter-count-of-a-basic-block}

Assume a Transformer block has model dimension \(d\), number of heads
\(h\), and feedforward dimension \(d_{\mathrm{ff}}\). Suppose each head
uses

\[
d_k=d_v=d/h.
\]

The query, key, and value projections across all heads together have
approximately

\[
3d^2
\]

weights. The output projection has

\[
d^2
\]

weights. Therefore multi-head attention has about

\[
4d^2
\]

weights, ignoring biases.

The feedforward sublayer has

\[
dd_{\mathrm{ff}}+d_{\mathrm{ff}}d=2dd_{\mathrm{ff}}
\]

weights, ignoring biases. Layer normalization contributes \(2d\)
parameters per normalization layer: scale \(\gamma\) and shift
\(\beta\).

Thus a rough block parameter count is

\[
4d^2+2dd_{\mathrm{ff}}+4d,
\]

for a block with two layer normalization modules and no bias counting in
the linear layers.

A common choice is

\[
d_{\mathrm{ff}}=4d.
\]

Then the feedforward sublayer has about \(8d^2\) weights, which is often
more than the attention sublayer.

\section{15.11 Computational
complexity}\label{computational-complexity-1}

Self-attention forms the score matrix

\[
S=QK^T\in R^{T\times T}.
\]

Computing \(S\) costs on the order of

\[
O(T^2d)
\]

operations. Multiplying the attention matrix by the values also costs
about

\[
O(T^2d).
\]

The feedforward sublayer costs

\[
O(Tdd_{\mathrm{ff}}).
\]

Thus the cost of attention grows quadratically with sequence length
\(T\). This is the main computational bottleneck for long-context
Transformers.

RNNs process sequences sequentially with cost roughly linear in \(T\),
but they are hard to parallelize over time. Transformers use \(T^2\)
pairwise comparisons, but these comparisons can be computed in parallel
on modern hardware.

\textbf{Tradeoff.} RNNs have sequential recurrence. Transformers replace
recurrence with parallel pairwise interaction.

\section{15.12 Interactive: Transformer block geometry
explorer}\label{interactive-transformer-block-geometry-explorer}

The following interactive uses a two-dimensional toy sequence. It is not
a real Transformer model, but it visualizes three structural ideas:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  attention mixes token positions;
\item
  residual connections pull the transformed representation back toward
  the input;
\item
  the feedforward sublayer bends the representation coordinatewise.
\end{itemize}

Try increasing the attention mixing parameter and residual strength.
Notice that a Transformer layer is not simply a classifier or a lookup
table; it is a learned geometric transformation of a whole sequence
matrix.
