\section{15.13 Python example: layer
normalization}\label{python-example-layer-normalization}

The following implementation applies layer normalization row by row to a
token matrix.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch15-layernorm}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{np.set\_printoptions(precision}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, suppress}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ layer\_norm(X, gamma}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, beta}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, eps}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1e{-}5}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{"""Layer normalization for X with shape (T, d)."""}
\NormalTok{    X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(X, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    mu }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    var }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ((X }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ mu) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{).mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ mu) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(var }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ eps)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ gamma }\KeywordTok{is} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        gamma }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.ones(X.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ beta }\KeywordTok{is} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        beta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(X.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ gamma }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ beta}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{4.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{6.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{8.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{3.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{7.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{4.0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ layer\_norm(X)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(Y)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"row means after LN:"}\NormalTok{, Y.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"row variances after LN:"}\NormalTok{, Y.var(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[[-1.3416 -0.4472  0.4472  1.3416]
 [-0.8165 -0.8165  0.      1.633 ]
 [-1.3416 -0.4472  0.4472  1.3416]]
row means after LN: [0. 0. 0.]
row variances after LN: [1. 1. 1.]
\end{verbatim}

Layer normalization changes the feature coordinates of each token
vector, but it does not mix token positions.

\section{15.14 Python example: multi-head attention from
scratch}\label{python-example-multi-head-attention-from-scratch}

The next example implements a small multi-head self-attention layer. The
purpose is dimension bookkeeping, not performance.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch15-mha-from-scratch}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}
\NormalTok{model\_dim }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{8}
\NormalTok{num\_heads }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{head\_dim }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ model\_dim }\OperatorTok{//}\NormalTok{ num\_heads}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(T, model\_dim))}

\NormalTok{WQ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(num\_heads, model\_dim, head\_dim))}
\NormalTok{WK }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(num\_heads, model\_dim, head\_dim))}
\NormalTok{WV }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(num\_heads, model\_dim, head\_dim))}
\NormalTok{WO }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(num\_heads }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ head\_dim, model\_dim))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax\_rows(S):}
\NormalTok{    S\_shift }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ S }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ S.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(S\_shift)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ E }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ E.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ multi\_head\_attention(X, WQ, WK, WV, WO, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    head\_outputs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{    attention\_matrices }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ r }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(WQ.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]):}
\NormalTok{        Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ WQ[r]}
\NormalTok{        K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ WK[r]}
\NormalTok{        V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ WV[r]}
\NormalTok{        scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (Q }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ K.T) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(Q.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ mask }\KeywordTok{is} \KeywordTok{not} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scores }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ mask}
\NormalTok{        A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax\_rows(scores)}
\NormalTok{        Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V}
\NormalTok{        head\_outputs.append(Z)}
\NormalTok{        attention\_matrices.append(A)}
\NormalTok{    Z\_all }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.concatenate(head\_outputs, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z\_all }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ WO, attention\_matrices}

\NormalTok{Y, As }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ multi\_head\_attention(X, WQ, WK, WV, WO)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"X shape:"}\NormalTok{, X.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"head attention shape:"}\NormalTok{, As[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{].shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"output shape:"}\NormalTok{, Y.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"row sums of first attention matrix:"}\NormalTok{, As[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
X shape: (5, 8)
head attention shape: (5, 5)
output shape: (5, 8)
row sums of first attention matrix: [1. 1. 1. 1. 1.]
\end{verbatim}

The row sums are approximately one because each attention matrix is
row-stochastic.

\section{15.15 Python example: a full Transformer encoder
block}\label{python-example-a-full-transformer-encoder-block}

Now we add residual connections, layer normalization, and a
position-wise feedforward network.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch15-transformer-block}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{2026}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{8}
\NormalTok{h }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{dh }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ d }\OperatorTok{//}\NormalTok{ h}
\NormalTok{dff }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(T, d))}

\NormalTok{params }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"WQ"}\NormalTok{: rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(h, d, dh)),}
    \StringTok{"WK"}\NormalTok{: rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(h, d, dh)),}
    \StringTok{"WV"}\NormalTok{: rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(h, d, dh)),}
    \StringTok{"WO"}\NormalTok{: rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(h }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ dh, d)),}
    \StringTok{"W1"}\NormalTok{: rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, dff)),}
    \StringTok{"b1"}\NormalTok{: np.zeros(dff),}
    \StringTok{"W2"}\NormalTok{: rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(dff, d)),}
    \StringTok{"b2"}\NormalTok{: np.zeros(d),}
\NormalTok{\}}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ relu(U):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(U, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ ffn(H, params):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ relu(H }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ params[}\StringTok{"W1"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ params[}\StringTok{"b1"}\NormalTok{]) }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ params[}\StringTok{"W2"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ params[}\StringTok{"b2"}\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ transformer\_encoder\_block(X, params):}
\NormalTok{    attn\_out, attention\_mats }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ multi\_head\_attention(}
\NormalTok{        X,}
\NormalTok{        params[}\StringTok{"WQ"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{        params[}\StringTok{"WK"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{        params[}\StringTok{"WV"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{        params[}\StringTok{"WO"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    )}
\NormalTok{    H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ layer\_norm(X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ attn\_out)}
\NormalTok{    Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ layer\_norm(H }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ ffn(H, params))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Y, attention\_mats}

\NormalTok{Y, attention\_mats }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ transformer\_encoder\_block(X, params)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"input shape:"}\NormalTok{, X.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"output shape:"}\NormalTok{, Y.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"first token before:"}\NormalTok{, X[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"first token after:"}\NormalTok{, Y[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
input shape: (6, 8)
output shape: (6, 8)
first token before: [-0.7931  0.2406 -1.8963  1.3958  0.6383 -0.292  -0.3119  0.3038]
first token after: [-0.757   0.0496 -1.8095  0.6765  1.1463 -0.6849 -0.0028  1.3818]
\end{verbatim}

The block maps \(R^{T\times d}\) to \(R^{T\times d}\). The sequence
length and model dimension are preserved.

\section{15.16 Python example: causal decoder
mask}\label{python-example-causal-decoder-mask}

A decoder-only Transformer uses a causal mask so that position \(i\)
cannot attend to position \(j>i\).

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch15-causal-mask}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}
\NormalTok{causal\_mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.triu(np.ones((T, T)), k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{causal\_mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.where(causal\_mask }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1e9}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(causal\_mask)}

\NormalTok{Y\_causal, causal\_As }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ multi\_head\_attention(}
\NormalTok{    X[:T],}
\NormalTok{    params[}\StringTok{"WQ"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    params[}\StringTok{"WK"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    params[}\StringTok{"WV"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    params[}\StringTok{"WO"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    mask}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{causal\_mask}
\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"First head causal attention matrix:"}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(causal\_As[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"largest future attention weight:"}\NormalTok{, np.triu(causal\_As[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{], k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
[[ 0.e+00 -1.e+09 -1.e+09 -1.e+09 -1.e+09 -1.e+09]
 [ 0.e+00  0.e+00 -1.e+09 -1.e+09 -1.e+09 -1.e+09]
 [ 0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00 -1.e+09 -1.e+09 -1.e+09]
 [ 0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00 -1.e+09 -1.e+09]
 [ 0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00 -1.e+09]
 [ 0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00  0.e+00]]
First head causal attention matrix:
[[1.     0.     0.     0.     0.     0.    ]
 [0.5115 0.4885 0.     0.     0.     0.    ]
 [0.3315 0.3412 0.3272 0.     0.     0.    ]
 [0.3058 0.2589 0.2758 0.1595 0.     0.    ]
 [0.1792 0.1936 0.1667 0.2458 0.2147 0.    ]
 [0.1508 0.1865 0.1687 0.1265 0.1511 0.2164]]
largest future attention weight: 0.0
\end{verbatim}

The largest future attention weight should be numerically close to zero.

\section{15.17 Python example: output probabilities for language
modeling}\label{python-example-output-probabilities-for-language-modeling}

The final hidden state at each position is converted into vocabulary
logits and then probabilities.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch15-output-probabilities}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{15}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"\textless{}bos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"the"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"model"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"learns"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"."}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{V }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)}
\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Y\_causal.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Y\_causal.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{WU }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, V))}
\NormalTok{bU }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(V)}

\NormalTok{logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Y\_causal }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ WU }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ bU}
\NormalTok{probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax\_rows(logits)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ t }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(T):}
\NormalTok{    top }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.argmax(probs[t]))}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"position }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{t}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{: top next{-}token candidate = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{vocab[top]}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}8s\}}\SpecialStringTok{, probability = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{probs[t, top]}\SpecialCharTok{:.3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
position 0: top next-token candidate =    <bos>, probability = 0.248
position 1: top next-token candidate =    <bos>, probability = 0.223
position 2: top next-token candidate =    <bos>, probability = 0.181
position 3: top next-token candidate =      the, probability = 0.183
position 4: top next-token candidate =      the, probability = 0.181
position 5: top next-token candidate =    <bos>, probability = 0.195
\end{verbatim}

During training, the true next token is known, so the model is trained
by minimizing cross-entropy across positions.

\section{15.18 Parameter-count function}\label{parameter-count-function}

The following function computes the rough parameter count from Section
15.10.

\protect\phantomsection\label{py-ch15-parameter-count}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ transformer\_block\_parameter\_count(d, dff, include\_bias}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    attention }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d}
\NormalTok{    feedforward }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ dff}
\NormalTok{    layernorm }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{4} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d}
\NormalTok{    total }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ attention }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ feedforward }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ layernorm}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ include\_bias:}
\NormalTok{        total }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{4} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d      }\CommentTok{\# Q, K, V, O biases approximately}
\NormalTok{        total }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ dff }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ d    }\CommentTok{\# FFN biases}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ \{}
        \StringTok{"attention\_weights"}\NormalTok{: attention,}
        \StringTok{"feedforward\_weights"}\NormalTok{: feedforward,}
        \StringTok{"layernorm\_parameters"}\NormalTok{: layernorm,}
        \StringTok{"total"}\NormalTok{: total,}
\NormalTok{    \}}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ d }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{128}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{256}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{512}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ transformer\_block\_parameter\_count(d}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{d, dff}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{d)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"d=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{d}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{, dff=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\DecValTok{4}\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{d}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{, total parameters per block ≈ }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{counts[}\StringTok{\textquotesingle{}total\textquotesingle{}}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{:,\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
d=128, dff=512, total parameters per block ≈ 197,120
d=256, dff=1024, total parameters per block ≈ 787,456
d=512, dff=2048, total parameters per block ≈ 3,147,776
\end{verbatim}

This calculation explains why feedforward layers are often a major part
of the parameter budget.

\section{15.19 Encoder-only, decoder-only, and encoder-decoder
models}\label{encoder-only-decoder-only-and-encoder-decoder-models}

The three main Transformer families differ in their attention pattern
and task objective.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Architecture
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Attention pattern
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Main output
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Typical tasks
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Encoder-only & bidirectional self-attention & contextual input
representation & classification, retrieval, tagging \\
Decoder-only & causal self-attention & next-token distribution &
generation, completion, chat \\
Encoder-decoder & source encoder plus target decoder cross-attention &
conditional target distribution & translation, summarization \\
\end{longtable}
}

Mathematically, encoder-only models estimate representations useful for
conditional predictions such as

\[
P(y\mid x_1,\ldots,x_T).
\]

Decoder-only models estimate left-to-right conditional distributions
such as

\[
P(w_{t+1}\mid w_1,\ldots,w_t).
\]

Encoder-decoder models estimate conditional sequence distributions such
as

\[
P(y_1,\ldots,y_m\mid x_1,\ldots,x_T)
=\prod_{t=1}^m P(y_t\mid y_1,\ldots,y_{t-1},x_1,\ldots,x_T).
\]

\section{15.20 Mathematical comparison with
RNNs}\label{mathematical-comparison-with-rnns}

An RNN computes hidden states recursively:

\[
h_t=f(h_{t-1},x_t).
\]

Thus information from token \(j\) reaches token \(i\) through a chain of
intermediate states. A Transformer computes direct token-token scores:

\[
s_{ij}=q_i^Tk_j/\sqrt{d_k}.
\]

Thus token \(i\) can attend directly to token \(j\) in one layer. This
shorter interaction path is one reason Transformers can model long-range
dependencies effectively.

However, the direct interaction comes with quadratic cost in \(T\). The
mathematical tradeoff is:

\[
\text{recurrence path length }O(T)\quad\text{versus}\quad\text{attention score matrix size }O(T^2).
\]

\section{15.21 AI-assisted learning
activities}\label{ai-assisted-learning-activities-1}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic, not just as a code
generator.

\subsection{Prompt 1: dimension audit}\label{prompt-1-dimension-audit-2}

Give the assistant the formulas for multi-head attention and ask:

\begin{quote}
Check every matrix dimension in this Transformer block. Identify the
shape of each intermediate matrix and explain where shape errors are
most likely.
\end{quote}

Then verify the response by doing the calculation yourself.

\subsection{Prompt 2: residual-gradient
explanation}\label{prompt-2-residual-gradient-explanation}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Explain why \(R(X)=X+G(X)\) helps gradient flow. Give both a scalar
explanation and a matrix derivative explanation.
\end{quote}

A good response should mention the identity term in the derivative.

\subsection{Prompt 3: architecture
classification}\label{prompt-3-architecture-classification}

Give the assistant several tasks such as sentiment classification,
next-token prediction, translation, semantic search, and summarization.
Ask it to classify which Transformer family is most natural and justify
the answer mathematically.

\subsection{Prompt 4: implementation
debugging}\label{prompt-4-implementation-debugging}

Paste your NumPy Transformer block and ask:

\begin{quote}
Find possible shape, masking, and numerical-stability bugs. Do not
rewrite the whole program. Explain each issue mathematically.
\end{quote}

\section{15.22 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-4}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing attention with the entire Transformer.} Attention is
  one sublayer. A Transformer block also uses residual connections,
  normalization, feedforward networks, and output projections.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting the causal mask in decoder-only language models.}
  Without causal masking, training leaks future tokens.
\item
  \textbf{Applying softmax over the wrong axis.} Attention softmax
  should usually be row-wise over key positions for each query position.
\item
  \textbf{Thinking layer normalization mixes tokens.} Layer
  normalization standardizes feature coordinates within each token row.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming attention weights are explanations.} Attention
  weights are useful diagnostics, but they are not automatically causal
  explanations of model behavior.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring sequence length cost.} The \(T\times T\) score matrix
  can dominate memory and computation for long sequences.
\end{enumerate}

\section{15.23 Exercises}\label{exercises-14}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Dimension check.} Let \(T=12\), \(d=64\), \(h=4\), and
  \(d_k=d_v=16\). Write the shapes of \(Q_r\), \(K_r\), \(V_r\),
  \(Q_rK_r^T\), \(A_r\), \(Z_r\),
  \(\operatorname{concat}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_h)\), and the final multi-head
  output.
\item
  \textbf{Residual derivative.} Suppose \(g:R\to R\) and
  \(R(x)=x+g(x)\). Show that \(R'(x)=1+g'(x)\). Explain why this is
  helpful in a deep composition.
\item
  \textbf{Layer normalization.} Compute layer normalization by hand for
  \(x=(1,3,5)\) with \(\gamma=(1,1,1)\), \(\beta=(0,0,0)\), and
  \(\varepsilon=0\).
\item
  \textbf{Parameter count.} For \(d=768\), \(h=12\), and
  \(d_{\mathrm{ff}}=3072\), compute the approximate number of parameters
  in one Transformer block, ignoring biases.
\item
  \textbf{Causal mask.} Write the causal mask matrix for \(T=5\).
  Explain why row \(3\) can attend to columns \(1,2,3\) but not columns
  \(4,5\) if indexing starts at \(1\).
\item
  \textbf{Encoder versus decoder.} Give one mathematical reason why
  bidirectional attention is inappropriate for next-token prediction
  training if no mask is used.
\item
  \textbf{Complexity.} Compare the attention cost for sequence lengths
  \(T=512\), \(T=2048\), and \(T=8192\), assuming \(d\) is fixed. How
  many times larger is \(T^2\) when \(T\) quadruples?
\item
  \textbf{Implementation.} Modify the Python multi-head attention
  example so that \(h=4\) and \(d=8\). What must be true about \(d\) and
  \(h\)?
\item
  \textbf{Interpretation.} In the interactive, set residual strength
  near \(1\). What happens to the transformed points? Explain this using
  the formula \(X+G(X)\).
\item
  \textbf{Model families.} Classify each task as encoder-only,
  decoder-only, or encoder-decoder: spam detection, machine translation,
  autocomplete, named-entity recognition, and abstractive summarization.
\end{enumerate}

\section{15.24 Mini-project: Build a tiny Transformer encoder
block}\label{mini-project-build-a-tiny-transformer-encoder-block}

Build a small Transformer encoder block from scratch in NumPy.

Your project should include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  token embeddings for a toy vocabulary;
\item
  positional encodings or learned position vectors;
\item
  multi-head self-attention;
\item
  residual connections;
\item
  layer normalization;
\item
  a position-wise feedforward network;
\item
  a short report checking all dimensions.
\end{enumerate}

Then compare two inputs that contain the same words in different orders.
Explain how positional information changes the output.

\section{15.25 Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-6}

The Chapter 15 lab should ask students to implement a minimal
Transformer block step by step. Students should first verify shapes
using small matrices, then add masking, and finally connect the block to
a simple next-token prediction objective.

Suggested lab sections:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  matrix shapes and token embeddings;
\item
  row-wise softmax and attention;
\item
  multi-head attention;
\item
  residual connections and layer normalization;
\item
  feedforward network;
\item
  causal masking;
\item
  output logits and cross-entropy;
\item
  reflection questions comparing RNNs and Transformers.
\end{enumerate}

The goal is not to train a large model. The goal is to understand the
mathematical architecture well enough to debug real implementations.

\chapter{Positional Encoding and Sequence
Geometry}\label{positional-encoding-and-sequence-geometry}

How order enters attention-based language models

\hfill\break

Self-attention compares tokens by content. If the input to a Transformer
is only a matrix of token embeddings, then self-attention sees a set of
token vectors rather than an ordered sentence. This is a serious
mathematical problem: the sentences

\[
\text{the dog chased the cat}
\]

and

\[
\text{the cat chased the dog}
\]

contain nearly the same words, but they have different meanings because
their order is different. Positional encoding is the mechanism by which
a Transformer receives information about order.

This chapter studies position from a mathematical point of view. We
begin with permutation equivariance, then study absolute positional
embeddings, sinusoidal positional encodings, Fourier-feature geometry,
relative positions, rotary positional embeddings, and attention biases.
The goal is not to memorize architectural variations, but to understand
what mathematical information about order is injected into a sequence
model.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-15}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  explain why vanilla self-attention without position is permutation
  equivariant;
\item
  distinguish token embeddings, position embeddings, and contextual
  embeddings;
\item
  write the sinusoidal positional encoding formulas and check their
  dimensions;
\item
  explain sinusoidal encoding as a finite collection of Fourier
  features;
\item
  compute dot products between sinusoidal position vectors and interpret
  them as functions of relative distance;
\item
  compare learned absolute position embeddings with fixed sinusoidal
  encodings;
\item
  describe relative-position attention, rotary positional embeddings,
  and additive attention biases;
\item
  implement positional encodings in NumPy;
\item
  visualize position vectors and their similarity structure with
  Plotly.js;
\item
  identify common mathematical mistakes involving position in
  Transformers.
\end{enumerate}

\section{16.1 The order problem}\label{the-order-problem}

Let a sequence of length \(T\) be represented by a matrix

\[
X =
\begin{bmatrix}
- & x_1^T & - \\
- & x_2^T & - \\
  & \vdots &   \\
- & x_T^T & -
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{T\times d},
\]

where \(x_t\in R^d\) is the input representation of the token at
position \(t\). A self-attention layer computes

\[
\operatorname{Attn}(X)
=
\operatorname{softmax}\left(
\frac{XW_Q(XW_K)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
\right)XW_V.
\]

This formula compares rows of \(X\) using dot products. If the rows are
permuted, the dot-product matrix is permuted in the same way. Thus
self-attention respects the symmetry of the input row order unless we
explicitly break that symmetry by adding position information.

\textbf{Key issue.} A sequence is not only a multiset of tokens. A
sequence has an order. A Transformer must therefore represent both
content and position.

For example, the two sequences

\[
(w_1,w_2,w_3)=(\text{students},\text{use},\text{AI})
\]

and

\[
(w_1,w_2,w_3)=(\text{AI},\text{use},\text{students})
\]

have the same bag of words but different syntax and meaning.
Bag-of-words models from Chapters 2--3 intentionally discard order.
Transformers should not.

\section{16.2 Permutation equivariance of
self-attention}\label{permutation-equivariance-of-self-attention}

Let \(P\in R^{T\times T}\) be a permutation matrix. Multiplying \(X\) on
the left by \(P\) permutes the rows of \(X\):

\[
X' = PX.
\]

For a single self-attention head without position, define

\[
Q=XW_Q,
\qquad
K=XW_K,
\qquad
V=XW_V.
\]

For the permuted input \(X'=PX\),

\[
Q'=PXW_Q=PQ,
\qquad
K'=PK,
\qquad
V'=PV.
\]

The score matrix becomes

\[
S'
=
\frac{Q'(K')^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
=
\frac{(PQ)(PK)^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}
=
P\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)P^T.
\]

The row-wise softmax satisfies

\[
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(PSP^T)
=
P\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S)P^T.
\]

Therefore

\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{Attn}(PX)
&=
\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S')V' \\
&=
P\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S)P^T PV \\
&=
P\operatorname{Attn}(X).
\end{aligned}
\]

So self-attention is \textbf{permutation equivariant}:

\[
\operatorname{Attn}(PX)=P\operatorname{Attn}(X).
\]

This is not wrong; it is often a useful symmetry. But for language, the
original row index matters. Positional encoding breaks pure permutation
symmetry by replacing the token-only representation with a
content-plus-position representation.

\section{16.3 Content vectors plus position
vectors}\label{content-vectors-plus-position-vectors}

Let \(e:V\to R^d\) be a token embedding map. If token \(w_t\) appears at
position \(t\), the token embedding is

\[
x_t=e(w_t).
\]

A simple positional strategy creates a vector \(p_t\in R^d\) for every
position \(t\), then uses

\[
z_t = x_t + p_t.
\]

The matrix input to the Transformer is then

\[
Z = X + P_{\text{pos}},
\]

where

\[
P_{\text{pos}}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
- & p_1^T & - \\
- & p_2^T & - \\
  & \vdots &   \\
- & p_T^T & -
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{T\times d}.
\]

The addition is simple but mathematically powerful. Because the vector
at row \(t\) now contains both token identity and position identity,
attention scores can depend on position through inner products such as

\[
(z_i W_Q)(z_j W_K)^T.
\]

Expanding \(z_i=x_i+p_i\) and \(z_j=x_j+p_j\) shows the possible
interactions:

\[
(z_i W_Q)(z_j W_K)^T
=
(x_iW_Q)(x_jW_K)^T
+
(x_iW_Q)(p_jW_K)^T
+
(p_iW_Q)(x_jW_K)^T
+
(p_iW_Q)(p_jW_K)^T.
\]

These terms allow the model to learn rules involving content, source
position, target position, and relative placement.

\section{16.4 Learned absolute position
embeddings}\label{learned-absolute-position-embeddings}

The most direct approach is to learn a position-embedding matrix

\[
E_{\text{pos}}\in R^{T_{\max}\times d},
\]

where row \(t\) is the learned vector \(p_t^T\). For a sequence of
length \(T\le T_{\max}\), use the first \(T\) rows.

The trainable parameters are

\[
T_{\max}d.
\]

This method is flexible because the model learns the position vectors
that help the training objective. But it has two limitations.

First, the model is usually trained with a fixed maximum length
\(T_{\max}\). Extrapolating beyond this length is not natural unless
additional design choices are made.

Second, learned absolute embeddings do not automatically encode a smooth
geometry of distance. The model must learn from data that positions 10
and 11 are closer than positions 10 and 500.

\textbf{Absolute position viewpoint.} Learned absolute position
embeddings identify each index \(t\) with a trainable vector \(p_t\).
They are flexible labels for positions, but they do not automatically
impose translation or distance structure.

\section{16.5 Sinusoidal positional
encoding}\label{sinusoidal-positional-encoding}

The original Transformer introduced a fixed sinusoidal positional
encoding. Suppose \(d\) is even. For position \(t\) and coordinate pair
indexed by \(i=0,1,\ldots,d/2-1\), define

\[
PE(t,2i)=\sin\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right),
\]

and

\[
PE(t,2i+1)=\cos\left(\frac{t}{10000^{2i/d}}\right).
\]

Thus each position \(t\) is mapped to a vector

\[
p_t = PE(t)\in R^d.
\]

The denominator

\[
10000^{2i/d}
\]

creates wavelengths on a logarithmic scale. Low-index coordinate pairs
vary rapidly with \(t\); high-index coordinate pairs vary slowly.

Equivalently, define frequencies

\[
\omega_i = 10000^{-2i/d}.
\]

Then the coordinate pair is

\[
(\sin(\omega_i t),\cos(\omega_i t)).
\]

This shows the Fourier-feature structure: sinusoidal encoding represents
each position through multiple periodic functions at different
frequencies.

\section{16.6 Geometry of sinusoidal
encodings}\label{geometry-of-sinusoidal-encodings}

For a single frequency \(\omega\), define

\[
u_t(\omega)=(\sin(\omega t),\cos(\omega t))\in R^2.
\]

Then

\[
\|u_t(\omega)\|_2^2
=
\sin^2(\omega t)+\cos^2(\omega t)=1.
\]

The dot product between two positions is

\[
\begin{aligned}
u_t(\omega)^T u_s(\omega)
&=\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega s)+\cos(\omega t)\cos(\omega s)\\
&=\cos(\omega(t-s)).
\end{aligned}
\]

Therefore the similarity between two sinusoidal position vectors depends
on the relative displacement \(t-s\). With multiple frequencies,

\[
p_t^T p_s
=
\sum_i \cos(\omega_i(t-s)).
\]

This is a crucial mathematical property: although the encoding is
absolute because it assigns a vector to each \(t\), inner products
between position vectors naturally contain relative-distance
information.

\textbf{Relative-distance property.} For sinusoidal encodings, the dot
product \(p_t^T p_s\) is a function of \(t-s\). Thus the geometry of
position vectors contains relative offset information.

\section{16.7 Linear transformations of sinusoidal
encodings}\label{linear-transformations-of-sinusoidal-encodings}

There is another useful property. For a fixed shift \(\Delta\), the pair

\[
(\sin(\omega(t+\Delta)),\cos(\omega(t+\Delta)))
\]

can be obtained from

\[
(\sin(\omega t),\cos(\omega t))
\]

by a two-dimensional rotation. Using angle-addition formulas,

\[
\sin(\omega(t+\Delta))
=
\sin(\omega t)\cos(\omega\Delta)
+
\cos(\omega t)\sin(\omega\Delta),
\]

and

\[
\cos(\omega(t+\Delta))
=
\cos(\omega t)\cos(\omega\Delta)
-
\sin(\omega t)\sin(\omega\Delta).
\]

In matrix form,

\[
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin(\omega(t+\Delta))\\
\cos(\omega(t+\Delta))
\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos(\omega\Delta) & \sin(\omega\Delta)\\
-\sin(\omega\Delta) & \cos(\omega\Delta)
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}
\sin(\omega t)\\
\cos(\omega t)
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

So a fixed relative shift is represented by a block-diagonal linear map
across the sinusoidal coordinate pairs. This helps explain why
sinusoidal encodings can support relative-position reasoning.

\section{16.8 Scaling token embeddings and position
embeddings}\label{scaling-token-embeddings-and-position-embeddings}

In many Transformer implementations, token embeddings are scaled before
adding positions:

\[
z_t=\sqrt{d}\,x_t+p_t.
\]

The reason is variance control. Suppose the coordinates of \(x_t\) have
typical scale around \(1/\sqrt{d}\). Then

\[
\|x_t\|_2
\]

may be order 1. Multiplying by \(\sqrt{d}\) changes the coordinate scale
and can balance the token content against the added positional signal,
depending on how embeddings are initialized.

From a mathematical perspective, the relative magnitude of \(x_t\) and
\(p_t\) matters because attention scores involve dot products. If
\(p_t\) is too small, the model may ignore order. If \(p_t\) is too
large, the model may overemphasize position and underemphasize content.

\section{16.9 Relative position
representations}\label{relative-position-representations}

Absolute position embeddings assign vectors to positions:

\[
t\mapsto p_t.
\]

Relative-position methods instead emphasize offsets:

\[
(i,j)\mapsto r_{i-j}.
\]

In attention, a relative-position term may be added to the score between
query position \(i\) and key position \(j\):

\[
S_{ij}
=
\frac{q_i^T k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}
+
 b_{i-j}.
\]

Here \(b_{i-j}\) is a learned or prescribed scalar bias depending on
relative displacement. This gives the model direct access to information
such as ``nearby tokens should often matter more'' or ``previous tokens
matter in a causal language model.''

A vector-valued version uses relative embeddings \(r_{i-j}\in R^{d_k}\),
for example

\[
S_{ij}
=
\frac{q_i^T(k_j+r_{i-j})}{\sqrt{d_k}}.
\]

The main idea is that attention scores become functions of both token
similarity and relative location.

\section{16.10 Rotary positional
embeddings}\label{rotary-positional-embeddings}

Rotary positional embeddings, often abbreviated RoPE, encode position by
rotating query and key vectors. The simplest version applies a
two-dimensional rotation to each coordinate pair.

For a vector pair \((a,b)\) and angle \(\theta\), define

\[
R_\theta
\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}
\cos\theta & -\sin\theta\\
\sin\theta & \cos\theta
\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}a\\ b\end{bmatrix}.
\]

At position \(t\), coordinate pair \(i\) is rotated by angle

\[
\theta_{t,i}=\omega_i t.
\]

Let \(R_t\) denote the resulting block-diagonal rotation matrix. RoPE
uses

\[
\tilde q_t = R_t q_t,
\qquad
\tilde k_s = R_s k_s.
\]

The attention score uses

\[
\tilde q_t^T\tilde k_s
=
q_t^T R_t^T R_s k_s.
\]

Because rotations satisfy

\[
R_t^T R_s = R_{s-t},
\]

the score depends on the relative offset \(s-t\) through the rotation
matrix. Thus RoPE builds relative position directly into dot-product
attention.

\textbf{RoPE viewpoint.} Instead of adding a position vector to the
token vector, RoPE rotates query and key coordinates. Dot products
between rotated vectors naturally encode relative displacement.

\section{16.11 Attention bias and distance
decay}\label{attention-bias-and-distance-decay}

Another common approach is to add a deterministic or learned distance
bias to attention scores:

\[
S_{ij}
=\frac{q_i^T k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}} + b(i,j).
\]

For a causal decoder, \(b(i,j)\) may include the mask

\[
b(i,j)=
\begin{cases}
0, & j\le i,\\
-\infty, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\]

A distance-decay bias may take the form

\[
b(i,j)=-\lambda |i-j|,
\]

or, in causal form,

\[
b(i,j)=-\lambda(i-j)\quad \text{for } j\le i.
\]

This bias makes attention to distant positions less likely unless the
content score is strong enough to overcome the penalty. From the
perspective of probability, the row-wise softmax turns scores into a
distribution over positions, so additive biases act like log-prior
preferences over where attention should be placed.

\section{16.12 Positional encoding as feature
design}\label{positional-encoding-as-feature-design}

Before deep learning, feature engineering was a central part of NLP.
Positional encoding is a modern version of feature design. It chooses a
map

\[
\psi:\{1,2,\ldots,T_{\max}\}\to R^d
\]

and combines it with the token embedding map

\[
e:V\to R^d.
\]

The model receives

\[
z_t=e(w_t)+\psi(t).
\]

Different choices of \(\psi\) encode different assumptions:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2308}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3077}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2308}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 6\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2308}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Method
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft

extrapolation \\

The correct choice depends on the task, sequence length, training data,
and architecture.

\section{16.14 Python example: sinusoidal encodings from
scratch}\label{python-example-sinusoidal-encodings-from-scratch}

The following code constructs the sinusoidal matrix

\[
P\in R^{T\times d}
\]

and checks its shape.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}


\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sinusoidal\_encoding(T, d, scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{10000.0}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{"""Return a T by d matrix of sinusoidal positional encodings."""}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ d }\OperatorTok{\%} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{!=} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{raise} \PreprocessorTok{ValueError}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"d must be even for paired sine/cosine coordinates."}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    positions }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(T)[:, }\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    pair\_ids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(d }\OperatorTok{//} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)[}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :]}
\NormalTok{    denominators }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scale }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ pair\_ids }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ d)}
\NormalTok{    angles }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ positions }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ denominators}

\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((T, d))}
\NormalTok{    P[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{::}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.sin(angles)}
\NormalTok{    P[:, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{::}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.cos(angles)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ P}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sinusoidal\_encoding(T}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, d}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(P.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(P[:}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(8, 6)
[[ 0.     1.     0.     1.     0.     1.   ]
 [ 0.841  0.54   0.046  0.999  0.002  1.   ]
 [ 0.909 -0.416  0.093  0.996  0.004  1.   ]]
\end{verbatim}

Each row is the position vector for one index. Each pair of columns is
one sine-cosine frequency pair.

\section{16.15 Python example: similarity depends on relative
offset}\label{python-example-similarity-depends-on-relative-offset}

For sinusoidal encodings, the dot product \(p_t^T p_s\) depends on
\(t-s\). The following experiment checks this numerically.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{20}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{16}
\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sinusoidal\_encoding(T, d)}

\NormalTok{G }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ P.T}

\CommentTok{\# Compare pairs with the same offset.}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ offset }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ t }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(T }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ offset):}
\NormalTok{        values.append(G[t, t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ offset])}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"offset"}\NormalTok{, offset, }\StringTok{"min"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(values), }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{), }\StringTok{"max"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(values), }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
offset 1 min 7.485166 max 7.485166
offset 2 min 6.368277 max 6.368277
offset 5 min 6.13704 max 6.13704
\end{verbatim}

The values are nearly identical for each fixed offset. Small numerical
differences may appear because of floating-point arithmetic, but the
symbolic formula says the values depend only on the offset.

\section{16.16 Python example: adding position to token
embeddings}\label{python-example-adding-position-to-token-embeddings}

The next example illustrates the standard input to a Transformer block:

\[
Z=X+P_{\text{pos}}.
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}
\NormalTok{d }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{8}
\NormalTok{vocab\_size }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{12}

\CommentTok{\# A small token{-}embedding matrix.}
\NormalTok{E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(vocab\_size, d))}

\CommentTok{\# A tokenized sequence represented by integer ids.}
\NormalTok{token\_ids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ E[token\_ids]}
\NormalTok{P\_pos }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sinusoidal\_encoding(T, d)}
\NormalTok{Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ P\_pos}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Token embedding matrix X:"}\NormalTok{, X.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Position matrix P\_pos:"}\NormalTok{, P\_pos.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Transformer input Z:"}\NormalTok{, Z.shape)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Token embedding matrix X: (6, 8)
Position matrix P_pos: (6, 8)
Transformer input Z: (6, 8)
\end{verbatim}

This example also shows why position and token embeddings must have the
same dimension \(d\) when they are combined by addition.

\section{16.17 Python example: permutation equivariance without
position}\label{python-example-permutation-equivariance-without-position}

The following simple self-attention function demonstrates the
permutation-equivariance property numerically.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ row\_softmax(S):}
\NormalTok{    S\_shifted }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ S }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ S.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    E }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(S\_shifted)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ E }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ E.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}


\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ self\_attention\_no\_position(X, Wq, Wk, Wv):}
\NormalTok{    Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Wq}
\NormalTok{    K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Wk}
\NormalTok{    V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Wv}
\NormalTok{    S }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ K.T }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(Q.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{    A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_softmax(S)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{T, d, dk, dv }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}
\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(T, d))}
\NormalTok{Wq }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, dk))}
\NormalTok{Wk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, dk))}
\NormalTok{Wv }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(d, dv))}

\NormalTok{perm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{Pmat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.eye(T)[perm]}

\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ self\_attention\_no\_position(X, Wq, Wk, Wv)}
\NormalTok{Y\_perm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ self\_attention\_no\_position(Pmat }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ X, Wq, Wk, Wv)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(np.allclose(Y\_perm, Pmat }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Y))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
True
\end{verbatim}

The output \texttt{True} means that permuting the input rows only
permutes the output rows. Without position, the layer does not know
which row was originally first, second, or third.

\section{16.18 Python example: rotary position
operation}\label{python-example-rotary-position-operation}

Here is a simple implementation of paired coordinate rotations. For
clarity, this code uses the same frequency pattern as sinusoidal
encoding.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ apply\_rope(X, scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{10000.0}\NormalTok{):}
    \CommentTok{"""Apply rotary position rotations to a T by d matrix X with even d."""}
\NormalTok{    T, d }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ d }\OperatorTok{\%} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{!=} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{raise} \PreprocessorTok{ValueError}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"d must be even for pairwise rotations."}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    positions }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(T)[:, }\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    pair\_ids }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.arange(d }\OperatorTok{//} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)[}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :]}
\NormalTok{    omega }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scale }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ (}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ pair\_ids }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ d)}
\NormalTok{    theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ positions }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ omega}

\NormalTok{    cos }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.cos(theta)}
\NormalTok{    sin }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.sin(theta)}

\NormalTok{    X\_even }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{::}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    X\_odd }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X[:, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{::}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{    Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.empty\_like(X)}
\NormalTok{    Y[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{::}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X\_even }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ cos }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ X\_odd }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ sin}
\NormalTok{    Y[:, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{::}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X\_even }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ sin }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ X\_odd }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ cos}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Y}

\NormalTok{Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{Q\_rot }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ apply\_rope(Q)}
\NormalTok{K\_rot }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ apply\_rope(K)}
\NormalTok{S\_rot }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q\_rot }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ K\_rot.T }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(Q.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(S\_rot.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(S\_rot[:}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, :}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(6, 6)
[[ 0.812 -0.286 -1.151  0.467]
 [-0.245 -0.604 -0.397 -0.75 ]]
\end{verbatim}

RoPE is not just a position vector added to \(X\). It changes the
geometry of dot products by rotating queries and keys according to their
positions.

visualization}\label{python-example-plotly-visualization}

The interactive above is written directly in JavaScript so it works in
the rendered HTML book. The same idea can be explored in Python with

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ plotly.graph\_objects }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ go}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ plotly.subplots }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ make\_subplots}

\NormalTok{T }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{80}

\NormalTok{    row}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, col}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{fig.add\_trace(}

\NormalTok{fig.update\_yaxes(title\_text}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"cos coordinate"}\NormalTok{, row}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, col}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{fig.update\_xaxes(title\_text}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"offset from position 0"}\NormalTok{, row}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, col}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{fig.update\_yaxes(title\_text}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"normalized dot product"}\NormalTok{, row}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, col}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{fig.update\_layout(height}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{420}\NormalTok{, showlegend}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
