\section{16.20 AI-assisted learning
components}\label{ai-assisted-learning-components-1}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic, not only as a code
generator.

\subsection{Prompt 1: prove the symmetry
problem}\label{prompt-1-prove-the-symmetry-problem}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Prove that self-attention without positional information is permutation
equivariant. Use matrices and explain every dimension.
\end{quote}

Then check whether the proof correctly uses

\[
P^TP=I
\]

and whether it handles the row-wise softmax carefully.

\subsection{Prompt 2: compare position
methods}\label{prompt-2-compare-position-methods}

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Compare learned absolute positional embeddings, sinusoidal encodings,
relative-position biases, and RoPE from the viewpoint of inner products
and extrapolation to longer sequences.
\end{quote}

A good answer should mention trainable tables, Fourier features,
additive score biases, and rotations of query/key coordinates.

\subsection{Prompt 3: audit an
implementation}\label{prompt-3-audit-an-implementation}

Give the assistant your positional-encoding code and ask:

\begin{quote}
Check the dimension conventions. Are positions rows or columns? Are sine
and cosine coordinates interleaved correctly? Does the code work for odd
embedding dimension?
\end{quote}

Then verify the answer by running tests yourself.

\section{16.21 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-5}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing token order with vocabulary order.} The vocabulary
  index of a token is not its sentence position.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting that self-attention is permutation equivariant
  without position.} Attention alone does not create order information.
\item
  \textbf{Using mismatched dimensions.} If token and position vectors
  are added, both must lie in \(R^d\).
\item
  \textbf{Assuming sinusoidal encoding is random.} It is deterministic
  and structured.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming all positional methods are equivalent.} Absolute
  embeddings, relative biases, and RoPE affect the model in different
  mathematical ways.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring sequence length.} A method that works for short
  sequences may behave differently for long-context modeling.
\end{enumerate}

\section{16.22 Worked calculation}\label{worked-calculation-1}

Let \(d=4\) and frequencies \(\omega_0=1\), \(\omega_1=0.1\). The
sinusoidal position vector is

\[
p_t=(\sin t,\cos t,\sin(0.1t),\cos(0.1t)).
\]

Then

\[
p_t^Tp_s
=
\cos(t-s)+\cos(0.1(t-s)).
\]

In particular,

\[
p_3^Tp_1
=\cos(2)+\cos(0.2).
\]

The result depends on \(3-1=2\), not on the absolute pair \((3,1)\)
separately. This illustrates how sinusoidal encodings provide
relative-offset information through inner products.

\section{16.23 Exercises}\label{exercises-15}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Prove that if \(F(X)=XW\) is applied row-wise, then \(F(PX)=PF(X)\)
  for every permutation matrix \(P\).
\item
  Prove the permutation-equivariance result for a single self-attention
  head.
\item
  Show that the row-wise softmax satisfies
  \(\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(PSP^T)=P\operatorname{softmax}_{\text{row}}(S)P^T\).
\item
  For a sinusoidal encoding with one frequency \(\omega\), prove that
  \(u_t(\omega)^Tu_s(\omega)=\cos(\omega(t-s))\).
\item
  Derive the block rotation matrix that maps \(u_t(\omega)\) to
  \(u_{t+\Delta}(\omega)\).
\item
  Implement sinusoidal encoding for \(T=100\) and \(d=32\). Plot the
  similarity matrix \(PP^T\).
\item
  Compare learned absolute position embeddings and sinusoidal encodings
  in terms of parameter count.
\item
  Implement a relative-position bias matrix \(B\) with entries
  \(B_{ij}=-\lambda |i-j|\). How does increasing \(\lambda\) change
  attention weights?
\item
  Implement the causal relative bias \(B_{ij}=-\infty\) for \(j>i\) and
  \(B_{ij}=-\lambda(i-j)\) for \(j\le i\).
\item
  Use RoPE on random queries and keys. Compare attention score matrices
  before and after rotation.
\item
  Explain why RoPE requires an even number of rotated coordinates, or
  else a convention for the leftover coordinate.
\item
  Write a short mathematical paragraph explaining why position is not a
  small implementation detail but a structural part of the Transformer
  model.
\end{enumerate}

\section{16.24 Mini-project}\label{mini-project-2}

Choose one short corpus, such as course descriptions, news headlines, or
theorem statements. Build a tiny Transformer-style input representation
in three ways:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  token embeddings only;
\item
  token embeddings plus learned absolute position embeddings;
\item
  token embeddings plus sinusoidal position encodings.
\end{enumerate}

For each method, compute the self-attention score matrix before training
using the same random \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\). Compare how the score
structure changes. Your report should include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  the mathematical formulas for the three input representations;
\item
  at least one heatmap for each score matrix;
\item
  a discussion of permutation equivariance;
\item
  a discussion of whether the model can distinguish word order before
  training.
\end{itemize}

\section{16.25 Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-7}

The accompanying lab for this chapter should ask students to build
positional encodings from scratch, test permutation equivariance,
visualize sinusoidal similarity matrices, implement RoPE, and compare
attention weights with and without distance biases.

A useful independent-study lab structure is:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  implement sinusoidal position encoding;
\item
  visualize the encoding matrix and similarity matrix;
\item
  prove and test permutation equivariance of attention;
\item
  add absolute position vectors and show that equivariance is broken in
  the desired way;
\item
  implement relative-position bias;
\item
  implement RoPE;
\item
  write a short reflection on how sequence geometry changes attention.
\end{enumerate}

\section{16.26 Summary}\label{summary-2}

Self-attention is powerful because every token can compare itself with
every other token. But without position information, self-attention is
permutation equivariant: it does not know the original order of the
rows. Positional encoding solves this problem by injecting order into
the input vectors or attention scores.

The simplest method adds position vectors to token embeddings. Learned
absolute embeddings are flexible but may not extrapolate naturally.
Sinusoidal encodings use Fourier features and have dot products that
depend on relative offsets. Relative-position biases add displacement
information directly to attention scores. RoPE rotates query and key
vectors so their dot products encode relative displacement.

From a mathematical perspective, positional encoding is the study of how
to represent the ordered set

\[
\{1,2,\ldots,T\}
\]

inside the geometry of a Transformer. It is where sequence structure
enters attention-based language modeling.

\part{Part VI. Large Language Models and Retrieval}

\chapter{Autoregressive Language
Models}\label{autoregressive-language-models}

Next-token prediction, likelihood, and mathematical generation

\hfill\break

This chapter begins the part of the book on large language models. The
goal is to explain an autoregressive language model as a clean
mathematical object: a conditional probability model for the next token.
Once this viewpoint is clear, training, perplexity, temperature,
top-\(k\) sampling, nucleus sampling, greedy decoding, and beam search
become consequences of probability and optimization rather than
mysterious engineering tricks.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-16}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Write the probability of a token sequence using the autoregressive
  chain rule.
\item
  Explain next-token prediction as conditional distribution estimation.
\item
  Derive the negative log-likelihood and cross-entropy objective for
  language modeling.
\item
  Compute sentence log-probability and perplexity from next-token
  probabilities.
\item
  Compare greedy decoding, sampling, temperature scaling, top-\(k\)
  sampling, nucleus sampling, and beam search.
\item
  Explain why causal masking is required in decoder-only Transformer
  language models.
\item
  Implement a small autoregressive generator and decoding methods from
  scratch in Python.
\end{itemize}

\section{17.1 The basic object: a distribution on
sequences}\label{the-basic-object-a-distribution-on-sequences}

Let \(V\) be a finite vocabulary with \(|V|=d\). A token sequence of
length \(T\) is

\[
w_{1:T} = (w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T) \in V^T.
\]

A language model assigns probabilities to sequences. For a fixed length
\(T\), this means a probability mass function

\[
P(w_{1:T}), \qquad w_{1:T} \in V^T,
\]

satisfying

\[
P(w_{1:T}) \geq 0, \qquad \sum_{w_{1:T} \in V^T} P(w_{1:T}) = 1.
\]

The space \(V^T\) has size \(d^T\), so directly specifying \(P\) is
impossible except for tiny vocabularies and tiny lengths. The central
mathematical idea is to factor the joint distribution into conditional
distributions.

By the chain rule of probability,

\[
P(w_{1:T})
=
P(w_1)P(w_2 \mid w_1)P(w_3 \mid w_{1:2})\cdots P(w_T \mid w_{1:T-1}).
\]

Equivalently,

\[
P(w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T} P(w_t \mid w_{<t}),
\]

where \(w_{<t}=(w_1,\ldots,w_{t-1})\). This identity is exact. An
autoregressive language model is a parameterized approximation of these
conditional probabilities.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Autoregressive viewpoint}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

An \textbf{autoregressive language model} estimates

\[
p_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t})
\]

for each position \(t\). The model then defines a sequence distribution
by

\[
p_\theta(w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^{T} p_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}).
\]

\end{tcolorbox}

The word \emph{autoregressive} means that the model generates each new
token using previously generated tokens as input. In time series
notation, the future is predicted from the past. In NLP notation, the
next token is predicted from the prefix.

\section{17.2 Prefixes, contexts, and conditional
distributions}\label{prefixes-contexts-and-conditional-distributions}

For every prefix \(c=w_{<t}\), an autoregressive model outputs a
probability vector

\[
p_\theta(\cdot \mid c) \in \Delta^{d-1},
\]

where

\[
\Delta^{d-1}
=
\left\{p\in R^d: p_j\geq 0,\; \sum_{j=1}^d p_j=1\right\}
\]

is the probability simplex. If the vocabulary is ordered as

\[
V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\},
\]

then the model output is

\[
p_\theta(\cdot \mid c)
=
\left(p_\theta(v_1\mid c),\ldots,p_\theta(v_d\mid c)\right).
\]

A neural language model usually produces real-valued logits

\[
z_\theta(c) \in R^d,
\]

and converts them to probabilities by the softmax map

\[
p_\theta(v_j\mid c)
=
\frac{\exp(z_j(c))}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\exp(z_\ell(c))}.
\]

The logits are scores. The softmax turns scores into a categorical
distribution.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Representation, model, and probability}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For a prefix \(c\), a modern neural language model usually has the form

\[
c \longmapsto h_\theta(c) \in R^m
\longmapsto z_\theta(c)=Wh_\theta(c)+b \in R^d
\longmapsto p_\theta(\cdot\mid c)=\operatorname{softmax}(z_\theta(c)).
\]

The representation \(h_\theta(c)\) is not itself a probability
distribution. The probability distribution appears after the output
logits are transformed by softmax.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{17.3 Training data and maximum
likelihood}\label{training-data-and-maximum-likelihood}

Suppose the training corpus consists of token sequences

\[
D=\{w^{(i)}_{1:T_i}: i=1,\ldots,n\}.
\]

The likelihood of the data under an autoregressive model is

\[
L(\theta;D)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}\prod_{t=1}^{T_i}
p_\theta\left(w_t^{(i)} \mid w_{<t}^{(i)}\right).
\]

The log-likelihood is

\[
\ell(\theta;D)
=
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta\left(w_t^{(i)} \mid w_{<t}^{(i)}\right).
\]

Training usually minimizes the negative log-likelihood,

\[
\mathcal L(\theta)
=
-
\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta\left(w_t^{(i)} \mid w_{<t}^{(i)}\right).
\]

This is also the sum of cross-entropy losses. At each position \(t\),
the target is the one-hot vector for the observed next token. If \(y_t\)
is the index of \(w_t\), then the one-position loss is

\[
\ell_t(\theta)=-\log p_\theta(y_t\mid w_{<t}).
\]

For logits \(z\in R^d\) and target class \(y\), the gradient of the
softmax cross-entropy is

\[
\frac{\partial}{\partial z_j}\left[-\log \operatorname{softmax}(z)_y\right]
=
\operatorname{softmax}(z)_j - 1\{j=y\}.
\]

This simple formula is one reason next-token prediction scales well
computationally.

\section{17.4 Teacher forcing}\label{teacher-forcing}

During training, the model is given the true prefix from the corpus. For
example, from the sentence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models predict the next token}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

we form training pairs:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{prefix: language                 target: models}
\NormalTok{prefix: language models          target: predict}
\NormalTok{prefix: language models predict  target: the}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

This training approach is called \textbf{teacher forcing}. The model
learns from correct prefixes even though, at generation time, it must
condition on tokens that it generated itself.

Mathematically, training minimizes empirical conditional cross-entropy
under the empirical distribution of true prefixes. Generation samples
from the model distribution over its own prefixes. This mismatch is one
source of error accumulation in generated text.

\section{17.5 Sentence probability, average loss, and
perplexity}\label{sentence-probability-average-loss-and-perplexity}

For one sequence \(w_{1:T}\), the model log-probability is

\[
\log p_\theta(w_{1:T})
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t}).
\]

The average negative log-likelihood per token is

\[
\bar{\mathcal L}
=
-
\frac{1}{T}
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t}).
\]

The perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{PPL}
=
\exp(\bar{\mathcal L}).
\]

Perplexity can be interpreted as an effective average number of
plausible next-token choices. Lower perplexity usually means the model
assigns higher probability to the observed text, but perplexity is not a
complete measure of usefulness or truthfulness.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Perplexity is not understanding}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A model can have low perplexity on a dataset by learning strong
statistical regularities. This does not imply that it reasons correctly,
uses facts reliably, or understands meaning in a human sense. Perplexity
is a likelihood-based metric, not a complete evaluation of language
behavior.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{17.6 Decoder-only Transformers as autoregressive
models}\label{decoder-only-transformers-as-autoregressive-models}

A decoder-only Transformer represents the prefix \(w_{<t}\) using a
stack of causal self-attention blocks. If the input sequence is

\[
w_{1:T},
\]

then each position \(t\) produces a hidden vector \(h_t\in R^m\). The
output logits for the next token are often computed by

\[
z_t = Wh_t + b \in R^d,
\]

and the next-token distribution is

\[
p_\theta(w_{t+1}=v_j\mid w_{1:t})
=
\frac{\exp((z_t)_j)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\exp((z_t)_\ell)}.
\]

The causal mask ensures that the hidden vector at position \(t\) cannot
use tokens from positions greater than \(t\). Without causal masking, a
language model trained to predict the next token could leak information
from the future.

For a sequence length \(T\), the causal attention mask has entries

\[
M_{ij}=
\begin{cases}
0, & j\leq i,\\
-\infty, & j>i.
\end{cases}
\]

The attention weights are computed as

\[
A=\operatorname{softmax}\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}+M\right),
\]

where the softmax is applied row by row.

\section{17.7 Generation as repeated
sampling}\label{generation-as-repeated-sampling}

Once a model produces \(p_\theta(\cdot\mid c)\), generation repeats
three steps:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Compute logits \(z_\theta(c)\) for the current context \(c\).
\item
  Convert logits to a probability distribution, possibly modified by a
  decoding rule.
\item
  Choose the next token and append it to the context.
\end{enumerate}

This gives a recursive stochastic process:

\[
W_t \sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid W_{<t}),
\qquad t=1,2,\ldots.
\]

Different decoding rules define different stochastic or deterministic
processes.

\section{17.8 Greedy decoding}\label{greedy-decoding}

Greedy decoding chooses the most likely next token:

\[
\hat w_t
=
\arg\max_{v\in V} p_\theta(v\mid \hat w_{<t}).
\]

Greedy decoding is deterministic. It is simple and often produces fluent
text, but it can become repetitive and may miss globally better
sequences. It is a local optimization rule, not a global
maximum-likelihood sequence search.

\section{17.9 Temperature scaling}\label{temperature-scaling}

Given logits \(z\in R^d\), temperature scaling defines

\[
p_j(\tau)
=
\frac{\exp(z_j/\tau)}{\sum_{\ell=1}^{d}\exp(z_\ell/\tau)},
\qquad \tau>0.
\]

Small temperature sharpens the distribution. Large temperature flattens
it. As \(\tau\to 0\), the distribution concentrates on the largest
logit. As \(\tau\to \infty\), it approaches the uniform distribution.

Temperature does not change the ordering of logits, but it changes
entropy. The entropy is

\[
H(p(\tau))=-\sum_{j=1}^{d}p_j(\tau)\log p_j(\tau).
\]

In applications, temperature is a diversity-control parameter.

\section{\texorpdfstring{17.10 Top-\(k\)
sampling}{17.10 Top-k sampling}}\label{top-k-sampling}

Top-\(k\) sampling keeps only the \(k\) highest-probability tokens. Let
\(S_k\) be the set of \(k\) token indices with largest probabilities.
The top-\(k\) distribution is

\[
q_j
=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{p_j}{\sum_{\ell\in S_k}p_\ell}, & j\in S_k,\\
0, & j\notin S_k.
\end{cases}
\]

Then the next token is sampled from \(q\). Top-\(k\) sampling prevents
extremely unlikely tokens from being selected while still allowing
randomness among likely tokens.

\section{\texorpdfstring{17.11 Nucleus sampling, or top-\(p\)
sampling}{17.11 Nucleus sampling, or top-p sampling}}\label{nucleus-sampling-or-top-p-sampling}

Nucleus sampling chooses the smallest set \(S_p\) of high-probability
tokens whose cumulative probability is at least a threshold \(p_0\).
After sorting probabilities in descending order,

\[
p_{(1)}\geq p_{(2)}\geq \cdots \geq p_{(d)},
\]

choose the smallest \(m\) such that

\[
\sum_{r=1}^{m}p_{(r)}\geq p_0.
\]

The nucleus is

\[
S_p=\{(1),\ldots,(m)\}.
\]

Then probabilities are renormalized on \(S_p\). Unlike top-\(k\), the
number of allowed tokens changes with the confidence of the
distribution. If the distribution is sharp, the nucleus may be small. If
the distribution is flat, the nucleus may be larger.

\section{17.12 Beam search}\label{beam-search}

Beam search is an approximate search for a high-probability sequence. It
maintains a set of \(B\) candidate prefixes called the beam. At each
step, each candidate prefix is extended by possible next tokens, and
only the \(B\) highest-scoring extended prefixes are kept.

The score of a sequence is usually its log-probability:

\[
s(w_{1:T})
=
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t}).
\]

Because log-probabilities are usually negative, longer sequences tend to
have smaller scores. Some implementations use length normalization, for
example

\[
s_\alpha(w_{1:T})
=
\frac{1}{T^\alpha}
\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t}),
\]

where \(\alpha\geq 0\).

Beam search is common in translation and structured generation, but for
open-ended generation it can produce dull or repetitive text because it
aggressively seeks high-probability continuations.

\section{17.13 Worked example: likelihood and
perplexity}\label{worked-example-likelihood-and-perplexity}

Suppose a vocabulary contains four tokens:

\[
V=\{\texttt{math},\texttt{models},\texttt{learn},\texttt{data}\}.
\]

A model assigns the following next-token probabilities to the observed
sequence

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{math models learn data}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

at the four positions:

\[
0.40,\quad 0.25,\quad 0.50,\quad 0.20.
\]

The sequence probability is

\[
0.40\cdot 0.25\cdot 0.50\cdot 0.20=0.01.
\]

The log-probability is

\[
\log(0.01)\approx -4.6052.
\]

The average negative log-likelihood is

\[
-\frac{1}{4}\log(0.01)\approx 1.1513.
\]

The perplexity is

\[
\exp(1.1513)\approx 3.1623.
\]

This means that, on average, the model behaves as if it were choosing
among about \(3.16\) equally likely next-token options at each step.

\section{17.14 Python example: softmax, likelihood, and
perplexity}\label{python-example-softmax-likelihood-and-perplexity}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch17-softmax-perplexity}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{np.set\_printoptions(precision}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, suppress}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits, temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(logits, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ temperature}
\NormalTok{    shifted }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ logits }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(logits)}
\NormalTok{    exp\_scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(shifted)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ exp\_scores }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ exp\_scores.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sequence\_log\_probability(next\_token\_probabilities):}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(next\_token\_probabilities, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{any}\NormalTok{(probs }\OperatorTok{\textless{}=} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{):}
        \ControlFlowTok{raise} \PreprocessorTok{ValueError}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"All observed{-}token probabilities must be positive."}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.log(probs).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ perplexity(next\_token\_probabilities):}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(next\_token\_probabilities, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    avg\_nll }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.log(probs).mean()}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.exp(avg\_nll))}

\NormalTok{observed\_probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.40}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.50}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{logp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sequence\_log\_probability(observed\_probs)}
\NormalTok{ppl }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ perplexity(observed\_probs)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Sequence log{-}probability:"}\NormalTok{, logp)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Perplexity:"}\NormalTok{, ppl)}

\NormalTok{logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Softmax probabilities:"}\NormalTok{, softmax(logits))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Temperature 0.5:"}\NormalTok{, softmax(logits, temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Temperature 2.0:"}\NormalTok{, softmax(logits, temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

Perplexity: 3.162277660168379
Softmax probabilities: [0.5672 0.2548 0.1266 0.0515]
Temperature 0.5: [0.7937 0.1602 0.0395 0.0065]
Temperature 2.0: [0.4092 0.2743 0.1933 0.1232]

\section{17.16 Python example: decoding
rules}\label{python-example-decoding-rules}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch17-decoding-rules}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"proof"}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{base\_logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ top\_k\_filter(probs, k):}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(probs, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ k }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(probs):}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ probs }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ probs.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\NormalTok{    keep }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(probs)[::}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][:k]}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(probs)}
\NormalTok{    q[keep] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ probs[keep]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ q.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ top\_p\_filter(probs, p\_threshold):}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(probs, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(probs)[::}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    cumulative }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.cumsum(probs[order])}
\NormalTok{    m }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.searchsorted(cumulative, p\_threshold, side}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"left"}\NormalTok{)) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{    keep }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ order[:m]}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(probs)}
\NormalTok{    q[keep] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ probs[keep]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ q.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\NormalTok{p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(base\_logits, temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Base distribution"}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(vocab, p):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{token}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}9s\}}\SpecialStringTok{: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Top{-}k distribution, k=3"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{qk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ top\_k\_filter(p, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(vocab, qk):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{token}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}9s\}}\SpecialStringTok{: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Top{-}p distribution, p=0.80"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{qp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ top\_p\_filter(p, p\_threshold}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(vocab, qp):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{token}\SpecialCharTok{:\textgreater{}9s\}}\SpecialStringTok{: }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{prob}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{sampled\_token }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.choice(vocab, p}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{qp)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Sample from top{-}p distribution:"}\NormalTok{, sampled\_token)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{17.17 Python example: a tiny autoregressive
generator}\label{python-example-a-tiny-autoregressive-generator}

The following example is intentionally simple. It uses a hand-built
bigram-like table so that the mathematics of generation is visible.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch17-tiny-generator}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{2026}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"\textless{}bos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"from"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{idx }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{w: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}

\CommentTok{\# Rows are contexts, columns are next{-}token logits.}
\NormalTok{Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.full((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)), }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{3.0}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ set\_logits(context, scores):}
\NormalTok{    row }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ idx[context]}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, score }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ scores.items():}
\NormalTok{        Z[row, idx[token]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ score}

\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"\textless{}bos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.8}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.5}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.4}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.2}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"from"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.4}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"from"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.3}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"from"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.6}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{2.2}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{set\_logits(}\StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{, \{}\StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{3.0}\NormalTok{\})}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ next\_distribution(context\_token, temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, top\_k}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, top\_p}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(Z[idx[context\_token]], temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{temperature)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ top\_k }\KeywordTok{is} \KeywordTok{not} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ top\_k\_filter(probs, top\_k)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ top\_p }\KeywordTok{is} \KeywordTok{not} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ top\_p\_filter(probs, top\_p)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ probs}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ generate(max\_steps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{, temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, top\_k}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, top\_p}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"\textless{}bos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{]}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(max\_steps):}
\NormalTok{        probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ next\_distribution(tokens[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{temperature, top\_k}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{top\_k, top\_p}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{top\_p)}
\NormalTok{        next\_token }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.choice(vocab, p}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{probs)}
\NormalTok{        tokens.append(next\_token)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ next\_token }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{break}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ tokens}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ temp }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.8}\NormalTok{]:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"temperature=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{temp}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{:"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{" "}\NormalTok{.join(generate(temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{temp, top\_p}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{)))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
temperature=0.5: <bos> math models learn from data <eos>
temperature=1.0: <bos> language models learn from language data <eos>
temperature=1.8: <bos> language models language models learn from data <eos>
\end{verbatim}

\section{17.18 Python example: beam
search}\label{python-example-beam-search}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch17-beam-search}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ math}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ beam\_search(beam\_width}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, max\_steps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    beam }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [([}\StringTok{"\textless{}bos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{], }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)]}
\NormalTok{    completed }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}

    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(max\_steps):}
\NormalTok{        candidates }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tokens, score }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ beam:}
            \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tokens[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"\textless{}eos\textgreater{}"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{                completed.append((tokens, score))}
\NormalTok{                candidates.append((tokens, score))}
                \ControlFlowTok{continue}
\NormalTok{            probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ next\_distribution(tokens[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], temperature}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{)}
            \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, prob }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(probs):}
                \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ prob }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{                    new\_tokens }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tokens }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ [vocab[j]]}
\NormalTok{                    new\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ score }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ math.log(prob)}
\NormalTok{                    candidates.append((new\_tokens, new\_score))}

        \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ normalized\_score(item):}
\NormalTok{            tokens, score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ item}
\NormalTok{            length }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tokens) }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
            \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ score }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (length }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ alpha)}

\NormalTok{        candidates.sort(key}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{normalized\_score, reverse}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        beam }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ candidates[:beam\_width]}

\NormalTok{    completed.extend(beam)}
\NormalTok{    completed.sort(key}\OperatorTok{=}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ item: item[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(item[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]) }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ alpha), reverse}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ completed[:beam\_width]}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tokens, score }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ beam\_search(beam\_width}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, max\_steps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, alpha}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.6}\NormalTok{):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"score=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{score}\SpecialCharTok{: .4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{ |"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{" "}\NormalTok{.join(tokens))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
score=-2.0655 | <bos> math models learn from data <eos>
score=-2.1205 | <bos> language models learn from data <eos>
score=-2.6012 | <bos> math models from data <eos>
\end{verbatim}

\section{17.21 AI-assisted learning
activities}\label{ai-assisted-learning-activities-2}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical tutor, not as a black box. Good
prompts force the assistant to state the conditioning, the probability
distribution, and the loss function.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Prompt 1: identify the distribution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Ask:

\begin{quote}
In the sentence \texttt{language\ models\ predict\ tokens}, list the
autoregressive training pairs. For each pair, identify the prefix, the
target token, and the conditional probability that appears in the
likelihood.
\end{quote}

Then check whether the answer correctly distinguishes
\(p(w_t\mid w_{<t})\) from \(p(w_{<t}\mid w_t)\).

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Prompt 2: decoding audit}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Ask:

\begin{quote}
Explain the difference between temperature, top-k sampling, and nucleus
sampling using probability notation. Give one example where top-k and
top-p keep different numbers of tokens.
\end{quote}

Then verify the explanation by computing the filtered distributions
yourself.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Prompt 3: perplexity interpretation}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Ask:

\begin{quote}
A language model has average negative log-likelihood 1.7 nats per token.
What is its perplexity? What does this number mean, and what does it not
mean?
\end{quote}

A good answer should mention \(\exp(1.7)\) and should not claim that
perplexity measures factual correctness.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{17.22 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-6}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Confusing the chain rule with a Markov assumption.} The
  factorization \(P(w_{1:T})=\prod_t P(w_t\mid w_{<t})\) is exact. A
  Markov model makes the additional approximation
  \(P(w_t\mid w_{<t})\approx P(w_t\mid w_{t-r:t-1})\).
\item
  \textbf{Treating logits as probabilities.} Logits can be any real
  numbers. Probabilities appear after softmax.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring length in sequence scores.} The raw log-probability
  of a sequence usually decreases as length increases. Comparing
  sequences of different lengths requires care.
\item
  \textbf{Believing sampling is the same as training.} Training usually
  uses teacher forcing. Generation conditions on previously generated
  tokens.
\item
  \textbf{Thinking low perplexity guarantees high-quality answers.}
  Perplexity is a likelihood metric. It does not by itself measure
  truthfulness, fairness, safety, or usefulness.
\end{enumerate}

\section{17.23 Exercises}\label{exercises-16}

\subsection{Conceptual exercises}\label{conceptual-exercises-7}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Let \(V=\{a,b,c\}\). Write the full chain-rule factorization of
  \(P(w_1,w_2,w_3,w_4)\).
\item
  Explain why the autoregressive factorization is exact but an
  \(n\)-gram approximation is not exact in general.
\item
  Suppose two models assign the following probabilities to the observed
  next tokens:

  \[
  (0.5,0.4,0.25,0.5)
  \quad\text{and}\quad
  (0.8,0.1,0.8,0.1).
  \]

  Compute the average negative log-likelihood and perplexity for each.
  Which model has better likelihood?
\item
  Show that temperature scaling does not change the identity of the
  largest-probability token when there is a unique largest logit.
\item
  Give an example where top-\(k\) sampling with \(k=3\) keeps less total
  probability mass than top-\(p\) sampling with \(p_0=0.90\).
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Mathematical exercises}\label{mathematical-exercises-6}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{5}
\item
  Derive the gradient

  \[
  \nabla_z[-\log \operatorname{softmax}(z)_y]
  =
  \operatorname{softmax}(z)-e_y.
  \]
\item
  Let \(p(\tau)=\operatorname{softmax}(z/\tau)\). Compute
  \(\lim_{\tau\to\infty}p(\tau)\).
\item
  Let \(M\) be the causal mask with \(M_{ij}=-\infty\) for \(j>i\) and
  \(0\) otherwise. Prove that the row-wise softmax of \(S+M\) assigns
  zero weight to future positions.
\item
  Suppose a model generates tokens by
  \(W_t\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid W_{<t})\). Explain why this defines a
  stochastic process on \(V^*\).
\item
  In beam search, explain why raw log-probability favors shorter
  sequences when end-of-sequence tokens are allowed.
\end{enumerate}

\subsection{Computational exercises}\label{computational-exercises-4}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\setcounter{enumi}{10}
\item
  Implement top-\(k\) and top-\(p\) filtering for a probability vector.
  Test your code on at least three distributions: sharp, medium, and
  flat.
\item
  Write a function that takes a list of observed next-token
  probabilities and returns log-probability, average NLL, and
  perplexity.
\item
  Build a tiny bigram language model from a small corpus. Generate text
  using greedy decoding, temperature sampling, top-\(k\) sampling, and
  top-\(p\) sampling.
\item
  Implement beam search for your tiny bigram model. Compare results for
  beam widths \(1\), \(3\), and \(5\).
\item
  Simulate generation under different temperatures and estimate the
  empirical entropy of generated next tokens.
\end{enumerate}

\section{17.24 Mini-project: a mathematical decoding
report}\label{mini-project-a-mathematical-decoding-report}

Choose a small corpus related to a course topic, for example mathematics
course descriptions, research abstracts, or advising FAQ text. Build a
simple autoregressive model using bigram or trigram probabilities. Then
write a short mathematical report containing:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  the vocabulary construction,
\item
  the estimated conditional probabilities,
\item
  the training negative log-likelihood,
\item
  generated examples under at least four decoding rules,
\item
  a comparison of entropy, diversity, repetition, and coherence,
\item
  a discussion of how these ideas scale to Transformer language models.
\end{enumerate}

The goal is not to build a strong model. The goal is to make the
probability structure of generation completely explicit.

\section{What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-5}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  An autoregressive language model estimates
  \(p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t})\).
\item
  The sequence probability is the product of next-token conditional
  probabilities.
\item
  Training usually minimizes next-token negative log-likelihood.
\item
  Perplexity is the exponential of average negative log-likelihood.
\item
  Generation is a recursive process in which sampled tokens become
  future context.
\item
  Temperature, top-\(k\), and top-\(p\) modify the next-token
  distribution before sampling.
\item
  Causal masking prevents a decoder-only model from seeing future
  tokens.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-9}

This chapter connects the probabilistic language-modeling ideas from
Chapters 4 and 5 with the Transformer machinery developed in Chapters
13--16. Classical background includes statistical language modeling and
information theory. Modern autoregressive models build on neural
sequence modeling, attention, and large-scale maximum likelihood
training.

\chapter{Training Large Language
Models}\label{training-large-language-models}

Pretraining, fine-tuning, instruction tuning, and alignment as
optimization problems

\hfill\break

Chapter 17 described an autoregressive language model as a conditional
probability model for the next token. This chapter explains how such a
model is trained. The main mathematical idea is simple: training a large
language model is empirical risk minimization over token sequences.
Pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning, preference
learning, and alignment differ mainly in the data distribution, the loss
function, and the constraints placed on the updated model.

\section{Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-17}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Write language-model pretraining as maximum likelihood estimation.
\item
  Derive the token-level cross-entropy loss from the autoregressive
  factorization.
\item
  Explain teacher forcing, causal masking, and padding masks in the
  training objective.
\item
  Compute the gradient of the softmax cross-entropy loss with respect to
  logits.
\item
  Distinguish pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, instruction tuning,
  and preference tuning.
\item
  Explain KL-regularized fine-tuning as constrained distributional
  movement away from a reference model.
\item
  Describe pairwise preference modeling using the Bradley--Terry
  logistic model.
\item
  Interpret RLHF and DPO-style methods as optimization problems on
  conditional distributions.
\item
  Implement small pieces of the training objective from scratch in
  Python.
\end{itemize}

\section{18.1 From a language model to a statistical
estimator}\label{from-a-language-model-to-a-statistical-estimator}

Let \(V\) be a finite vocabulary and let a token sequence be

\[
w_{1:T}=(w_1,\ldots,w_T) \in V^T.
\]

An autoregressive language model with parameters \(\theta\) defines

\[
p_\theta(w_{1:T})
=
\prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}).
\]

Training means choosing \(\theta\) using data. Suppose the training
corpus consists of \(N\) token sequences

\[
D=\{w^{(1)}_{1:T_1},\ldots,w^{(N)}_{1:T_N}\}.
\]

The maximum likelihood estimator is

\[
\hat \theta
=
\arg\max_\theta
\prod_{i=1}^N
p_\theta(w^{(i)}_{1:T_i}).
\]

Because products of many small probabilities are numerically unstable,
we maximize log-likelihood or equivalently minimize negative
log-likelihood:

\[
\hat\theta
=
\arg\min_\theta
\left[-\sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(w^{(i)}_{1:T_i})\right].
\]

Using the autoregressive factorization,

\[
-\log p_\theta(w^{(i)}_{1:T_i})
=
-\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta(w_t^{(i)} \mid w_{<t}^{(i)}).
\]

Thus the training problem is a large supervised learning problem in
disguise. Each prefix \(w_{<t}\) is an input and the next token \(w_t\)
is the label.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Pretraining objective}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The standard autoregressive pretraining loss is

\[
L_{\text{pre}}(\theta)
=
-\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta(w_t^{(i)} \mid w_{<t}^{(i)}),
\]

where \(M=\sum_i T_i\) is the number of predicted tokens. This is the
empirical cross-entropy between the data distribution and the model
distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{18.2 Training data as samples from an unknown
distribution}\label{training-data-as-samples-from-an-unknown-distribution}

A mathematically clean way to view the corpus is as a sample from an
unknown population distribution \(P_{\text{data}}\) on token sequences.
The population risk for language modeling is

\[
R(\theta)
=
E_{W_{1:T}\sim P_{\text{data}}}
\left[
-\sum_{t=1}^T \log p_\theta(W_t \mid W_{<t})
\right].
\]

The empirical training loss replaces the expectation by an average over
the observed corpus. This gives the usual statistical learning picture:

\[
\text{population risk} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{empirical risk} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{optimization algorithm}.
\]

For MS Statistics students, this viewpoint is important because the
training corpus is not neutral. It induces an empirical distribution.
The model learns from that distribution and inherits its coverage,
imbalances, style, and noise.

\section{18.3 Tokens, contexts, and
labels}\label{tokens-contexts-and-labels}

Given a sequence

\[
w_{1:T}=(w_1,w_2,\ldots,w_T),
\]

training forms the pairs

\[
(w_{<1},w_1),\;(w_{<2},w_2),\;\ldots,\;(w_{<T},w_T).
\]

The first context \(w_{<1}\) is usually represented by a
beginning-of-sequence token. The target at position \(t\) is not the
entire future. It is only the next token \(w_t\). However, minimizing
next-token loss over many positions encourages the model to capture
long-range structure because the prefix may contain earlier semantic and
syntactic information.

For a vocabulary ordered as \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_d\}\), the model produces
logits

\[
z_\theta(w_{<t})\in R^d.
\]

The probability assigned to token \(v_j\) is

\[
p_\theta(v_j\mid w_{<t})
=
\frac{\exp(z_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^d \exp(z_k)}.
\]

If the true next token is \(v_y\), the token loss is

\[
\ell(z,y)
=
-\log \frac{\exp(z_y)}{\sum_{k=1}^d \exp(z_k)}
=
-z_y+\log\sum_{k=1}^d \exp(z_k).
\]

This is the same softmax cross-entropy loss used in multiclass
classification, applied at every token position.

\section{18.4 Gradient of token-level
cross-entropy}\label{gradient-of-token-level-cross-entropy}

Let

\[
p=\operatorname{softmax}(z).
\]

Let \(e_y\in R^d\) be the one-hot vector for the correct class. The
token loss is

\[
\ell(z,y)=-\log p_y.
\]

A direct calculation gives

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_j}=p_j-(e_y)_j.
\]

Therefore,

\[
\nabla_z \ell = p-e_y.
\]

This simple formula is central. The model is pushed to decrease
probabilities assigned to incorrect tokens and increase the probability
assigned to the observed token.

\textbf{Interpretation.} If the model assigns too little probability to
the observed next token, the residual \(p-e_y\) is large in the
direction that corrects the logits. Training a language model is
therefore repeated probability calibration over a huge number of
next-token classification problems.

\section{18.5 Teacher forcing}\label{teacher-forcing-1}

During training, the model is given the true previous tokens as context.
This is called \textbf{teacher forcing}. For example, if the training
sequence is

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\textless{}bos\textgreater{} math models learn from data \textless{}eos\textgreater{}}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

then the model is trained on contexts such as

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{\textless{}bos\textgreater{} math models}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

with target

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{learn}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The model does not train on its own generated mistakes at this stage.
Mathematically, the loss uses contexts from the empirical data
distribution, not contexts produced by the model. This difference is one
source of the gap between training and generation.

\section{18.6 Batching, padding, and
masks}\label{batching-padding-and-masks}

In practice, sequences of different lengths are placed into a
rectangular array. Suppose a batch has \(B\) sequences and maximum
length \(T_{\max}\). The token array has shape

\[
B\times T_{\max}.
\]

Shorter sequences are padded. Let

\[
m_{i,t}\in \{0,1\}
\]

be a mask indicating whether token position \((i,t)\) is real or
padding. The masked training loss is

\[
L(\theta)
=
-
\frac{1}{\sum_{i,t}m_{i,t}}
\sum_{i=1}^B\sum_{t=1}^{T_{\max}}
 m_{i,t}
\log p_\theta(w_{i,t}\mid w_{i,<t}).
\]

Padding positions must not contribute to the loss. In decoder-only
Transformers, causal masks are also used so that position \(t\) cannot
attend to positions greater than \(t\).

\section{18.7 Optimization: stochastic gradients and
AdamW}\label{optimization-stochastic-gradients-and-adamw}

The loss function for a large language model is nonconvex and
high-dimensional. Let \(\theta\in R^P\) denote all parameters. A generic
stochastic-gradient update is

\[
\theta_{s+1}
=
\theta_s-\eta_s \widehat{\nabla L}(\theta_s),
\]

where \(\widehat{\nabla L}\) is a gradient estimate computed from a
minibatch and \(\eta_s\) is a learning rate.

Modern training often uses adaptive optimizers. A simplified Adam-style
update maintains moving averages of gradients and squared gradients:

\[
m_s=\beta_1m_{s-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_s,
\]

\[
v_s=\beta_2v_{s-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_s\odot g_s.
\]

Then the parameter update has the coordinatewise form

\[
\theta_{s+1}
=
\theta_s
-
\eta_s
\frac{\widehat m_s}{\sqrt{\widehat v_s}+\epsilon}.
\]

AdamW separates weight decay from the gradient update. A schematic
update is

\[
\theta_{s+1}
=
(1-\eta_s\lambda)\theta_s
-
\eta_s
\frac{\widehat m_s}{\sqrt{\widehat v_s}+\epsilon}.
\]

Here \(\lambda\) controls weight decay. From an applied mathematics
viewpoint, AdamW is a stochastic, adaptive, preconditioned first-order
method with explicit shrinkage.

\section{18.8 Validation loss, overfitting, and early
stopping}\label{validation-loss-overfitting-and-early-stopping}

The training loss estimates performance on the training distribution. To
estimate generalization, we hold out validation data and compute

\[
L_{\text{val}}(\theta)
=
-
\frac{1}{M_{\text{val}}}
\sum_{(i,t)\in \text{validation}}
\log p_\theta(w_t^{(i)}\mid w_{<t}^{(i)}).
\]

A useful diagnostic is the training-validation gap:

\[
L_{\text{val}}(\theta)-L_{\text{train}}(\theta).
\]

A large positive gap suggests overfitting, distribution mismatch, or
both. In very large pretraining, the situation is more subtle because
data diversity, model capacity, optimization budget, and evaluation
distribution interact.

\section{18.9 Supervised fine-tuning}\label{supervised-fine-tuning}

Pretraining learns a broad next-token model. \textbf{Supervised
fine-tuning} updates the model on a more targeted dataset. For
instruction tuning, each training example often has a prompt and a
desired response:

\[
x_i=\text{prompt},\qquad y_i=\text{response}.
\]

The conditional fine-tuning objective is

\[
L_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)
=
-
\frac{1}{M}
\sum_{i=1}^N\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x_i,y_{i,<t}).
\]

The prompt tokens provide context, but the loss is often applied only to
the response tokens. This is an important masking detail. If prompt
tokens are included in the loss, the model is trained to reproduce
prompts rather than only to generate useful responses.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Masking matters}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

For instruction fine-tuning, one often wants

\[
\text{loss on response tokens only}.
\]

The mask determines which tokens count as labels. This small
implementation choice changes the statistical problem being solved.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{18.10 Fine-tuning as distributional
movement}\label{fine-tuning-as-distributional-movement}

Let \(p_0\) be the pretrained reference model and let \(p_\theta\) be
the fine-tuned model. Fine-tuning changes conditional distributions:

\[
p_0(\cdot\mid c)
\quad \longrightarrow \quad
p_\theta(\cdot\mid c).
\]

If the fine-tuning dataset is small, moving too far from the reference
model can reduce general ability. A common mathematical safeguard is a
KL penalty:

\[
L_{\text{KL-SFT}}(\theta)
=
L_{\text{SFT}}(\theta)
+
\beta
E_c\left[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(
 p_\theta(\cdot\mid c)\;\|\;p_0(\cdot\mid c)
\right)
\right].
\]

The KL divergence is

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)=\sum_{j=1}^d p_j\log\frac{p_j}{q_j}.
\]

The coefficient \(\beta\geq 0\) controls how strongly the fine-tuned
model is discouraged from moving away from the reference model.

\section{18.11 Preference data and reward
models}\label{preference-data-and-reward-models}

Some training data does not specify a single correct response. Instead,
it gives preferences. For a prompt \(x\), suppose humans or another
evaluator prefer response \(y^+\) over response \(y^-\). A common model
assumes there is a scalar reward function

\[
r_\phi(x,y)\in R
\]

and that preference probabilities follow a Bradley--Terry logistic
model:

\[
P_\phi(y^+ \succ y^-\mid x)
=
\sigma\left(r_\phi(x,y^+)-r_\phi(x,y^-)\right),
\]

where

\[
\sigma(a)=\frac{1}{1+\exp(-a)}.
\]

The negative log-likelihood for one preference pair is

\[
\ell_{\text{pref}}(\phi)
=
-
\log \sigma\left(r_\phi(x,y^+)-r_\phi(x,y^-)\right).
\]

This is logistic regression on pairwise differences of rewards.

\section{18.12 KL-regularized policy optimization
viewpoint}\label{kl-regularized-policy-optimization-viewpoint}

A language model can also be viewed as a policy. Given a prompt \(x\),
it samples a response \(Y\) from

\[
Y\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid x).
\]

Suppose a reward model \(r_\phi(x,Y)\) assigns a scalar score. A
KL-regularized objective is

\[
J(\theta)
=
E_{Y\sim p_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}[r_\phi(x,Y)]
-
\beta
D_{\mathrm{KL}}\left(
 p_\theta(\cdot\mid x)\;\|\;p_0(\cdot\mid x)
\right).
\]

The first term encourages high-reward responses. The second term
prevents the model from drifting too far from a reference model. This is
the mathematical core behind many alignment-style training procedures.

The optimization is difficult because the response \(Y\) is a discrete
sequence. Gradient estimates can have high variance. Practical
algorithms introduce approximations, clipping, baselines, and minibatch
estimates. The mathematical principle, however, is the same: maximize
reward while controlling distributional change.

\section{18.13 Direct preference optimization
viewpoint}\label{direct-preference-optimization-viewpoint}

Preference tuning can sometimes be written directly in terms of
log-probabilities rather than explicitly training a separate reward
model. A common form compares the preferred response \(y^+\) and
rejected response \(y^-\) under the current model and a reference model.

Define

\[
\Delta_\theta
=
\log p_\theta(y^+\mid x)-\log p_\theta(y^-\mid x),
\]

and

\[
\Delta_0
=
\log p_0(y^+\mid x)-\log p_0(y^-\mid x).
\]

A direct preference loss has the logistic form

\[
L_{\text{DPO}}(\theta)
=
-
\log \sigma\left(\beta(\Delta_\theta-\Delta_0)\right).
\]

This encourages the updated model to increase the relative
log-probability of the preferred response compared with the reference
model. The reference model acts as a statistical anchor.

\section{18.14 Parameter-efficient
fine-tuning}\label{parameter-efficient-fine-tuning}

Fine-tuning every parameter can be expensive. A parameter-efficient
method freezes most of the pretrained model and trains only a small
number of new parameters.

A simple mathematical model is a low-rank update to a weight matrix.
Suppose a pretrained layer contains

\[
W_0\in R^{m\times n}.
\]

Instead of training all entries of \(W_0\), we train matrices

\[
A\in R^{r\times n},\qquad B\in R^{m\times r},
\]

where \(r\ll \min(m,n)\), and use

\[
W=W_0+BA.
\]

The update \(BA\) has rank at most \(r\). This turns a large update in
\(R^{m\times n}\) into a smaller optimization problem with \(r(m+n)\)
trainable parameters.

\textbf{Linear algebra viewpoint.} Parameter-efficient fine-tuning
restricts the update direction to a low-dimensional subspace or manifold
of the full parameter space.

\section{18.16 Python example: token-level
cross-entropy}\label{python-example-token-level-cross-entropy}

The next examples use small arrays so that every quantity is visible.

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch18-cross-entropy}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{np.set\_printoptions(precision}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, suppress}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits):}
\NormalTok{    logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(logits, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    shifted }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ logits }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ logits.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    exp\_values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(shifted)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ exp\_values }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ exp\_values.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cross\_entropy\_from\_logits(logits, targets):}
\NormalTok{    probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits)}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(targets)}
\NormalTok{    losses }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.log(probs[np.arange(n), targets])}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ losses, losses.mean(), probs}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"learn"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.1}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{targets }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{losses, mean\_loss, probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ cross\_entropy\_from\_logits(logits, targets)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"probabilities:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{, probs)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"token losses:"}\NormalTok{, losses)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"mean loss:"}\NormalTok{, mean\_loss)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"perplexity:"}\NormalTok{, np.exp(mean\_loss))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
probabilities:
 [[0.6439 0.2369 0.0871 0.0321]
 [0.1122 0.5559 0.2761 0.0557]
 [0.053  0.1067 0.6458 0.1945]]
token losses: [0.4402 1.2871 1.6373]
mean loss: 1.1215378808659175

\section{18.17 Python example: gradient with respect to
logits}\label{python-example-gradient-with-respect-to-logits}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch18-logit-gradient}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits)}
\NormalTok{one\_hot }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(probs)}
\NormalTok{one\_hot[np.arange(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(targets)), targets] }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1.0}

\NormalTok{grad\_logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (probs }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ one\_hot) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(targets)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"gradient of mean cross{-}entropy with respect to logits:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{, grad\_logits)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"row sums should be zero:"}\NormalTok{, grad\_logits.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
gradient of mean cross-entropy with respect to logits:
 [[-0.1187  0.079   0.029   0.0107]
 [ 0.0374  0.1853 -0.2413  0.0186]
 [ 0.0177  0.0356  0.2153 -0.2685]]
row sums should be zero: [ 0. -0.  0.]
\end{verbatim}

The row sums are zero because adding the same constant to all logits
does not change the softmax distribution.

\section{18.18 Python example: masked response
loss}\label{python-example-masked-response-loss}

Instruction fine-tuning often uses a loss mask. In the following toy
example, prompt tokens have mask value \(0\) and response tokens have
mask value \(1\).

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch18-masked-loss}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Shape: batch size 2, length 5, vocabulary size 4.}
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{18}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{logits\_batch }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{target\_batch }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{])}

\CommentTok{\# Only response tokens count.}
\NormalTok{loss\_mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{probs\_batch }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(logits\_batch)}
\NormalTok{selected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ probs\_batch[}
\NormalTok{    np.arange(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{)[:, }\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    np.arange(}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{)[}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :],}
\NormalTok{    target\_batch}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{token\_losses }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.log(selected)}
\NormalTok{masked\_mean }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (token\_losses }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ loss\_mask).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ loss\_mask.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"token losses:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{, token\_losses)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"loss mask:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{, loss\_mask)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"masked mean loss:"}\NormalTok{, masked\_mean)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{18.19 Python example: KL penalty between current and reference
models}\label{python-example-kl-penalty-between-current-and-reference-models}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch18-kl-penalty}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ kl\_divergence(p, q):}
\NormalTok{    p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(p, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(q, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(p }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (np.log(p }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.log(q }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)), axis}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{current\_logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{2.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.1}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{reference\_logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.6}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{p\_current }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(current\_logits)}
\NormalTok{p\_reference }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax(reference\_logits)}
\NormalTok{kl\_values }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ kl\_divergence(p\_current, p\_reference)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"current probabilities:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{, p\_current)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"reference probabilities:}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{"}\NormalTok{, p\_reference)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"KL(current || reference):"}\NormalTok{, kl\_values)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"mean KL:"}\NormalTok{, kl\_values.mean())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

current probabilities:
 [[0.6101 0.2741 0.0747 0.041 ]
 [0.0773 0.2567 0.6313 0.0347]]
reference probabilities:
 [[0.4993 0.3029 0.1231 0.0747]
 [0.1258 0.2799 0.51   0.0843]]
KL(current || reference): [0.0331 0.044 ]

\section{18.20 Python example: preference
loss}\label{python-example-preference-loss}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch18-preference-loss}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sigmoid(x):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \FloatTok{1.0} \OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\FloatTok{1.0} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.exp(}\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ preference\_loss(reward\_chosen, reward\_rejected):}
\NormalTok{    margin }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ reward\_chosen }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ reward\_rejected}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.log(sigmoid(margin) }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{reward\_chosen }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{reward\_rejected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{losses }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ preference\_loss(reward\_chosen, reward\_rejected)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"reward margins:"}\NormalTok{, reward\_chosen }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ reward\_rejected)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"preference probabilities:"}\NormalTok{, sigmoid(reward\_chosen }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ reward\_rejected))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"preference losses:"}\NormalTok{, losses)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"mean preference loss:"}\NormalTok{, losses.mean())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
reward margins: [ 1.5 -0.3  1.5  0.2]
preference probabilities: [0.8176 0.4256 0.8176 0.5498]
preference losses: [0.2014 0.8544 0.2014 0.5981]
mean preference loss: 0.46383016745225225
\end{verbatim}

\section{18.21 Python example: low-rank
adaptation}\label{python-example-low-rank-adaptation}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch18-low-rank-adaptation}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{1818}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{m, n, r }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{W0 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(m, n))}
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(r, n))}
\NormalTok{B }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(m, r))}

\NormalTok{Delta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ B }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ A}
\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W0 }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Delta}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"W0 shape:"}\NormalTok{, W0.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"A shape:"}\NormalTok{, A.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"B shape:"}\NormalTok{, B.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"rank of update B A:"}\NormalTok{, np.linalg.matrix\_rank(Delta))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"trainable full matrix parameters:"}\NormalTok{, m }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ n)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"trainable low{-}rank parameters:"}\NormalTok{, r }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (m }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ n))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
