\section{18.22 Interactive: training objective
explorer}\label{interactive-training-objective-explorer}

This interactive shows how three ingredients affect a stylized training
curve: learning rate, batch size, and KL regularization strength. It is
not a physical law of neural-network training; it is a visualization of
the qualitative roles of step size, gradient noise, and distributional
anchoring.

\section{18.23 AI-assisted learning
components}\label{ai-assisted-learning-components-2}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic, not as an authority. The
following prompts are designed for students to check understanding.

\subsection{Prompt 1: identify the
objective}\label{prompt-1-identify-the-objective}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I am studying language model training.  Given a training setup, help me identify the data distribution, model distribution, loss function, mask, and optimization variable.  Do not give code first.  Start with mathematical notation.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Prompt 2: audit a fine-tuning
dataset}\label{prompt-2-audit-a-fine-tuning-dataset}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{I have a prompt{-}response fine{-}tuning dataset.  Help me decide which tokens should be included in the loss mask and explain how the choice changes the statistical objective.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Prompt 3: compare alignment
objectives}\label{prompt-3-compare-alignment-objectives}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Compare supervised fine{-}tuning, reward{-}model training, KL{-}regularized policy optimization, and direct preference optimization.  For each one, state the objective function and the random variables.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\subsection{Prompt 4: detect
overclaiming}\label{prompt-4-detect-overclaiming}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{A student says: "RLHF makes a model truthful."  Critique this statement mathematically.  Discuss what objective is optimized and why optimizing that objective does not automatically prove truthfulness.}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{18.24 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-7}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing pretraining with memorization.} The objective
  estimates conditional token distributions. Memorization may occur, but
  it is not the mathematical objective.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring masks.} The mask determines which tokens are treated
  as labels.
\item
  \textbf{Treating KL divergence as symmetric.} In general,
  \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\neq D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\).
\item
  \textbf{Assuming lower training loss always means better behavior.}
  Fine-tuning may improve one distribution while hurting another.
\item
  \textbf{Equating reward with truth.} A reward model estimates
  preferences or scores, not a theorem about correctness.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting the reference model.} Many preference objectives
  are meaningful only relative to a reference distribution.
\end{enumerate}

\section{18.25 Worked calculation}\label{worked-calculation-2}

Suppose a vocabulary has three tokens and the model assigns
probabilities

\[
p_\theta(\cdot\mid c)=(0.70,0.20,0.10).
\]

If the observed token is token \(2\), the token loss is

\[
\ell=-\log(0.20)\approx 1.609.
\]

If a reference model has

\[
p_0(\cdot\mid c)=(0.60,0.30,0.10),
\]

then

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_0)
=0.70\log\frac{0.70}{0.60}
+0.20\log\frac{0.20}{0.30}
+0.10\log\frac{0.10}{0.10}.
\]

Numerically,

\[
D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p_\theta\|p_0)
\approx 0.70(0.154)-0.20(0.405)+0
\approx 0.027.
\]

With \(\beta=0.5\), the KL-regularized token objective is approximately

\[
1.609+0.5(0.027)=1.6225.
\]

The penalty is small here because the current model is close to the
reference distribution.

\section{18.26 Exercises}\label{exercises-17}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Pretraining objective.} Starting from the autoregressive
  factorization, derive the negative log-likelihood loss for a corpus of
  variable-length sequences.
\item
  \textbf{Softmax gradient.} Prove that \(\nabla_z\ell=p-e_y\) for the
  multiclass cross-entropy loss.
\item
  \textbf{Masking.} Construct a prompt-response example and write a
  binary mask that applies loss only to the response tokens.
\item
  \textbf{KL direction.} Compute both \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(p\|q)\) and
  \(D_{\mathrm{KL}}(q\|p)\) for \(p=(0.8,0.2)\) and \(q=(0.5,0.5)\).
\item
  \textbf{Preference loss.} For rewards \(r^+=1.4\) and \(r^-=0.2\),
  compute the Bradley--Terry preference probability and loss.
\item
  \textbf{Low-rank update.} If \(W_0\in R^{4096\times 4096}\) and rank
  \(r=8\), compare the number of full fine-tuning parameters with the
  number of low-rank update parameters.
\item
  \textbf{Validation gap.} Suppose training loss decreases but
  validation loss increases. Give at least two mathematical
  explanations.
\item
  \textbf{Objective comparison.} Write one paragraph comparing
  supervised fine-tuning and preference tuning as empirical risk
  minimization problems.
\end{enumerate}

\section{18.27 Mini-project}\label{mini-project-3}

Choose a small text dataset and implement a miniature training pipeline.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item

\item
  Construct next-token input-target pairs.
\item
  Train a simple model such as a bigram table, linear classifier, or
  tiny neural model.
\item
  Track training loss and validation loss.
\item

\item

\section{18.29 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-6}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Pretraining is maximum likelihood estimation for next-token
  prediction.
\item
  The token-level loss is multiclass cross-entropy.
\item
  Teacher forcing uses true previous tokens during training.
\item
  Masks define which tokens contribute to the empirical risk.
\item
  Fine-tuning changes a pretrained conditional distribution.
\item
  KL penalties control movement away from a reference model.
\item
  Preference data can be modeled with pairwise logistic losses.
\item
  Alignment-style objectives optimize mathematical proxies for desired
  behavior; they do not automatically prove correctness, truthfulness,
  or safety.
\end{itemize}

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-10}

This chapter connects maximum likelihood estimation, stochastic
optimization, preference learning, and modern language-model training.
Useful background sources include Jurafsky and Martin (2024), Bishop
(2006b), Goodfellow et al. (2016b), Vaswani et al. (2017), {Brown et
al.} (2020), {Ouyang et al.} (2022a), and Rafailov et al. (2023a).

\chapter{Chapter 19. Embeddings, Retrieval, and
RAG}\label{chapter-19.-embeddings-retrieval-and-rag}

Semantic search, nearest neighbors, and retrieval-augmented generation

\hfill\break

\section{19.1 Why retrieval belongs in a mathematical NLP
book}\label{why-retrieval-belongs-in-a-mathematical-nlp-book}

Large language models estimate conditional distributions over tokens. In
an autoregressive model, the central object is

\[
p_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}).
\]

This distribution is learned from training data and depends on the
information contained in the prompt. A model may have learned general
linguistic and statistical patterns, but it may not know the contents of
a new course policy, a recent paper, a private document collection, or a
local advising rule. Retrieval-augmented generation, usually abbreviated
as \textbf{RAG}, addresses this limitation by adding an explicit search
step.

A RAG system separates two mathematical operations:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Retrieval:} given a query \(q\), choose documents or chunks
  \(c_1,\dots,c_k\) from a collection \(C\).
\item
  \textbf{Generation:} produce an answer from a conditional model using
  both the query and the retrieved context.
\end{enumerate}

A simplified RAG model has the form

\[
p_\theta(y \mid q)
\approx
p_\theta(y \mid q, r_k(q)),
\]

where

\[
r_k(q) = (c_{i_1},\dots,c_{i_k})
\]

is the top-\(k\) retrieved context. In a more probabilistic formulation,
the retrieved document is treated as a latent variable:

\[
p(y \mid q)
= \sum_{c \in C} p_\theta(y \mid q,c) p_\eta(c \mid q).
\]

This chapter studies the mathematics behind \(p_\eta(c \mid q)\):
embeddings, similarity functions, nearest-neighbor search, vector
indexes, ranking, and retrieval evaluation. The emphasis is not on
building a production search engine, but on understanding the objects
that make semantic retrieval possible.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Main mathematical theme}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

RAG turns part of language modeling into a problem in finite-dimensional
geometry. Queries and documents are mapped into vectors; retrieval
becomes an optimization problem over a point cloud; generation becomes
conditional modeling with selected external evidence.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{19.2 Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-18}

After studying this chapter, students should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  define a sentence or document embedding as a map into \(R^m\);
\item
  compare sparse lexical retrieval and dense semantic retrieval;
\item
  compute dot-product, cosine, and Euclidean nearest neighbors;
\item
  explain why normalization changes retrieval geometry;
\item
  formulate retrieval as a maximum-score optimization problem;
\item
  understand approximate nearest-neighbor search at a high level;
\item
  explain chunking, indexing, retrieval, reranking, and context
  construction;
\item
  evaluate retrieval using precision, recall, MRR, and nDCG;
\item
  describe failure modes of RAG using probability and geometry.
\end{itemize}

\section{19.3 From word embeddings to document
embeddings}\label{from-word-embeddings-to-document-embeddings}

In Chapter 8 we represented individual words using an embedding map

\[
e: V \to R^m.
\]

For retrieval, we usually need embeddings of longer text units: queries,
sentences, paragraphs, document chunks, or full documents. Let \(T\)
denote the set of all finite token sequences. A text embedding model is
a map

\[
f_\theta: T \to R^m.
\]

For a query \(q \in T\) and a document chunk \(c \in T\), we compute

\[
z_q = f_\theta(q),
\qquad
z_c = f_\theta(c).
\]

The retrieval score is then a function

\[
s(q,c) = S(z_q,z_c),
\]

where \(S:R^m \times R^m \to R\) is a similarity measure. Common choices
are

\[
S_{\text{dot}}(z_q,z_c)=z_q^T z_c,
\]

\[
S_{\text{cos}}(z_q,z_c)=\frac{z_q^T z_c}{\|z_q\|\|z_c\|},
\]

and

\[
S_{\text{neg-dist}}(z_q,z_c)=-\|z_q-z_c\|_2^2.
\]

The top-\(k\) retrieval problem is

\[
\operatorname{TopK}(q)
=
\operatorname{argtopk}_{c \in C} S(f_\theta(q),f_\theta(c)).
\]

This is a finite optimization problem over a collection of vectors.

\section{19.4 Sparse retrieval versus dense
retrieval}\label{sparse-retrieval-versus-dense-retrieval}

Classical information retrieval often represents a document by a sparse
vector. If the vocabulary has size \(d\), then a document \(c\) may be
represented as

\[
x_c \in R^d,
\]

where \(x_{cj}\) is a count or TF-IDF weight for token \(j\). A query
\(q\) is represented similarly by \(x_q\), and the score is often a dot
product or cosine similarity.

Dense retrieval instead represents the same text by

\[
z_c \in R^m,
\]

where \(m\) is usually much smaller than \(d\), and the coordinates are
learned. Dense embeddings are designed so that semantically related
texts can be close even when they do not share exact words.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1875}}
  >{\raggedleft\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.2500}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1875}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1875}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 8\tabcolsep) * \real{0.1875}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Representation
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedleft
Vector dimension
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright

\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot

matching & weak semantic matching \\
Dense embedding & \(m\) & learned features & semantic matching & can
miss exact constraints \\
Hybrid retrieval & both & lexical and semantic & often robust & more
complex \\
\end{longtable}
}

The mathematical difference is important. Sparse retrieval mostly uses
explicit coordinates corresponding to words. Dense retrieval uses an
embedding map learned from data. Thus, dense retrieval transfers part of
the retrieval problem into representation learning.

\section{19.5 Similarity geometry}\label{similarity-geometry}

Suppose all embeddings are nonzero. Define normalized embeddings by

\[
\widehat z = \frac{z}{\|z\|_2}.
\]

For normalized vectors,

\[
\widehat z_q^T \widehat z_c
= \cos(\widehat z_q,\widehat z_c).
\]

Also,

\[
\|\widehat z_q - \widehat z_c\|_2^2
= \|\widehat z_q\|^2 + \|\widehat z_c\|^2 - 2\widehat z_q^T\widehat z_c
= 2 - 2\widehat z_q^T\widehat z_c.
\]

Therefore, for normalized vectors, maximizing cosine similarity is
equivalent to minimizing Euclidean distance:

\[
\operatorname{argmax}_c \widehat z_q^T \widehat z_c
=
\operatorname{argmin}_c \|\widehat z_q-\widehat z_c\|_2.
\]

This is why many vector databases support both inner-product search and
Euclidean nearest-neighbor search. With normalized embeddings, these
objectives are equivalent up to a monotone transformation.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Normalization changes the retrieval problem}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Without normalization, the dot product depends on both direction and
vector length:

\[
z_q^T z_c = \|z_q\|\|z_c\|\cos(z_q,z_c).
\]

Thus, a long vector can score highly because of its norm, not only
because of semantic alignment. Cosine similarity removes this norm
effect.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{19.6 Retrieval as matrix
multiplication}\label{retrieval-as-matrix-multiplication}

Let the collection contain \(n\) chunks \(c_1,\dots,c_n\). Stack their
embeddings as rows of a matrix

\[
Z =
\begin{bmatrix}
- z_{c_1}^T - \\
- z_{c_2}^T - \\
\vdots \\
- z_{c_n}^T -
\end{bmatrix}
\in R^{n \times m}.
\]

For a query embedding \(z_q \in R^m\), dot-product scores are

\[
s = Z z_q \in R^n.
\]

The \(i\)th component is

\[
s_i = z_{c_i}^T z_q.
\]

For cosine retrieval, first normalize each row of \(Z\) and the query
vector:

\[
\widehat Z_i = \frac{z_{c_i}}{\|z_{c_i}\|},
\qquad
\widehat z_q = \frac{z_q}{\|z_q\|}.
\]

Then

\[
s = \widehat Z \widehat z_q.
\]

So dense retrieval is mathematically simple: compute an embedding,
multiply by a matrix, sort the scores.

\section{19.7 A small retrieval
example}\label{a-small-retrieval-example}

Consider six short chunks:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  ``students may transfer graduate credits with approval''
\item
  ``the course covers stochastic processes and Markov chains''
\item
  ``the library has study rooms and research databases''
\item
  ``machine learning uses embeddings and optimization''
\item
  ``applied mathematics students study probability and linear algebra''
\item
  ``transfer credit forms require the program director signature''
\end{enumerate}

A query such as ``How do I transfer credits?'' should retrieve chunks 1
and 6. A query such as ``What math background is needed for machine
learning?'' should retrieve chunks 4 and 5.

A sparse lexical system will rely on words like ``transfer'' and
``credit.'' A dense embedding system may also learn that ``approval,''
``form,'' and ``signature'' are related to administrative transfer
rules. The central question is how well the embedding map preserves the
task-relevant notion of similarity.

\section{19.8 Python: dense retrieval from scratch with toy
embeddings}\label{python-dense-retrieval-from-scratch-with-toy-embeddings}

The following example builds a tiny semantic search engine using
manually designed low-dimensional embeddings. The goal is not to train a
real embedding model; the goal is to make the retrieval geometry
transparent.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\NormalTok{chunks }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"students may transfer graduate credits with approval"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"the course covers stochastic processes and Markov chains"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"the library has study rooms and research databases"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"machine learning uses embeddings and optimization"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"applied mathematics students study probability and linear algebra"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"transfer credit forms require the program director signature"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{]}

\CommentTok{\# Coordinates are interpretable toy semantic features:}
\CommentTok{\# [administration, probability/math, ML/AI, campus resources]}
\NormalTok{toy\_embeddings }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.98}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{queries }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"How do I transfer credits?"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"What math background helps ML?"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.03}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.03}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"Where can I study on campus?"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.02}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.05}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{]),}
\NormalTok{\}}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ normalize\_rows(A):}
\NormalTok{    norms }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(A, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(norms, }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cosine\_search(query\_vec, doc\_matrix, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ normalize\_rows(doc\_matrix)}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ query\_vec }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(query\_vec), }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q}
\NormalTok{    order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(scores)[::}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][:k]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
        \StringTok{"rank"}\NormalTok{: np.arange(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(order) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{),}
        \StringTok{"chunk"}\NormalTok{: [chunks[i] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ order],}
        \StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{: scores[order].}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    \})}

\NormalTok{cosine\_search(queries[}\StringTok{"How do I transfer credits?"}\NormalTok{], toy\_embeddings, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch19-toy-dense-retrieval}
{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& rank & chunk & score \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1 & transfer credit forms require the program dire... & 1.000 \\
1 & 2 & students may transfer graduate credits with ap... & 0.998 \\
2 & 3 & applied mathematics students study probability... & 0.116 \\
\end{longtable}
}

The retrieval score is not a probability. It is a geometric score. Later
we may convert scores to a probability-like distribution using a
softmax, but this adds modeling assumptions.

\section{19.9 Sparse retrieval with
TF-IDF}\label{sparse-retrieval-with-tf-idf}

Dense retrieval is not always better than sparse retrieval. If a query
contains a precise course number, policy phrase, chemical name, theorem
name, or error message, exact lexical matching can be essential.

The following code builds a small TF-IDF retriever without relying on a
specialized library.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ re}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ re.findall(}\VerbatimStringTok{r"}\PreprocessorTok{[a{-}z]}\OperatorTok{+}\VerbatimStringTok{"}\NormalTok{, text.lower())}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(token }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ chunks }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenize(c)))}
\NormalTok{idx }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{w: j }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(chunks), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)))}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, c }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(chunks):}
\NormalTok{    counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(tokenize(c))}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ counts.items():}
\NormalTok{        X[i, idx[w]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ count}

\CommentTok{\# smoothed IDF}
\NormalTok{n\_docs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (X }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{idf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log((}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ n\_docs) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ df)) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{X\_tfidf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ idf}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ vectorize\_query(text):}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}
\NormalTok{    counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(tokenize(text))}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ counts.items():}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ idx:}
\NormalTok{            q[idx[w]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ count}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ idf}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sparse\_search(query, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ vectorize\_query(query)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ normalize\_rows(X\_tfidf)}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(q), }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q}
\NormalTok{    order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(scores)[::}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][:k]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
        \StringTok{"rank"}\NormalTok{: np.arange(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(order) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{),}
        \StringTok{"chunk"}\NormalTok{: [chunks[i] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ order],}
        \StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{: scores[order].}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    \})}

\NormalTok{sparse\_search(}\StringTok{"transfer credit approval form"}\NormalTok{, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch19-tfidf-retrieval}
{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& rank & chunk & score \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 1 & students may transfer graduate credits with ap... & 0.406 \\
1 & 2 & transfer credit forms require the program dire... & 0.383 \\
2 & 3 & applied mathematics students study probability... & 0.000 \\
\end{longtable}
}

TF-IDF can be understood as a diagonal rescaling of a document-term
matrix. If \(X \in R^{n \times d}\) is a count matrix and
\(D \in R^{d \times d}\) is a diagonal matrix of
inverse-document-frequency weights, then the TF-IDF matrix is

\[
X_{\text{tfidf}} = X D.
\]

Retrieval is then performed using row-normalized vectors from
\(X_{\text{tfidf}}\).

\section{19.10 Hybrid retrieval}\label{hybrid-retrieval}

In many applications, sparse and dense retrieval are complementary. One
simple hybrid score is

\[
s_{\text{hybrid}}(q,c)
= \lambda s_{\text{dense}}(q,c)
+ (1-\lambda)s_{\text{sparse}}(q,c),
\qquad 0 \leq \lambda \leq 1.
\]

Here \(\lambda\) controls the tradeoff between semantic matching and
exact-word matching. This formula is simple but useful. It also makes a
conceptual point: retrieval design is often a choice of scoring
function.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ dense\_scores(query\_vec):}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ normalize\_rows(toy\_embeddings)}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ query\_vec }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(query\_vec), }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ sparse\_scores(query\_text):}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ vectorize\_query(query\_text)}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ normalize\_rows(X\_tfidf)}
\NormalTok{    q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ q }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(q), }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ hybrid\_search(query\_text, query\_vec, lam}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    d }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ dense\_scores(query\_vec)}
\NormalTok{    s }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sparse\_scores(query\_text)}
\NormalTok{    score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ lam }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ d }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ lam) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ s}
\NormalTok{    order }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(score)[::}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{][:k]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
        \StringTok{"rank"}\NormalTok{: np.arange(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(order) }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{),}
        \StringTok{"chunk"}\NormalTok{: [chunks[i] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ order],}
        \StringTok{"dense"}\NormalTok{: d[order].}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
        \StringTok{"sparse"}\NormalTok{: s[order].}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
        \StringTok{"hybrid"}\NormalTok{: score[order].}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    \})}

\NormalTok{hybrid\_search(}
    \StringTok{"transfer credit approval form"}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{    queries[}\StringTok{"How do I transfer credits?"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    lam}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{    k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{,}
\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{19.11 Reranking}\label{reranking}

A common retrieval pipeline has two stages:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Retriever:} quickly returns a candidate set \(C_k(q)\).
\item
  \textbf{Reranker:} applies a more expensive scoring function to
  reorder the candidates.
\end{enumerate}

Mathematically, the first stage solves an approximate top-\(k\) problem:

\[
C_k(q) \approx \operatorname{argtopk}_{c \in C} S_1(q,c).
\]

The reranker then solves

\[
\operatorname{argtopr}_{c \in C_k(q)} S_2(q,c),
\qquad r \leq k.
\]

The first score \(S_1\) is usually cheap, such as vector similarity. The
second score \(S_2\) may use a cross-encoder or a larger language model
that jointly reads the query and candidate chunk. This is more expensive
because the representation of the pair \((q,c)\) must be computed
jointly for each candidate.

\section{19.12 Chunking as a mathematical design
choice}\label{chunking-as-a-mathematical-design-choice}

Before indexing a document collection, long documents are usually split
into chunks. Let a document be a sequence

\[
d = (w_1,\dots,w_T).
\]

A chunking function maps \(d\) to shorter subsequences:

\[
g(d) = (c_1,\dots,c_M).
\]

For example, fixed-length chunking with length \(L\) and stride \(s\)
creates chunks

\[
c_j = (w_{1+(j-1)s},\dots,w_{L+(j-1)s}).
\]

Chunking is not merely a technical preprocessing step. It affects
retrieval quality.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  If chunks are too short, they may lack context.
\item
  If chunks are too long, they may contain irrelevant material and waste
  the model context window.
\item
  If chunks overlap too much, the index becomes redundant.
\item
  If chunks do not respect document structure, important definitions or
  assumptions may be separated.
\end{itemize}

In mathematical terms, chunking determines the finite candidate set
\(C\) over which retrieval is performed. A poor candidate set cannot be
fixed completely by a good similarity function.

\section{19.13 RAG as conditional
generation}\label{rag-as-conditional-generation}

A simple RAG pipeline is:

\[
q \xrightarrow{\text{embed}} z_q
\xrightarrow{\text{retrieve}} c_{i_1},\dots,c_{i_k}
\xrightarrow{\text{prompt}} x
\xrightarrow{\text{LM}} y.
\]

The context-augmented prompt may be written as

\[
x = \operatorname{concat}(q,c_{i_1},\dots,c_{i_k},I),
\]

where \(I\) denotes the instruction template. The generator then samples
or chooses

\[
y \sim p_\theta(\cdot \mid x).
\]

This clarifies an important point: retrieval does not force the
generator to be correct. Retrieval changes the conditioning information.
The final answer still depends on the conditional distribution learned
by the language model and on the decoding procedure.

\section{19.14 A probabilistic latent-document
view}\label{a-probabilistic-latent-document-view}

A more formal RAG model treats retrieved documents as latent variables.
Let \(C\) be the collection. Then

\[
p(y \mid q)
= \sum_{c \in C} p_\theta(y \mid q,c) p_\eta(c \mid q).
\]

In practice, summing over all \(c \in C\) is expensive, so we
approximate by the top-\(k\) retrieved chunks:

\[
p(y \mid q)
\approx
\sum_{c \in C_k(q)} p_\theta(y \mid q,c) p_\eta(c \mid q).
\]

If the retriever assigns scores \(s(q,c)\), a soft retrieval
distribution can be defined by

\[
p_\eta(c \mid q)
= \frac{\exp(s(q,c)/\tau)}{\sum_{c' \in C} \exp(s(q,c')/\tau)}.
\]

The temperature \(\tau\) controls concentration. A small \(\tau\)
concentrates probability on the top chunks. A large \(\tau\) spreads
probability across many chunks.

This formulation makes retrieval uncertainty explicit. If several chunks
have similar scores, then the system should be less confident about
which evidence is most relevant.

\section{19.15 Evaluating retrieval}\label{evaluating-retrieval}

Suppose for a query \(q\) we know a set of relevant documents
\(R(q) \subseteq C\). If a retriever returns an ordered list

\[
L_k(q) = (c_{i_1},\dots,c_{i_k}),
\]

then precision at \(k\) is

\[
\operatorname{Precision@}k(q)
= \frac{|L_k(q) \cap R(q)|}{k}.
\]

Recall at \(k\) is

\[
\operatorname{Recall@}k(q)
= \frac{|L_k(q) \cap R(q)|}{|R(q)|}.
\]

The reciprocal rank is

\[
\operatorname{RR}(q)
= \frac{1}{\min\{j:c_{i_j}\in R(q)\}},
\]

if a relevant result appears, and \(0\) otherwise. Mean reciprocal rank
averages this quantity over queries.

For graded relevance labels \(rel_j\), discounted cumulative gain is

\[
\operatorname{DCG@}k
= \sum_{j=1}^k \frac{2^{rel_j}-1}{\log_2(j+1)}.
\]

Normalized DCG divides by the best possible DCG:

\[
\operatorname{nDCG@}k
= \frac{\operatorname{DCG@}k}{\operatorname{IDCG@}k}.
\]

These metrics measure retrieval, not necessarily final answer quality. A
RAG system can retrieve the right document and still generate a poor
answer; it can also retrieve incomplete evidence and produce an answer
that sounds plausible but is unsupported.

\section{19.16 Python: retrieval
metrics}\label{python-retrieval-metrics}

\protect\phantomsection\label{ch19-retrieval-metrics}
\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{retrieved }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"c6"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"c1"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"c4"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"c2"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"c3"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{relevant }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"c1"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"c6"}\NormalTok{\}}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ precision\_at\_k(retrieved, relevant, k):}
\NormalTok{    top }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ retrieved[:k]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(item }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ relevant }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ item }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ top) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ k}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ recall\_at\_k(retrieved, relevant, k):}
\NormalTok{    top }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ retrieved[:k]}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(item }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ relevant }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ item }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ top) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(relevant)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ reciprocal\_rank(retrieved, relevant):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j, item }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(retrieved, start}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ item }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ relevant:}
            \ControlFlowTok{return} \DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ j}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \FloatTok{0.0}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ dcg\_at\_k(relevances, k):}
\NormalTok{    relevances }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(relevances[:k], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    discounts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log2(np.arange(}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, k }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ relevances }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ discounts)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Precision@3:"}\NormalTok{, precision\_at\_k(retrieved, relevant, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Recall@3:"}\NormalTok{, recall\_at\_k(retrieved, relevant, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Reciprocal rank:"}\NormalTok{, reciprocal\_rank(retrieved, relevant))}

\NormalTok{relevance\_scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{ideal\_scores }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(relevance\_scores, reverse}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{ndcg3 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ dcg\_at\_k(relevance\_scores, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ dcg\_at\_k(ideal\_scores, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"nDCG@3:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(ndcg3, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
Precision@3: 0.6666666666666666
Recall@3: 1.0
Reciprocal rank: 1.0
nDCG@3: 1.0
\end{verbatim}

\section{19.17 Approximate nearest-neighbor
search}\label{approximate-nearest-neighbor-search}

Exact retrieval by matrix multiplication requires computing \(Zz_q\)
over all \(n\) stored vectors. This costs \(O(nm)\) per query. For small
\(n\), this is fine. For millions or billions of chunks, exact search
may be too expensive.

Approximate nearest-neighbor methods build an index that returns a
candidate set quickly. The mathematical tradeoff is between:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{speed:} how fast queries are answered;
\item
  \textbf{memory:} how large the index is;
\item
  \textbf{recall:} how often the true nearest neighbors are returned;
\item
  \textbf{update cost:} how hard it is to add or remove vectors.
\end{itemize}

At a high level, many methods use one of the following ideas.

\subsection{Partitioning}\label{partitioning}

Partition the vector space into regions. Search only regions near the
query. This reduces the number of candidate vectors.

\subsection{Graph search}\label{graph-search}

Build a graph whose vertices are stored vectors and whose edges connect
nearby vectors. Starting from an entry point, greedily move through the
graph toward vectors closer to the query.

\subsection{Quantization}\label{quantization}

Approximate vectors by compressed codes. Search is faster and uses less
memory, but distances are approximate.

For this book, the key point is that vector indexing is an algorithmic
approximation to the mathematical top-\(k\) problem.

\section{19.18 Worked calculation: cosine
retrieval}\label{worked-calculation-cosine-retrieval}

Suppose a query and three chunk embeddings are

\[
z_q = (1,1),
\qquad
z_1=(2,2),
\qquad
z_2=(2,0),
\qquad
z_3=(0,3).
\]

Dot-product scores are

\[
z_1^Tz_q=4,
\qquad
z_2^Tz_q=2,
\qquad
z_3^Tz_q=3.
\]

Thus dot-product retrieval ranks \(z_1,z_3,z_2\). Cosine scores are

\[
\cos(z_q,z_1)=1,
\]

\[
\cos(z_q,z_2)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2}\cdot 2}=\frac{1}{\sqrt 2},
\]

\[
\cos(z_q,z_3)=\frac{3}{\sqrt{2}\cdot 3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}.
\]

Under cosine similarity, \(z_2\) and \(z_3\) tie. The difference occurs
because dot product rewards the longer norm of \(z_3\).

\section{19.19 Interactive: dense retrieval and hybrid
scoring}\label{interactive-dense-retrieval-and-hybrid-scoring}

The interactive below uses a two-dimensional toy embedding space. Each
point is a document chunk. The query direction can be changed, and the
slider \(\lambda\) blends dense semantic score with sparse lexical
score:

\[
s_{\text{hybrid}} = \lambda s_{\text{dense}} + (1-\lambda)s_{\text{sparse}}.
\]

\section{19.21 Error modes in RAG}\label{error-modes-in-rag}

RAG systems can fail for mathematically distinct reasons.

\subsection{Retrieval failure}\label{retrieval-failure}

The relevant chunk is not retrieved:

\[
R(q) \cap L_k(q) = \varnothing.
\]

This may happen because the embedding model fails to place the query
near the right document, because the relevant document was not indexed,
or because the chunking strategy split the answer from its context.

\subsection{Ranking failure}\label{ranking-failure}

A relevant chunk is retrieved, but ranked too low to be included in the
final context. This is a recall and ranking problem.

\subsection{Context overload}\label{context-overload}

Too many chunks are provided. The answer-relevant evidence may be
present, but the generator may attend to the wrong material or combine
incompatible chunks.

\subsection{Generation failure}\label{generation-failure}

The correct evidence is present, but the language model misreads it,
ignores it, or produces unsupported text.

\subsection{Citation failure}\label{citation-failure}

The answer may be mostly correct but cite the wrong chunk. This is a
mismatch between answer generation and evidence attribution.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{A useful diagnostic separation}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

When debugging a RAG system, separate three questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Did retrieval find the right evidence?
\item
  Did the prompt place the evidence in a usable form?
\item
  Did the generator faithfully use the evidence?
\end{enumerate}

These are different mathematical and engineering problems.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{19.22 RAG for academic advising and course
resources}\label{rag-for-academic-advising-and-course-resources}

A university resource chatbot is a natural RAG application. The document
collection may include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  program requirements;
\item
  course descriptions;
\item
  transfer-credit policies;
\item
  advising FAQs;
\item
  academic calendar pages;
\item
  graduate catalog entries;
\item
  official forms and procedures.
\end{itemize}

For such a system, mathematical care matters. The answer should be
grounded in retrieved official sources, and the system should
communicate uncertainty when retrieval is weak.

A minimal retrieval-aware answer generator should keep track of:

\[
\text{query},\quad
\text{retrieved chunks},\quad
\text{similarity scores},\quad
\text{source metadata},\quad
\text{answer}.
\]

The source metadata are essential. Without them, the system may generate
fluent but unverifiable responses.

\section{19.23 AI-assisted learning
activities}\label{ai-assisted-learning-activities-3}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic, not only as a code
generator.

\subsection{Activity 1: explain the scoring
geometry}\label{activity-1-explain-the-scoring-geometry}

Ask an AI assistant:

\begin{quote}
In dense retrieval, explain the difference between dot-product
similarity and cosine similarity. Give a two-dimensional example where
they rank documents differently.
\end{quote}

Then verify the example by hand.

\subsection{Activity 2: audit a RAG
pipeline}\label{activity-2-audit-a-rag-pipeline}

Give the assistant a proposed RAG design and ask:

\begin{quote}
Identify possible retrieval failure modes, ranking failure modes, and
generation failure modes. For each one, suggest a quantitative
diagnostic.
\end{quote}

Check whether the suggested metrics actually correspond to the failure
modes.

\subsection{Activity 3: create adversarial
queries}\label{activity-3-create-adversarial-queries}

Ask the assistant to produce queries that are likely to confuse a
retriever:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  queries with synonyms;
\item
  queries with exact codes or course numbers;
\item
  queries requiring negation;
\item
  queries requiring date-sensitive information;
\item
  queries requiring multiple documents.
\end{itemize}

Then test whether dense, sparse, or hybrid retrieval handles each case
better.

\section{19.24 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-8}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Treating similarity scores as probabilities.} A cosine score
  is not automatically a calibrated probability of relevance.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring chunking.} Retrieval quality depends on the candidate
  units.
\item
  \textbf{Using only dense retrieval.} Exact keywords, identifiers, and
  policy names often require lexical matching.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming retrieved means true.} Retrieved text may be
  outdated, irrelevant, or misinterpreted.
\item
  \textbf{Evaluating only final answers.} Retrieval metrics and
  generation metrics should be separated.
\item
  \textbf{Overloading the context window.} More retrieved text is not
  always better.
\end{enumerate}

\section{19.25 Exercises}\label{exercises-18}

\subsection{Exercise 1: normalized dot
product}\label{exercise-1-normalized-dot-product}

Prove that for unit vectors \(u\) and \(v\),

\[
\|u-v\|_2^2 = 2 - 2u^Tv.
\]

Explain why nearest-neighbor search by Euclidean distance is equivalent
to maximum cosine similarity on the unit sphere.

\subsection{Exercise 2: hybrid score}\label{exercise-2-hybrid-score}

Suppose two chunks have scores

\[
(s_{\text{dense}},s_{\text{sparse}})_1=(0.9,0.1),
\]

and

\[
(s_{\text{dense}},s_{\text{sparse}})_2=(0.6,0.8).
\]

For which values of \(\lambda\) does chunk 1 rank above chunk 2 under

\[
s_{\text{hybrid}}=\lambda s_{\text{dense}}+(1-\lambda)s_{\text{sparse}}?
\]

\subsection{Exercise 3: retrieval
metrics}\label{exercise-3-retrieval-metrics}

For a query, the returned list is

\[
(c_3,c_5,c_1,c_2,c_4),
\]

and the relevant set is

\[
\{c_1,c_4,c_6\}.
\]

Compute Precision@3, Recall@3, and reciprocal rank.

\subsection{Exercise 4: chunking
design}\label{exercise-4-chunking-design}

Consider a 4000-token document. You use chunk length \(L=500\) and
stride \(s=250\). How many chunks are produced if every chunk must fit
inside the document? What changes if the last partial chunk is kept?

\subsection{Exercise 5: latent-document
RAG}\label{exercise-5-latent-document-rag}

Starting from

\[
p(y \mid q)=\sum_{c \in C}p_\theta(y\mid q,c)p_\eta(c\mid q),
\]

explain why top-\(k\) truncation can introduce bias. When might the
approximation be reasonable?

\section{19.26 Mini-project: build a small mathematical RAG
retriever}\label{mini-project-build-a-small-mathematical-rag-retriever}

Build a small retriever for a collection of course or program documents.

Minimum requirements:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Split documents into chunks.
\item
  Implement sparse TF-IDF retrieval.
\item
  Implement dense retrieval using either a toy embedding, a pretrained
  sentence embedding model, or an API embedding model.
\item
  Implement hybrid scoring.
\item
  Create at least 10 test queries with known relevant chunks.
\item
  Report Precision@3, Recall@3, and MRR.
\item
  Analyze at least three failure cases.
\end{enumerate}

A strong project should also include reranking, source metadata, and a
short discussion of how retrieval affects generated answers.

\section{19.27 Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-8}

The companion lab for this chapter should guide students through:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  constructing a document collection;
\item
  chunking text;
\item
  building TF-IDF vectors;
\item
  building dense vectors;
\item
  comparing cosine and dot-product retrieval;
\item
  implementing hybrid search;
\item
  computing retrieval metrics;
\item
  connecting retrieved chunks to a simple answer-generation prompt.
\end{itemize}

The lab should emphasize that RAG is not magic. It is a pipeline made of
mathematical components: representation maps, similarity functions,
ranking rules, and conditional generation.

\section{19.28 Summary}\label{summary-3}

Retrieval-augmented generation combines language modeling with search.
The retrieval part is fundamentally geometric: map queries and chunks to
vectors, compute similarities, and return top-ranked evidence. The
generation part is probabilistic: condition a language model on the
query and retrieved context.

The main mathematical objects in this chapter were:

\[
f_\theta:T \to R^m,
\]

\[
S(z_q,z_c),
\]

\[
\operatorname{TopK}(q)=\operatorname{argtopk}_{c\in C}S(f_\theta(q),f_\theta(c)),
\]

and

\[
p(y\mid q)\approx p_\theta(y\mid q,r_k(q)).
\]

Understanding these objects helps us design better retrieval systems,
evaluate them separately from generation, and diagnose failure modes in
applied NLP systems.

\section{19.29 Further reading}\label{further-reading}

The original retrieval-augmented generation framework is due to Lewis et
al. ({Lewis et al.} 2020). For approximate nearest-neighbor search and
vector indexing, see Johnson, Douze, and Jegou (Johnson et al. 2019).
For background on vector space models and embeddings, see earlier
chapters and the references on latent semantic analysis, Word2Vec,
GloVe, and Transformers.

\chapter{Chapter 20. Evaluation of Language
Models}\label{chapter-20.-evaluation-of-language-models}

Metrics, Uncertainty, Calibration, and Responsible Measurement

\hfill\break

\chapter{Chapter 20. Evaluation of Language
Models}\label{chapter-20.-evaluation-of-language-models-1}

Evaluation is the mathematical discipline of asking whether a language
system is doing what we want it to do. For a small classifier,
evaluation may mean accuracy on a labeled test set. For a language
model, evaluation may mean perplexity on held-out text. For a
summarizer, evaluation may compare generated summaries with reference
summaries. For a retrieval-augmented generation system, evaluation must
include both retrieval quality and answer quality. For a deployed
assistant, evaluation must also consider calibration, robustness,
factuality, bias, latency, privacy, and human usefulness.

The purpose of this chapter is not to collect many disconnected scores.
The goal is to show that most evaluation methods have a common
statistical structure:

\[
\text{model} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{predictions} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{loss or score} \quad \longrightarrow \quad \text{statistical estimate}.
\]

For MA Applied Mathematics and MS Statistics students, this chapter
should feel familiar. Evaluation is estimation. A reported score is
usually a sample average, a ratio of random counts, or a function of
empirical distributions. Therefore, every evaluation score has
assumptions, variance, failure modes, and a domain of validity.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Guiding principle}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A metric is not a property of a model alone. It is a property of a
model, a data distribution, a task definition, an annotation procedure,
and a scoring rule.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{20.1 Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-19}

After studying this chapter, you should be able to:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  express NLP evaluation as estimation of expected loss or expected
  utility;
\item
  compute accuracy, precision, recall, \(F_1\), and confusion matrices
  from first principles;
\item
  derive cross-entropy and perplexity for language models;
\item
  explain calibration, Brier score, and expected calibration error;
\item
  distinguish token-level, sequence-level, retrieval-level, and
  human-centered evaluation;
\item
  implement overlap-based metrics such as ROUGE-style recall and
  BLEU-style precision;
\item
  evaluate retrieval and RAG pipelines using Precision@\(k\),
  Recall@\(k\), MRR, and nDCG;
\item
  quantify uncertainty in evaluation using standard errors and bootstrap
  confidence intervals;
\item
  critique metric choice using mathematical reasoning.
\end{enumerate}

\section{20.2 The mathematical form of
evaluation}\label{the-mathematical-form-of-evaluation}

Let \((X,Y)\) be a random input-output pair drawn from an unknown
population distribution \(P\). A model \(f_\theta\) maps an input \(x\)
to either a prediction, a score vector, a probability distribution, or a
generated sequence. A loss function compares the model output to the
target:

\[
L(f_\theta(X),Y).
\]

The population risk is

\[
R(\theta) = E_P[L(f_\theta(X),Y)].
\]

Since \(P\) is unknown, we estimate risk from a test set

\[
D_{\text{test}} = \{(x_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n.
\]

The empirical risk is

\[
\widehat R(\theta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n L(f_\theta(x_i),y_i).
\]

This formula is the mathematical backbone of evaluation. Different NLP
tasks use different forms of \(X\), \(Y\), \(f_\theta\), and \(L\).

The important statistical question is:

\[
\widehat R(\theta) \approx R(\theta)?
\]

This approximation depends on sample size, test-set quality,
distribution shift, and whether the metric faithfully measures the
desired behavior.

\section{20.3 Data splits and the danger of
leakage}\label{data-splits-and-the-danger-of-leakage}

A standard supervised workflow uses three data sets:

\[
D_{\text{train}}, \qquad D_{\text{validation}}, \qquad D_{\text{test}}.
\]

The training set is used to fit parameters. The validation set is used
to choose hyperparameters, thresholds, prompts, decoding strategies,
retrieval settings, and checkpoints. The test set is used only once for
final evaluation.

If decisions are repeatedly made using the test set, then the test score
becomes optimistically biased. This is a form of selection bias. For
example, suppose we try many models \(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_m\) and
report the best test score. Even if all models have the same population
risk, the minimum empirical risk

\[
\min_{1 \le j \le m} \widehat R(\theta_j)
\]

will usually be smaller than the true risk of the selected model.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Test-set leakage}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A test set is not a data bank for repeated design decisions. It is an
estimator of future performance. Once it guides design choices, it
starts functioning like a validation set.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{20.4 Classification metrics}\label{classification-metrics}

Consider a classification task with classes \(\{1,\ldots,K\}\). Let
\(y_i\) be the true class and \(\hat y_i\) be the predicted class. The
accuracy is

\[
\operatorname{Accuracy}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \mathbf 1\{\hat y_i=y_i\}.
\]

Accuracy is simple and useful when classes are balanced and errors have
similar cost. However, for imbalanced tasks, accuracy can be misleading.
A classifier that always predicts the majority class may have high
accuracy but low usefulness.

\subsection{Binary confusion matrix}\label{binary-confusion-matrix}

For binary classification, let the positive class be \(1\) and the
negative class be \(0\). The confusion counts are:

\[
TP = \sum_i \mathbf 1\{y_i=1,\hat y_i=1\},
\]

\[
FP = \sum_i \mathbf 1\{y_i=0,\hat y_i=1\},
\]

\[
FN = \sum_i \mathbf 1\{y_i=1,\hat y_i=0\},
\]

\[
TN = \sum_i \mathbf 1\{y_i=0,\hat y_i=0\}.
\]

Precision measures how reliable positive predictions are:

\[
\operatorname{Precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP}.
\]

Recall measures how many true positives are found:

\[
\operatorname{Recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.
\]

The \(F_1\) score is the harmonic mean:

\[
F_1 = \frac{2\cdot \operatorname{Precision}\cdot \operatorname{Recall}}{\operatorname{Precision}+\operatorname{Recall}}.
\]

The harmonic mean is small if either precision or recall is small. Thus
\(F_1\) rewards balance.

\subsection{Thresholds and decision
rules}\label{thresholds-and-decision-rules}

Many classifiers output a score \(s(x)\) or probability estimate
\(p_\theta(y=1\mid x)\). A threshold \(\tau\) produces a hard
prediction:

\[
\hat y_\tau(x)=\mathbf 1\{p_\theta(y=1\mid x)\ge \tau\}.
\]

Changing \(\tau\) changes \(TP\), \(FP\), \(FN\), and \(TN\). Therefore
precision, recall, and \(F_1\) are not properties of the probability
model alone. They are properties of the probability model plus the
threshold.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Mathematical viewpoint}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A threshold is a decision rule. The same probabilistic model can produce
many classifiers depending on how probabilities are converted into
actions.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{20.5 Python example: classification metrics from
scratch}\label{python-example-classification-metrics-from-scratch}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\CommentTok{\# A small binary text{-}classification evaluation example.}
\NormalTok{y\_true }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{p\_score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{0.92}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.62}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.55}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.48}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.40}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.36}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.22}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ binary\_metrics(y\_true, p\_score, threshold}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    y\_pred }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (p\_score }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ threshold).astype(}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    tp }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{    fp }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{    fn }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{    tn }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{    accuracy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ tn) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(y\_true)}
\NormalTok{    precision }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{    recall }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{    f1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ precision }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ recall }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (precision }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ recall) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ precision }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ recall }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ \{}
        \StringTok{"threshold"}\NormalTok{: threshold,}
        \StringTok{"TP"}\NormalTok{: tp,}
        \StringTok{"FP"}\NormalTok{: fp,}
        \StringTok{"FN"}\NormalTok{: fn,}
        \StringTok{"TN"}\NormalTok{: tn,}
        \StringTok{"accuracy"}\NormalTok{: accuracy,}
        \StringTok{"precision"}\NormalTok{: precision,}
        \StringTok{"recall"}\NormalTok{: recall,}
        \StringTok{"f1"}\NormalTok{: f1,}
\NormalTok{    \}}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tau }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.7}\NormalTok{]:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(binary\_metrics(y\_true, p\_score, tau))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
{'threshold': 0.3, 'TP': 4, 'FP': 4, 'FN': 1, 'TN': 1, 'accuracy': 0.5, 'precision': 0.5, 'recall': 0.8, 'f1': 0.6153846153846154}
{'threshold': 0.5, 'TP': 3, 'FP': 1, 'FN': 2, 'TN': 4, 'accuracy': 0.7, 'precision': 0.75, 'recall': 0.6, 'f1': 0.6666666666666665}
{'threshold': 0.7, 'TP': 2, 'FP': 0, 'FN': 3, 'TN': 5, 'accuracy': 0.7, 'precision': 1.0, 'recall': 0.4, 'f1': 0.5714285714285715}
\end{verbatim}

\section{20.6 Macro, micro, and weighted
averaging}\label{macro-micro-and-weighted-averaging}

For multiclass classification, we can compute precision, recall, and
\(F_1\) separately for each class. For class \(c\), treat \(c\) as
positive and all other classes as negative. This gives \(F_{1,c}\).

Macro averaging gives equal weight to each class:

\[
F_{1,\text{macro}} = \frac{1}{K}\sum_{c=1}^K F_{1,c}.
\]

Weighted averaging weights each class by its support \(n_c\):

\[
F_{1,\text{weighted}} = \sum_{c=1}^K \frac{n_c}{n}F_{1,c}.
\]

Micro averaging pools all true positives, false positives, and false
negatives across classes before computing the score. For single-label
multiclass classification, micro \(F_1\) equals accuracy.

The choice matters. Macro \(F_1\) emphasizes minority classes. Weighted
\(F_1\) is closer to the empirical class distribution. Micro metrics
emphasize overall instance-level performance.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y\_true\_mc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"stats"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"stats"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cs"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cs"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"stats"}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{y\_pred\_mc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"stats"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"stats"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"stats"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"math"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cs"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"cs"}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{classes }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(y\_true\_mc) }\OperatorTok{|} \BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(y\_pred\_mc))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ per\_class\_f1(y\_true, y\_pred, classes):}
\NormalTok{    rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ c }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ classes:}
\NormalTok{        tp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ c) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ c))}
\NormalTok{        fp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ c) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ c))}
\NormalTok{        fn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{((y\_true }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ c) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y\_pred }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ c))}
\NormalTok{        precision }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{        recall }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{        f1 }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ precision }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ recall }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (precision }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ recall) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ precision }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ recall }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}
\NormalTok{        support }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(y\_true }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ c))}
\NormalTok{        rows.append((c, support, precision, recall, f1))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ rows}

\NormalTok{rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ per\_class\_f1(y\_true\_mc, y\_pred\_mc, classes)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ row }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ rows:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(row)}

\NormalTok{macro\_f1 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean([row[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ row }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ rows])}
\NormalTok{weighted\_f1 }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(row[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ row[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ row }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ rows) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(y\_true\_mc)}
\NormalTok{accuracy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean(y\_true\_mc }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ y\_pred\_mc)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"macro F1:"}\NormalTok{, macro\_f1)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"weighted F1:"}\NormalTok{, weighted\_f1)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"accuracy:"}\NormalTok{, accuracy)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
('cs', 2, 0.5, 0.5, 0.5)
('math', 3, 0.6666666666666666, 0.6666666666666666, 0.6666666666666666)
('stats', 3, 0.6666666666666666, 0.6666666666666666, 0.6666666666666666)
macro F1: 0.611111111111111
weighted F1: 0.625
accuracy: 0.625
\end{verbatim}

\section{20.7 Language-model evaluation: cross-entropy and
perplexity}\label{language-model-evaluation-cross-entropy-and-perplexity}

For a language model, the target is usually the next token. Given a
sequence \(w_{1:T}\), an autoregressive model assigns

\[
p_\theta(w_{1:T}) = \prod_{t=1}^T p_\theta(w_t \mid w_{<t}).
\]

The average negative log-likelihood per token is

\[
\widehat H = -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^N \log p_\theta(w_i \mid \text{context}_i),
\]

where \(N\) is the number of evaluated target tokens. This quantity is
also called empirical cross-entropy when the tokens are sampled from a
data distribution.

Perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{PPL} = \exp(\widehat H)
\]

when natural logarithms are used. If logarithms base \(2\) are used,
then

\[
\operatorname{PPL}=2^{\widehat H_2}.
\]

Perplexity can be interpreted as an effective average branching factor.
A lower perplexity means the model assigns higher probability to the
observed next tokens.

\subsection{Important limitations of
perplexity}\label{important-limitations-of-perplexity}

Perplexity is useful for comparing models under the same tokenizer and
evaluation distribution. However, it can be misleading across
tokenizers. A model using shorter subword units may have a different
number of tokens than a model using longer tokens. Per-token perplexity
is therefore not automatically comparable across tokenization schemes.

Also, low perplexity does not guarantee usefulness, factuality, safety,
or reasoning quality. A model may predict common text well but fail on
specialized mathematical or institutional questions.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Token{-}level negative log{-}likelihood and perplexity.}
\CommentTok{\# Rows are time steps; columns are vocabulary items.}
\NormalTok{logits }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.2}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\FloatTok{1.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{targets }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ log\_softmax(z):}
\NormalTok{    z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(z, axis}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.log(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(np.exp(z), axis}\OperatorTok{={-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{log\_probs }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ log\_softmax(logits)}
\NormalTok{nll }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{log\_probs[np.arange(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(targets)), targets]}
\NormalTok{mean\_nll }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean(nll)}
\NormalTok{perplexity }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(mean\_nll)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"token NLL values:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(nll, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"mean NLL:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(mean\_nll, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"perplexity:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(perplexity, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
token NLL values: [0.4076 0.3254 0.2529 1.2152]
mean NLL: 0.5503
perplexity: 1.7337
\end{verbatim}

\section{20.8 Calibration and probabilistic
honesty}\label{calibration-and-probabilistic-honesty}

Accuracy measures whether predictions are correct. Calibration measures
whether predicted probabilities mean what they say.

A binary classifier is calibrated if

\[
P(Y=1 \mid \hat p(X)=q)=q
\]

for all probability values \(q\). In practice, probabilities are binned.
For bin \(B_m\), define

\[
\operatorname{conf}(B_m)=\frac{1}{|B_m|}\sum_{i\in B_m}\hat p_i,
\]

and

\[
\operatorname{acc}(B_m)=\frac{1}{|B_m|}\sum_{i\in B_m}y_i.
\]

The expected calibration error is approximated by

\[
\operatorname{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{n}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_m)-\operatorname{conf}(B_m)\right|.
\]

A related proper scoring rule is the Brier score:

\[
\operatorname{Brier}=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (\hat p_i-y_i)^2.
\]

A proper scoring rule rewards honest probability estimates.
Cross-entropy and Brier score are both proper scoring rules for
probabilistic prediction.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.88}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.82}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.76}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.69}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.55}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.52}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.45}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.37}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.28}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.21}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.08}\NormalTok{])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ calibration\_table(y, p, bins}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linspace(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, bins }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{    ece }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(bins):}
\NormalTok{        lo, hi }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ edges[j], edges[j }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ j }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ bins }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (p }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ lo) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (p }\OperatorTok{\textless{}=}\NormalTok{ hi)}
        \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (p }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ lo) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (p }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ hi)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(mask) }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{continue}
\NormalTok{        conf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean(p[mask])}
\NormalTok{        acc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean(y[mask])}
\NormalTok{        weight }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean(mask)}
\NormalTok{        ece }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ weight }\OperatorTok{*} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(acc }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ conf)}
\NormalTok{        rows.append((lo, hi, }\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(np.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(mask)), conf, acc))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ rows, ece}

\NormalTok{rows, ece }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ calibration\_table(y, p, bins}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ row }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ rows:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(row)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"ECE:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(ece, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"Brier:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(np.mean((p }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ y) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{), }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
(0.0, 0.25, 2, 0.145, 0.5)
(0.25, 0.5, 3, 0.3666666666666667, 0.3333333333333333)
(0.5, 0.75, 3, 0.5866666666666667, 0.3333333333333333)
(0.75, 1.0, 4, 0.8525, 0.75)
ECE: 0.165
Brier: 0.2654
\end{verbatim}

\section{20.9 Interactive: threshold, precision, recall, and
calibration}\label{interactive-threshold-precision-recall-and-calibration}

The following interactive example shows how a single set of probability
scores can lead to different classification metrics as the decision
threshold changes. It also shows how temperature scaling changes
probabilistic confidence.

\section{20.10 Overlap metrics for generated
text}\label{overlap-metrics-for-generated-text}

Generated text is difficult to evaluate because there may be many
correct answers. For example, two summaries can be semantically similar
while sharing few exact words. Nevertheless, overlap metrics remain
useful as quick baselines.

Let \(G\) be a generated sequence and \(R\) be a reference sequence. For
a token \(n\)-gram \(g\), let \(c_G(g)\) and \(c_R(g)\) be its counts. A
clipped precision score is

\[
P_n = \frac{\sum_g \min\{c_G(g),c_R(g)\}}{\sum_g c_G(g)}.
\]

BLEU-style evaluation combines clipped \(n\)-gram precisions with a
brevity penalty. A simplified version is

\[
\operatorname{BLEU}_N = BP \cdot \exp\left(\frac{1}{N}\sum_{n=1}^N \log P_n\right),
\]

where

\[
BP = \begin{cases}
1, & |G| > |R|,\\
\exp(1-|R|/|G|), & |G| \le |R|.
\end{cases}
\]

ROUGE-style evaluation often emphasizes recall. For unigrams, a simple
ROUGE-1 recall score is

\[
\operatorname{ROUGE\text{-}1\ recall} = \frac{\sum_g \min\{c_G(g),c_R(g)\}}{\sum_g c_R(g)}.
\]

The conceptual difference is important:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  BLEU-style precision asks: how much of the generated text is supported
  by the reference?
\item
  ROUGE-style recall asks: how much of the reference was covered by the
  generated text?
\end{itemize}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ math}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize\_simple(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ text.lower().replace(}\StringTok{"."}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{""}\NormalTok{).replace(}\StringTok{","}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{""}\NormalTok{).split()}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ ngrams(tokens, n):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ [}\BuiltInTok{tuple}\NormalTok{(tokens[i:i}\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{n]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(tokens) }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ n }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ clipped\_precision(generated, reference, n):}
\NormalTok{    g\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(ngrams(generated, n))}
\NormalTok{    r\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(ngrams(reference, n))}
\NormalTok{    overlap }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(count, r\_counts[gram]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ gram, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ g\_counts.items())}
\NormalTok{    total }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(g\_counts.values())}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ overlap }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ total }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ total }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ rouge1\_recall(generated, reference):}
\NormalTok{    g\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(generated)}
\NormalTok{    r\_counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(reference)}
\NormalTok{    overlap }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(g\_counts[token], count) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ r\_counts.items())}
\NormalTok{    total }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(r\_counts.values())}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ overlap }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ total }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ total }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else} \FloatTok{0.0}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ bleu\_like(generated, reference, max\_n}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, eps}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{):}
