\section{21.27 Summary}\label{summary-5}

Information theory gives a common mathematical vocabulary for many parts
of NLP. Entropy measures uncertainty, cross-entropy measures predictive
loss, KL divergence measures distributional mismatch, and mutual
information measures statistical dependence. Perplexity is the
exponential form of average cross-entropy and is central to
language-model evaluation. PMI connects co-occurrence statistics with
word embeddings. KL regularization connects information theory with
fine-tuning and alignment.

The most important lesson is that information-theoretic quantities are
always defined relative to random variables and probability
distributions. Before computing entropy, perplexity, or mutual
information, first identify the tokenization, the sample space, the data
distribution, and the model distribution.

\section{Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-11}

Classical information theory begins with Shannon (1948) and is developed
systematically in Cover and Thomas (2006). For statistical NLP
connections, see Manning and Schuetze (1999) and Jurafsky and Martin
(2024). For neural language modeling and cross-entropy training, see
Bengio et al. (2003), Goodfellow et al. (2016b), and Vaswani et al.
(2017).

\chapter{Optimization for NLP}\label{optimization-for-nlp}

Gradients, stochasticity, and large-scale training

\hfill\break

Modern NLP models are trained by solving very large optimization
problems. The model may be a linear classifier, a recurrent network, a
Transformer, or a retrieval-augmented system with trainable components,
but the mathematical core is the same: choose parameters, define a loss,
estimate a gradient from data, and update the parameters. This chapter
develops optimization for NLP from a clean mathematical point of view.

\section{22.1 Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-21}

After reading this chapter, students should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  formulate NLP training as empirical risk minimization;
\item
  derive gradients for softmax cross-entropy losses;
\item
  distinguish full-batch gradients from stochastic mini-batch gradients;
\item
  explain how SGD, momentum, RMSProp, Adam, and AdamW update parameters;
\item
  interpret learning rate, batch size, gradient noise, clipping, and
  regularization mathematically;
\item
  understand why optimization in neural NLP is nonconvex but still
  useful in practice;
\item
  implement small optimization algorithms from scratch in Python;
\item
  use AI tools to audit an optimization setup without treating them as
  black boxes.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Guiding question}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

When an NLP model improves during training, what mathematical object is
changing?

The answer is not simply ``the model learns language.'' More precisely,
the parameter vector \(\theta\) changes so that a loss function, usually
an empirical estimate of an expected negative log-likelihood, becomes
smaller on the training distribution.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{22.2 The optimization problem behind
NLP}\label{the-optimization-problem-behind-nlp}

Let \(z\) denote an NLP input. Depending on the task, \(z\) may be a
token, a document, a sentence pair, a prompt, or a sequence prefix. Let
\(y\) denote the target. A model with parameters \(\theta \in R^p\)
defines either a prediction function

\[
f_\theta(z)
\]

or a conditional probability distribution

\[
p_\theta(y \mid z).
\]

A loss function measures the cost of a prediction. In supervised text
classification, a common loss is

\[
\ell(\theta;z,y) = -\log p_\theta(y\mid z).
\]

Given training data

\[
D_n = \{(z_i,y_i)\}_{i=1}^n,
\]

the empirical risk is

\[
L_n(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(\theta;z_i,y_i).
\]

Training means solving, approximately,

\[
\hat \theta \in \arg\min_{\theta \in R^p} L_n(\theta).
\]

The population risk is

\[
L(\theta)=E_{(Z,Y)\sim P}\left[\ell(\theta;Z,Y)\right],
\]

where \(P\) is the data-generating distribution. Since \(P\) is unknown,
the empirical risk \(L_n\) is used as an estimate.

\textbf{Optimization viewpoint.} NLP training is the numerical problem
of minimizing \(L_n(\theta)\), but statistical learning is about whether
small \(L_n(\theta)\) also implies small \(L(\theta)\).

\section{22.3 Token-level losses for language
models}\label{token-level-losses-for-language-models}

For autoregressive language modeling, a training sequence is

\[
w_{1:T}=(w_1,\ldots,w_T).
\]

The model defines next-token probabilities

\[
p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t}).
\]

The negative log-likelihood for one sequence is

\[
\ell(\theta;w_{1:T})
= -\sum_{t=1}^T \log p_\theta(w_t\mid w_{<t}).
\]

For a corpus with sequences \(w^{(1)},\ldots,w^{(n)}\), the average
token-level loss is

\[
L_n(\theta)
= -\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^n\sum_{t=1}^{T_i}
\log p_\theta\left(w_t^{(i)}\mid w_{<t}^{(i)}\right),
\]

where

\[
N = \sum_{i=1}^n T_i.
\]

The corresponding perplexity is

\[
\operatorname{PPL}(\theta)=\exp(L_n(\theta))
\]

when the loss uses natural logarithms.

This gives a direct connection between optimization and language
modeling:

\begin{quote}
Lower training loss means the model assigns higher probability to the
observed tokens under teacher forcing.
\end{quote}

\section{22.4 Softmax cross-entropy and its
gradient}\label{softmax-cross-entropy-and-its-gradient}

Many NLP objectives end with a softmax. Suppose a model produces logits

\[
z = (z_1,\ldots,z_K) \in R^K.
\]

The softmax probabilities are

\[
p_j = \frac{\exp(z_j)}{\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(z_k)}.
\]

For a one-hot target vector \(e_y\), the cross-entropy loss is

\[
\ell(z,y)=-\log p_y.
\]

Equivalently,

\[
\ell(z,y)= -z_y + \log\left(\sum_{k=1}^K \exp(z_k)\right).
\]

Differentiating gives the fundamental gradient identity

\[
\frac{\partial \ell}{\partial z_j}=p_j-1_{j=y}.
\]

In vector form,

\[
\nabla_z \ell = p-e_y.
\]

This identity appears throughout NLP:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  in text classifiers;
\item
  in masked language models;
\item
  in next-token prediction;
\item
  in instruction tuning;
\item
  in preference losses after reduction to logits.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Interpretation}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

The gradient \(p-e_y\) says: decrease the logit of classes assigned too
much probability and increase the logit of the correct class. The size
of the correction depends on the model's current probability error.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{22.5 From logits to parameter
gradients}\label{from-logits-to-parameter-gradients}

Let the logits depend on parameters \(\theta\) through a differentiable
map

\[
z=f_\theta(x).
\]

The chain rule gives

\[
\nabla_\theta \ell(\theta;x,y)
= J_\theta f_\theta(x)^T (p-e_y),
\]

where \(J_\theta f_\theta(x)\) is the Jacobian of the logits with
respect to the parameters.

For a linear softmax classifier,

\[
z = Wh+b,
\]

where \(h \in R^d\), \(W \in R^{K\times d}\), and \(b \in R^K\). Then

\[
\nabla_W \ell = (p-e_y)h^T,
\]

\[
\nabla_b \ell = p-e_y,
\]

and

\[
\nabla_h \ell = W^T(p-e_y).
\]

This small calculation is the local building block of backpropagation.

\section{22.6 Gradient descent}\label{gradient-descent}

Gradient descent updates parameters by moving in the direction of
steepest local decrease:

\[
\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k - \eta_k \nabla L_n(\theta_k),
\]

where \(\eta_k>0\) is the learning rate.

For a quadratic loss

\[
L(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\theta^T A \theta - b^T \theta,
\]

with \(A\) symmetric positive definite, the gradient is

\[
\nabla L(\theta)=A \theta-b.
\]

Gradient descent converges when the learning rate is small enough. If
\(\lambda_{\max}(A)\) is the largest eigenvalue of \(A\), then a
constant learning rate satisfying

\[
0<\eta<\frac{2}{\lambda_{\max}(A)}
\]

ensures convergence for this quadratic problem.

This idealized result matters because neural-network losses are locally
approximated by quadratic functions through Taylor expansion:

\[
L(\theta+u)\approx L(\theta)+\nabla L(\theta)^T u + \frac{1}{2}u^T H(\theta)u.
\]

Large curvature directions require smaller steps.

\section{22.7 Stochastic gradients}\label{stochastic-gradients}

For large NLP corpora, the full gradient

\[
\nabla L_n(\theta)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \nabla \ell(\theta;z_i,y_i)
\]

is expensive. Mini-batch stochastic gradient descent uses a random
subset \(B_k\subset \{1,\ldots,n\}\):

\[
g_k=\frac{1}{|B_k|}\sum_{i\in B_k}\nabla \ell(\theta_k;z_i,y_i).
\]

If the mini-batch is sampled uniformly, then

\[
E[g_k\mid \theta_k]=\nabla L_n(\theta_k).
\]

Thus \(g_k\) is an unbiased estimator of the full gradient. Its variance
decreases as the batch size increases. Under idealized independent
sampling,

\[
\operatorname{Var}(g_k)\approx \frac{1}{B}\Sigma(\theta_k),
\]

where \(B=|B_k|\) and \(\Sigma(\theta_k)\) is the covariance matrix of
per-example gradients.

The SGD update is

\[
\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\eta_k g_k.
\]

\textbf{Statistical view of SGD.} SGD replaces an exact derivative by a
noisy but cheaper estimator. The learning rate controls how much of this
noise is converted into parameter motion.

\section{22.8 Learning rate as a scale
parameter}\label{learning-rate-as-a-scale-parameter}

The learning rate is not merely a software option. It determines the
scale of parameter movement:

\[
\|\theta_{k+1}-\theta_k\| = \eta_k \|g_k\|.
\]

If \(\eta_k\) is too small, learning is slow. If it is too large, the
iterates may oscillate or diverge. In neural NLP, useful learning-rate
schedules often include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{warmup}, where the learning rate increases gradually at the
  beginning;
\item
  \textbf{constant phase}, where the learning rate remains approximately
  stable;
\item
  \textbf{decay}, where the learning rate decreases to refine the
  solution.
\end{enumerate}

A simple inverse-square-root schedule is

\[
\eta_k = c\min\{k^{-1/2}, k w^{-3/2}\},
\]

where \(w\) is the warmup length. A cosine decay schedule is

\[
\eta_k = \eta_{\min}
+\frac{1}{2}(\eta_{\max}-\eta_{\min})
\left(1+\cos\left(\frac{\pi k}{K}\right)\right).
\]

The mathematical purpose of a schedule is to balance exploration and
stabilization.

\section{22.9 Momentum}\label{momentum}

Momentum keeps a running average of past gradients:

\[
v_{k+1}=\mu v_k + g_k,
\]

\[
\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\eta v_{k+1},
\]

where \(0\leq \mu <1\). When gradients point in a consistent direction,
momentum accelerates movement. When gradients oscillate, momentum can
average out some oscillation.

For a long sequence of gradients, the velocity is

\[
v_{k+1}=g_k+\mu g_{k-1}+\mu^2 g_{k-2}+\cdots.
\]

Thus momentum is an exponentially weighted history of gradients.

\section{22.10 Adaptive methods: AdaGrad, RMSProp, and
Adam}\label{adaptive-methods-adagrad-rmsprop-and-adam}

NLP models often have sparse or highly uneven gradients. Some parameters
update frequently; others update rarely. Adaptive methods rescale
coordinates based on historical gradient magnitudes.

\subsection{AdaGrad}\label{adagrad}

AdaGrad accumulates squared gradients coordinatewise:

\[
s_{k+1}=s_k+g_k\odot g_k,
\]

\[
\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\eta \frac{g_k}{\sqrt{s_{k+1}}+\epsilon}.
\]

Coordinates with large accumulated gradients receive smaller future
steps.

\subsection{RMSProp}\label{rmsprop}

RMSProp uses an exponential moving average instead of a cumulative sum:

\[
s_{k+1}=\rho s_k+(1-\rho)(g_k\odot g_k),
\]

\[
\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\eta \frac{g_k}{\sqrt{s_{k+1}}+\epsilon}.
\]

\subsection{Adam}\label{adam}

Adam combines momentum and coordinatewise scaling:

\[
m_{k+1}=\beta_1 m_k+(1-\beta_1)g_k,
\]

\[
v_{k+1}=\beta_2 v_k+(1-\beta_2)(g_k\odot g_k).
\]

Bias-corrected estimates are

\[
\hat m_{k+1}=\frac{m_{k+1}}{1-\beta_1^{k+1}},
\qquad
\hat v_{k+1}=\frac{v_{k+1}}{1-\beta_2^{k+1}}.
\]

The update is

\[
\theta_{k+1}=\theta_k-\eta\frac{\hat m_{k+1}}{\sqrt{\hat v_{k+1}}+\epsilon}.
\]

Adam is popular in neural NLP because it handles noisy,
high-dimensional, and unevenly scaled gradients well.

\section{22.11 Weight decay and AdamW}\label{weight-decay-and-adamw}

A common regularized objective is

\[
L_{\lambda}(\theta)=L_n(\theta)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2.
\]

For ordinary gradient descent, this gives

\[
\theta_{k+1}
=\theta_k-\eta \left(\nabla L_n(\theta_k)+\lambda \theta_k\right)
=(1-\eta\lambda)\theta_k-\eta\nabla L_n(\theta_k).
\]

The regularizer shrinks parameters toward zero.

For adaptive optimizers, directly adding \(\lambda \theta\) to the
gradient interacts with coordinatewise scaling. AdamW decouples weight
decay from the adaptive gradient step:

\[
\theta_{k+1}
=(1-\eta\lambda)\theta_k
-\eta\frac{\hat m_{k+1}}{\sqrt{\hat v_{k+1}}+\epsilon}.
\]

This is often a cleaner implementation of shrinkage for Transformer
models.

\section{22.12 Gradient clipping}\label{gradient-clipping-1}

RNNs and Transformers can produce very large gradients. Gradient
clipping limits the step size by replacing \(g\) with

\[
\tilde g = g\min\left\{1,\frac{c}{\|g\|}\right\}.
\]

If \(\|g\|\leq c\), then \(\tilde g=g\). If \(\|g\|>c\), then
\(\|\tilde g\|=c\).

Clipping is not the same as fixing the model. It is a numerical
stabilization method. It prevents one unusually large mini-batch
gradient from causing a destructive update.

\section{22.13 Optimization and
generalization}\label{optimization-and-generalization}

Optimization minimizes training loss, but the goal is usually good
performance on new data. A model with very low empirical risk can still
have high population risk if it overfits.

Important sources of implicit or explicit regularization include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  weight decay;
\item
  dropout;
\item
  early stopping;
\item
  data augmentation;
\item
  label smoothing;
\item
  small-batch gradient noise;
\item
  learning-rate schedules;
\item
  architecture constraints;
\item
  parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
\end{itemize}

From a statistical point of view, the optimizer is part of the learning
algorithm. Two optimizers can reach different solutions with similar
training losses but different generalization behavior.

\section{22.14 Nonconvexity in neural
NLP}\label{nonconvexity-in-neural-nlp}

Linear regression with squared loss is convex. Logistic regression is
convex in its parameters. Neural NLP models are typically nonconvex
because they are compositions of many nonlinear maps:

\[
f_\theta = f_L\circ f_{L-1}\circ \cdots \circ f_1.
\]

The loss surface may contain many critical points where

\[
\nabla L_n(\theta)=0.
\]

These can be local minima, saddle points, or flat regions. In
high-dimensional neural networks, saddle points and nearly flat valleys
are especially important.

A second-order Taylor approximation near \(\theta\) is

\[
L_n(\theta+u)
\approx L_n(\theta)+\nabla L_n(\theta)^Tu+\frac{1}{2}u^T H(\theta)u.
\]

The Hessian eigenvalues describe local curvature. Large positive
eigenvalues indicate sharp directions. Small eigenvalues indicate flat
directions. Negative eigenvalues indicate directions of local decrease.

In modern NLP, the parameter dimension \(p\) is often much larger than
the number of human-interpretable modeling choices. Therefore
optimization analysis focuses less on finding the unique global
minimizer and more on stability, scaling, gradient quality, and
generalization.

\section{22.15 Numerical stability}\label{numerical-stability-1}

Optimization can fail because of numerical issues, not because the
mathematical model is conceptually wrong. Common stability tricks
include:

\subsection{Stable log-sum-exp}\label{stable-log-sum-exp}

Instead of computing

\[
\log\sum_j \exp(z_j),
\]

use

\[
m + \log\sum_j \exp(z_j-m),
\qquad m=\max_j z_j.
\]

This avoids overflow when logits are large.

\subsection{Loss masks}\label{loss-masks}

For padded sequences, the loss should ignore padding tokens. If
\(M_{i,t}\in\{0,1\}\) is a mask, then

\[
L(\theta)=
-\frac{1}{\sum_{i,t} M_{i,t}}
\sum_{i,t} M_{i,t}
\log p_\theta(w_{i,t}\mid w_{i,<t}).
\]

\subsection{Mixed precision}\label{mixed-precision}

Large models often use lower precision arithmetic to save memory and
increase speed. This introduces a tradeoff between numerical efficiency
and stability. Loss scaling and careful normalization help prevent
underflow and overflow.

\section{22.16 Interactive: optimization
dynamics}\label{interactive-optimization-dynamics}

The following interactive compares gradient descent, momentum, and Adam
on a two-dimensional quadratic loss

\[
L(x,y)=\frac{1}{2}(a x^2+b y^2).
\]

The parameter \(b/a\) controls the condition number. A large condition
number creates a narrow valley, where plain gradient descent may zigzag.

\section{22.17 Python example: softmax regression
gradient}\label{python-example-softmax-regression-gradient}

This example derives and checks the gradient for a small text
classifier. The model is

\[
z_i = W x_i + b,
\qquad
p_i=\operatorname{softmax}(z_i),
\]

with average cross-entropy loss.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{    [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{K }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{n, d }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(K, d))}
\NormalTok{b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(K)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax\_rows(Z):}
\NormalTok{    Z\_shift }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ Z.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    expZ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(Z\_shift)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ expZ }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ expZ.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ loss\_and\_grad(W, b, X, y):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W.T }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b}
\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax\_rows(Z)}
\NormalTok{    loss }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{np.mean(np.log(P[np.arange(n), y]))}
\NormalTok{    G }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P.copy()}
\NormalTok{    G[np.arange(n), y] }\OperatorTok{{-}=} \FloatTok{1.0}
\NormalTok{    G }\OperatorTok{/=}\NormalTok{ n}
\NormalTok{    grad\_W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ G.T }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ X}
\NormalTok{    grad\_b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ G.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ loss, grad\_W, grad\_b}

\NormalTok{loss, grad\_W, grad\_b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_and\_grad(W, b, X, y)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"loss:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(loss, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grad\_W shape:"}\NormalTok{, grad\_W.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"grad\_b:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(grad\_b, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
loss: 0.736831
grad_W shape: (2, 4)
grad_b: [-0.069829  0.069829]
\end{verbatim}

The shapes are important:

\[
X\in R^{n\times d},
\qquad
W\in R^{K\times d},
\qquad
\nabla_W L\in R^{K\times d}.
\]

\section{22.18 Python example: finite-difference gradient
check}\label{python-example-finite-difference-gradient-check}

A gradient check compares an analytic derivative with a numerical
approximation:

\[
\frac{\partial L}{\partial \theta_j}
\approx
\frac{L(\theta+\epsilon e_j)-L(\theta-\epsilon e_j)}{2\epsilon}.
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{eps }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1e{-}5}
\NormalTok{j, k }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{W\_plus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W.copy()}
\NormalTok{W\_minus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W.copy()}
\NormalTok{W\_plus[j, k] }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ eps}
\NormalTok{W\_minus[j, k] }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ eps}
\NormalTok{loss\_plus, \_, \_ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_and\_grad(W\_plus, b, X, y)}
\NormalTok{loss\_minus, \_, \_ }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_and\_grad(W\_minus, b, X, y)}
\NormalTok{finite\_difference }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (loss\_plus }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ loss\_minus) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{2} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ eps)}
\NormalTok{analytic }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ grad\_W[j, k]}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"finite difference:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(finite\_difference, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"analytic gradient:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(analytic, }\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"absolute error:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(finite\_difference }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ analytic))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
finite difference: 0.11785573
analytic gradient: 0.11785573
absolute error: 7.044365091246618e-13
\end{verbatim}

Gradient checking is useful when writing custom training code. It is too
expensive for normal training, but it is excellent for debugging.

\section{22.19 Python example: GD, momentum, and Adam on a
quadratic}\label{python-example-gd-momentum-and-adam-on-a-quadratic}

The next example mirrors the interactive figure.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.diag([}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{20.0}\NormalTok{])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ quad\_loss(theta):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \FloatTok{0.5} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ theta }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ theta}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ quad\_grad(theta):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ theta}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ optimize(method}\OperatorTok{=}\StringTok{"gd"}\NormalTok{, lr}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.08}\NormalTok{, steps}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{60}\NormalTok{, beta}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{2.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{2.2}\NormalTok{], dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    path }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [theta.copy()]}
\NormalTok{    losses }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [quad\_loss(theta)]}
\NormalTok{    m }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(theta)}
\NormalTok{    v }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(theta)}
\NormalTok{    beta1, beta2 }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.9}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.99}
\NormalTok{    eps }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1e{-}8}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ t }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, steps }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{        g }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ quad\_grad(theta)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ method }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"gd"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ theta }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ g}
        \ControlFlowTok{elif}\NormalTok{ method }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"momentum"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            m }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ beta }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ m }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ g}
\NormalTok{            theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ theta }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ m}
        \ControlFlowTok{elif}\NormalTok{ method }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"adam"}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            m }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ beta1 }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ m }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ beta1) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ g}
\NormalTok{            v }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ beta2 }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ v }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ beta2) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (g }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ g)}
\NormalTok{            m\_hat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ m }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ beta1 }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ t)}
\NormalTok{            v\_hat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ v }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ beta2 }\OperatorTok{**}\NormalTok{ t)}
\NormalTok{            theta }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ theta }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ m\_hat }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (np.sqrt(v\_hat) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ eps)}
\NormalTok{        path.append(theta.copy())}
\NormalTok{        losses.append(quad\_loss(theta))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.array(path), np.array(losses)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ method }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"gd"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"momentum"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"adam"}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    path, losses }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ optimize(method}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{method)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{method}\SpecialCharTok{:8s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ final theta = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{np}\SpecialCharTok{.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(path[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{, final loss = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{losses[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}\SpecialCharTok{:.6f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
gd       final theta = [0.0188 0.    ], final loss = 0.000177
momentum final theta = [-0.0146 -0.1004], final loss = 0.100870
adam     final theta = [-0.1226 -0.0936], final loss = 0.095036
\end{verbatim}

A quadratic example is simple, but it teaches three practical lessons:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  curvature affects stable step sizes;
\item
  momentum can reduce zigzagging;
\item
  adaptive scaling can help when coordinates have very different
  curvature.
\end{enumerate}

\section{22.20 Python example: mini-batch gradient
noise}\label{python-example-mini-batch-gradient-noise}

Mini-batch gradients are random estimates of the full gradient. The
variance decreases with batch size.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{2026}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{N }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1000}
\NormalTok{true\_grad }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.25}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{per\_example\_grads }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ true\_grad }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\FloatTok{2.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{], size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(N, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{full\_grad }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ per\_example\_grads.mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ B }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{16}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{64}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{256}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    estimates }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{500}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{        idx }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.choice(N, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{B, replace}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        estimates.append(per\_example\_grads[idx].mean(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    estimates }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array(estimates)}
\NormalTok{    avg\_error\_norm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(estimates }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ full\_grad, axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{).mean()}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"batch size }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{B}\SpecialCharTok{:3d\}}\SpecialStringTok{: mean gradient{-}estimation error norm = }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{avg\_error\_norm}\SpecialCharTok{:.4f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
batch size   1: mean gradient-estimation error norm = 2.0634
batch size   4: mean gradient-estimation error norm = 1.0484
batch size  16: mean gradient-estimation error norm = 0.5055
batch size  64: mean gradient-estimation error norm = 0.2485
batch size 256: mean gradient-estimation error norm = 0.1095
\end{verbatim}

Larger batches give more accurate gradient estimates, but they are more
expensive and may reduce the useful exploratory noise of SGD.

\section{22.21 Python example: gradient
clipping}\label{python-example-gradient-clipping}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ clip\_gradient(g, threshold):}
\NormalTok{    norm }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(g)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ norm }\OperatorTok{\textless{}=}\NormalTok{ threshold:}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ g.copy()}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ g }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (threshold }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ norm)}

\NormalTok{gradients }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
\NormalTok{    np.array([}\FloatTok{0.2}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.3}\NormalTok{]),}
\NormalTok{    np.array([}\FloatTok{5.0}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{4.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{3.0}\NormalTok{]),}
\NormalTok{    np.array([}\FloatTok{40.0}\NormalTok{, }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{20.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{10.0}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{threshold }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{2.0}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ g }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ gradients:}
\NormalTok{    clipped }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ clip\_gradient(g, threshold)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"original norm:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(g), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
          \StringTok{" clipped norm:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.norm(clipped), }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{),}
          \StringTok{" clipped vector:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(clipped, }\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
original norm: 0.374  clipped norm: 0.374  clipped vector: [ 0.2 -0.1  0.3]
original norm: 7.071  clipped norm: 2.0  clipped vector: [ 1.414 -1.131  0.849]
original norm: 45.826  clipped norm: 2.0  clipped vector: [ 1.746 -0.873  0.436]
\end{verbatim}

Clipping preserves direction but changes magnitude when the gradient is
too large.

\section{22.22 Python example: training a tiny text
classifier}\label{python-example-training-a-tiny-text-classifier}

The following code trains a softmax classifier using averaged
token-count features. This is not a state-of-the-art NLP model. Its
purpose is to show the complete optimization loop in a transparent way.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}

\NormalTok{train\_texts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"excellent clear helpful explanation"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"useful clear lecture helpful"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"confusing unclear poor explanation"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"poor confusing lecture unclear"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"clear useful examples"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"unclear poor examples"}
\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{train\_y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(word }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ text }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ train\_texts }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ text.split()))}
\NormalTok{word\_to\_id }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{w: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(train\_texts), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)))}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, text }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(train\_texts):}
\NormalTok{    counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Counter(text.split())}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, count }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ counts.items():}
\NormalTok{        X[i, word\_to\_id[word]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ count}
\NormalTok{    X[i] }\OperatorTok{/=} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, X[i].}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{())}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{11}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{K, d }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{, X.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.01}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(K, d))}
\NormalTok{b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(K)}

\NormalTok{lr }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.8}
\NormalTok{loss\_history }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ epoch }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    loss, grad\_W, grad\_b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ loss\_and\_grad(W, b, X, train\_y)}
\NormalTok{    W }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_W}
\NormalTok{    b }\OperatorTok{{-}=}\NormalTok{ lr }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ grad\_b}
\NormalTok{    loss\_history.append(loss)}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ softmax\_rows(X }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W.T }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ b)}
\NormalTok{pred }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ P.argmax(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"vocabulary:"}\NormalTok{, vocab)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"final loss:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(loss\_history[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{4}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"predictions:"}\NormalTok{, pred.tolist())}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"training accuracy:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.mean(pred }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ train\_y)))}

\NormalTok{weights\_for\_positive }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ W[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ W[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, weight }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{zip}\NormalTok{(vocab, weights\_for\_positive), key}\OperatorTok{=}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ x: }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{x[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]):}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{word}\SpecialCharTok{:12s\}}\SpecialStringTok{ }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{weight}\SpecialCharTok{: .3f\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
vocabulary: ['clear', 'confusing', 'examples', 'excellent', 'explanation', 'helpful', 'lecture', 'poor', 'unclear', 'useful']
final loss: 0.0819
predictions: [1, 1, 0, 0, 1, 0]
training accuracy: 1.0
clear         4.177
useful        2.818
helpful       2.564
excellent     1.373
explanation   0.115
examples     -0.013
lecture      -0.053
confusing    -2.508
poor         -4.111
unclear      -4.118
\end{verbatim}

This example connects optimization with interpretability. The learned
weight difference \(W_1-W_0\) gives a linear score direction for the
positive class.

\section{22.23 AI-assisted learning
prompts}\label{ai-assisted-learning-prompts}

Use an AI assistant as a mathematical critic rather than a replacement
for derivation.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Prompt 1: audit an objective}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

I am training a text classifier with softmax cross-entropy. Write the
empirical risk \(L_n(\theta)\) explicitly, identify the model
probabilities, and explain which terms depend on \(\theta\). Then check
whether my notation distinguishes logits, probabilities, and labels.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Prompt 2: verify a gradient}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Here is my derivation of the softmax cross-entropy gradient. Check each
line and identify the first incorrect equality, if any. Do not skip
dimension checks.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Prompt 3: diagnose optimization instability}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

My training loss sometimes becomes \texttt{nan}. Give a mathematical
checklist involving log-sum-exp, learning rate, gradient norm, loss
masking, division by small numbers, and probability clipping. Separate
likely numerical causes from modeling causes.

\end{tcolorbox}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{AI caution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

An AI assistant may correctly name Adam or SGD while giving an
incomplete formula. Always ask for the update equations, the role of
each hyperparameter, and the dimensions of the quantities involved.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{22.24 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-11}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing logits and probabilities.} Softmax converts logits
  into probabilities. Cross-entropy should usually be computed using a
  numerically stable log-softmax.
\item
  \textbf{Averaging over padding tokens.} Padding tokens should be
  masked out of token-level losses.
\item
  \textbf{Using a learning rate without checking gradient scale.} The
  product \(\eta\|g\|\) controls step size.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming smaller training loss means better model.} Training
  loss and test performance can move differently.
\item
  \textbf{Treating Adam as magic.} Adam rescales coordinates using
  gradient moments; it still requires learning-rate tuning and
  regularization.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring random variation.} Mini-batch order, initialization,
  and hardware can change training trajectories.
\end{enumerate}

\section{22.25 Worked calculation}\label{worked-calculation-4}

Suppose a three-class model outputs probabilities

\[
p=(0.20,0.60,0.20)
\]

and the correct class is class \(2\). With one-hot target

\[
e_2=(0,1,0),
\]

the gradient with respect to logits is

\[
\nabla_z\ell=p-e_2=(0.20,-0.40,0.20).
\]

If the logit model is \(z=Wh+b\) with

\[
h=(1,2)^T,
\]

then

\[
\nabla_W\ell=(p-e_2)h^T
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.20 \\
-0.40 \\
0.20
\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & 2
\end{pmatrix}
=
\begin{pmatrix}
0.20 & 0.40 \\
-0.40 & -0.80 \\
0.20 & 0.40
\end{pmatrix}.
\]

Thus gradient descent subtracts a positive multiple of this matrix. The
row for the correct class increases in the direction of \(h\), while the
rows for incorrect classes decrease in that direction.

\section{22.26 Exercises}\label{exercises-21}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Softmax gradient.} Starting from \[
  \ell(z,y)=-z_y+\log\sum_k \exp(z_k),
  \] derive \(\partial \ell/\partial z_j=p_j-1_{j=y}\).
\item
  \textbf{Linear classifier gradient.} For \(z=Wh+b\), derive
  \(\nabla_W\ell\), \(\nabla_b\ell\), and \(\nabla_h\ell\).
\item
  \textbf{Learning-rate stability.} Consider
  \(L(\theta)=\frac{1}{2}\lambda \theta^2\). Show that gradient descent
  converges if \(0<\eta<2/\lambda\).
\item
  \textbf{Mini-batch variance.} Suppose per-example gradients have
  covariance \(\Sigma\). Under independent sampling, show that the
  mini-batch gradient covariance is approximately \(\Sigma/B\).
\item
  \textbf{Gradient clipping.} Prove that the clipped gradient \[
  \tilde g=g\min\{1,c/\|g\|\}
  \] has norm at most \(c\).
\item
  \textbf{Adam update.} Write one full Adam update for the scalar
  gradient sequence \(g_1=2\), \(g_2=1\), using \(\beta_1=0.9\),
  \(\beta_2=0.99\), and \(\epsilon=10^{-8}\).
\item
  \textbf{Loss masking.} Create a small padded batch of token labels and
  logits. Compute the masked average cross-entropy by hand.
\item
  \textbf{Optimization versus generalization.} Describe an experiment
  comparing two optimizers that achieve similar training loss but
  different validation loss.
\end{enumerate}

\section{22.27 Mini-project: optimizer comparison for text
classification}\label{mini-project-optimizer-comparison-for-text-classification}

Build a small text classifier using count vectors, TF-IDF vectors, or
learned embeddings. Compare at least three optimizers:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  SGD;
\item
  SGD with momentum;
\item
  Adam or AdamW.
\end{enumerate}

For each optimizer, report:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  training loss curve;
\item
  validation loss curve;
\item
  gradient norm curve;
\item
  final classification metrics;
\item
  sensitivity to learning rate;
\item
  an explanation of the observed behavior using the mathematics of this
  chapter.
\end{itemize}

The final report should separate three questions:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Which optimizer minimized training loss fastest?
\item
  Which optimizer gave the best validation performance?
\item
  Which optimizer was most stable across random seeds?
\end{enumerate}

\section{22.29 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-7}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Most NLP training objectives are empirical risks built from negative
  log-likelihood or cross-entropy.
\item
  The softmax cross-entropy gradient is \(p-e_y\).
\item
  Backpropagation is repeated use of the chain rule.
\item
  SGD uses noisy but inexpensive gradient estimates.
\item
  Momentum averages gradient directions over time.
\item
  Adam rescales coordinates using first and second gradient moments.
\item
  AdamW separates weight decay from adaptive gradient scaling.
\item
  Gradient clipping controls the norm of extreme updates.
\item
  Optimization performance and statistical generalization are related
  but not identical.
\item
  In mathematical NLP, every training run should specify the model, data
  distribution, loss, optimizer, schedule, and evaluation metric.
\end{itemize}

\section{22.30 Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-12}

Optimization for NLP draws on numerical optimization, stochastic
approximation, statistical learning, and deep learning. For broader
background, see Boyd and Vandenberghe (2004) for convex optimization,
Nocedal and Wright (2006) for numerical optimization, Goodfellow et al.
(2016a) for deep learning, and Vaswani et al. (2017) for Transformer
training context. Adam was introduced in Kingma and Ba (2015a), and
decoupled weight decay in AdamW is associated with Loshchilov and Hutter
(2019a).

\chapter{Graphs and Language}\label{graphs-and-language-1}

Dependency, knowledge, and message passing

\hfill\break

Language is not only a sequence. A sentence has syntactic relations, a
document collection has citation and hyperlink structure, a knowledge
base has subject-relation-object triples, and a corpus has co-occurrence
patterns among words. Graphs provide a mathematical language for
representing these relational structures. This chapter develops
graph-based NLP from a clean mathematical point of view: nodes, edges,
matrices, Laplacians, walks, propagation, and message passing.

\section{23.1 Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-22}

After reading this chapter, students should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  represent linguistic objects as graphs;
\item
  convert graphs into adjacency, degree, incidence, and Laplacian
  matrices;
\item
  distinguish directed, undirected, weighted, bipartite, heterogeneous,
  and relational graphs;
\item
  construct word co-occurrence graphs, dependency graphs, document-term
  graphs, and knowledge graphs;
\item
  interpret graph walks, centrality, PageRank, and label propagation
  mathematically;
\item
  derive one layer of graph neural message passing;
\item
  explain graph convolution, graph attention, and relation-specific
  message passing;
\item
  implement small graph algorithms from scratch in Python;
\item
  use AI tools to audit graph construction choices rather than simply
  generate graph code.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Guiding question}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

When should an NLP problem be represented as a graph rather than as a
sequence or a bag of words?

A graph is useful when the relational structure is part of the signal.
The important mathematical decision is not ``use a graph neural
network'' but first: choose nodes, choose edges, choose weights, and
decide what invariances the representation should have.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{23.2 From sequences to relational
objects}\label{from-sequences-to-relational-objects}

Earlier chapters represented a text as a sequence

\[
w_{1:T}=(w_1,\\ldots,w_T)
\]

over a vocabulary \(V\), or as a vector \(x\in R^d\). These
representations are powerful but not always natural for relational
information.

A graph representation starts with a set of nodes

\[
\mathcal V = \{1,2,\ldots,n\}
\]

and a set of edges

\[
\mathcal E \subseteq \mathcal V \times \mathcal V.
\]

In NLP, nodes may represent:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  tokens in a sentence;
\item
  word types in a vocabulary;
\item
  documents in a corpus;
\item
  entities in a knowledge base;
\item
  concepts in an ontology;
\item
  users, questions, courses, or resources in an advising system.
\end{itemize}

Edges may represent:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  adjacency in a sentence;
\item
  syntactic dependency;
\item
  word co-occurrence;
\item
  citation or hyperlink;
\item
  semantic relation;
\item
  membership of a word in a document;
\item
  retrieval similarity.
\end{itemize}

Thus a graph is not just a data structure. It is a modeling assumption
about which relations are relevant.

\textbf{Graph modeling decision.} A graph-based NLP model begins with a
map

\[
\text{text data} \longmapsto G=(\mathcal V,\mathcal E,W,X),
\]

where \(W\) stores edge weights and \(X\) stores node features. The
quality of the downstream model depends strongly on this construction.

\section{23.3 Basic graph definitions}\label{basic-graph-definitions}

An undirected weighted graph on \(n\) nodes is described by a symmetric
adjacency matrix

\[
A\in R^{n\times n},
\qquad
A_{ij}=A_{ji}\ge 0.
\]

Here \(A_{ij}>0\) means that nodes \(i\) and \(j\) are connected, and
\(A_{ij}\) gives the edge weight. For an unweighted graph,
\(A_{ij}\in \{0,1\}\).

A directed graph uses a possibly nonsymmetric adjacency matrix. Then
\(A_{ij}>0\) may mean an edge from node \(i\) to node \(j\). The
direction convention must be stated because different software packages
use different conventions.

The weighted degree of node \(i\) is

\[
d_i = \sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}.
\]

The degree matrix is diagonal:

\[
D=\operatorname{diag}(d_1,\ldots,d_n).
\]

For undirected graphs, the combinatorial graph Laplacian is

\[
L=D-A.
\]

The normalized adjacency matrix is often written

\[
S=D^{-1/2} A D^{-1/2},
\]

and the normalized Laplacian is

\[
L_{\mathrm{norm}} = I-D^{-1/2}AD^{-1/2}=I-S.
\]

When isolated nodes occur, \(d_i=0\), and the inverse degree factors
must be handled carefully.

\section{23.4 Why the Laplacian
matters}\label{why-the-laplacian-matters}

For a scalar function \(f\in R^n\) on nodes, the quadratic form of the
Laplacian is

\[
f^T L f
= \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j=1}^n A_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2.
\]

This identity is central. It says that \(f^T L f\) is small when
connected nodes have similar values. In NLP, \(f_i\) may be a label
score, a semantic score, or one coordinate of a node embedding.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Smoothness prior on graphs}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A graph Laplacian encodes the prior that connected nodes should have
similar predictions or representations. For example, if two documents
are very similar, a classifier may penalize assigning very different
label scores to them.

\end{tcolorbox}

The Laplacian also appears in spectral clustering. Eigenvectors
associated with small eigenvalues reveal low-frequency graph signals,
meaning functions that vary slowly across edges. This is the graph
analogue of using low-frequency Fourier modes to describe a smooth
signal.

\section{23.5 A sentence as a dependency
graph}\label{a-sentence-as-a-dependency-graph}

A dependency parse represents a sentence by directed grammatical
relations. For example, consider

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{language models predict tokens}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A possible simplified dependency graph is:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{predict {-}\textgreater{} models}
\NormalTok{models  {-}\textgreater{} language}
\NormalTok{predict {-}\textgreater{} tokens}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

The words are nodes. Directed edges represent syntactic relations. The
main verb \texttt{predict} is connected to subject-like and object-like
components.

Mathematically, for a sentence with \(T\) tokens, a dependency graph has
an adjacency matrix

\[
A\in \{0,1\}^{T\times T}.
\]

If \(A_{ij}=1\) means token \(i\) points to token \(j\), then row \(i\)
lists outgoing syntactic neighbors. A graph-based model may update a
token representation by aggregating information from its syntactic
neighbors rather than from all tokens.

Dependency graphs are useful because they remove some irrelevant
word-distance effects. In a long sentence, two syntactically related
words may be far apart in the sequence but close in the dependency
graph.

\section{23.6 Word co-occurrence
graphs}\label{word-co-occurrence-graphs}

A word co-occurrence graph has one node per word type. Two words are
connected if they occur near each other in a corpus. A simple
construction uses a window size \(r\). For every occurrence of word
\(w_t\), connect it to words \(w_s\) satisfying

\[
0 < |s-t| \le r.
\]

The edge weight may count co-occurrence frequency:

\[
A_{ij}=\#\{(s,t): w_s=i, w_t=j, 0<|s-t|\le r\}.
\]

After symmetrization, \(A\) becomes an undirected weighted graph. This
graph captures the distributional hypothesis: words appearing in similar
neighborhoods tend to have related meanings.

This connects graph methods to Chapter 8. Co-occurrence matrices, PMI
matrices, and word graphs are different views of the same empirical
object.

\section{23.7 Document-term graphs as bipartite
graphs}\label{document-term-graphs-as-bipartite-graphs}

A document-term matrix

\[
X\in R^{m\times d}
\]

can be interpreted as a bipartite graph. One part contains document
nodes

\[
\{D_1,\ldots,D_m\},
\]

and the other part contains term nodes

\[
\{t_1,\ldots,t_d\}.
\]

There is an edge between document \(D_i\) and term \(t_j\) with weight
\(X_{ij}\). The full adjacency matrix has block form

\[
A_{\\text{bip}}=
\begin{bmatrix}
0 & X \\
X^T & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

This construction lets information propagate between documents through
shared terms and between terms through shared documents. For example,
two documents need not share a direct edge; they may become related
through paths of length two:

\[
D_i \to t_j \to D_k.
\]

The document-document similarity matrix is

\[
XX^T,
\]

and the term-term similarity matrix is

\[
X^T X.
\]

Thus the familiar Gram matrices from vector-space NLP are also two-step
walk matrices in a bipartite graph.

\section{23.8 Knowledge graphs}\label{knowledge-graphs}

A knowledge graph stores triples

\[
(h,r,t),
\]

where \(h\) is a head entity, \(r\) is a relation, and \(t\) is a tail
entity. For example:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{(Transformer, is\_a, neural\_architecture)}
\NormalTok{(BERT, uses, self\_attention)}
\NormalTok{(NLP, uses, probability)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A knowledge graph is not merely a graph; it is usually a labeled
directed multigraph. Different relations should not always be treated as
the same type of edge.

For \(R\) relation types, one may define relation-specific adjacency
matrices

\[
A^{(1)},\ldots,A^{(R)}.
\]

The entry \(A^{(r)}_{ij}=1\) means that relation \(r\) connects entity
\(i\) to entity \(j\). This creates an adjacency tensor

\[
\mathcal A\in R^{R\times n\times n}.
\]

Relation-specific structure is important. The relation \texttt{is\_a} is
not the same as \texttt{part\_of}, and neither is the same as
\texttt{cites} or \texttt{teaches}.

\section{23.9 Random walks and
centrality}\label{random-walks-and-centrality}

Graphs support random walks. For an undirected weighted graph with
degree matrix \(D\), the row-stochastic transition matrix is

\[
P=D^{-1}A.
\]

If \(p_t\in R^n\) is a row vector distribution over nodes at time \(t\),
then

\[
p_{t+1}=p_t P.
\]

A stationary distribution satisfies

\[
\pi = \pi P.
\]

For connected non-bipartite undirected graphs, the stationary
distribution is proportional to degree:

\[
\pi_i = \frac{d_i}{\sum_j d_j}.
\]

Random walks appear in NLP through ranking, graph-based disambiguation,
label propagation, and representation learning. PageRank modifies the
walk by adding teleportation:

\[
p_{t+1}=\alpha p_t P + (1-\alpha)v,
\]

where \(v\) is a restart distribution and \(0<\alpha<1\).

\section{23.10 Label propagation}\label{label-propagation}

Suppose a graph has a small set of labeled nodes and many unlabeled
nodes. Let \(Y\in R^{n\times K}\) store label scores. A simple label
propagation iteration is

\[
F^{(k+1)} = \alpha S F^{(k)} + (1-\alpha)Y,
\]

where \(S\) is a normalized adjacency matrix. At convergence, if
\(0<\alpha<1\), the fixed point satisfies

\[
F^* = \alpha S F^* + (1-\alpha)Y,
\]

so

\[
F^* = (1-\alpha)(I-\alpha S)^{-1}Y,
\]

provided the inverse exists.

This formula shows that label propagation is not magic. It is repeated
averaging over a graph with a restart to the initial labels.

In NLP, this can be used to propagate sentiment labels through a word
graph, topic labels through a document graph, or resource categories
through a knowledge graph.

\section{23.11 Message passing as the common
abstraction}\label{message-passing-as-the-common-abstraction}

Many graph neural networks use message passing. Each node \(i\) has a
hidden state

\[
h_i^{(\ell)}\in R^{d_\ell}
\]

at layer \(\ell\). A generic message passing layer has the form

\[
m_i^{(\ell)} = \operatorname{AGG}^{(\ell)}\left(\{\psi^{(\ell)}(h_i^{(\ell)},h_j^{(\ell)},e_{ij}) : j\in N(i)\}\right),
\]

then

\[
h_i^{(\ell+1)} = \phi^{(\ell)}\left(h_i^{(\ell)},m_i^{(\ell)}\right).
\]

Here:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(N(i)\) is the neighborhood of node \(i\);
\item
  \(e_{ij}\) may store edge features;
\item
  \(\psi\) creates messages;
\item
  \(\operatorname{AGG}\) aggregates messages, often by sum, mean, or
  attention;
\item
  \(\phi\) updates the node state.
\end{itemize}

The aggregation should usually be permutation invariant with respect to
the ordering of neighbors. This is the graph analogue of a set function.

\section{23.12 A graph convolution
layer}\label{a-graph-convolution-layer}

A common simplified graph convolution layer is

\[
H^{(\ell+1)} = \sigma(\tilde S H^{(\ell)} W^{(\ell)}),
\]

where:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \(H^{(\ell)}\in R^{n\times d_\ell}\) stores node features;
\item
  \(W^{(\ell)}\in R^{d_\ell\times d_{\ell+1}}\) is a trainable weight
  matrix;
\item
  \(\sigma\) is a nonlinear activation;
\item
  \(\tilde S\) is a normalized adjacency matrix, often built after
  adding self-loops.
\end{itemize}

With self-loops,

\[
\tilde A = A + I,
\qquad
\tilde D_{ii}=\sum_j \tilde A_{ij},
\]

and

\[
\tilde S = \tilde D^{-1/2}\tilde A\tilde D^{-1/2}.
\]

The layer has two operations:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  mix nearby node features by multiplying by \(\tilde S\);
\item
  transform feature coordinates by multiplying by \(W^{(\ell)}\).
\end{enumerate}

\textbf{Graph convolution as smoothing plus learning.} The matrix
\(\tilde S\) performs graph smoothing. The matrix \(W^{(\ell)}\) learns
feature combinations. Their product creates a trainable local averaging
operator on graph signals.

\section{23.13 Graph attention}\label{graph-attention}

Self-attention from Chapters 13 and 14 allows every token to attend to
every other token. Graph attention restricts attention to graph
neighborhoods. For node \(i\), compute a score for each neighbor
\(j\in N(i)\):

\[
e_{ij} = a(h_i,h_j).
\]

Then normalize over the neighborhood:

\[
\alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp(e_{ij})}{\sum_{k\in N(i)}\exp(e_{ik})}.
\]

The update is

\[
h_i' = \sigma\left(\sum_{j\in N(i)} \alpha_{ij} W h_j\right).
\]

This is attention on a sparse graph. In NLP, it can be used on
dependency graphs, document graphs, entity graphs, and hybrid graphs
connecting documents, passages, entities, and concepts.

\section{23.14 Relational message
passing}\label{relational-message-passing}

Knowledge graphs require relation-specific updates. A simple relational
message passing layer is

\[
h_i' = \sigma\left(
W_0 h_i + \sum_{r=1}^R\sum_{j\in N_r(i)} \frac{1}{c_{i,r}} W_r h_j
\right),
\]

where \(N_r(i)\) is the set of neighbors connected to \(i\) by relation
\(r\), \(W_r\) is a relation-specific matrix, and \(c_{i,r}\) is a
normalization constant.

This is important because edge labels carry meaning. Treating all
relations as identical may lose the distinction between syntactic,
semantic, citation, and membership relations.

\section{23.15 Interactive: graph message
passing}\label{interactive-graph-message-passing}

The following interactive shows a small word graph. Node colors
represent a scalar graph signal. Each message-passing step replaces a
node's value by a convex combination of its current value and the
average value of its neighbors:

\[
f^{(k+1)} = (1-\alpha)f^{(0)} + \alpha P f^{(k)}.
\]

The parameter \(\alpha\) controls how strongly information propagates
through the graph.

\section{23.16 Python example: build a word co-occurrence
graph}\label{python-example-build-a-word-co-occurrence-graph}

The following example builds a weighted undirected word graph from a
tiny corpus. The code avoids external graph libraries so that the
matrices are visible.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}
\ImportTok{from}\NormalTok{ collections }\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ Counter}

\NormalTok{corpus }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
    \StringTok{"graph models represent language structure"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"language models use tokens and context"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"probability models describe uncertainty"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"graph neural networks pass messages"}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"tokens cooccur with context in language"}
\NormalTok{]}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ tokenize(text):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ text.lower().split()}

\NormalTok{tokenized }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [tokenize(doc) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ corpus]}
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(tok }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tok }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ doc))}
\NormalTok{index }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{w: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(vocab)\}}

\NormalTok{window }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{2}
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)), dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ doc }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ tokenized:}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ t, w }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(doc):}
\NormalTok{        i }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ index[w]}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ s }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, t }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ window), }\BuiltInTok{min}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(doc), t }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ window }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)):}
            \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ s }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ t:}
                \ControlFlowTok{continue}
\NormalTok{            j }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ index[doc[s]]}
\NormalTok{            A[i, j] }\OperatorTok{+=} \DecValTok{1}

\CommentTok{\# Symmetrize the directed window counts.}
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.5} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (A }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ A.T)}

\NormalTok{degrees }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{summary }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{: vocab, }\StringTok{"degree"}\NormalTok{: degrees\}).sort\_values(}\StringTok{"degree"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(summary.head(}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{).to\_string(index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
     word  degree
   models     9.0
 language     7.0
   tokens     6.0
  context     6.0
 networks     4.0
      use     4.0
represent     4.0
     with     4.0
\end{verbatim}

The matrix \(A\) is a weighted adjacency matrix. The degree of a word is
the total co-occurrence weight attached to it.

\section{23.17 Python example: Laplacian and
smoothness}\label{python-example-laplacian-and-smoothness}

For an undirected graph, the Laplacian is \(L=D-A\). The quantity
\(f^TLf\) measures how much a signal varies across edges.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{D }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.diag(A.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{L }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ D }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ A}

\NormalTok{f }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, value }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ \{}\StringTok{"graph"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"uncertainty"}\NormalTok{: }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{\}.items():}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ word }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ index:}
\NormalTok{        f[index[word]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ value}

\NormalTok{energy\_matrix }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(f.T }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ L }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ f)}
\NormalTok{energy\_sum }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)):}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab)):}
\NormalTok{        energy\_sum }\OperatorTok{+=} \FloatTok{0.5} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ A[i, j] }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (f[i] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ f[j]) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"f\^{}T L f:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(energy\_matrix, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"edge{-}sum formula:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(energy\_sum, }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"smallest Laplacian eigenvalues:"}\NormalTok{, np.}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(np.linalg.eigvalsh(L)[:}\DecValTok{5}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
f^T L f: 9.61
edge-sum formula: 9.61
smallest Laplacian eigenvalues: [-0.        0.245177  0.686777  1.208809  2.      ]
\end{verbatim}

The two values agree up to numerical precision. This verifies the
identity

\[
f^T L f = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j} A_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2.
\]

\section{23.18 Python example: random walk and
PageRank}\label{python-example-random-walk-and-pagerank}

We now convert the adjacency matrix to a row-stochastic transition
matrix.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ row\_stochastic(A):}
\NormalTok{    row\_sums }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, keepdims}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros\_like(A, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_sums[:, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}
\NormalTok{    P[mask] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A[mask] }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ row\_sums[mask]}
\NormalTok{    P[}\OperatorTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{mask, }\OperatorTok{\textasciitilde{}}\NormalTok{mask] }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{1.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ P}

\NormalTok{P }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ row\_stochastic(A)}

\NormalTok{alpha }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.85}
\NormalTok{n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{v }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.ones(n) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ n}
\NormalTok{p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ v.copy()}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{100}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    p }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (p }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ P) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ v}

\NormalTok{pagerank }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{: vocab, }\StringTok{"pagerank"}\NormalTok{: p\}).sort\_values(}\StringTok{"pagerank"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(pagerank.head(}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{).to\_string(index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{))}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"sum of scores:"}\NormalTok{, }\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(p.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(), }\DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
     word  pagerank
   models  0.112016
 language  0.084972
  context  0.072496
   tokens  0.072312
 networks  0.062037
    graph  0.056305
represent  0.053312
     with  0.050625
sum of scores: 1.0
\end{verbatim}

PageRank is a smoothed centrality measure. In a word graph, high
PageRank words are connected to many other important words, but this
should not be confused with semantic importance in every task.

\section{23.19 Python example: label
propagation}\label{python-example-label-propagation}

Suppose we label a few words as mathematical/technical and a few as
nontechnical. Label propagation spreads these scores across the graph.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ word, value }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"graph"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"probability"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"neural"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"tokens"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"uncertainty"}\NormalTok{: }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"and"}\NormalTok{: }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"with"}\NormalTok{: }\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{0.5}
\NormalTok{\}.items():}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ word }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ index:}
\NormalTok{        Y[index[word]] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ value}

\NormalTok{alpha }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.7}
\NormalTok{F }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Y.copy()}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ \_ }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{20}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    F }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ alpha }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ (P }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ F) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ alpha) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ Y}

\NormalTok{propagation }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{: vocab, }\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{: F\}).sort\_values(}\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(propagation.head(}\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{).to\_string(index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
       word    score
     neural 0.517939
      graph 0.480214
probability 0.426963
uncertainty 0.366963
   networks 0.239906
   describe 0.218831
       pass 0.213894
   messages 0.158832
     models 0.143921
  represent 0.128022
\end{verbatim}

The formula is simple, but the modeling choices matter. If the graph is
noisy, propagation spreads noise. If the graph is meaningful,
propagation spreads useful information.

\section{23.20 Python example: one graph convolution
layer}\label{python-example-one-graph-convolution-layer}

We implement one normalized graph convolution layer

\[
H' = \operatorname{ReLU}(\tilde S H W).
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{7243}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{A\_tilde }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ np.eye(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(vocab))}
\NormalTok{d\_tilde }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ A\_tilde.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{D\_inv\_sqrt }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.diag(}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(np.maximum(d\_tilde, }\FloatTok{1e{-}12}\NormalTok{)))}
\NormalTok{S\_tilde }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ D\_inv\_sqrt }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ A\_tilde }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ D\_inv\_sqrt}

\CommentTok{\# Simple node features: degree, PageRank, and seeded label score.}
\NormalTok{H }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.column\_stack([}
\NormalTok{    degrees }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(degrees.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(), }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    p }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ p.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(),}
\NormalTok{    Y}
\NormalTok{])}

\NormalTok{W }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.5}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(H.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{], }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{Z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ S\_tilde }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ H }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ W}
\NormalTok{H\_next }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(Z, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{)}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"H shape:"}\NormalTok{, H.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"W shape:"}\NormalTok{, W.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"H\_next shape:"}\NormalTok{, H\_next.shape)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(pd.DataFrame(H\_next, index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{vocab, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\StringTok{"coord\_1"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"coord\_2"}\NormalTok{]).head())}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
H shape: (19, 3)
W shape: (3, 2)
H_next shape: (19, 2)
          coord_1   coord_2
and           0.0  0.000000
context       0.0  0.000000
cooccur       0.0  0.000000
describe      0.0  0.429837
graph         0.0  0.341356
\end{verbatim}

This example is not meant to train a useful model. It is meant to make
the dimensions visible.

\section{23.21 Python example: relation-specific knowledge graph
matrices}\label{python-example-relation-specific-knowledge-graph-matrices}

For a small knowledge graph, we can build one adjacency matrix per
relation.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{triples }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"BERT"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"uses"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"self\_attention"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"Transformer"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"uses"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"self\_attention"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"NLP"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"uses"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"probability"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"NLP"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"uses"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"linear\_algebra"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"BERT"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"is\_a"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"Transformer"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"Transformer"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"is\_a"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"neural\_model"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"GCN"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"is\_a"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"graph\_model"}\NormalTok{),}
\NormalTok{    (}\StringTok{"GAT"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"is\_a"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"graph\_model"}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{entities }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{([h }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ h, r, t }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ triples] }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ [t }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ h, r, t }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ triples]))}
\NormalTok{relations }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{sorted}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{set}\NormalTok{(r }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ h, r, t }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ triples))}
\NormalTok{ent\_index }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{e: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, e }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(entities)\}}
\NormalTok{rel\_index }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{r: i }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, r }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(relations)\}}

\NormalTok{A\_rel }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(relations), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(entities), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(entities)))}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ h, r, t }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ triples:}
\NormalTok{    A\_rel[rel\_index[r], ent\_index[h], ent\_index[t]] }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}

\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"relations:"}\NormalTok{, relations)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"entities:"}\NormalTok{, entities)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"adjacency tensor shape:"}\NormalTok{, A\_rel.shape)}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ r }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ relations:}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"}\CharTok{\textbackslash{}n}\StringTok{Relation:"}\NormalTok{, r)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(pd.DataFrame(A\_rel[rel\_index[r]], index}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{entities, columns}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{entities).astype(}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}
