\section{23.22 Python example: graph attention
weights}\label{python-example-graph-attention-weights}

The following code computes attention weights over graph neighbors for
one node. It mirrors the attention formulas from Chapters 13 and 14 but
restricts the normalization to neighbors.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Use H as node features from the previous example.}
\NormalTok{q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{H.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{k }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{H.shape[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{node }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ index[}\StringTok{"models"}\NormalTok{] }\ControlFlowTok{if} \StringTok{"models"} \KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ index }\ControlFlowTok{else} \DecValTok{0}
\NormalTok{neighbors }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.where(A[node] }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ neighbors:}
\NormalTok{    score }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (H[node] }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ q) }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ (H[j] }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ k)}
\NormalTok{    scores.append(score)}
\NormalTok{scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array(scores)}
\NormalTok{weights }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(scores }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ scores.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{())}
\NormalTok{weights }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ weights }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ weights.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}

\NormalTok{attn\_table }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"neighbor"}\NormalTok{: [vocab[j] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ neighbors],}
    \StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{: scores,}
    \StringTok{"attention\_weight"}\NormalTok{: weights}
\NormalTok{\}).sort\_values(}\StringTok{"attention\_weight"}\NormalTok{, ascending}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\StringTok{"central node:"}\NormalTok{, vocab[node])}
\BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(attn\_table.to\_string(index}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{))}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
central node: models
   neighbor     score  attention_weight
   language -0.055853          0.187169
  represent -0.235786          0.156347
        use -0.254089          0.153511

Graph attention is local self-attention on a specified graph. The graph
determines which attention scores are even allowed to exist.

\section{23.23 AI-assisted learning
activity}\label{ai-assisted-learning-activity}

Use an AI assistant as a graph-construction critic.

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Give the assistant a small NLP problem, such as course-resource
  recommendation, document search, sentiment lexicon expansion, or
  mathematical-concept mapping.
\item
  Ask for three possible graph constructions.
\item
  For each construction, require the assistant to state:

  \begin{itemize}
  \tightlist
  \item
    node types;
  \item
    edge types;
  \item
    edge weights;
  \item
    whether the graph is directed;
  \item
    what information is lost;
  \item
    what bias the graph introduces.
  \end{itemize}
\item
  Ask for the adjacency matrix form and the corresponding
  message-passing update.
\item
  Critique the answer manually.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{AI caution}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

An AI tool may suggest a graph because it sounds modern. Your job is to
ask whether the graph represents a real relation in the data and whether
the proposed edge weights estimate anything meaningful.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{23.24 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-12}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Confusing a graph with a drawing.} The graph is the pair
  \((\mathcal V,\mathcal E)\) and its weights, not the plotted layout.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting direction.} A dependency relation and its reverse
  are not the same unless explicitly symmetrized.
\item
  \textbf{Using unnormalized adjacency blindly.} High-degree nodes can
  dominate message passing.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring edge labels.} Knowledge graph relations often require
  relation-specific parameters.
\item
  \textbf{Over-smoothing.} Too many propagation layers can make node
  representations too similar.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming graph edges are true semantics.} Edges are
  constructed from data and assumptions; they may be noisy.
\end{enumerate}

\section{23.25 Worked calculation}\label{worked-calculation-5}

Consider the undirected path graph with three nodes:

\[
1-2-3.
\]

The adjacency matrix is

\[
A=\begin{bmatrix}
0 & 1 & 0\\
1 & 0 & 1\\
0 & 1 & 0
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The degree matrix is

\[
D=\begin{bmatrix}
1 & 0 & 0\\
0 & 2 & 0\\
0 & 0 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

The Laplacian is

\[
L=D-A=
\begin{bmatrix}
1 & -1 & 0\\
-1 & 2 & -1\\
0 & -1 & 1
\end{bmatrix}.
\]

For a signal \(f=(1,0,-1)^T\),

\[
Lf = (1,0,-1)^T,
\]

so

\[
f^TLf = 2.
\]

Using the edge formula gives

\[
(1-0)^2 + (0-(-1))^2 = 2.
\]

Thus the Laplacian energy equals the sum of squared differences over
undirected edges.

\section{23.26 Exercises}\label{exercises-22}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Adjacency matrix.} Construct the adjacency matrix for a
  dependency graph with five tokens. State clearly whether \(A_{ij}=1\)
  means \(i\to j\) or \(j\to i\).
\item
  \textbf{Laplacian identity.} Prove that
  \(f^TLf = \frac{1}{2}\sum_{i,j}A_{ij}(f_i-f_j)^2\) for an undirected
  weighted graph.
\item
  \textbf{Bipartite text graph.} Given a \(3\times 4\) document-term
  matrix \(X\), write the block adjacency matrix of the document-term
  graph.
\item
  \textbf{Two-step walks.} Show that \(XX^T\) counts weighted two-step
  paths from documents to documents through terms.
\item
  \textbf{Random walk.} For a small graph, compute \(P=D^{-1}A\) and run
  two steps of a random walk by hand.
\item
  \textbf{Label propagation.} Derive the fixed-point formula for
  \(F^* = \alpha S F^* + (1-\alpha)Y\).
\item
  \textbf{Graph convolution.} Check the dimensions in
  \(H'=\sigma(\tilde S H W)\) when \(H\in R^{n\times d}\) and
  \(W\in R^{d\times m}\).
\item
  \textbf{Graph attention.} Explain how graph attention differs from
  Transformer self-attention.
\item
  \textbf{Knowledge graph.} Build relation-specific adjacency matrices
  for a set of five triples.
\item
  \textbf{Model critique.} Choose an NLP task and compare a sequence
  model, a bag-of-words model, and a graph model for that task.
\end{enumerate}

Build a small graph-based course-resource recommender.

  webpage or policy document;

Suggested edge types:

\begin{itemize}

  question mentions topic;

Tasks:

\section{23.29 What to remember}\label{what-to-remember-8}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A graph representation is a modeling decision about relations.
\item
  Matrices make graph structure computable: \(A\), \(D\), \(L\), \(P\),
  and \(S\).
\item
  The Laplacian measures variation of signals across edges.
\item
  Bipartite document-term graphs connect vector-space NLP with graph
  walks.
\item
  Message passing is local aggregation followed by transformation.
\item
  Graph attention is attention restricted by an edge set.
\item
  Knowledge graphs require relation-specific structure.
\item
  Graph methods are powerful when edges represent meaningful relations
  and risky when edges are noisy or arbitrary.
\end{itemize}

\section{23.30 Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-13}

Classical graph-based thinking in NLP is connected to dependency parsing
and information retrieval in Manning and Schuetze (1999), Jurafsky and
Martin (2024), and Manning et al. (2008). Spectral graph ideas are
treated in Chung (1997). PageRank was introduced in Brin and Page
(1998). Graph convolution and graph neural message passing are
associated with Kipf and Welling (2017a) and Hamilton et al. (2017).
Graph attention is developed in Velickovic et al. (2018). Knowledge
graph embeddings are surveyed in Wang et al. (2017).

\chapter{Topology and Geometry of Language
Representations}\label{topology-and-geometry-of-language-representations}

Metric spaces, persistent homology, and representation diagnostics

\hfill\break

Modern NLP represents words, sentences, documents, and prompts as
high-dimensional vectors. Once language objects become vectors, a corpus
becomes a point cloud, a similarity graph, or a finite metric space.
Linear algebra explains directions, projections, and low-rank structure;
probability explains uncertainty and likelihood; topology asks a
complementary question: what qualitative shape is present in the
representation space? This chapter develops the topology and geometry of
language representations from a clean mathematical point of view, with
emphasis on finite metric spaces, neighborhood graphs, simplicial
complexes, persistent homology, and representation diagnostics.

\section{24.1 Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-23}

After reading this chapter, students should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  view a collection of language embeddings as a finite metric space;
\item
  construct neighborhood graphs and Vietoris--Rips complexes from
  pairwise distances;
\item
  compute and interpret Betti numbers in dimensions 0 and 1;
\item
  explain persistent homology as a multiscale summary of shape;
\item
  distinguish geometric summaries from topological summaries;
\item
  understand how clustering, loops, anisotropy, and intrinsic dimension
  appear in embedding spaces;
\item
  use persistent features carefully as diagnostics rather than as
  automatic semantic truths;
\item
  implement small topological summaries from scratch in Python;
\item
  use AI tools to critique representation geometry and topology
  responsibly.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Guiding question}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

What is the shape of a language representation space?

A linear-algebra answer might examine singular values, principal
components, and distances. A statistical answer might estimate class
separation or uncertainty. A topological answer asks whether the data
form connected components, branching structures, loops, voids, or other
multiscale patterns that persist across distance thresholds.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{24.2 From embeddings to point
clouds}\label{from-embeddings-to-point-clouds}

Let \(T\) be a collection of language objects. Depending on the problem,
the objects may be:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  words in a vocabulary;
\item
  tokens in one sentence;
\item
  sentence embeddings from a corpus;
\item
  document embeddings;
\item
  contextual token embeddings from one layer of a Transformer;
\item
  prompts, questions, answers, or retrieved chunks.
\end{itemize}

An embedding model is a map

\[
f_\theta:T\to R^d.
\]

For objects \(t_1,\ldots,t_n\), define

\[
x_i=f_\theta(t_i)\in R^d,
\qquad
X=\{x_1,\ldots,x_n\}\subset R^d.
\]

Thus a finite collection of language objects becomes a finite point
cloud. The point cloud may be studied by Euclidean distances,

\[
d_E(x_i,x_j)=\|x_i-x_j\|_2,
\]

cosine distances,

\[
d_C(x_i,x_j)=1-\frac{x_i^T x_j}{\|x_i\|_2\|x_j\|_2},
\]

or other task-dependent dissimilarities.

\textbf{Finite metric-space viewpoint.} For topological data analysis,
the central object is often not the coordinate matrix
\(X\in R^{n\times d}\) itself, but the pairwise distance matrix

\[
D=(d_{ij}),
\qquad
d_{ij}=d(x_i,x_j).
\]

Many topological constructions use only \(D\), so they can be applied to
Euclidean embeddings, cosine embeddings, edit-distance spaces, or
learned similarity spaces.

\section{24.3 Geometry versus topology}\label{geometry-versus-topology}

Geometry studies quantities such as lengths, angles, curvature,
projections, and distances. Topology studies qualitative features that
are stable under continuous deformation, such as connected components
and holes.

For language embeddings, geometry asks questions such as:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Which sentence is nearest to a query?
\item
  Which direction separates two topics?
\item
  How much variance is explained by the first few principal components?
\item
  Are embeddings anisotropic?
\end{itemize}

Topology asks questions such as:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  How many connected clusters appear at a given scale?
\item
  Do clusters merge gradually or suddenly?
\item
  Is there evidence of loop-like structure among semantic groups?
\item
  Does the same qualitative shape persist across several scales?
\end{itemize}

A simple example helps. Suppose sentence embeddings lie approximately on
a circle because the sentences describe a cyclic process such as
morning, afternoon, evening, night, and morning again. PCA may show a
two-dimensional plane. Clustering may find local groups. Persistent
homology can detect a one-dimensional loop.

\section{24.4 Neighborhood graphs}\label{neighborhood-graphs}

A first topological construction is the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood
graph. Given a finite metric space \((X,d)\) and a scale parameter
\(\varepsilon\ge 0\), define a graph

\[
G_\varepsilon=(V,E_\varepsilon),
\qquad
V=\{1,\ldots,n\},
\]

where

\[
(i,j)\in E_\varepsilon
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
d(x_i,x_j)\le \varepsilon.
\]

As \(\varepsilon\) increases, the graph changes:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  for very small \(\varepsilon\), every point is isolated;
\item
  at moderate \(\varepsilon\), nearby points form local clusters;
\item
  at larger \(\varepsilon\), clusters merge;
\item
  for sufficiently large \(\varepsilon\), the graph becomes connected.
\end{itemize}

The number of connected components is the zeroth Betti number:

\[
\beta_0(G_\varepsilon)=\text{number of connected components of }G_\varepsilon.
\]

For a graph, the number of independent cycles is the graph cycle rank:

\[
\beta_1^{\mathrm{graph}}(G_\varepsilon)=|E_\varepsilon|-|V|+\beta_0(G_\varepsilon).
\]

This graph quantity counts cycles before considering whether triangular
cycles should be filled in. Persistent homology refines this idea by
using simplicial complexes.

\section{24.5 Simplicial complexes}\label{simplicial-complexes}

A simplicial complex is a collection of finite subsets closed under
taking subsets. Its elements are called simplices.

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  A 0-simplex is a vertex.
\item
  A 1-simplex is an edge.
\item
  A 2-simplex is a filled triangle.
\item
  A 3-simplex is a filled tetrahedron.
\end{itemize}

If \(\sigma\) is a simplex and \(\tau\subseteq \sigma\), then \(\tau\)
must also be a simplex. This closure condition is important: if a filled
triangle is present, then its three edges and three vertices must be
present.

For a finite metric space, the most common construction is the
Vietoris--Rips complex.

\textbf{Vietoris--Rips complex.} Given \((X,d)\) and
\(\varepsilon\ge 0\), the Vietoris--Rips complex
\(\operatorname{VR}_\varepsilon(X)\) contains a simplex
\(\{i_0,\ldots,i_k\}\) whenever all pairwise distances are at most
\(\varepsilon\):

\[
d(x_{i_a},x_{i_b})\le \varepsilon
\quad
\text{for all }a,b.
\]

Equivalently, \(\operatorname{VR}_\varepsilon(X)\) is the clique complex
of the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood graph.

This construction is useful for language embeddings because it converts
similarity information into a multiscale combinatorial object.

\section{24.6 Betti numbers}\label{betti-numbers}

Betti numbers count independent topological features. Informally:

\[
\beta_0 = \text{number of connected components},
\]

\[
\beta_1 = \text{number of independent one-dimensional loops},
\]

\[
\beta_2 = \text{number of independent two-dimensional voids}.
\]

For a graph without filled triangles, the formula

\[
\beta_1=|E|-|V|+\beta_0
\]

counts independent graph cycles. For a simplicial complex, some graph
cycles become boundaries of filled triangles and therefore should not
count as holes.

For a 2-dimensional simplicial complex with vertices, edges, and
triangles, one can compute

\[
\beta_1 = \dim \ker \partial_1 - \operatorname{rank}\partial_2,
\]

where

\[
\partial_1:C_1\to C_0
\]

maps oriented edges to differences of endpoints, and

\[
\partial_2:C_2\to C_1
\]

maps oriented triangles to signed sums of boundary edges.

Since

\[
\dim\ker \partial_1 = |E| - \operatorname{rank}\partial_1,
\]

and for a graph

\[
\operatorname{rank}\partial_1 = |V|-\beta_0,
\]

we get

\[
\beta_1
=
|E|-|V|+\beta_0-\operatorname{rank}\partial_2.
\]

This formula shows why filled triangles matter: the rank of
\(\partial_2\) subtracts cycles that have become triangle boundaries.

\section{24.7 Filtrations and persistent
homology}\label{filtrations-and-persistent-homology}

A single value of \(\varepsilon\) is arbitrary. Persistent homology
studies all scales at once. Since

\[
\varepsilon_1\le \varepsilon_2
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\operatorname{VR}_{\varepsilon_1}(X)\subseteq \operatorname{VR}_{\varepsilon_2}(X),
\]

we obtain a nested sequence

\[
\operatorname{VR}_{\varepsilon_1}(X)
\subseteq
\operatorname{VR}_{\varepsilon_2}(X)
\subseteq
\cdots
\subseteq
\operatorname{VR}_{\varepsilon_m}(X).
\]

This is called a filtration.

As \(\varepsilon\) increases, features appear and disappear. A connected
component is born when a point appears and dies when it merges with an
older component. A loop is born when edges close a cycle and dies when
the loop becomes filled by triangles.

A persistent homology summary records intervals

\[
[b_i,d_i),
\]

where \(b_i\) is the birth scale and \(d_i\) is the death scale of a
feature. The persistence length is

\[
d_i-b_i.
\]

Longer intervals are usually interpreted as more stable multiscale
features. Short intervals are often interpreted as local noise, although
this interpretation depends on the problem.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-warning-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-warning-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-warning-color}{\faExclamationTriangle}\hspace{0.5em}{Interpretation warning}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A persistent loop in an embedding space is not automatically a
linguistic fact. It may come from semantic structure, sampling design,
normalization, model architecture, dimensionality reduction, or
numerical artifacts. Topology gives diagnostics; interpretation still
requires domain reasoning.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{24.8 Why topology can help
NLP}\label{why-topology-can-help-nlp}

Topological summaries are useful because they are less tied to a
particular coordinate system than raw embedding coordinates. If two
embedding spaces are transformed by rotations or small metric
perturbations, their large-scale topological summaries may remain
similar.

In NLP, topology can help analyze:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  whether sentence embeddings form topic clusters;
\item
  whether generated texts cover the same representation shape as human
  texts;
\item
  whether contextual embeddings collapse into a narrow cone;
\item
  whether different layers of a Transformer gradually change
  representation geometry;
\item
  whether retrieval chunks form disconnected semantic islands;
\item
  whether class labels align with connected components or cut across
  them.
\end{itemize}

This is especially useful for mathematical NLP because it gives students
a way to ask structural questions beyond accuracy.

\section{24.9 Local dimension and
anisotropy}\label{local-dimension-and-anisotropy}

Topology should be combined with geometry. Two important geometric
diagnostics are local intrinsic dimension and anisotropy.

Let \(x_i\) be a point and let \(N_k(i)\) be its \(k\) nearest
neighbors. Let

\[
Y_i = \{x_j-x_i:j\in N_k(i)\}.
\]

The local covariance matrix is

\[
C_i = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{j\in N_k(i)} (x_j-x_i)(x_j-x_i)^T.
\]

If the eigenvalues of \(C_i\) are

\[
\lambda_1\ge \lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_d\ge 0,
\]

then the number of large eigenvalues gives a local dimension heuristic.
For example, a curve has approximately one large local eigenvalue, a
surface has approximately two, and a full-dimensional cloud has many.

Anisotropy means that vectors concentrate in a narrow cone or a few
dominant directions. One diagnostic is the spectrum of the centered
covariance matrix

\[
C=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-\bar x)(x_i-\bar x)^T.
\]

A very steep spectrum indicates that the cloud is dominated by a few
directions. This can affect nearest-neighbor retrieval and apparent
topological structure.

\section{24.10 Persistent homology and representation
layers}\label{persistent-homology-and-representation-layers}

For a Transformer, each layer produces a representation matrix

\[
H^{(\ell)}\in R^{T\times d},
\]

for tokens in a sentence, or a collection of sentence embeddings across
a dataset. We can treat the rows of \(H^{(\ell)}\) as a point cloud and
compare topological summaries across layers.

For each layer \(\ell\), one may compute a persistence summary

\[
\operatorname{PH}_k(H^{(\ell)}),
\]

where \(k=0\) studies components and \(k=1\) studies loops. This gives a
layerwise diagnostic:

\[
\ell \mapsto \operatorname{PH}_k(H^{(\ell)}).
\]

Possible observations include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  early layers preserve local lexical neighborhoods;
\item
  middle layers separate syntactic or semantic roles;
\item
  later layers may collapse task-relevant examples into decision
  regions;
\item
  instruction-tuned models may reshape prompt and answer
  representations.
\end{itemize}

These are hypotheses to test, not universal laws.

\section{24.11 Stability viewpoint}\label{stability-viewpoint}

A major reason persistent homology is attractive is stability.
Informally, if two point clouds are close as metric spaces, then their
persistence diagrams are close. The precise form of stability depends on
the construction and the metric used on diagrams.

Let \(D_X\) and \(D_Y\) be persistence diagrams for two point clouds. A
common diagram distance is the bottleneck distance

\[
d_B(D_X,D_Y),
\]

which matches points in one diagram to points in the other, allowing
points to be matched to the diagonal. The diagonal represents
zero-persistence features.

The stability principle says, informally,

\[
\text{small perturbation of distances}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\text{small perturbation of persistence diagrams}.
\]

For NLP, this matters because embeddings are noisy and model-dependent.
A diagnostic that changes wildly under tiny perturbations is not
reliable.

\section{24.12 Mapper and semantic
organization}\label{mapper-and-semantic-organization}

Another topological method is Mapper. Mapper starts with:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  a point cloud \(X\);
\item
  a filter function \(g:X\to R^q\);
\item
  a cover of the filter range;
\item
  a clustering method inside each cover element.
\end{enumerate}

The output is a graph whose nodes are local clusters and whose edges
indicate overlap. In NLP, possible filter functions include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  first principal component score;
\item
  sentiment score;
\item
  document length;
\item
  perplexity under a language model;
\item
  retrieval score;
\item
  topic probability;
\item
  projection onto a semantic direction.
\end{itemize}

Mapper can reveal branching or circular organization, but it has tuning
choices: cover size, overlap, clustering method, and distance metric.

\section{24.13 A worked example: six sentence
embeddings}\label{a-worked-example-six-sentence-embeddings}

Suppose six short sentence embeddings have pairwise distances arranged
so that points \(1,2,3\) are close to each other and points \(4,5,6\)
are close to each other, with a larger distance between the two groups.

At a small scale \(\varepsilon\), all six points are disconnected:

\[
\beta_0=6,
\qquad
\beta_1=0.
\]

At a moderate scale, each group forms a triangle. If the triangles are
filled in the Rips complex, each group is contractible:

\[
\beta_0=2,
\qquad
\beta_1=0.
\]

At a larger scale, the two groups connect by at least one edge:

\[
\beta_0=1.
\]

This is a topological version of clustering. The death times of
connected components encode inter-cluster distances. In dimension 0,
persistent homology is closely related to single-linkage hierarchical
clustering.

\section{24.14 Interactive: Vietoris--Rips complex for a toy embedding
cloud}\label{interactive-vietorisrips-complex-for-a-toy-embedding-cloud}

The interactive below uses a two-dimensional toy embedding cloud with
two semantic arcs and a bridge point. Move the distance threshold
\(\varepsilon\). The plot draws the neighborhood graph. The summary
reports connected components, edges, filled triangles, and an exact
\(\beta_1\) value for the clique complex up to dimension 2.

\section{24.16 Python example: neighborhood graph and
components}\label{python-example-neighborhood-graph-and-components}

The following code builds the \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood graph and
counts connected components.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ epsilon\_edges(D, eps):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ D.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n):}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(i }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, n):}
            \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ D[i, j] }\OperatorTok{\textless{}=}\NormalTok{ eps:}
\NormalTok{                edges.append((i, j))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ edges}

\KeywordTok{class}\NormalTok{ UnionFind:}
    \KeywordTok{def} \FunctionTok{\_\_init\_\_}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{, n):}
        \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{list}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n))}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ find(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{, a):}
        \ControlFlowTok{while} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent[a] }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ a:}
            \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent[a] }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent[}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent[a]]}
\NormalTok{            a }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent[a]}
        \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ a}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ union(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{, a, b):}
\NormalTok{        ra, rb }\OperatorTok{=} \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.find(a), }\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.find(b)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ ra }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ rb:}
            \VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent[rb] }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ra}

    \KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ count\_components(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{):}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(\{}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.find(i) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(}\VariableTok{self}\NormalTok{.parent))\})}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ beta0\_graph(D, eps):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ D.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    uf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ UnionFind(n)}
\NormalTok{    edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ epsilon\_edges(D, eps)}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i, j }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ edges:}
\NormalTok{        uf.union(i, j)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ uf.count\_components(), edges}

\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ eps }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.5}\NormalTok{]:}
\NormalTok{    b0, edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ beta0\_graph(D, eps)}
    \BuiltInTok{print}\NormalTok{(}\SpecialStringTok{f"epsilon=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{eps}\SpecialCharTok{:.1f\}}\SpecialStringTok{, edges=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(edges)}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{, beta0=}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{b0}\SpecialCharTok{\}}\SpecialStringTok{"}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
epsilon=0.4, edges=0, beta0=8
epsilon=0.8, edges=4, beta0=4
epsilon=1.1, edges=8, beta0=1
epsilon=1.5, edges=15, beta0=1
\end{verbatim}

\section{24.17 Python example: Betti numbers for a Rips complex up to
dimension
2}\label{python-example-betti-numbers-for-a-rips-complex-up-to-dimension-2}

Now we include filled triangles. The function below computes \(\beta_0\)
and \(\beta_1\) for the clique complex up to dimension 2.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ rips\_edges\_triangles(D, eps):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ D.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ epsilon\_edges(D, eps)}
\NormalTok{    edge\_index }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{edge: k }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ k, edge }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(edges)\}}
\NormalTok{    triangles }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(n):}
        \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(i }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, n):}
            \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ k }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(j }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, n):}
                \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ ((i, j) }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ edge\_index }\KeywordTok{and}
\NormalTok{                    (i, k) }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ edge\_index }\KeywordTok{and}
\NormalTok{                    (j, k) }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ edge\_index):}
\NormalTok{                    triangles.append((i, j, k))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ edges, edge\_index, triangles}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ rank\_matrix(A, tol}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{1e{-}10}\NormalTok{):}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ A.size }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \DecValTok{0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.matrix\_rank(A, tol}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{tol)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ betti\_0\_1\_rips(D, eps):}
\NormalTok{    n }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ D.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    beta0, edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ beta0\_graph(D, eps)}
\NormalTok{    edges, edge\_index, triangles }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rips\_edges\_triangles(D, eps)}

\NormalTok{    graph\_cycle\_rank }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(edges) }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ n }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ beta0}

    \CommentTok{\# Boundary matrix partial\_2: C\_2 {-}\textgreater{} C\_1.}
\NormalTok{    B2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.zeros((}\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(edges), }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(triangles)))}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ col, (i, j, k) }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{enumerate}\NormalTok{(triangles):}
        \CommentTok{\# oriented boundary: [j,k] {-} [i,k] + [i,j]}
\NormalTok{        B2[edge\_index[(j, k)], col] }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{        B2[edge\_index[(i, k)], col] }\OperatorTok{=} \OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}
\NormalTok{        B2[edge\_index[(i, j)], col] }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{1}

\NormalTok{    rank\_b2 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rank\_matrix(B2)}
\NormalTok{    beta1 }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ graph\_cycle\_rank }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ rank\_b2}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ \{}
        \StringTok{"epsilon"}\NormalTok{: eps,}
        \StringTok{"vertices"}\NormalTok{: n,}
        \StringTok{"edges"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(edges),}
        \StringTok{"triangles"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(triangles),}
        \StringTok{"beta0"}\NormalTok{: beta0,}
        \StringTok{"graph\_cycle\_rank"}\NormalTok{: graph\_cycle\_rank,}
        \StringTok{"rank\_boundary\_2"}\NormalTok{: rank\_b2,}
        \StringTok{"beta1"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(}\BuiltInTok{round}\NormalTok{(beta1)),}
\NormalTok{    \}}

\NormalTok{summary }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [betti\_0\_1\_rips(D, eps) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ eps }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ [}\FloatTok{0.4}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.8}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.5}\NormalTok{]]}
\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(summary)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\endhead

\endlastfoot

\section{24.19 Python example: local intrinsic
dimension}\label{python-example-local-intrinsic-dimension}

We estimate local dimension by looking at the spectrum of local
covariance matrices.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ local\_dimension\_scores(X, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    D }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(((X[:, }\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ X[}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :, :]) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ i }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(X.shape[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]):}
\NormalTok{        nn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.argsort(D[i])[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:k}\OperatorTok{+}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{        Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ X[nn] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ X[i]}
\NormalTok{        C }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (Y.T }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ Y) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ k}
\NormalTok{        eigvals }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.eigvalsh(C)[::}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{        ratio }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ eigvals[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ eigvals.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ eigvals.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ np.nan}
\NormalTok{        scores.append(\{}
            \StringTok{"point"}\NormalTok{: labels[i],}
            \StringTok{"lambda1"}\NormalTok{: eigvals[}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{],}
            \StringTok{"lambda2"}\NormalTok{: eigvals[}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{],}
            \StringTok{"lambda1\_fraction"}\NormalTok{: ratio,}
\NormalTok{        \})}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(scores)}

\NormalTok{local\_dimension\_scores(X, k}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{3}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{24.20 Python example: topology as a representation
diagnostic}\label{python-example-topology-as-a-representation-diagnostic}

The next code compares a circular cloud and a two-cluster cloud. Both
may have similar variance, but their topological summaries behave
differently.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{24}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{angles }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linspace(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{np.pi, }\DecValTok{18}\NormalTok{, endpoint}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{False}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{circle }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.c\_[np.cos(angles), np.sin(angles)] }\OperatorTok{+} \FloatTok{0.05} \OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{18}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}

\NormalTok{cluster\_a }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(loc}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{], scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.18}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{9}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{cluster\_b }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.normal(loc}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{[}\FloatTok{1.0}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.0}\NormalTok{], scale}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.18}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{(}\DecValTok{9}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}
\NormalTok{clusters }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.vstack([cluster\_a, cluster\_b])}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ distance\_matrix(X):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(((X[:, }\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :] }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ X[}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{, :, :]) }\OperatorTok{**} \DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{(axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{2}\NormalTok{))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ betti\_curve(X, eps\_grid):}
\NormalTok{    D }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ distance\_matrix(X)}
\NormalTok{    rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ eps }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ eps\_grid:}
\NormalTok{        rows.append(betti\_0\_1\_rips(D, }\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(eps)))}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(rows)}

\NormalTok{eps\_grid }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linspace(}\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{7}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{circle\_curve }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ betti\_curve(circle, eps\_grid)}
\NormalTok{cluster\_curve }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ betti\_curve(clusters, eps\_grid)}

\NormalTok{comparison }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"epsilon"}\NormalTok{: eps\_grid,}
    \StringTok{"circle\_beta0"}\NormalTok{: circle\_curve[}\StringTok{"beta0"}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"circle\_beta1"}\NormalTok{: circle\_curve[}\StringTok{"beta1"}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"clusters\_beta0"}\NormalTok{: cluster\_curve[}\StringTok{"beta0"}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"clusters\_beta1"}\NormalTok{: cluster\_curve[}\StringTok{"beta1"}\NormalTok{],}
\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{comparison}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\endlastfoot
0 & 0.15 & 18 & 0 & 8 & 0 \\
1 & 0.25 & 18 & 0 & 7 & 0 \\
2 & 0.35 & 7 & 0 & 4 & 0 \\
3 & 0.45 & 1 & 0 & 2 & 0 \\
4 & 0.55 & 1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\
5 & 0.65 & 1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\
6 & 0.75 & 1 & 1 & 2 & 0 \\
\end{longtable}
}

The circular cloud tends to develop a one-dimensional loop over an
intermediate range of scales. The two-cluster cloud emphasizes component
merging instead.

\section{24.21 Python Plotly
visualization}\label{python-plotly-visualization}

The following code produces a Plotly visualization in Python. It is

\section{24.22 AI-assisted learning: topology audit
prompts}\label{ai-assisted-learning-topology-audit-prompts}

AI tools can be helpful for brainstorming diagnostics, but they should
not replace mathematical checks. Students can use the following prompts:

\textbf{Prompt 1: representation-space audit}

I have sentence embeddings from two models. Suggest a mathematical plan
for comparing their geometry and topology. Include distance choices,
normalization choices, PCA/SVD diagnostics, connected-component
persistence, and possible failure modes.

\textbf{Prompt 2: interpretation critique}

A persistent loop appears in a sentence-embedding point cloud. Give at
least five possible explanations, including semantic explanations and
artifact explanations. For each explanation, propose a test.

\textbf{Prompt 3: code review}

Review my Python code for a Vietoris--Rips complex. Check whether I
incorrectly count graph cycles as topological loops after triangles are
filled. Explain the role of the boundary matrix \(\partial_2\).

\section{24.23 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-13}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Confusing a graph cycle with a topological loop.} A triangle
  in a graph is a cycle, but in a Rips complex it is usually filled, so
  it does not contribute to \(\beta_1\).
\item
  \textbf{Using dimensionality reduction as evidence of topology.} A
  loop in a two-dimensional visualization may be introduced or destroyed
  by projection. Compute topology from the original metric when
  possible.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring normalization.} Euclidean distance and cosine
  distance can give very different filtrations.
\item
  \textbf{Overinterpreting short bars.} Low-persistence features may be
  noise or sampling artifacts.
\item
  \textbf{Forgetting sample-size effects.} Persistent homology depends
  on how densely the underlying shape is sampled.
\item
  \textbf{Treating persistent homology as a black box.} Students should
  understand vertices, edges, triangles, boundary maps, and Betti
  numbers before using a library.
\end{enumerate}

\section{24.24 Exercises}\label{exercises-23}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  Let \(X\) be four points forming the corners of a square. Compute
  \(\beta_0\) and graph cycle rank for the neighborhood graph at a scale
  where adjacent corners are connected but diagonals are not.
\item
  For the same square, decide whether the Vietoris--Rips complex has a
  one-dimensional loop at that scale.
\item
  Increase the scale until the diagonals appear. What happens to the
  Rips complex and \(\beta_1\)?
\item
  Let \(X\) be three points forming a triangle. Explain why the graph
  cycle rank is 1 but the Rips complex has \(\beta_1=0\) once the filled
  triangle appears.
\item
  Suppose two embedding models produce the same nearest-neighbor
  classification accuracy. Design a topological diagnostic that could
  still distinguish them.
\item
  Explain why cosine distance may be preferable to Euclidean distance
  for sentence embeddings that vary strongly in norm.
\item
  Derive the formula
  \(\beta_1=|E|-|V|+\beta_0-\operatorname{rank}\partial_2\) for a
  2-dimensional simplicial complex.
\item
  Construct a toy dataset of 12 points sampled from two circles. Predict
  how \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) should behave as \(\varepsilon\)
  increases.
\item
  In a retrieval system, suppose retrieved document chunks form three
  disconnected components in embedding space. Give two possible good
  interpretations and two possible bad interpretations.
\item
  Use an AI tool to generate a topological interpretation of a point
  cloud, then write a critique explaining which parts are supported by
  mathematics and which parts are speculative.
\end{enumerate}

\section{24.25 Mini-project: topology of course-advising
embeddings}\label{mini-project-topology-of-course-advising-embeddings}

Build a small corpus of 30--60 short documents about university advising
topics such as registration, transfer credit, degree requirements,
co-op, graduate electives, and academic standing. Compute embeddings
using any available method, for example TF-IDF/SVD or a sentence
embedding model. Then:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  choose a distance metric;
\item
  compute a distance matrix;
\item
  build \(\varepsilon\)-neighborhood graphs over a range of thresholds;
\item
  plot \(\beta_0\) as a function of \(\varepsilon\);
\item
  compute simple graph cycle ranks and, if possible, Rips \(\beta_1\)
  values;
\item
  compare the topology with known document categories;
\item
  write a short interpretation and a cautionary note.
\end{enumerate}

This project connects topology, retrieval, and responsible
interpretation.

\section{24.26 Lab connection}\label{lab-connection-10}

The accompanying lab should guide students through:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  constructing a point cloud from small text embeddings;
\item
  computing Euclidean and cosine distance matrices;
\item
  building neighborhood graphs;
\item
  computing connected components;
\item
  computing \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) for small Rips complexes;
\item
  plotting Betti curves;
\item
  comparing circular, clustered, and noisy point clouds;
\item
  applying the same tools to a small NLP corpus.
\end{itemize}

\section{24.27 Summary}\label{summary-6}

This chapter introduced a topological viewpoint on NLP representation
spaces. The central idea is simple: embeddings turn language objects
into points, distances turn point clouds into finite metric spaces, and
filtrations turn metric spaces into multiscale topological summaries.
Betti numbers and persistent homology provide tools for studying
connected components, loops, and other qualitative structures. These
tools are most valuable when used together with linear algebra,
probability, and domain knowledge. In mathematical NLP, topology is not
a replacement for modeling or evaluation; it is a structural lens for
asking better questions about representation spaces.

\chapter{Ethics, Bias, and Mathematical
Responsibility}\label{ethics-bias-and-mathematical-responsibility}

Fairness, uncertainty, privacy, and responsible NLP deployment

\hfill\break

Modern NLP systems are mathematical systems deployed in social
environments. A language model is trained on data, optimized under a
loss function, evaluated by metrics, and then used by people. Ethical
analysis therefore cannot be separated from mathematical analysis.
Before we can ask whether a system is fair, safe, or trustworthy, we
must specify the random variables, the population, the representation,
the target, the loss, the metric, and the deployment setting.

This chapter develops a mathematical language for responsibility in NLP.
The goal is not to reduce ethics to formulas. Rather, the goal is to
make assumptions visible. A formula can clarify what is being measured,
what is being ignored, and where statistical uncertainty enters.

\section{25.1 Learning goals}\label{learning-goals-24}

After reading this chapter, students should be able to:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  formulate bias, fairness, uncertainty, and privacy questions using
  random variables and distributions;
\item
  distinguish sampling bias, measurement bias, label bias,
  representation bias, optimization bias, and deployment bias;
\item
  compute common group fairness metrics from a confusion matrix;
\item
  explain why different fairness metrics can conflict;
\item
  analyze distribution shift using training and deployment
  distributions;
\item
  compute calibration error and understand why accuracy alone is
  insufficient;
\item
  use embedding association scores to audit representation bias;
\item
  describe selective prediction, abstention, and uncertainty-aware
  deployment;
\item
  connect mathematical clarity with responsible AI-assisted NLP
  practice.
\end{itemize}

\section{25.2 The statistical object behind a responsible NLP
system}\label{the-statistical-object-behind-a-responsible-nlp-system}

Let \(X\) denote an input text, such as a document, prompt, search
query, or conversation. Let \(Y\) denote the target variable, such as a
class label, relevance judgment, next token, toxicity rating, or
answer-quality score. Let \(A\) denote a group attribute or context
variable relevant for auditing. Depending on the application, \(A\) may
represent language variety, geography, institution type, dialect,
writing style, document source, demographic group, or another variable
that may affect model behavior.

A responsible statistical analysis begins with a joint distribution

\[
P(X,A,Y).
\]

A trained NLP model is a function, or a conditional distribution, built
from data:

\[
f_\theta:X \mapsto \widehat{Y},
\qquad
p_\theta(y\mid x).
\]

A deployment decision is usually not just the model output. It also
includes a threshold, abstention rule, retrieval rule, or human-review
rule. We therefore write the full deployed rule as

\[
d(x)=\text{decision made after observing }x.
\]

A performance claim has mathematical meaning only relative to a
distribution and a loss. If \(L(d(X),Y)\) is the loss, then the
population risk is

\[
R(d)=E_P[L(d(X),Y)].
\]

The empirical risk computed on a test set is an estimator:

\[
\widehat{R}(d)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n L(d(x_i),y_i).
\]

The key point is simple but important: \textbf{a metric is not an
ethical conclusion}. A metric is a statistic computed under assumptions.

\textbf{Responsible NLP as a mathematical workflow.}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Specify the population \(P(X,A,Y)\).
\item
  Specify the model or decision rule \(d\).
\item
  Specify the loss \(L\).
\item
  Estimate performance and uncertainty.
\item
  Audit performance conditionally on relevant subpopulations.
\item
  Study behavior under distribution shift.
\item
  Decide whether the system should be deployed, constrained, redesigned,
  or rejected.
\end{enumerate}

\section{25.3 Sources of bias in NLP}\label{sources-of-bias-in-nlp}

The word \textbf{bias} has several meanings. In statistics, bias often
refers to

\[
\operatorname{Bias}(\widehat{\theta})=E[\widehat{\theta}]-\theta.
\]

In responsible NLP, bias is broader. It often refers to systematic
error, unequal performance, stereotyped representation, or harmful
behavior. These notions are related, but not identical.

A useful mathematical decomposition is the following.

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Source
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mathematical form
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
NLP example
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Sampling bias & \(P_{\text{train}}(X,A,Y) \ne P_{\text{target}}(X,A,Y)\)
& training corpus overrepresents certain genres \\
Measurement bias & observed \(\widetilde{Y}\) differs from intended
\(Y\) & noisy toxicity labels or vague annotation instructions \\
Representation bias & \(\phi(X)\) loses relevant information &
tokenization fails for names, dialects, or multilingual text \\
Label bias & \(P(\widetilde{Y}\mid X,A)\) reflects annotator/systematic
bias & same text rated differently depending on dialect \\
Optimization bias & objective weights some errors more than others &
minimizing average loss hides subgroup error \\
Deployment bias & use differs from training/evaluation assumptions &
classifier used as a gatekeeping tool outside original context \\
Feedback bias & future data depends on earlier model decisions & search
ranking affects what users click next \\
\end{longtable}
}

For MA Applied Math and MS Statistics students, the important habit is
to ask:

\[
\text{Which distribution generated the data, and which distribution will use the model?}
\]

If those distributions differ, a test-set score may not estimate
deployment behavior.

\section{25.4 Group fairness metrics}\label{group-fairness-metrics}

Consider a binary decision problem with label \(Y\in\{0,1\}\) and
prediction \(\widehat{Y}\in\{0,1\}\). Suppose \(A\) is a group variable.
For a fixed group \(a\), define:

\[
\operatorname{TPR}_a=P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid Y=1,A=a),
\]

\[
\operatorname{FPR}_a=P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid Y=0,A=a),
\]

\[
\operatorname{PPV}_a=P(Y=1\mid \widehat{Y}=1,A=a),
\]

\[
\operatorname{SR}_a=P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid A=a),
\]

where TPR is true positive rate, FPR is false positive rate, PPV is
positive predictive value, and SR is selection rate.

Common fairness criteria include:

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}
  >{\raggedright\arraybackslash}p{(\linewidth - 4\tabcolsep) * \real{0.3333}}@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
\begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Criterion
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Mathematical condition
\end{minipage} & \begin{minipage}[b]{\linewidth}\raggedright
Interpretation
\end{minipage} \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
Demographic parity &
\(P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid A=a)=P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid A=b)\) & equal selection
rates \\
Equal opportunity &
\(P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid Y=1,A=a)=P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid Y=1,A=b)\) & equal
true positive rates \\
Equalized odds & \(\widehat{Y}\perp A\mid Y\) & equal TPR and FPR \\
Predictive parity &
\(P(Y=1\mid \widehat{Y}=1,A=a)=P(Y=1\mid \widehat{Y}=1,A=b)\) & equal
precision among selected cases \\
Calibration by group & \(P(Y=1\mid S=s,A=a)=s\) & scores mean the same
probability in each group \\
\end{longtable}
}

Here \(S\in[0,1]\) is a model score, such as a predicted probability.

These criteria are not merely technical. They encode different normative
choices. Equalizing selection rates, equalizing error rates, and
equalizing predictive values may lead to different thresholds and
different social consequences.

\section{25.5 Why fairness metrics can
conflict}\label{why-fairness-metrics-can-conflict}

Suppose the base rates differ:

\[
P(Y=1\mid A=a)\ne P(Y=1\mid A=b).
\]

If a classifier is calibrated within each group and is not perfect, then
it is generally impossible to also equalize all error rates across
groups. This is not a paradox. It is a constraint imposed by conditional
probability.

To see the tension, write the selection rate for group \(a\) as

\[
P(\widehat{Y}=1\mid A=a)
=
\operatorname{TPR}_a P(Y=1\mid A=a)
+
\operatorname{FPR}_a P(Y=0\mid A=a).
\]

If the base rate \(P(Y=1\mid A=a)\) changes across groups, then equal
TPR and equal FPR generally imply different selection rates. Conversely,
forcing equal selection rates may require unequal error rates.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-important-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-important-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-important-color}{\faExclamation}\hspace{0.5em}{Important}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

Fairness metrics should not be selected mechanically. In a real
application, one must ask what the decision means, what errors cost, who
is affected, what appeal process exists, and whether the model should be
used at all.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{25.6 Confusion matrices by
group}\label{confusion-matrices-by-group}

For a fixed group \(a\), the confusion matrix counts are

\[
\begin{array}{c|cc}
& Y=1 & Y=0 \\
\hline
\widehat{Y}=1 & TP_a & FP_a \\
\widehat{Y}=0 & FN_a & TN_a
\end{array}
\]

From these counts,

\[
\operatorname{TPR}_a=\frac{TP_a}{TP_a+FN_a},
\qquad
\operatorname{FPR}_a=\frac{FP_a}{FP_a+TN_a},
\]

\[
\operatorname{PPV}_a=\frac{TP_a}{TP_a+FP_a},
\qquad
\operatorname{SR}_a=\frac{TP_a+FP_a}{TP_a+FP_a+FN_a+TN_a}.
\]

The following Python example computes these quantities.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\NormalTok{data }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"group"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"A"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{8} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"B"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{:     [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,  }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"yhat"}\NormalTok{:  [}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{,  }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{\})}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ group\_metrics(frame):}
\NormalTok{    rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ g, df }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ frame.groupby(}\StringTok{"group"}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{        y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ df[}\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy()}
\NormalTok{        yhat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ df[}\StringTok{"yhat"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy()}
\NormalTok{        tp }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{())}
\NormalTok{        fp }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{())}
\NormalTok{        fn }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{())}
\NormalTok{        tn }\OperatorTok{=} \BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{())}
\NormalTok{        rows.append(\{}
            \StringTok{"group"}\NormalTok{: g,}
            \StringTok{"TP"}\NormalTok{: tp,}
            \StringTok{"FP"}\NormalTok{: fp,}
            \StringTok{"FN"}\NormalTok{: fn,}
            \StringTok{"TN"}\NormalTok{: tn,}
            \StringTok{"TPR"}\NormalTok{: tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ np.nan,}
            \StringTok{"FPR"}\NormalTok{: fp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (fp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ tn) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ fp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ tn }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ np.nan,}
            \StringTok{"PPV"}\NormalTok{: tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ np.nan,}
            \StringTok{"selection\_rate"}\NormalTok{: (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(df),}
            \StringTok{"base\_rate"}\NormalTok{: y.mean()}
\NormalTok{        \})}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(rows)}

\NormalTok{group\_metrics(data)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lllllllllll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& group & TP & FP & FN & TN & TPR & FPR & PPV & selection\_rate &
base\_rate \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & A & 2 & 1 & 2 & 3 & 0.5 & 0.250000 & 0.666667 & 0.375 & 0.50 \\
1 & B & 1 & 1 & 1 & 5 & 0.5 & 0.166667 & 0.500000 & 0.250 & 0.25 \\
\end{longtable}
}

The output is not the end of the analysis. It is the beginning. A
subgroup with a small sample size may have high uncertainty, so
confidence intervals or bootstrap intervals are often needed.

\section{25.8 Python example: threshold metrics by
group}\label{python-example-threshold-metrics-by-group}

The interactive above uses the same mathematical idea as the following
Python simulation. We generate scores \(S\), choose a threshold \(t\),
and compute group-wise rates.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ numpy }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ np}
\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ pandas }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ pd}

\NormalTok{rng }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.random.default\_rng(}\DecValTok{2025}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{nA }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{400}
\NormalTok{nB }\OperatorTok{=} \DecValTok{400}
\NormalTok{YA }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.binomial(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.45}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{nA)}
\NormalTok{YB }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ rng.binomial(}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{nB)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ clipped\_normal(mean, sd, size):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.clip(rng.normal(mean, sd, size}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{size), }\FloatTok{0.01}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.99}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{SA }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.where(YA }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, clipped\_normal(}\FloatTok{0.70}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.14}\NormalTok{, nA), clipped\_normal(}\FloatTok{0.32}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, nA))}
\NormalTok{SB }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.where(YB }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, clipped\_normal(}\FloatTok{0.64}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, nB), clipped\_normal(}\FloatTok{0.30}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{, nB))}

\NormalTok{scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"group"}\NormalTok{: np.r\_[np.repeat(}\StringTok{"A"}\NormalTok{, nA), np.repeat(}\StringTok{"B"}\NormalTok{, nB)],}
    \StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{: np.r\_[YA, YB],}
    \StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{: np.r\_[SA, SB]}
\NormalTok{\})}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ threshold\_report(df, threshold):}
\NormalTok{    out }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ g, sub }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ df.groupby(}\StringTok{"group"}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{        y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ sub[}\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy()}
\NormalTok{        yhat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (sub[}\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ threshold).astype(}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{        tp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\NormalTok{        fp }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\NormalTok{        fn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\NormalTok{        tn }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ ((yhat }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (y }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)).}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\NormalTok{        out.append(\{}
            \StringTok{"group"}\NormalTok{: g,}
            \StringTok{"base\_rate"}\NormalTok{: y.mean(),}
            \StringTok{"selection\_rate"}\NormalTok{: yhat.mean(),}
            \StringTok{"TPR"}\NormalTok{: tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fn),}
            \StringTok{"FPR"}\NormalTok{: fp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (fp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ tn),}
            \StringTok{"PPV"}\NormalTok{: tp }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp) }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ fp }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ np.nan,}
            \StringTok{"accuracy"}\NormalTok{: (tp }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ tn) }\OperatorTok{/} \BuiltInTok{len}\NormalTok{(sub)}
\NormalTok{        \})}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(out)}

\NormalTok{threshold\_report(scores, threshold}\OperatorTok{=}\FloatTok{0.50}\NormalTok{)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{25.9 Calibration and
uncertainty}\label{calibration-and-uncertainty}

A model score \(S\in[0,1]\) is calibrated if

\[
P(Y=1\mid S=s)=s.
\]

In practice we approximate this condition using bins. If bin \(B_m\)
contains examples whose scores lie in an interval, define

\[
\operatorname{acc}(B_m)=\frac{1}{|B_m|}\sum_{i\in B_m} y_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{conf}(B_m)=\frac{1}{|B_m|}\sum_{i\in B_m} s_i.
\]

The expected calibration error is commonly estimated by

\[
\operatorname{ECE}=\sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{n}\left|\operatorname{acc}(B_m)-\operatorname{conf}(B_m)\right|.
\]

Calibration matters because a score of \(0.9\) should not merely rank
higher than a score of \(0.6\); it should mean something probabilistic.
In NLP, calibration is important for moderation, retrieval confidence,
question-answering uncertainty, and decision support.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ calibration\_table(y, s, bins}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(y)}
\NormalTok{    s }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(s)}
\NormalTok{    edges }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linspace(}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, bins }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\NormalTok{    ece }\OperatorTok{=} \FloatTok{0.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ j }\KeywordTok{in} \BuiltInTok{range}\NormalTok{(bins):}
\NormalTok{        left, right }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ edges[j], edges[j }\OperatorTok{+} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ j }\OperatorTok{==}\NormalTok{ bins }\OperatorTok{{-}} \DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (s }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ left) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (s }\OperatorTok{\textless{}=}\NormalTok{ right)}
        \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{            mask }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (s }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ left) }\OperatorTok{\&}\NormalTok{ (s }\OperatorTok{\textless{}}\NormalTok{ right)}
        \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ mask.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
            \ControlFlowTok{continue}
\NormalTok{        acc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ y[mask].mean()}
\NormalTok{        conf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ s[mask].mean()}
\NormalTok{        weight }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ mask.mean()}
\NormalTok{        ece }\OperatorTok{+=}\NormalTok{ weight }\OperatorTok{*} \BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(acc }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ conf)}
\NormalTok{        rows.append(\{}
            \StringTok{"bin"}\NormalTok{: }\SpecialStringTok{f"[}\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{left}\SpecialCharTok{:.2f\}}\SpecialStringTok{, }\SpecialCharTok{\{}\NormalTok{right}\SpecialCharTok{:.2f\}}\SpecialStringTok{]"}\NormalTok{,}
            \StringTok{"count"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{(mask.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()),}
            \StringTok{"accuracy"}\NormalTok{: acc,}
            \StringTok{"mean\_score"}\NormalTok{: conf,}
            \StringTok{"abs\_gap"}\NormalTok{: }\BuiltInTok{abs}\NormalTok{(acc }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ conf)}
\NormalTok{        \})}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(rows), ece}

\NormalTok{cal\_table, ece }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ calibration\_table(scores[}\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{], scores[}\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{], bins}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{8}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{cal\_table, ece}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

 0  [0.00, 0.12]     54  0.000000    0.057371  0.057371
 1  [0.12, 0.25]    133  0.015038    0.199292  0.184255
 2  [0.25, 0.38]    173  0.023121    0.316975  0.293854
 3  [0.38, 0.50]    137  0.218978    0.433008  0.214030

 7  [0.88, 1.00]     21  1.000000    0.939546  0.060454,
 0.21286359605060212)

A classifier can have high accuracy and poor calibration. Conversely, a
calibrated classifier may not have the best thresholded accuracy. These
are different mathematical properties.

\section{25.10 Distribution shift}\label{distribution-shift}

Let \(P\) be the training distribution and \(Q\) be the deployment
distribution. Distribution shift means

\[
P(X,A,Y)\ne Q(X,A,Y).
\]

Important special cases include:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Covariate shift:} \(P(X)\ne Q(X)\) but
  \(P(Y\mid X)=Q(Y\mid X)\).
\item
  \textbf{Label shift:} \(P(Y)\ne Q(Y)\) but \(P(X\mid Y)=Q(X\mid Y)\).
\item
  \textbf{Concept shift:} \(P(Y\mid X)\ne Q(Y\mid X)\).
\end{itemize}

In text applications, distribution shift appears when a model trained on
one source is used on another source: social media versus formal essays,
one university's policy pages versus another's, one time period versus
another, or one language variety versus another.

Under covariate shift, if the density ratio \(w(x)=q(x)/p(x)\) is known
or estimated, then

\[
R_Q(d)=E_Q[L(d(X),Y)]
=E_P\left[\frac{q(X)}{p(X)}L(d(X),Y)\right].
\]

Thus weighted empirical risk can estimate deployment risk:

\[
\widehat{R}_Q(d)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n w(x_i)L(d(x_i),y_i).
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# A toy covariate{-}shift example with two text sources.}
\NormalTok{shift\_df }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"source"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"train"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{6} \OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"deploy"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{*} \DecValTok{6}\NormalTok{,}
    \StringTok{"text\_type"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"short"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"short"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"short"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"short"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"short"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"long"}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"loss"}\NormalTok{: [}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{\})}

\NormalTok{train }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ shift\_df[shift\_df[}\StringTok{"source"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"train"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{deploy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ shift\_df[shift\_df[}\StringTok{"source"}\NormalTok{] }\OperatorTok{==} \StringTok{"deploy"}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{p\_train }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ train[}\StringTok{"text\_type"}\NormalTok{].value\_counts(normalize}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{p\_deploy }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ deploy[}\StringTok{"text\_type"}\NormalTok{].value\_counts(normalize}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{True}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{weights }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ train[}\StringTok{"text\_type"}\NormalTok{].}\BuiltInTok{map}\NormalTok{(}\KeywordTok{lambda}\NormalTok{ z: p\_deploy[z] }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ p\_train[z])}
\NormalTok{unweighted\_risk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ train[}\StringTok{"loss"}\NormalTok{].mean()}
\NormalTok{weighted\_risk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.average(train[}\StringTok{"loss"}\NormalTok{], weights}\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{weights)}
\NormalTok{deploy\_risk }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ deploy[}\StringTok{"loss"}\NormalTok{].mean()}

\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"estimate"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"unweighted train risk"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"weighted train risk"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"observed deploy risk"}\NormalTok{],}
    \StringTok{"risk"}\NormalTok{: [unweighted\_risk, weighted\_risk, deploy\_risk]}
\NormalTok{\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\toprule\noalign{}

\endhead

\endlastfoot

The weighted estimate moves toward the deployment risk because it
accounts for the changed mixture of text types. In real NLP, estimating
\(q(x)/p(x)\) is itself a hard statistical problem.

\section{25.11 Embedding association and representation
bias}\label{embedding-association-and-representation-bias}

Embedding models represent words, sentences, or documents as vectors.
Bias can appear as geometric association. Let \(X\) and \(Y\) be two
sets of target words, and let \(A\) and \(B\) be two sets of attribute
words. A simple association score is

\[
s(w,A,B)=\frac{1}{|A|}\sum_{a\in A}\cos(e_w,e_a)
-
\frac{1}{|B|}\sum_{b\in B}\cos(e_w,e_b).
\]

A set-level effect score is

\[
S(X,Y,A,B)=\sum_{x\in X}s(x,A,B)-\sum_{y\in Y}s(y,A,B).
\]

This type of score is inspired by word-embedding association tests and
related representation-auditing methods Caliskan et al. (2017),
Bolukbasi, Chang, Zou, Saligrama, and Adam Tauman Kalai (2016).

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# A small toy embedding audit.  These numbers are artificial and for pedagogy only.}
\NormalTok{emb }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{}
    \StringTok{"nurse"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"engineer"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"teacher"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.70}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"programmer"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.75}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.20}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"care"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{1.00}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"family"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"logic"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{1.00}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.00}\NormalTok{]),}
    \StringTok{"machine"}\NormalTok{: np.array([}\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{]),}
\NormalTok{\}}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cosine(u, v):}
\NormalTok{    u }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(u)}
\NormalTok{    v }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(v)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(u }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ v }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (np.linalg.norm(u) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(v)))}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ assoc(word, A, B):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.mean([cosine(emb[word], emb[a]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ a }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ A]) }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.mean([cosine(emb[word], emb[b]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ b }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ B])}

\NormalTok{X }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"nurse"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"teacher"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{Y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"engineer"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"programmer"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"care"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"family"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{B }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"logic"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"machine"}\NormalTok{]}

\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{: X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y,}
    \StringTok{"association\_to\_A\_minus\_B"}\NormalTok{: [assoc(w, A, B) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y]}
\NormalTok{\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& word & association\_to\_A\_minus\_B \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & nurse & 0.820412 \\
1 & teacher & 0.648967 \\
2 & engineer & -0.820412 \\
3 & programmer & -0.669537 \\
\end{longtable}
}

A linear debiasing operation can be written as orthogonal projection. If
\(b\) is a unit direction representing an unwanted association, then the
projection removing that direction is

\[
\Pi_{b^\perp}(v)=v-(v^Tb)b.
\]

This operation is mathematically clean, but it is not a complete
solution. Bias may be nonlinear, contextual, or encoded in many
directions. Projection can also remove useful information or create a
false sense of safety.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\CommentTok{\# Remove the direction from "logic/machine" to "care/family" in the toy example.}
\NormalTok{mean\_A }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean([emb[a] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ a }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ A], axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{mean\_B }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.mean([emb[b] }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ b }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ B], axis}\OperatorTok{=}\DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{bias\_direction }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ mean\_A }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ mean\_B}
\NormalTok{bias\_direction }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ bias\_direction }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(bias\_direction)}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ remove\_direction(v, b):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ v }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ (v }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ b) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ b}

\NormalTok{emb\_projected }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ \{w: remove\_direction(v, bias\_direction) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ w, v }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ emb.items()\}}

\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ assoc\_projected(word, A, B):}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ np.mean([cosine(emb\_projected[word], emb\_projected[a]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ a }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ A]) }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.mean([cosine(emb\_projected[word], emb\_projected[b]) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ b }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ B])}

\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"word"}\NormalTok{: X }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ Y,}

\NormalTok{\})}
