\section{25.12 Selective prediction and
abstention}\label{selective-prediction-and-abstention}

Responsible deployment often requires a model not to answer every query.
A selective classifier returns either a prediction or an abstention
symbol \(\bot\):

\[
g(x)\in\{0,1,\bot\}.
\]

For a confidence score \(c(x)\) and threshold \(\tau\), a simple rule is

\[
g_\tau(x)=
\begin{cases}
\widehat{y}(x), & c(x)\ge \tau,\\
\bot, & c(x)<\tau.
\end{cases}
\]

Two quantities are central:

\[
\operatorname{coverage}(\tau)=P(c(X)\ge \tau),
\]

\[
\operatorname{selective\ risk}(\tau)
=E[L(\widehat{Y},Y)\mid c(X)\ge \tau].
\]

Increasing \(\tau\) often decreases risk among answered cases but also
decreases coverage.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{conf }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.maximum(scores[}\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy(), }\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ scores[}\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy())}
\NormalTok{y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scores[}\StringTok{"y"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy()}
\NormalTok{yhat }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (scores[}\StringTok{"score"}\NormalTok{].to\_numpy() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=} \FloatTok{0.50}\NormalTok{).astype(}\BuiltInTok{int}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{loss }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ (yhat }\OperatorTok{!=}\NormalTok{ y).astype(}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}

\NormalTok{selective\_rows }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ []}
\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ tau }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ np.linspace(}\FloatTok{0.50}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.95}\NormalTok{, }\DecValTok{10}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    keep }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ conf }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}=}\NormalTok{ tau}
\NormalTok{    selective\_rows.append(\{}
        \StringTok{"confidence\_threshold"}\NormalTok{: tau,}
        \StringTok{"coverage"}\NormalTok{: keep.mean(),}
        \StringTok{"selective\_error"}\NormalTok{: loss[keep].mean() }\ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ keep.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{() }\OperatorTok{\textgreater{}} \DecValTok{0} \ControlFlowTok{else}\NormalTok{ np.nan}
\NormalTok{    \})}

\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(selective\_rows)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}llll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& confidence\_threshold & coverage & selective\_error \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 0.50 & 1.00000 & 0.088750 \\
1 & 0.55 & 0.88125 & 0.052482 \\
2 & 0.60 & 0.76000 & 0.026316 \\
3 & 0.65 & 0.60250 & 0.014523 \\
4 & 0.70 & 0.45000 & 0.011111 \\
5 & 0.75 & 0.33250 & 0.011278 \\
6 & 0.80 & 0.20625 & 0.012121 \\
7 & 0.85 & 0.11750 & 0.010638 \\
8 & 0.90 & 0.07000 & 0.000000 \\
9 & 0.95 & 0.04375 & 0.000000 \\
\end{longtable}

In high-stakes applications, abstention should usually trigger a defined
alternative process, such as human review, retrieval of source
documents, or refusal to answer.

\section{25.13 Privacy and memorization}\label{privacy-and-memorization}

NLP systems can leak information from training data, prompts, logs, or
retrieved documents. A mathematical privacy guarantee should describe
how the output distribution changes when one individual's data is
changed.

A randomized algorithm \(M\) is \(\varepsilon\)-differentially private
if for all neighboring datasets \(D\) and \(D'\) differing in one
individual, and for all measurable output sets \(S\),

\[
P(M(D)\in S)\le e^\varepsilon P(M(D')\in S).
\]

Smaller \(\varepsilon\) means stronger privacy. Differential privacy is
not the only privacy concept, but it is mathematically precise Dwork and
Roth (2014).

A simple example is randomized response. Suppose a private binary answer
is \(Y\in\{0,1\}\). The released answer \(Z\) equals \(Y\) with
probability \(p\) and is flipped with probability \(1-p\). The privacy
parameter is

\[
\varepsilon=\log\frac{p}{1-p}.
\]

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{ps }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([}\FloatTok{0.55}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.60}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.70}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.80}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.90}\NormalTok{])}
\NormalTok{eps }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.log(ps }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ (}\DecValTok{1} \OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ ps))}
\NormalTok{pd.DataFrame(\{}\StringTok{"truth\_probability\_p"}\NormalTok{: ps, }\StringTok{"epsilon"}\NormalTok{: eps\})}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

{\def\LTcaptype{none} % do not increment counter
\begin{longtable}[]{@{}lll@{}}
\toprule\noalign{}
& truth\_probability\_p & epsilon \\
\midrule\noalign{}
\endhead
\bottomrule\noalign{}
\endlastfoot
0 & 0.55 & 0.200671 \\
1 & 0.60 & 0.405465 \\
2 & 0.70 & 0.847298 \\
3 & 0.80 & 1.386294 \\
4 & 0.90 & 2.197225 \\
\end{longtable}
}

Privacy has a utility tradeoff. As \(p\) approaches \(1/2\), the
released answer becomes more private but less informative. As \(p\)
approaches \(1\), the answer is accurate but less private.

\section{25.14 Hallucination, factuality, and RAG
responsibility}\label{hallucination-factuality-and-rag-responsibility}

For a generated answer \(Z\) to a prompt \(X\), factuality cannot be
determined from fluency alone. A response may be syntactically excellent
and factually false. A clean way to describe a retrieval-augmented
system is

\[
D_1,\ldots,D_k \sim r_\eta(d\mid x),
\qquad
Z\sim p_\theta(z\mid x,D_1,\ldots,D_k).
\]

Errors can enter through retrieval or generation:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  relevant documents may not be retrieved;
\item
  retrieved documents may be outdated, ambiguous, or contradictory;
\item
  the generator may ignore retrieved evidence;
\item
  the generator may blend evidence with unsupported prior knowledge;
\item
  the final answer may omit uncertainty or citations.
\end{itemize}

For mathematical responsibility, it is useful to separate:

\[
P(\text{correct answer})
=P(\text{retrieval sufficient})P(\text{generation faithful}\mid \text{retrieval sufficient})+
\cdots.
\]

This is not a complete causal model, but it forces students to separate
retrieval failure from generation failure.

\section{25.15 AI-assisted auditing
workflow}\label{ai-assisted-auditing-workflow}

AI tools can help audit NLP systems, but they should not replace
statistical reasoning. A useful AI-assisted workflow is:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Ask the AI system to state the task, target variable, decision rule,
  and possible harms.
\item
  Ask it to propose subgroup variables that might matter.
\item
  Ask it to list plausible distribution shifts.
\item
  Convert the suggestions into mathematical quantities.
\item
  Compute metrics and uncertainty using data.
\item
  Ask the AI system to critique the audit for missing assumptions.
\item
  Document the final human judgment.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-note-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-note-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-note-color}{\faInfo}\hspace{0.5em}{Note}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

AI assistance is useful for brainstorming failure modes and drafting
audit checklists. It is not evidence. Evidence comes from data, source
documents, mathematical definitions, and careful evaluation.

\end{tcolorbox}

\section{25.16 Worked example: two classifiers with the same
accuracy}\label{worked-example-two-classifiers-with-the-same-accuracy}

Suppose two classifiers have the same overall accuracy, but their
group-specific errors differ.

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{comparison }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ pd.DataFrame(\{}
    \StringTok{"model"}\NormalTok{: [}\StringTok{"M1"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"M1"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"M2"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"M2"}\NormalTok{],}

    \StringTok{"FPR"}\NormalTok{: [}\FloatTok{0.10}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.22}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.16}\NormalTok{, }\FloatTok{0.15}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{\})}
\NormalTok{comparison}

The mathematical lesson is that aggregation is a projection. It can

\section{25.17 Common mistakes}\label{common-mistakes-14}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{Treating accuracy as responsibility.} Accuracy is one
  statistic, not an ethical guarantee.
\item
  \textbf{Ignoring the deployment distribution.} A test set estimates
  performance only for the distribution it represents.
\item
  \textbf{Using group metrics without uncertainty.} Small subgroups can
  produce unstable estimates.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming one fairness metric is always correct.} Different
  metrics encode different choices.
\item
  \textbf{Assuming debiasing projection solves bias.} Geometric
  correction can help but is incomplete.
\item
  \textbf{Confusing fluency with factuality.} Language quality does not
  imply truth.
\item
  \textbf{Using AI critiques as evidence.} AI-generated audits must be
  checked against data and definitions.
\end{enumerate}

\section{25.18 Exercises}\label{exercises-24}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\item
  \textbf{Group metrics.} Given the following counts for groups A and B,
  compute TPR, FPR, PPV, selection rate, and accuracy. Which fairness
  criteria are approximately satisfied?
\item
  \textbf{Threshold tradeoff.} For a score-based classifier, write code
  that searches over thresholds and plots TPR gap, FPR gap,
  selection-rate gap, and accuracy.
\item
  \textbf{Calibration.} Construct a model that has high accuracy but
  poor calibration. Compute ECE.
\item
  \textbf{Distribution shift.} Suppose the training data contains
  \(70\%\) formal text and \(30\%\) informal text, but deployment
  contains \(30\%\) formal text and \(70\%\) informal text. If error
  rates differ by text type, compute the shifted risk.
\item
  \textbf{Embedding association.} Build a small toy embedding example
  and compute association scores before and after projection.
\item
  \textbf{Selective prediction.} For a classifier with confidence
  scores, compute coverage and selective risk as functions of the
  abstention threshold.
\item
  \textbf{Privacy.} For randomized response with \(p=0.75\), compute
  \(\varepsilon\). Interpret the result.
\item
  \textbf{RAG audit.} Design separate metrics for retrieval sufficiency
  and generation faithfulness.
\end{enumerate}

\section{25.19 Mini-project: mathematical audit of an NLP
classifier}\label{mini-project-mathematical-audit-of-an-nlp-classifier}

Choose a small text classification task, such as sentiment
classification, topic classification, helpfulness prediction, or
moderation. Your project should include:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  a precise definition of \(X\), \(Y\), and any auditing variable \(A\);
\item
  a baseline model and decision rule;
\item
  group-wise confusion matrices;
\item
  at least two fairness metrics;
\item
  calibration analysis;
\item
  a distribution-shift experiment;
\item
  an uncertainty discussion;
\item
  a written statement about whether the model should be used and under
  what constraints.
\end{enumerate}

The goal is not to produce the highest-performing model. The goal is to
practice mathematically responsible evaluation.

\section{25.21 Chapter summary}\label{chapter-summary-4}

Ethics in NLP is not only a philosophical add-on after model training.
It begins when we choose the data distribution, target variable,
representation, model class, objective function, metric, and deployment
rule. Mathematics helps because it forces these choices to become
explicit.

The core lessons are:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  responsible NLP starts with random variables and distributions;
\item
  bias can enter through data, measurement, representation,
  optimization, and deployment;
\item
  fairness metrics are conditional probabilities, not universal moral
  truths;
\item
  different fairness metrics can conflict when base rates differ;
\item
  calibration, uncertainty, and distribution shift are central to
  deployment;
\item
  privacy and factuality require separate mathematical treatment;
\item
  AI assistance can support auditing, but evidence must come from
  definitions, data, and transparent evaluation.
\end{itemize}

\section{25.22 Notes and references}\label{notes-and-references-14}

This chapter connects statistical evaluation, fairness in machine
learning, privacy, and representation auditing. Useful background
includes the fairness text of Barocas, Hardt, and Narayanan Barocas et
al. (2019a), the equalized-odds framework of Hardt, Price, and Srebro
Hardt et al. (2016a), differential privacy foundations Dwork and Roth
(2014), embedding bias studies Bolukbasi, Chang, Zou, Saligrama, and
Adam Tauman Kalai (2016), Caliskan et al. (2017), and broader
discussions of dataset and language-model risk Buolamwini and Gebru
(2018), Bender et al. (2021a).

\chapter{Computer Labs}\label{computer-labs-1}

Google Colab Notebooks for Independent Study

\hfill\break

The computer labs for \emph{Mathematical Foundations of Natural Language
Processing} are designed for independent study. Each lab begins with the
necessary mathematical and conceptual background before programming,
then develops the ideas through small transparent examples in Python.

The labs are stored in the \texttt{labs/} folder of the GitHub
repository:

\url{https://github.com/wanghemath/Book-MathNLP}

Each notebook can be opened directly in Google Colab. Students do not
need to install Python locally, although the notebooks can also be
downloaded and run in JupyterLab.

\section{How to use the labs}\label{how-to-use-the-labs}

A good workflow for each chapter is:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  read the corresponding textbook chapter;
\item
  open the lab notebook in Google Colab;
\item
  run the notebook from top to bottom once without changing code;
\item
  return to each section and explain the mathematical idea in your own
  words;
\item
  complete the exercises;
\item
  complete the mini-project or extension task;
\item
  write a short reflection on assumptions, limitations, and possible
  improvements.
\end{enumerate}

The labs emphasize understanding before automation. Many examples
intentionally use small toy corpora so that students can inspect the
data, compute intermediate quantities by hand, and see how the
mathematics becomes code.

\section{Suggested grading or self-study
structure}\label{suggested-grading-or-self-study-structure}

For a course, each lab can be used in one of three ways.

\subsection{Option A. Guided practice}\label{option-a.-guided-practice}

Students run the notebook, answer the short exercises, and submit
selected outputs. This is appropriate for weekly low-stakes assignments.

\subsection{Option B. Independent lab
report}\label{option-b.-independent-lab-report}

Students submit a short report containing:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  a summary of the main mathematical idea;
\item
  one key equation and its interpretation;
\item
  selected code output;
\item
  answers to exercises;
\item
  one limitation or failure mode;
\item
  one proposed extension.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Option C. Mini-project
pathway}\label{option-c.-mini-project-pathway}

Students use the mini-project section as a starting point for a longer
project. This is appropriate for final projects, research preparation,
or independent study.

\section{Recommended pacing}\label{recommended-pacing}

A semester course can use the labs at different depths.

A slower mathematical course may spend more time on Labs 4, 7, 8, 13,
15, 21, and 22. A more applied NLP course may spend more time on Labs 6,
10, 17, 19, 20, and 25.

\section{Technical notes}\label{technical-notes}

The labs are intended to run in Google Colab with common scientific
Python libraries:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  \texttt{numpy}
\item
  \texttt{pandas}
\item
  \texttt{matplotlib}
\item
  \texttt{scikit-learn}
\end{itemize}

Some notebooks use optional libraries when available, but the core
examples are designed to remain small and transparent. The emphasis is
on understanding the mathematical structure rather than training large
models.

\section{Student expectations}\label{student-expectations}

Students should keep the following principles in mind.

\begin{tcolorbox}[enhanced jigsaw, arc=.35mm, bottomrule=.15mm, bottomtitle=1mm, breakable, colback=white, colbacktitle=quarto-callout-tip-color!10!white, colframe=quarto-callout-tip-color-frame, coltitle=black, left=2mm, leftrule=.75mm, opacityback=0, opacitybacktitle=0.6, rightrule=.15mm, title=\textcolor{quarto-callout-tip-color}{\faLightbulb}\hspace{0.5em}{Tip}, titlerule=0mm, toprule=.15mm, toptitle=1mm]

A lab is not complete when the code runs. A lab is complete when you can
explain what mathematical object each variable represents and why the
output makes sense.

\end{tcolorbox}

For every model, ask:

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  What is the input space?
\item
  What is the output space?
\item
  What parameters are learned or chosen?
\item
  What loss, score, or criterion is being optimized?
\item
  What assumptions does the method make about language?
\item
  What failure modes should be checked?
\end{itemize}

\section{Instructor notes}\label{instructor-notes}

The labs can be used as weekly assignments, recitation materials,
independent-study notebooks, or project preparation. Because each lab
includes background before programming, students can also use them as
review materials after completing the corresponding chapter.

When assigning labs, it is useful to ask students to submit both code
output and written interpretation. The written interpretation helps
students connect Python arrays back to the mathematical ideas in the
textbook.

\chapter{Interactive HTML Modules}\label{interactive-html-modules}

Interactive HTML modules can be used for visual explanations of NLP
mathematics. Good candidates include tokenization, cosine similarity,
smoothing, SVD, embedding geometry, attention matrices, positional
encoding, sampling temperature, perplexity, and persistent homology.

\section{Design principles}\label{design-principles}

\begin{itemize}
\tightlist
\item
  Each module should teach one mathematical concept clearly.
\item
  Use Plotly.js or lightweight JavaScript visualizations when
  interactivity adds value.
\item
  Keep formulas in standard LaTeX format using MathJax.
\item
  Do not make the interactive component replace the explanation; it
  should support the explanation.
\end{itemize}

\chapter{Interactive diagnostics}\label{interactive-diagnostics-1}

This page helps diagnose whether the HTML interactives in the NLP book
can load Plotly.js.

\section{What should work}\label{what-should-work}

The following chapters contain embedded Plotly.js interactives:

\begin{itemize}

\item
  Chapter 1: classifier boundary explorer
\item
  Chapter 2: vocabulary threshold explorer
\item
  Chapter 3: TF-IDF retrieval explorer
\item
  Chapter 4: temperature/entropy explorer
\item
  Chapter 5: smoothing explorer
\item
  Chapter 6: Naive Bayes log-odds explorer
\item
  Chapter 7: rank-k latent semantic map
\item
  Chapter 8: embedding analogy explorer
\item
  Chapter 9: embedding geometry explorer
\item
  Chapter 10: softmax classifier explorer
\item
  Chapter 11: recurrent memory explorer
\end{itemize}

\section{Most common causes of a blank
interactive}\label{most-common-causes-of-a-blank-interactive}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  The local file \texttt{assets/plotly.min.js} was not copied into
  \texttt{\_book/assets/}.
\item
  A browser extension blocked JavaScript.
\item
  The page was rendered to PDF instead of HTML.
\item
  The output site is opened from a path where local scripts are blocked.
\item
  An older cached version of the page is being displayed.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Quick browser check}\label{quick-browser-check}

Open the HTML page and press \textbf{Option-Command-I} on macOS or
\textbf{Ctrl-Shift-I} on Windows/Linux. In the Console tab, run:

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\BuiltInTok{window}\OperatorTok{.}\AttributeTok{Plotly} \OperatorTok{\&\&}\NormalTok{ Plotly}\OperatorTok{.}\AttributeTok{version}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

A working page should print a Plotly version, such as \texttt{2.35.2}.

\chapter{Final Projects}\label{final-projects}

Final projects should combine mathematical explanation, computation, and
statistical evaluation. A strong project should state the
representation, model, loss function, dataset, metric, and limitations.

\section{Suggested projects}\label{suggested-projects-1}

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  \textbf{A small mathematical search engine.} Build TF-IDF and
  embedding-based search and compare the geometry of retrieval.
\item
  \textbf{Naive Bayes versus logistic regression versus transformers.}
  Compare assumptions, losses, and empirical behavior on a text
  classification task.
\item
  \textbf{Attention from scratch.} Implement scaled dot-product
  attention and analyze how attention weights change under
  perturbations.
\item
  \textbf{Geometry of sentence embeddings.} Study clustering, PCA,
  nearest neighbors, and bias directions.
\item
  \textbf{A small retrieval-augmented generation system.} Build a RAG
  prototype over official course or program documents and evaluate
  retrieval accuracy.
\item
  \textbf{Persistent homology of embedding spaces.} Compare topological
  summaries of sentence embeddings across genres, topics, or models.
\item
  \textbf{Information theory of language models.} Compare entropy,
  cross-entropy, KL divergence, and perplexity for small language
  models.
\item
  \textbf{Bias and distribution shift in text classification.} Study how
  model performance changes across groups, topics, or time periods.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Project report structure}\label{project-report-structure}

A recommended report has the following sections:

\begin{enumerate}
\def\labelenumi{\arabic{enumi}.}
\tightlist
\item
  Research question
\item
  Mathematical formulation
\item
  Data and preprocessing
\item
  Model or algorithm
\item
  Experiments
\item
  Evaluation and uncertainty
\item
  Limitations
\item
  Reproducible code appendix
\end{enumerate}

\bookmarksetup{startatroot}

\chapter{Python Reference}\label{python-reference}

goal is to keep code readable and mathematically connected.

\section{Core libraries}\label{core-libraries}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]

\ImportTok{import}\NormalTok{ matplotlib.pyplot }\ImportTok{as}\NormalTok{ plt}

\section{Count vectors}\label{count-vectors-1}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\NormalTok{vocab }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"model"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"statistics"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{doc }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ [}\StringTok{"language"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"model"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"model"}\NormalTok{, }\StringTok{"data"}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{counts }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.array([doc.count(token) }\ControlFlowTok{for}\NormalTok{ token }\KeywordTok{in}\NormalTok{ vocab])}
\NormalTok{counts}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\begin{verbatim}
array([1, 1, 2, 0])
\end{verbatim}

\section{Cosine similarity}\label{cosine-similarity-2}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ cosine\_similarity(x, y):}
\NormalTok{    x }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(x, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    y }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(y, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    denom }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(x) }\OperatorTok{*}\NormalTok{ np.linalg.norm(y)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ denom }\OperatorTok{==} \DecValTok{0}\NormalTok{:}
        \ControlFlowTok{return} \FloatTok{0.0}
    \ControlFlowTok{return} \BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{(np.dot(x, y) }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ denom)}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Softmax}\label{softmax}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ softmax(z):}
\NormalTok{    z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(z, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ z }\OperatorTok{{-}}\NormalTok{ np.}\BuiltInTok{max}\NormalTok{(z)}
\NormalTok{    exp\_z }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.exp(z)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ exp\_z }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ exp\_z.}\BuiltInTok{sum}\NormalTok{()}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\section{Scaled dot-product
attention}\label{scaled-dot-product-attention}

\begin{Shaded}
\begin{Highlighting}[]
\KeywordTok{def}\NormalTok{ attention(Q, K, V, mask}\OperatorTok{=}\VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{):}
\NormalTok{    Q }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(Q, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    K }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(K, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    V }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.asarray(V, dtype}\OperatorTok{=}\BuiltInTok{float}\NormalTok{)}
\NormalTok{    d\_k }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q.shape[}\OperatorTok{{-}}\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{]}
\NormalTok{    scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ Q }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ K.T }\OperatorTok{/}\NormalTok{ np.sqrt(d\_k)}
    \ControlFlowTok{if}\NormalTok{ mask }\KeywordTok{is} \KeywordTok{not} \VariableTok{None}\NormalTok{:}
\NormalTok{        scores }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ scores }\OperatorTok{+}\NormalTok{ mask}
\NormalTok{    weights }\OperatorTok{=}\NormalTok{ np.apply\_along\_axis(softmax, }\DecValTok{1}\NormalTok{, scores)}
    \ControlFlowTok{return}\NormalTok{ weights }\OperatorTok{@}\NormalTok{ V, weights}
\end{Highlighting}
\end{Shaded}

\chapter{References and Further
Reading}\label{references-and-further-reading}

This page collects the main references used throughout
\emph{Mathematical Foundations of Natural Language Processing}. The list
is intentionally broad: it includes classical NLP, probability and
information theory, linear algebra and retrieval, neural language
models, attention and transformers, retrieval-augmented generation,
evaluation, optimization, graph methods, topology, and responsible NLP.

\section{Core NLP references}\label{core-nlp-references}

For a broad introduction to natural language processing, the most useful
starting points are the classical statistical treatment of Manning and
Schuetze, the modern textbook by Jurafsky and Martin, the mathematically
clear introduction by Eisenstein, and the neural NLP text by Goldberg
(Manning and Schuetze 1999; Jurafsky and Martin 2024; Eisenstein 2019;
Goldberg 2017).

\section{Probability and information
theory}\label{probability-and-information-theory}

The probability, likelihood, entropy, cross-entropy, KL divergence, and
perplexity ideas used throughout the book are rooted in Shannon's
communication theory and standard information-theory treatments (Shannon
1948; Cover and Thomas 2006; MacKay 2003). For probabilistic modeling
and statistical learning background, see Bishop, Murphy, and
Hastie--Tibshirani--Friedman (Bishop 2006b; Murphy 2022; Hastie et al.
2009).

\section{Vector spaces, retrieval, and document
geometry}\label{vector-spaces-retrieval-and-document-geometry}

The document-vector view of language connects vector-space indexing,
latent semantic analysis, and probabilistic retrieval (Salton et al.
1975; Deerwester et al. 1990; Landauer and Dumais 1997; Robertson and
Zaragoza 2009; Manning et al. 2008). These sources support the chapters
on document-term matrices, TF-IDF, cosine similarity, low-rank
approximation, and retrieval.

\section{Tokenization and word
embeddings}\label{tokenization-and-word-embeddings}

Subword tokenization is central to modern NLP systems (Sennrich et al.
2016; Kudo and Richardson 2018). Word representations connect neural
prediction, matrix factorization, and distributional semantics (Bengio
et al. 2003; Mikolov, Chen, et al. 2013; Mikolov, Sutskever, et al.
2013; Pennington et al. 2014; Levy and Goldberg 2014).

\section{Sequence models, attention, and
transformers}\label{sequence-models-attention-and-transformers}

The sequence-modeling arc begins with recurrent networks, LSTM/GRU
memory mechanisms, and attention-based encoder-decoder models (Elman
1990; Hochreiter and Schmidhuber 1997; Cho et al. 2014; Bahdanau et al.
2015; Luong et al. 2015). Transformers and large language models build
on self-attention, positional structure, pretraining, scaling, and
instruction tuning (Vaswani et al. 2017; Devlin et al. 2019; Radford et
al. 2019; {Brown et al.} 2020; Kaplan et al. 2020; {Ouyang et al.}
2022b).

\section{Retrieval-augmented generation and semantic
search}\label{retrieval-augmented-generation-and-semantic-search}

The retrieval and RAG chapters use ideas from sentence embeddings, dense
retrieval, late interaction, large-scale similarity search, and
retrieval-augmented generation (Reimers and Gurevych 2019; Karpukhin et
al. 2020; Khattab and Zaharia 2020; Johnson et al. 2019; {Lewis et al.}
2020).

\section{Optimization and training}\label{optimization-and-training}

Gradient-based training, stochastic optimization, recurrent-gradient
pathologies, Adam, AdamW, and preference-based fine-tuning are supported
by the following sources (Goodfellow et al. 2016b; Boyd and Vandenberghe
2004; Pascanu et al. 2013; Kingma and Ba 2015b; Loshchilov and Hutter
2019b; Christiano et al. 2017; Rafailov et al. 2023b).

\section{Evaluation and calibration}\label{evaluation-and-calibration}

The evaluation chapter uses classical overlap metrics, probabilistic
scoring, calibration diagnostics, and modern model comparison ideas
(Papineni et al. 2002; Lin 2004; Brier 1950; Guo et al. 2017). These
references are not a substitute for task-specific human evaluation, but
they provide a mathematical starting point.

\section{Graphs and topology}\label{graphs-and-topology}

Graph-based language models, PageRank, graph neural networks, and graph
attention are connected to matrix operators on graphs (Page et al. 1999;
Kipf and Welling 2017b; Hamilton et al. 2017; Velickovic et al. 2018).
The topological viewpoint uses computational topology, persistent
homology, and Mapper-style summaries (Edelsbrunner and Harer 2010;
Carlsson 2009; Ghrist 2008; Singh et al. 2007).

\section{Ethics, bias, and
responsibility}\label{ethics-bias-and-responsibility}

The final chapter connects technical NLP modeling with fairness, bias
measurement, documentation, and responsible deployment (Barocas et al.
2019b; Dwork et al. 2012; Hardt et al. 2016b; Bolukbasi, Chang, Zou,
Saligrama, and Adam T. Kalai 2016; Caliskan et al. 2017; Blodgett et al.
2020; Bender et al. 2021b; Gebru et al. 2021; Mitchell et al. 2019).
